_childDocuments_.review: Pretty interesting first person shooter KIND of like the classic descent games or Sublevel Zero..or Overload, except you're piloting a submarine in an apocalyptic world were its dangerous to live on the surface because of nuclear winter and all kinds of bad news up there so as a result, whats left of humanity has to live in underwater cities where subs are pretty much the main method of transportation.I will say though, the combat can get a little repetative but what else is there to fight besides pirates and nano-sharks?  maybe I haven;t gone too far in but so far it's okay.   there is co-op for the main story.  competitive Multiplayer though?  Can't comment on that since literally no one plays that.
_childDocuments_.name: Aquanox Deep Descent

_childDocuments_.review: Frankly i'm a bit torn about this game. First let me state: I love Aquanox 1+2 and their predecessor. So i really wanted this game to rekindle this feeling and hopefully get a bigger audience... but gameplay-wise it lacks a lot. In terms of graphics it is ok. Not great or that good. One notices it's long delayed developement but it is still servicable. A bit too dark and muddy but... well it is the deep sea so kinda excusable. Still it could've been so much better. The maps look too much alike and i wished the terrain was more interactable. Like clouds of mud beeing raised when the engine of my boat gets to close to the ground or some parts beeing destroyable. Sadly it is quite static. The controls  with mouse and keyboard are ok. I learned a bit late how to side-dodge, since that wasn't well explained in the game but aside from that i got into it fast. The design of the boats are ok as well. Each one plays a bit different and i like the ability to upgrade them.On the plus-side: there also quite a few different weapon-types... but on the minus-side: many are just upgraded versions of earlier ones. Which i could tolerate but.... they are alle available at all time once unlocked - which is stupid. Why? Baceause that prolongs the time i need in combat to scroll through them just to find the one i want.  Why can't the better versions just replace the outdated? Why keeping both? They use up the same ammo and only differ in damage dealt. This is a stupid design-choice and one i  can't understand why this is still in to release after all this time in developement? And speaking of questionable design-choices: Why get the final upgrades for my boats to be unlocked, right before the finally, when there's no imminent way, to upgrade - since therefore i have to dock somewhere.  The AI ain't that good either and only gets to be a threat by numbers not by quality, but, well, to me that was kinda a given. Let's be frank, did anyone expect great bot-AI. I don't think so. The combat is ok but the missions are mostly "go there and shoot someone" or "go there and find something". The only reason for exploring the maps is for  looting materials to upgrade your ships or refill your ammunition. There should have been more fights like the one against the mutated whale. About the story: Well it's a reset of the classic Aquanox-storyline... and to my displeasure not a good one. I don't want to spoil too much, so let me just say it is generic and big plot-twists are easy to foresee. I really wished, they'd just remastered  Aquanox 1+2 and then continued the story with a sequel. The worls-building isn't well done. There're few character-interactions and lack of dialogues (yeah, i know many didn't like those talks in the predecessors but to me, they added much to the atmosphere and helped getting immersed). And it may be just me but the finaly felt rushed. All in all i prefer the adventures of Emerald Flint over this.All in all i would prefer if i could give this game neither a thumbs-up, nor thumbs-down... but since that's still not possible (seriuosly, steam?) i will let my nostalgia take over and give this a thumbs up (mainly in hope for a better sequel o r at least a remaster of the original-ones). If you don't have an emotional attachement to the series - like me - but you're curious and likewingcommander-like games, i would advise you to wait for a steam-sale to get this. Oh, and the multiplayer i did not touch since... well is there really anyone playing this for the multiplayer? I cannot imagine.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate leaving bad reviews... Let me first say I was just looking for something different for the squad to jump in together and the premise seemed legit. That being said underwater shooters are not my thing so maybe there are people who are accustomed to extremely slow wonky maneuvering craft and extremely poor almost guesswork targeting. The screen sticking was atrocious and it didn't seem like i could adjust the sensitivity high enough to not have to pick my mouse up 8 times to do a 180... also wasd felt fine but space and control which under normal circumstances would be fine for ascend/descend is wiped out because as one would like to feather space to correct descending too fast but if you double tap either it boosts you up or down respectively into the floor or ceiling... As I have said this game may just not be my cup of tea but after 3 failed attempts to get to Okabe (ON EASY MODE) due to the scene where Ishmael is "Protecting you... It left me with %10 hull and no repair kits at checkpoint... As with all games I still feel like it has potential but my overall first impression is lack luster and disappointed. Or maybe i just need to get gud. May buy again if they do a massive overhaul but am skeptical.

_childDocuments_.review: As log as you understand that this is a crowdfunded game, and that you can't compare it with its predecessors, you can definitely see that it's achieved its goal of reviving the Aquanox series.The story and voice acting are mediocre, but that seems to be down to the low budget, most of which was likely spent on designing the environment. Even that could use more work, but it uses a modern game engine (Unreal Engine) and the developers will gain more experience with it as time goes on.The subs offer some variation, but the unlocking of various customizations should have a different pace. As of writing, you barely unlock any interesting upgrades, most of which come as a waterfall towards the very end of the game.The weapons are fun, and the subs are easy to steer through the depths of Aqua, but future Aquanox games could use more simulation features -- at least as an option for hardcore enthusiasts. And it should be noted that combat feels like the mechanics were borrowed from a space sim. AI is in need of major rework.It might sound harsh, but one of the things that keep this game from being great is that its biggest promise was not fulfilled. I'm talking about exploration, of course. Exploring is not encouraged by anything other than scavenging parts, and there's very little reward for scouring the depths of the sea. The developers could definitely make exploration more compelling in future iterations.One more thing -- as someone who has played the entire series, I didn't mind the dialog interface and overall UI, but we're not in 2001. Actual 3D characters and the ability to do things in 3D inside stations would have been a welcome modernization of Aquanox. Budget shouldn't be an excuse, this IP has a lot of potential but needs more love from the publisher to get to where it needs to be. It's a different genre that could offer a breath of fresh air at a time when the game market is flooded with the same old, same old.Overall, I'd give this game a rating of 5.5/10, meaning it's passable. This should have been an episodic game, which would have allowed the relatively small budget to be used more efficiently. I do recommend this game to fans for the nostalgia factor, but otherwise buy on sale, not full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Hi!First of all I want to shoot down some of the BAD Reviews that this game has been given Yesterday and Today.I've been playing AquaNox Deep Descent for over 11 hours now and still I haven't seen a single problem with (AI doing Loops) or that "Homing Seeking Projectiles/Torpedoes" haven't been working (Might help if those people equipped the right weapons that has Homing Tech in them).The only "meh" things that I have seen is...#1: One of the big freighters clipped a wall a tiny bit with it's back engines while taking a turn. (oooooh)#2: One time the Subtitles and the Voice Actor didn't say the same thing. (Text: Be gone! Actor: Go away!)Now I've played the two first game and loved them. This game have been something that I've been waiting for a while now :)But there are things that I would have prefered if they had done differently.DODGING: I rather seen this had been a double tap then just a tap because there are times where you trigger it when you don't mean to trigger it (Slowly "Tap" to rise over a ridge to snipe someone.)WEAPONS: Here it would have been great IF you had the option to either sell the Low-Grade weapons when you get upgrades, that you can unequiped the Low-Grade weapons or that you can Upgrade the Low-Grade weapons to the newly obtained Level-Grade Weapon.JOURNAL: A marker for Unread Messages would be sweet, because there is a bunch of them.Beside these THREE things and the Meh stuff I think that this is a great game and it offers a good story.Happy Hunting and Stay Dry :)

_childDocuments_.review: Half an hour into the game. User interface is not intuitive at all. Can only save outside a ship. There's target lock, but it doesn't help targetting. No even help to lead a moving target. What is that target lock even for? And everywhere are the same force fields that make no sense whatsoever, but open as the plot demands. So many years in development, and the game is still this sloppy and low effort.

_childDocuments_.review: Update:Overall a Solid 6.8/10Finally beat it 100% all sidequests and story. Took around 13-14 Hours.The main issue with this game is that most of the good stuff in near the last couple of hours. Cool environments, story picks up, a few bosses, great weapons, better ships, better upgrades. This is a big problem as the beginning is slow and clunky. Enemies are boring and barely do anything. Your weapons are garbage. Later on, I am moving at great speeds, blasting everything with the Advanced Shard (pretty much a railgun), along with drones, a forcefield, railgun turrets, dodging missiles left and right. Unfortunately, most of the cool stuff is locked away at the end. The environments pick up too, going from a dull ocean to a really nice looking, colorful underwater arena. Also there was a racing mini game for one sidequest, it provided a break from the combat and I would like to see more of that. Exploration does reward you with a ton of stuff early on however most of it is crafting materials, which you end up selling for money since inventory space is limited. While I can see the makings of a great game, the flaws keep it back.I have to bring up the weapon system, you have 2 main weapon slots that you switch between weapons using the 1 and 2 button, for some reason you have EVERY weapon equipped at all times. If you are like me and did all the optional stuff then you have to cycle through about 15 different weapons until you get what you want. They need a weapon wheel badly. (Note: This was fixed apparently in the most recent update)Lastly, remember to turn on the headlights. The Ocean is dark.First impressions:Quicksave is the F5 button. Save often, Especially on escort missions.If you enjoyed the old Aquanox games you will probably love this one.To summarize this is a "spaceship game" underwater. More on the arcadish side of things.You can change the colors of your ship to whatever you want in the hanger. I wish more games would let you do this for fashion purposes.Movement is clumsy until you get a ton of upgrades even then it might take a while for people to get used to the movement, you are underwater afterall. Strongly recommend the tutorial and messing around with the options menu until you have a comfortable control scheme. (Same with most flight games) Also move carefully fighting only a few enemies at a time, the AI will rip you apart even the chance even normal mode is tough. The game features a "dash" option, great for dodging and getting around. Much faster than the boost function sometimes. In later areas / boss fight you need to dodge a lot.

_childDocuments_.review: Allow me to preface; if you are bored enough to get this game. See if you can turn off Voice Acting or voices. You'll have a much better experience as the VA is so bad it'll hurt your head.The game starts off as most do, its intriguing, set in an interesting world with a fun st of concepts. But as you play, as you move through the story you start to realise more and more that it is monotonous, stale gameplay. It gets clearer and clearer how terrible and annoying a lot of the voice acting is, the poor development of character makes them all tools to the means of an end. The story is incomplete and has no consequences it seems. (Then theres the fact half the NPCs aren't even Voice Acted)There is also plenty of "fun" gimmicks added in to help keep you busy, but offer no variance to gameplay whatsoever. Such as ship customization, ship upgrades (Which don't allow any variance in design, just a path from start to finish) and instead of making use of the interesting world, you instead have to go through the story to unlock these different ship variances and upgrades, none of which are reversible. There is only ONE weapon you find by the idea I proposed of going out to find them, the Biont Cannon, and you only get to use it for an incredibly short period of time despite it being as powerful as it is.The gameplay loop in and of itself is something to remark on, it too, is painstaking, seeing as you move so slowly no matter what ship you choose to use, every fight feels sluggish, slow, and an annoyance moreso to the latter half. The fights themselves are unsatisfying and don't leave you with a sense of "I wanna go back in and do it again!" Instead you tend to get annoyed that you used all your repair kits and shield kits.The villains of the game may as well be non-existent, as their morals are the usual slop. There is nothing interesting about this game.In short. This game is highly incomplete, boring and generally unsatisfying

_childDocuments_.review: Having Fond Memories of Archimedean Dynasty, I find this game not only faithful to the original, but also arouses some fond memories of Wing Commander. The character Voice Over is excellent, it would be nice to have a teeming city underwater like Bioshock, but I think for the scope of a kickstarter to have a full campaign and multiplayer is already terrific. If you’re looking for submarine simulations you’re barking up the wrong tree, if you want some cool ships, that are progressively better, with upgrades to spend your hard earned loot on, then this is the place to be. Fun and entertaining. One quick note because it's not a sim, I didn't see any way for me to bind a HOTAS to it, so that would be my only complaint.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think the Steam user rating does the game justice, as it's not a bad game and has the core mechanics of the previous Aquanox parts, while bringing the visuals to a new level. It's also correct that visually it's not triple A, and the amount of "epxloration" you can do in the mission is limited, but that was kind of to be expected.What is sad however is that the game missed many opportunities to polish the details to make it "feel" more like an Aquanox. For example, the dialogue is much to clean and often not immersive, the side missions are loose-ended, the main four characters not very much explored, the ending sequence is wrapping up things too quickly etc. Stations should have been made more unique (station visuals, sounds, maybe names for the bar as in previous titles), and more lore could have been added. I preferred the geographically motivated names of the original much over the ones chosen here ("CU Main Station?! seriously...)I didn't quite like the way of the connection to the original series, but I can somehow understand the reasons for doing so. Still, some Aquanox is better than none ;-)

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a huge disappointment definitely not worth the full price proposed by the devs (I suggest buying it when it's at least 70% off). Quests are bland, tedious and cheap (both main and side); storyline is banal and predictable; characters are shallow and undeveloped; AI is aggresive and stupid; ship models look fine but there's nothing remarkable or unique about them (which is a shame; part of the appeal for me was the idea of piloting a unique vessel, nowhere before seen in Aqua – instead you pilot stock ships available for everyone); in-game economy is garbage (literally and figuratively); enemy variety is scarce; the atmosphere is sort of there, but not really (the ocean feels dead and doesn't give off that feeling of dread and mystery present in the first Aquanox); ship physics are acceptable; visuals are fine; audio is acceptable; crafting is tedious and unnecessary; fights require no brainpower; ship upgrades are few and far between and leave you feeling dissatisfied and unimpressed.Altogether, it feels like there's at least 50% of the game missing; it feels rushed, unpolished and without proper direction. There's love here, for sure, for eg. level design looks solid (albeit lazy at times), the ocean floor seems varied and quite eyecatching, but I feel like that love was not felt by the entirety (heck, not even half) of the dev team.Is the game playable? Yes. However, it gets monotonous fast, so keep that in mind.Is the game fun? For like an hour or three, after that not so much.Haven't tried coop and am not going to.
_childDocuments_.name: Aquanox Deep Descent

_childDocuments_.review: Got this for the co-op. The save system in co-op is terrible. Only the host saves progress and all other players reset their upgrades and resources every session. For a game which involves earning money to upgrade weapons and buy ammo, this is unacceptable. for that reason alone I do not recommend overall. But I'll be fair and say that the gameplay feels like more of what made the original Aquanox fun, but more refined. I'm not sure if I like the open world structure... it makes sense and exploring, collecting resources is fun, but the mission structure often just becomes "go to place, fight a bunch of people, go to next place". I feel there was more mission variety in the original games.I don't get the impression that they are going to update the game, but if they improve the saving in co-op I'd happily revisit and update my review. Either have it so you bring your single player save into multiplayer when you join, and bring back the resources you earned, or have the save be tied to the host, to the individual characters, so as long as a player picks the same character as last time, they keep what they had.

_childDocuments_.review: First things first: Deep Descent plays like I remember Aquanox 2: You have a story told through dialogues (although at least from having played 6 hours, the story isn't that convincing). And you have missions that play like descent in slow motion. And on a surface level (pun intended), that could be it. But because this is 2020, it isn't. I really like the game as I liked Aquanox 2 etc. Because of that nostalgia. But that's basically the primary and maybe for some even only point Deep Descent makes (so far): It brings you back to a time looong ago. On the other hand, that's probably the reason why I'm forgiving the graphics that just don't evoke awe as they did then. Or the bad AI. But it _is_ something I can and have to forgive to like the game. It is not a bombastic sequel, neither technically nor from the story as far as I can tell, to Aquanox. It is more of the same and I'm not unhappy to have bought it. I'm just a bit sad about how I imagined it could have been, so many years later, in comparison to how it is 3 days after launch.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a decent successor to the old Aquanox games even though there is no joystick, VR nor TrackIR support; this is a small crowdfunded project instead of a triple A title. Mouse & keyboard are the best controllers for the game.Game is very stable(no crashing nor stuttering for me), AI is quite polished and there's quite a bit of detail and atmosphere. It's got enough campaign for 12 to 20 hours and thus the value for your money is pretty spot on. There are 60 buck games out there with a similar or even lesser amount of hours in them.  EDIT: The game has a very simplistic co-op mode where progress only saves for the host. Players who join get reset into the starter ship with 20 000 credits to upgrade it every time they rejoin the host. So if they wanted to have the same progress as host the campaign would have to be played through in one session. As a result of this I can't recommend the game for co-op anymore, and it gets 6/10 from me. With a more proper co-op, it would have been a solid 7/10. I play this with everything maxed out and at 2560x1440p. _childDocuments_.review: Yesterday I have spent the evening on playing Aquanox Deep Descent while streaming it live on Twitch TV. And playing it has been a blast for me since it brought back lots of nostalgia for me just like in December 2001. Getting back into the game was not much of a problem for me since I have not played these series for too many years. And levels and terrains are well detailed for an under-water game.The aspects of the game that has really get me going is the hazardous environment. You should be aware on where you are going or taking cover at otherwise you might damage your ship by bumping into the rocks or other objects.The combat mechanics are rather basic simply aim and start shooting and locking on enemies does give additional information on their status. While remembering yourself that you should lock on enemies the information is clearly shown by tags and symbols.Sometimes during the live stream, I was a bit distracted and did not heard the dialogs on which objective I should do next. Which was caused by the music and events happening on the chat but that was a human error on my end. When paying more attention to the location marker this becomes clearer and easier to get through the game.Score / Rating wise I would give the game an 8.4 and may add more information to my review within in the future.Want to watch Aquanox and judge it yourself on Twitch? I will be live streaming it for the upcoming days and will be happy to answer your questions!

_childDocuments_.review: I am considering myself an oldschool gamer, playing from 83 when I got ZX Spectrum. And in the same way I consider Archimedean Dynasty and Aquanox series an oldschool games. But oldschool games had their own beauty that I completely miss in this title.- no hand holding: this game begins with an absolutely useless tutorial that learns you - move, avoid dangerous area, shoot, collect stuff. Wow, such a complete tasks that cannot be communicated during the first mission, if someone considers them too complicated. For an oldskool game I expect to be thrown into the action and discovering what can be done is part of the fun- fully use the potential of the hardware: oldschool games look old, but have their charm, which comes from the fact, that in their time their were absolutely top and cleverly used lots of tricks to give player maximum eye candy with limited resources. Different kind of explosions, damaged enemies slowly disintegrating, loosing parts etc. And here we are underwater, one would expect that enemies will implode in different ways, that the shots will give you an impression they are actually fired underwater. Or at least that the shots are actually fired from your guns and move through the 3D space. But you get nothing from this here, shots do not follow the direction of the gun barrels but they simply converges in your reticule. There are no flashes of the shots in the cockpit, your sub is not pushed back by the recoil of heavy guns, there is  no feeling that you actually fire from heavy underwater guns, no matter how nicely they look.Even targeting itself is very simple, there might have been lots of happening in your HUD. There might have been beautiful underwater fights, pleasing your senses with underwater destruction and imploded wrecks of enemies slowly descending to the bottom of the sea- cleverly designed UI: the UI in good oldschool games might not look good but it was always working great. UI in this came is chaotic, contraintuitive and generally pain to use. Almost nothing is where you expect it and if you find it you dont know how to use it. The game has controller support but for the in games menus I simply had to use mouse, because the UI designers of this game probably never used a controller and came with over complicated schemes instead of leaving the user possibility to use a cursor and simply click on everything. Alternative ways how to navigate a menu with controller are nice to have but must be intuitive. For some items I simply didnt find a way how to activate them without a mouse- story and it's presentation: in oldschool game there is no need of voice acting. There is especially no need of bad voice acting. There is need of short and interesting dialogues. Here I had option to click through the unnecessary long dialogues with several persons they I had no interest to talk with, because there were just annoying and unwanted ballast on my shipGenerally after the log wait I expected something like an underwater Freelancer, but what I get is band 6dof shooter where underwater locations are just a background and if you swap them with space or anything else it will make absolutely no difference
_childDocuments_.name: Aquanox Deep Descent

_childDocuments_.review: Really makes you feel immersed in a devastated underwater world.Aquanox Deep Descent took a while to finally see the  of day but it was worth the wait in the end.The graphics and underwater landscapes are gorgeous, really great atmosphere here, i love it so far, well done Digital Arrow.Gameplay is great, didn't expected it to be so dynamic with the dodge system, underwater combat feels good and the weapons are satisfying.I'd say the mouse look inertia could have been improved a bit though, also the up/down dodge is a bit too touchy and can be annoying.It's not perfect but it still really feel like you are underwater, it's not a submarine sim by any means but there's enough inertia and resistance to make it feel authentic.If this concept looks interesting to you, give it a try, you won't be disappointed.I don't understand the negative reviews tbh, people have to keep in mind this is an indie game and not a huge triple A title.You get full campaign with up to four players coop + some pvp modes, well worth the price IMO.Aquanox Deep Descent overall is a fine game, it's exactly what i expected it to be minus not being a true 6DOF game.I'm not sure why it's tagged as being a 6DOF game because it's not, you can't roll in this game.Anyway man i'm so happy this game finally came out and turned to be a good one.

_childDocuments_.review: Well I was literally starting to build very large bases in subnautica when I started playing this game.  I never did play the original versions but frankly the world needs an underwater micro sub battle game.  I frankly wouldn't mind if they combined forces with the planetside 2 people but alas.  Keyboard is fully customizable but forces you to use keyboard and mouse.  Seems to be fine, hopefully get a joystick option eventually.  Game has a lot of commonality with descent if any reader is old enough to remember that far back.  Quite frankly that is a good thing in a world infested with flight sims and corny space combat with fluffy controls.  25 bucks is roughly the price of two modern movies.  Considering how awful hollywood is these days its a bargain.  Voice acting is a bit wonky and docking with the capital ships should probably have been made into a mini-game rather than a single click, but ok.  Underwater environments are incredibly beautiful and ship customization is fun.2.6 hours in and the crew voices are getting downright annoying.  its like having three backseat drivers that never shut up.  game is also becoming annoyingly linear.  be far better in an open world format.  many features from elite dangerous could be imported here.Underwater "warp gate" thing too prominent as well.  seems confused and weird.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATED REVIEW 2020-10-18RECOMMENDED TO:Space Shooter, Deep Sea Fans WAIT FOR SALEI just completed the game in 13 hours. While I enjoyed it, I wouldn't say it's worth 30€ after all, maybe 20€.Although the world map suggests it's a more open title, the game is very linear. Weapons and Upgrades are directly bound to missions (with a very few exceptions that you'll get from scavenging).The additional NPCs on most stations suggest that the devs planned for more missions but ultimately pulled the plug for release.While I enjoyed the graphics and the general atmosphere, the gameplay itself is rather simplistic. The best tactic is to keep most enemies out of the line of sight and pick em off one by one, till the odds are acceptable.What pissed me off somewhat is the final mission where you unlock all the rest of the weaponry but have to stick with your current loadout... that or I was simply too dumb to find any capital ship to dock at (or was I supposed to leave the area at the story's climax and dock at some far-off harbour to reequip?).If you're interested, wait for a discount. Maybe the game sees some updates till then to make it more worthwhile.----------------------Original reviewI can see why some backers are pissed off by the extra DLC but the negative reviews are misleading. For this price, Aquanox Deep Descent is a fine game.Digital Arrow did a great job depicting the water, screenshots only show half of it. There's limited sight, a lot of play with light, plankton, distortions and turbulences, all-in-all a great deal of movement to remind you that you're in deep-sea.In contrast to the former Aquanox titles, inertia seems a bit higher, it's still Arcade but it doesn't feel like Underwater-Doom anymore. I recommend Mouse + Keyboard as it seems more flexible than playing with controller and aiming is easier too. Joystick doesn't seem to be supported, sadly.I appreciate the developer's effort to create some story, all main quest dialogues are fully voiced. I don't know if some dialogue options have any impact other than expressing your playstyle, but I doubt it.I haven't played much of the game, but I think the current average rating is very unfair hence the early review. Will update it when I'm further into the game.The game runs smooth (100+ FPS) on my system, 2K resolution, all maxed.i7 8600k, RTX 2070 Super, 32 GB, M2 SSD, Soundblaster Z

Aquanox Deep Descent is a first person underwater vehicle shooter, in which players control a variety of customizable ships to engage in fierce battles in the dystopian deep sea world of Aqua. In the near future the Earth's surface has become uninhabitable. What remains of humankind lives in former mining and research stations, deep below the surface of the sea. Born and raised in the only world we know, the loose network of underwater settlements, torn by the war for resources and dominance between various factions.

Take control of a team of highly trained fighter pilots and experience an epic story in the dark world of Aquanox. Send your enemies down to Davy Jones's Locker with well-aimed torpedoes, mortars, mines and more. Explore the deepest corners of the oceans -- mysterious, hazardous, uncharted.

name: Shadow of the Ninja - Reborn
detailed_description: Asian Community About the Game Show off ninja skills in the remake of a legendary dark and futuristic classic! It’s 2029. A vicious dystopian future. And it’s up to two warriors of the night to save the nation! After 34 years in the shadows, prepare to see this legendary action adventure in a new light! Looking and playing better than ever before, Shadow of the Ninja - Reborn is Tengo Project’s remake of a cult classic, that the fans have been waiting for. An arsenal of deadly weapons: In this thrilling action-adventure, you will use your striking katana along with a wide variety of weaponry that has greatly expanded from the NES original, as well as the acrobatic finesse of a ninja to face the onslaught of powerful enemies. Although, the challenge does not end here! Jungle of concrete and steel: 6 complex, expansive, and masterfully designed stages test your skills through devious traps and challenging platform puzzles. Two ninjas are better than one: Critically acclaimed as one of the best 2-player co-ops of its time, Shadow of the Ninja—Reborn lets you play together locally as the legendary ninjas Hayate and Kaede. A Star-Studded, Rockin’ Soundtrack: In addition to the contributions of Tengo Project, this remake also features Iku Mizutani, the star composer who helped create the iconic Natsume sound and renowned tracks for various NES games. Fans of Mr. Mizutani and retro gamers across the world will find delight in his renowned guitar riffs and fast-paced retro melodies! A fresh new look: Our fearless heroes, Hayate and Kaede have undergone a massive visual upgrade over their original 8-bit models. And the improvements don’t stop there: From the deadly foes to the no-less deadly stages, every part of this title has been faithfully recreated in stunning high-quality sprites. The Lethal Tools of the Trade: Use your hard-earned points in the tool shop and customize your loadout for the next play session. Features: Caltrops, shuriken, and more! 5 completely recreated stages featuring devious traps and challenging platform puzzles. Plus, a 6th entirely new stage! Grab a friend and get ready for the critically acclaimed couch co-op! Beautiful modern sprite art as a faithful update to the 8-bit original. Play along with the legendary Hiroshi Iwatsuki’s and Iku Mizutani’s electrifying guitar riffs and fast-paced retro melodies. So, cloak yourself in shadows and slash your way through a treacherous concrete jungle of the future in this dark action gem Shadow of the Ninja – Reborn! Extraordinary Artists: As with the original version, Dynamic Pro handled the illustrations! The key visuals/character illustrations are also by Dynamic Productions, as was the case with the first version in 1990. Dynamic Production Since its establishment in 1969, Dynamic Productions has been engaged in the management of manga artists, novelists and manga authors, including Go Nagai, as well as producing newly drawn manga, planning various events and managing the copyrights of its artists. Mikio Tachibana Born 11 May 1976 in Saitama Prefecture.After working as an assistant to Go Nagai, he made his debut in 2004 and has since published serialised works such as Mazinger Otome and Mazinger Otome Taisen. He continues to publish short manga, newly drawn manga and illustrated works in all genres.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a review, but a rant. The recently mixed reception for this game is exactly why I don't listen to modern gamers about anything anymore. Especially the modern indie game fans that a game like this would generally appeal to typically.Softened by low difficulty and excess convenience in their games now, they cannot fathom one that doesn't just hand out victory for free. So this fantastic game, another by the lovely people at Tengo Project, sits at an undeserved mixed because scrubs thought this would be instantly recognizable and beaten in a sitting.God forbid a game make you learn some rules and new skills instead of being another cookie cutter, disposable title. If you were expecting yet more toothless nostalgia bait that won't back up it's classic aesthetics with classic gameplay, you're in the wrong place. Shadow of the Ninja doesn't reward your meager legacy skill from playing Kirby, Shovel Knight, and copy/pasted Metroidvanias all day. Treat it as the NES game it's reviving. You don't get overpowered air dashes. You don't get forced RPG upgrades to circumvent the challenge with """build variety""". You don't have 20 different course correcting jumps that keep you from engaging with enemy patterns and tight stage layouts. Your weapons demand actual strategy and positioning. Bosses are hard. Enemy placement is ruthless. Jumps are stressful. It's biting from the very start without patronizing tutorials or tutorial levels. And it's flagrant disregard for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is all very beautiful. This is a short game that wants you committed for the long haul like a proper, Japanese arcade style action game. And it does it with very few modern compromises. Accept the game's terms. Learn it's ACTUAL rules instead of the ones you preemptively decided it should have based on the presentation and improve. You will lose and lose hard. If that's not your cup of tea, I'm sure you have some Super Mario Wonder to be playing. Maybe get back to that instead of crying in the reviews in a bid to get one of the best games of 2024 pushed down. For those of you who are not weenies, this game is more than worth your time and money. Another excellent Natsume remake to the collection. The best yet, I'd say. Play it and recommend it to get it back up to blue like it deserves.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadow of the Ninja Reborn, to get the gameplay description out of the way, is an action platformer.  It is a decent game, I want to stress it is OKAY, but it does have some glaring issues regarding being annoying for no reason and not utilizing core features and some quality of life to a degree a game should if it's going to demand excellence from players on a gameplay level.Shadow of the Ninja Reborn is a remake of an NES action game that, frankly, is a much different game.  The new game emphasizes items that you can purchase if you can clear stages with those items still on your person.  This asks players to be able to win with their standard kit in specific stages, without using items, so that they can place items in the store.  From there, the game puts great incentive on getting a high score, your best score in Arcade Mode, the main game, becomes the budget you have to buy items for your future runs in Arcade Mode AND in the Time Attack Mode.I don't think the "depth" of having to purposefully offload items is really interesting, it would be more interesting to narrow down how much of an item you need, like actual strategy would suggest, and then make your run even more precise.  Instead, there's a lot of fluff in making the controls and gameplay "busy" in uninteresting or needless ways at times.This game is an acquired taste, it's decent, but not really a great remake in the sense of bringing some of the cool qualities of the original into a modern setting.  Shadow of the Ninja Reborn opts to be a Score and Time Attack based game, compared to the original's basic and, I'd argue, extremely elegant design.  So a major issue is that the game doesn't really do enough with the two characters and difficulty modes in spite of adding these new modes.  The problem this ultimately poses to players is that you have to be okay with designer indulgences that leave you bearing the brunt of any issues of the core design relative to some of the game's rough spots.  And boy is there one really unnecessary and stupid rough spot.To get the worst of this game's problems out of the way, I think it leaves a lot to be desired as a remake, and in this regard I view it as a failure.  But it is fun if you play it in very specific ways.  For instance, if you play as Hayate, and not Kaede, the system inevitably shines.  As long as you don't mind a few failures along the way and some challenging gameplay.  Spacing, pattern recognition, rhythm... the game will test you.Something players will face is the fact that your character will grab ledges, ladders, overhangs and other surfaces automatically, while also having techniques such as hovering or wall runs that require you to rapidly mash buttons.  If your hands hurt from repetitive motion, this may be a deal breaker depending on how invested you want to be with the game.  The severe flaw I alluded to relates to the two characters.  In the original Shadow of the Ninja, both characters function exactly the same.  While they didn't have differences, one character wasn't worse in an arbitrary and stupid way.  Yes, that's the problem.  Unlike Ninja Warriors Once Again/Ninja Saviours, nothing really sets Kaede apart from Hayate.  Their kits are standardized, she just runs faster on the ground and jumps slightly higher, but at the cost of any momentum she has slamming to a crawl the instant she takes to the air.  And so it goes, the brunt of my negative feelings about the game have to do with difficulty decisions the designers made to force errors, coupled with the fact that if you play as Kaede, you're just playing a really unfun character.  I don't think a game that demands this kind of excellence in platforming or, at the very least, the attention span and challenge Shadow of the Ninja Reborn requires, should have a character like this.  When I see elements in the game like how certain hitboxes require absolute precision in this asinine way, it means a lot of the depth, and Kaede is the biggest offender here, is just marketing flourish.  It's the kind of thing you can read on a list of taglines, but actually playing the game can be an extremely annoying experience.This means that if you play co-op and have to play as Kaede, you're getting the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ character.  I can think of really minute and specific reasons to justify her design, but for a game that pulls no punches in its platforming, I see no reason to be charitable.  This is an awful character and an awful decision for a platformer with huge vertical segments that require split decision making, on top of precise strategy and movement, to make.  It's trash.The difficulty in the game doesn't really feel meaningfully applied in this sense.  It's indulgent.  There are many challenges in the game that are platform based that just do not change with the difficulty and this game really won't shy away from knowledge checking you.  Stage 5 can be absolute hell if you don't understand what's happening.  So if you're using Kaede, her limited air momentum and mobility makes the game's challenges and difficulty more severe than they should be, because she'll often be behind on timing cycles or struggle in a lot of situations that Hayate just doesn't.  In Stage 5, her slow movement opens her up to being shot unless you really have the game memorized.  Kaede doesn't have her own categories in Score or Time Attack... that means there's even less reason to play her than there already was being some kind of picky, top tier enjoyer and nerd, I think that her jump momentum working the way it does is just lazy and cheap.  It's such a bad mistake, I cannot stop harping about it.  I want to be clear that it is the largest criticism I have against the game.  She is not all that rewarding to use and, in some contexts, she never will be relative to another character.  This may not bother you!So the good?  Well, I can play as Hayate!  I quite like the character Hayate.  He's really fun to play, but I spent my first 22 or so hours on stream and off playing as Kaede trying to iron out if she actually had much going for her.  If you're playing casually, for score or for time, I think Hayate is a solid pick.  He best exemplifies the system and the "Super Realism" concept of weighty moves the game has.So what it boils down to, to me, is that this game is just not that good if you are taking the brunt of its flaws.  This game is not like other platforming games in the sense that it wants to emphasize its animations and create a strategic experience that, while unique, I think asks much of the player that it doesn't earn out of players.  If the game was going to be this difficult, I think Normal Mode should have been put to better purpose and, in my mind, represent the design of the original game a little more closely.  To show the appeal of the game before forcing players to engage with its item management concept.Despite my negativity, I feel like this is one of the best looking and sounding games I've played.  That's to be expected from Tengo Project.  I think the gameplay can be snappy and varied.  I bet the game would even be fun with another player, but take note that if you play on co-op mode the game defaults to hard mode difficulty as a consequence and that I think is, yet again, something that Tengo Project still hasn't learned to do correctly.With massive caveats.  While I think the game has a lot of problems, a LOT of problems, it's decent.  It's your typical Tengo Project experience, I just think that while their remakes are becoming what I expect and sometimes better in ways, this game has a lot of slip ups that I won't ignore anymore.  They need to do difficulty much better, and a waste of space character is a complete joke.  If you can forgive that, you're in for some fun provided the demanding control scheme isn't a turn off.

_childDocuments_.review: [Addendum: I'll leave this review as it is, with its many edits, as a sort of chronicle of my journey with this game. TL;DR I kinda love the crap out of it now.]This is clearly one of those secret galaxy-brain games with really purposeful controls & mechanics that most people will find "clunky" (it's not like these devs haven't made plenty of games with more traditionally "good"/self-explanatory controls in the past) but I'm not smart enough to get the full extent of its design & what you can do in it. I can tell the jumping controls are like that for a reason & the very unique combat would likely feel immensely worse with a more traditional jump. I can tell the slow weapon-switching is meant to encourage clever planning & routing, and that the order in which you're handed weapons is very important - it's not just about hoarding them & quickly switching to whatever fits the given situation best. As of now though, I'm pretty terrible at this game & I feel like I'm missing a bunch. Still having a great time however and I'm sure once it clicks it'll click hard.Edit: Yeah it's not really a "click" as much as a steady learning process, everything making more & more sense with each step. There's a lot of strategizing after memorizing the levels & this game's a very replayable, mastery-based affair. I respect the devs for making design choices most people are going to find "cumbersome" for the sake of more thoughtful & unique gameplay. The controls become second nature the more you play & make for a pretty unique feeling.Edit 3: 1CCed Normal, reached the final stage on Hard. Any lingering misgivings I may have had about the design are gone. I guess some might take issue with how the jumping mechanics jive with the platforming, but they were mainly designed for the high-commitment combat and the jump extend (down + jump in midair, tap for more distance) immensely helps with non-combat jumping. Beyond that, I have no issues with the item system; having to go out of your way to avoid touching items you don't need to not mess up your inventory might bother people, but it's still something that's within your control and easy to deal with after multiple playthroughs with properly strategized routing. You won't have to kill yourself to avoid a crappy item a la Ghosts n' Goblins/Ghouls n' Ghosts.

_childDocuments_.review: In 2006 Capcom released a game called God Hand, which had a tagline, "Hard but fair." This byline was a philosophical statement as well as a promise made in earnest.Now, here in 2024 Tengo Project and NatsumeAtari have brought us an extremely sophisticated remake of a fairly hard but ultimately simplistic game for the Famicom/Nintendo Entertainment System that went by the the name of Shadow of the Ninja (1990). In remaking it, the developers have created a significantly more sophisticated experience than the title upon which it iterates. It's a whole new and different game. This remake adheres to that former philosophy of, "Hard but fair."Shadow of the Ninja Reborn asks a great deal of the player, but the ask is never terribly unreasonable. Master your full moveset, know what to do and when, think on your feet, prepare for a few seconds in advance as best you can, and act with conscious but swift deliberation. Every action takes a bit of time (down to even picking out inventory items), so the game is quick to punish an incorrect action. However, the punishment is never wholly unreasonable, and it's usually possible to recover from a simple mistake.The artwork and animations are beautiful. The developers really fleshed out the world in what was previously a rather bare-bones, spartan NES game. Alas, you might not get to really enjoy the art until you've mastered the game, because when you're playing it you need to be tuned in and focused on the tasks before you. The game never goes more than a few seconds without introducing a new series of challenges.There are a great many fun tools to use aside from the sword and the kusarigama (sickle on a chain), each with its own uses. An implicit goal when playing is to complete a Stage with unused tools in your inventory so that they are added to your collection and thus made available for purchase in future runs.The game does not treat the player with kid gloves. There is a sort of dodge/dash technique available, but it has NO i-frames to speak of. NONE. It's still useful when used appropriately, but there's no way to spam-dodge or anything of that sort. All of the techniques are similarly conditional, and knowing the right technique for a given set of conditions is essential. There's no way to prevail through spam. Again, the game demands that you be deliberate, and punishes lax reactions swiftly (though not in a way that feels overly harsh).The game piles on the excitement, even in platforming segments. You will be thrust into new screens that can often seem insurmountable at first glance, but once the initial trepidation subsides it becomes clear that the challenges are quite surmountable given proper technique and spacing.Spacing is a big part of the fights in this game. It's essential to be in the right position in any given encounter. In this respect the game can sometimes feel a bit like it channels certain aspects of the fighting in the Super Smash Brothers series, though most encounters resolve far quicker than in that game.The game never holds your hand, but it usually suggests the ideal approach to a given challenge by quietly eliminating avenues of approach and punishing bad decisions. It's easy to glean what it's trying to tell you.There is, however, one section where I had some difficulties figuring out how to land a particularly distant jump. It required combining two techniques, a hovering jump leading into a downward stab. You'll know it when you arrive at it.The checkpoints feel fairly spaced out, and you'll never feel that you're being made to slog through too much of a given section without relief. Each section of a level can be taken on its own without too much concern for being sent back an outrageously long way should you happen to perish.Perhaps the most difficult aspect of the game as it is here at the launch comes from mastering the controls. Many of the moves require button combinations that feel a bit oppositional to that which feels instinctually correct. A good example of this is hovering after a jump. This requires pressing down + jump, which is a very strange feeling to me for whatever reason. This is not to say that one cannot get used to these peculiar combos, since there are not that many of them, but they can be a bit offputting. Another example, and this one is a bit more nuanced in its irritation: mantling on ledges and grappling on overhead pipes and platforms is a bit fraught due to the button combinations yielding very different results dependent upon the conditions. If you grapple onto an overhanging platform, you pull yourself up by pressing up. If you're grappling onto the corner of a ledge, you pull yourself up by pressing jump. However, if you're grappling onto an overhanging platform and press jump then you will drop down. Do you see where this becomes tricky? It can lead to irritating outcomes in heated moments where the conditions mandate a lot of fast platforming over complex platform arrangements, as you will almost certainly react in the wrong way at some point and drop off a ledge you meant to climb up.Those minor gripes aside, the game rules! I love it! It is a lot of fun and if it seems as though it would appeal to you, and you're willing to take on a reasonable challenge then you would be well-served to scoop this one up. It's another banger from NatsumeAtari. They're some of the best out there serving up wonderful 8/16-bit era remakes. Their art is unmatched, and their designs are rock-solid. This is the sort of arcade excitement that I could only have dreamt of as a child.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow of the Ninja - Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: Superb. Tengo Project are on a roll and are now 4 for 4 with absolute bangers. This is a fairly tough action platformer, with absolutely gorgeous sprite art, beautiful animation and an awesome soundtrack. It's a joy watching just masters at their craft.The controls and movement will take a little bit of getting used to at first, especially if you haven't played any arcade or NES games for a while, and you will likely see some folks claim the controls are bad or clunky, but the game gives you all the tools you need to get through its challenges. There's a few things like the way you climb up or drop off ledges feeling a bit weird at first, but it's just a thing you learn and then you're fine. The range of movement and attack options is quite vast and each one feels like it has its benefits and restrictions, making each one a tool to learn and use well. For instance, you have no double jump, instead you can press down and jump in the air to do a twirl to extend or delay your landing, and mashing the jump will extend the twirl even further. Your chain attack has long reach and can be shot in multiple angles (including downwards if you're in the air), but it has longer recovery as you're stuck in the animation. But being closer to an enemy when you shoot it can allow you to hit multiple times.The sword beam extends your range a lot, but being very close to enemies lets you hit them with both the beam and the sword slash together. But you will lose it if you get hit a few times etc. Everything feels like it's been carefully calibrated with just the right amount of risk and reward.I for instance love the item system, how you don't pause the game and have to rummage through your bag in the middle of a fight. It initially feels devastating, but trying to find a safe spot during a hectic battle to switch items, then quickly move and find another safe spot to munch on a baguette, it is again, carefully calibrated to be rewarding and demanding. You pick up habits like selecting the item you quickly want access to before you enter the next boss etc. It's great stuff and the right call from the designer.Once you master it, it's very satisfying, but it'll take a while. Do not go into the game if you are hoping for a breezy button mashy "retro" time, Reborn definitely subscribes to the design philosophy that overcoming challenges is just as important part of making the player feel good as just simply giving them what they think they want instantly. That said, I am no longer particularly good at hard action games, especially "nintendo hard" ones, but the game isn't like sadistic. It is the fun kind of challenging, even if you will occasionally curse when you get knocked off a ledge or time a jump wrong.I have enjoyed every reimagining the group has put out, altho Pocky & Rocky Reshrined remains my favourite. It's exciting to see old veterans flex their muscle and present us with such fantastic action games. I can't wait to see what they tackle next.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow of the Ninja - Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: This game is relentlessly difficult. The entire game is built around the controls and how they function - so while they may feel "clunky" or even "bad" to some, the design that was amongst the best of what was possible at the time - and by especially clever or unique games, imitated on purpose - takes some time to get used to. Even on normal, you're not going to be able to open this up and crank through it in an afternoon.A few tips to get you going...*Make use of continues. You need practice!*The game rains tools on you to use, and you can only hold so many. Discard any notion of holding on to them. They all have their uses and in the times they are useful, are strictly better than hitting things with your sword. As you play more to learn how the tools work, and how the stages are laid out, you'll pick up on when and where you should hold on to something to deal with an upcoming problem enemy. When you're just starting, you don't know anything, so just use it and see what works where.*Don't come at this game with preconceived notions of what it SHOULD be, engage with what IT IS.

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the best example of a game that people should try to master before having any say on the quality. It is an extremely well-designed and beautiful remake of an NES classic. It is incredibly difficult but fair (for the most part) and very satisfying to master. The jump may feel clunky at first, but stick with it for a while and you'll get the hang of it.-The art and animation is excellent. Colors are great and the form of the environments, characters, and effects are excellent. You won't find many examples of better pixel art.-The levels feel very tuned to character movement. The more you get used to the controls, the move fun it is to navigate around. Your moveset also feels VERY intentional, with no redundancies in methods of moving around or attacking.-Items are good and fun, even if they feel like an afterthought sometimes. They can help make some parts easier, and you are rewarded for carrying certain items with you to the end, incentivizing low item usage. It's a nice give and take to help players improve gradually. They also add a lot of personality to the moveset. -For the most part, the game seems to prioritize fair damage. Most enemies and puzzles are given an introduction from afar so you can process your actions going forward. Most situations can be navigated out of if you are skilled enough. Theoretically, you CAN (probably) do a no damage run on your first try. It will jut be really hard. in my eyes a "perfect" run in any game should be achievable, so it is nice to see that such a thing may be possible.My main issue with this game is the fact that a lot of your movement options are context sensitive. For example, in most platformers you can jump through "soft" platforms from below. This game doesn't do that - you will GRAB the "soft" platforms to climb. The same thing goes for ledges, you will automatically grab an edge if you fall next to one. While the mechanic itself is cool, the way it just activates can create very frustrating situations. It can mean life or death when you mean to do something like escape by bailing off a ledge, only to grab it and eat damage. Personally, I believe grabbing ledges or a roof could've just been bound to another button to avoid this annoyance (or at least a togglable option). You can play around this, of course, but I think it messys the room for player expression when it comes up. It's one of the only things that really hamper the flow of the game.One other criticism I have is the difficulty of some bosses. It feels like the stage 4 boss is pretty RNG dependent. i have beaten it damageless exactly once, and I have not been able to replicate it since. It is BY FAR the hardest boss in the game. This and the slow-scrolling stage 6 section are the main headache when going for low-damage playthroughs. The semi-final boss also feels easier on hard mode for some reason, which is a shame.This is an incredibly fun, fair, and beautiful game with only a few real problems. If you dedicate just a little time to it and are open to bettering yourself, you will discover a very replayable and challenging game that will just make you feel good. Very excited to see what Tengo Project does next.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow of the Ninja - Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: Tengo Project’s latest remake, starts off deceptive with how simple it seems. Level and enemy design that seems very textbook, but subtle nuances such as player control, multi-hits, item management, enhance what comes off as an otherwise standard console-style action platformer.The first and most immediate thing you’ll probably notice is the controls. They’re not what you expect from a game where you play as a ninja. They’re very commital. Long delay for jumps, arcs that you only have a little control over, jumps off of ledge grabs being locked to arcs that you’re stuck to and can’t immediately attack out of, your chain weapon being something that locks you in place and has a lot of recovery, item management being real time and something you have to stop to do. I want to highlight the controls, not just because even by themselves it’s really fun to master and zip through levels but because of them it enhances almost every part of the game. It means even the tiniest bit of enemy rng such as them deciding to turn left instead of right now carries more gravity with it.I was surprised to find this game has a good scoring system, considering scoring in 99% of action platformers is ass (and not the good kind like Kaede’s) but it’s nice to have an exception. It mostly revolves around routing your throwing fan (weapon that gives you points with every hit and is good for long rows of enemies), your small mallet (weapon that doesn’t do much damage, but whatever you hit with it has a multiplied score on death), killing as much as you can as fast as you can, and holding onto high score items (usually food, but sometimes something completely useless), until the end of stage. It’s simple but ties into the core fundamentals of the game really nice because now you don’t wanna use your good healing items too much, but you also still want to be fast because that gives you more points. Just gotta be more efficient.Time trials seem like such a natural fit for a game like this so I was surprised to find out it was much less interesting. The time trials are strictly separated into their individual stages, so you can pick a super powerful item loadout for a stage that would otherwise be in the middle of a run and just blitz through it without much fanfare. It’s disappointing. They should either remove the ability to use loadouts or add an option for full game time trials.Anyways, this has become one of my favorite action platformers. Really solid fundamentally, visually gorgeous with mostly really fun bosses and levels that do a good job of setting themselves apart. Tengo Project really are some of the best devs around.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow of the Ninja - Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: This game is fantastic, but if you're not a fan of VERY challenging arcade games, you might not have as much fun. If you enjoy a challenge and are willing to sit and learn the game, it's 100% worth a buy.Having completed the game once or twice now casually I definitely have a lot of thoughts about the game. I would consider Reborn to be a straight upgrade in all ways (visual, audio, gameplay) to the original NES release from 1990. I have a few minor gripes that honestly could pretty easily be fixed and don't greatly impact the enjoyable nature of the game.The sprite art is a major selling point and it doesn't let the player down at all. From start to finish the game is gorgeous and all the stages, enemies, items, and animations are a joy to look at.The sound likewise got a huge upgrade with new arrangements at a higher fidelity by (I think) the original composer. Sound effects are great and didn't ever get annoying (to me).The gameplay is difficult. About 90% of the difficulty is intentional. You can't rush through this game, but you get a lot of options to help develop strategies. Each level is a bit like a multi-part puzzle that you need to crack apart. A couple of areas near the end of the game do get a little egregious with the hazards but it never breaks its own rules to make things harder.It's not perfect, though. The menus and continue menui are a little annoying when you want to get back to a new attempt immediately. Admittedly I don't think menus and such are Tengo's strong point. I'm a tiny bit bummed that there's still no netplay multiplayer (Hey, get ahold of Codemasters. They've worked wonders for SNK!) but there IS local multiplayer which is a cool addition.The last thing I want to point out is how happy I am we got this remake on PC and console near-simultaneously. It felt like forever waiting on Ninja Warriors Once Again to come to Steam and I'm hoping Natsume/Tengo continue making great games and bring them to Steam on launch day.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow of the Ninja - Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good. It is difficult but I see that as a good thing. Remember difficulty is content. As someone who has spent a lot of time playing games that don't challenge the player switching over to games like this is very refreshing. The game does not waste the player's time. When you press that start button you're right into the action. No walking sections or introduction segments that stand in the way of getting to the actual gameplay. If were to describe the gameplay I would compare it to the older Castlevania games where it's commitment heavy but also versatile since this game has a expanded moveset compared to the original. Some people have critiqued this game for deviating too much from the original but I believe it's different this time. If you compare this game to other remakes that are just other companies making fanfiction versions of the original, this one was done by the original developers who looked back at the original game with the knowledge they have now and made a game with more innovative gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is awesome!  Thank you Natsume for another well done remake and classic brought to PC!I was slightly worried originally when people on the discussion forums were stating that the controls were unresponsive, or that there was a huge delay in jumping or something in the demo that was on console, but when I played on PC, that was not the case at all.  The controls are very responsive from my experience.  Maybe it is because consoles naturally have more lag in its games and many do not the VRR ranges, refresh rates, or v-sync off that PC has access to for the fastest response times/lowest latency?  I don't know.  It is very responsive here on PC.Anyways, the game is pretty tough like most Arcade/classic games from the past and Natsume's library and this is no different.  The combat for this platformer and movement in general is definitely a bit more commitment focused (don't confuse that with clunky or unresponsive).  The controls also make sense to me on gamepad.  X/Y for Xbox (Square/triangle for Sony controllers) for your main attack and the ranged attack feels fine.  So does dropping down from platforms with down + A/(X for Sony) and so forth.  There are many things on screen setup like most platformers to stand in your way, multiple routes, and multiple tools to deal with enemies which is pretty cool.  Battles between bosses feel kinda like a fighting game in a sense.  The two playable characters play exactly the same from what I've gathered and read in the manual.  There also is no blocking in this game in contrast to another game of Natsume's that you may have played (Ninja Warriors/Savior...I ironically beat that game without blocking without realizing there was a block function because I did not read the manual lol, but I digress).The sprites/art in this game are gorgeous, but they don't really shine unless you play at a  lower resolution in windowed mode.  If you play full screen on a larger display, it will look less crisp.  There is a scanline feature under display settings, but it doesn't do a good job at mimicking the CRT look/feel.  I recommend downloading ReShade from the internet and attaching it to this game and use some of the Retroarch CRT Shaders as a mod to make the visuals look better--it's the next best thing without an actual CRT monitor.  I hope they provide more CRT filters in future titles.Other than that, the game has a nice challenge to it even on normal to start.  There is no online multiplayer sadly (likely due to costs), but remote play exists via Steam Remote Play Together and Parsec.  They're totally viable for this game as an alternative and this is a lightweight game to boot; I've  played with a friend in Asia all the way from North America.  I hope they add online co-op in future titles though regardless.Definitely recommend this game and hope for more titles in the future though!

_childDocuments_.review: I played and finished it on the hard difficulty.The game is still amazing even as a remake. Menus are nice and simple.Graphics are very good, the developers did and amazing job for this remake. The art style is different than what I expected, it's more light-hearted but still similar to the original. The atmosphere is still there but it's also more bright and while in some places it feels much better, some other areas are a bit too colourful.Sound is good, better than smashing robots. Music is still awesome, some songs do sound a bit more light-hearted as well in my opinion.Story is short and to the point like the old one.Game play is similar to what was before, but it's more interesting now with some extra mechanics and it gets pretty difficult. You get a lot more weapons and they help quite a lot in some locations but you can also run through with just your main weapons which I appreciate and can use both now. There is an entire new stage with a new boss which is an amazing addition to the game, although I did find the new boss just a bit more easier while other bosses got additional phases which made them harder but they are still great, even better. Enemy variety is great, stages look great and do a good job at looking different. Some parts can be very difficult but i did discover sometimes ways to make them easier and bosses have patterns that once you see, will decrease in difficulty. There are rankings which is a nice addition for a bit of competition. There is still a two player option to play the game and while some areas can be more difficult in two, other areas can be easier.       Small issues and things I would have liked:- There could have been more options in the settings for example it would have been nice to be able to change the music to the original or darken the colours.- In the old version, the later bosses, especially the last one have some extra life points that do not show on the screen which I very much enjoyed and it felt great when their life bar eventually started going down.- When the life bar of the old bosses would be near the end it would go red and the bosses would get more aggressive which this remake does not do.- The hard version is somewhat of a missed opportunity since it's almost the same as normal and could have added a couple of things from the old like the aggressive boss mechanic i specified and also it's own level achievements.    - When you reach a boss the first time, you only have one shot at it with the weapons you gathered and if you die you have to do it with just your main ones and also not upgraded which can drag a bit.- The female character voice can be a bit annoying. - Last boss arena is still great by design but for me the background change is not better and the second phase one isn't that good.   - The second phase fight of the last boss could have been better.- The game needed just a bit more polish.In the end, it's very fun, i enjoyed it a lot and i do hope a sequel will be made.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow of the Ninja - Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game for an hour the night before I wrote this review, got upset that it felt worse than the NES game, and contemplated a refund.I have now completed nearly two playthroughs and I am currently enjoying the crow I'm eating. Game's a little weighted in feeling and the responsiveness even with this intention in mind is not always top notch, but once you figure out its controls and its weird quirks (everything involving hanging and the wall) it gets very fun very fast. Presentation is top notch, this might be their best work yet in that regard.Realistically the worst things in this game are the autoscroller stages and to a lesser extent the boss fights. The autoscrollers all run way too long and way too slow while encompassing the absolute worst aspects of the game's level design (off-screen enemies in Stage 6 and general lack of clarity in Stage 4 on top of screen noise) but outside of these, it's fantastic. While I am not as fond of this one as I am the Ninja Saviors, this is worth your time if you give it a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadow of the Ninja Reborn's new features are welcome, but to be blunt, its presentation is what makes it worth checking out, all the more if you’re a sucker for pixel graphics. If the boss fights were at least a bit more interesting and memorable, the unforgiving scrolling scenes probably wouldn’t have bothered us as much and we’d have a better impression of the gameplay. But as it is, you put a lot of effort to overcome scrolling scenes just to land on battles that don’t really make up for the struggle.The boss fights and their mechanics are mostly untouched and haven’t aged very well. Taking advantage from the invincibility frames after being hurt to spam your buffed melee hits is often a good choice, usually safer and more effective than playing carefully. To put it simply, reworked boss fights would better fit the reworked player movement and attacks.Were it not for its delightful audiovisual, I’d be compelled to call it a  game rather than a  one. Some sections had us pulling our hairs out while we tried to find the best way through, and sometimes the answer was evidence we weren’t given the right tools to work with, almost as if the new level design had been tested solely with a playthrough buffed by the Prep Shop.Yet, Reborn is doubtlessly a much more fleshed out experience than the original entry, not to mention much more affordable and accessible even if progressing through stages for the first time prove to be excessively challenging.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me just say, the game is not bad, bad. But it annoyed me and any other friend I tried to play with to such extent, that giving it anything more than a non recommendation is the highest compliment I can possibly give. It starts out excellent, great music, great art, and awesome gameplay. Sounds promising, right? So what is the problem? Everything else! After the first stage, the cracks begin to show, and it gets gradually worse until the final stage that is the piece de resistance of crap. There are 2 major problems. The first is the stage design. It is almost.... I hasitate to say....like garbage. Every damn enemy placement and hazard is made to hit you with cheap shots again and again. Oh! Did you manage to get trough that jump or hazard? Sorry beatch! There was an enemy douche waiting for you almost off screen so he could shoot you the moment you thought that you made it. Oh! Did you think you could jump next to an enemy and duck when he shoots you? Well too bad! We placed a pipe next to him, so that your character would grab on to it automatically, and start hanging from it instead of landing so you could duck. Why did we do that? So the enemy could land yet another cheap shot on you of course….duh. Oh! Did you plan on using the wall run ability that we did not tell you about in any way shape or form to scale the wall, and grab that item. You presume too much, we placed an obstacle next to the edge so that you would not be able to grab or climb it. Why did we do that? Because we wanted you to climb it in the most annoying and non intuitive way possible…….we also placed a enemy that will shoot at you the moment you are in sight while you are struggeling with the controlls….kekekekeke.This type of ass-ho-le stage design only gets worse the more you progress in the game. It’s not about being hard. It’s about it being frustrating, and annoying at every step of the way. I would still be fine with this form of design if not for the 2nd problem, the horrible controls. Slightly delayed jumps, and the forced  slow animations that force you to commit to everything you do. Probably made so on purpose, so the enemy can land those cheap shots even more so. Also one of the characters, jumps a much shorter distance for no reason other than make the jumps even more annoying if you play with her, and that is probably made so........you guessed it! So that the enemy and the hazards may yet again land those pesky cheap shots. All this, in a game that demands precision and tight controls and does not have it. Often when using the hang mechanic I would hang on a platform and press up and jump so that my character would climb up, if I wanted to drop down I would press down and jump. Sounds reasonable because every game ever, does control like this. Except this one, if you so much as lick the jump button you will be dropping down even if you pressed up. So I was killing myself more than jumping in the later levels and struggling with the controls over and over for other reasons as well.Now you may be wondering. Ok maybe the game is a little too hard. Why don’t you play on normal? I can’t! Playing multiplayer with a friend automatically puts the game on hard and cannot be changed. Why!? Ask the developers!This type of idiotic design decisions are for some reason all over their recent games. Wild Guns Reloaded: no continues, and sharing lives when playing more than one player. Also, forcing hard which also dictates what stages may or may not be played.Pocky Rocky Reshinned: you may not play co-op multiplayer unless you finish the game once or punch in a secret cheat that is… a secret.What the hell!? Who made these decisions? The original games had none of these ”features” why are they here?So yes, in the end my experience was nothing if not frustrating. I still beat the game. But did I have fun? No! I was swearing trough the whole ordeal. This type of design is made for masochists or sadists and if you are one. Welcome, son! This is right up your alley.
