_childDocuments_.review: A weighty, decisive game taking after the tradition of Castlevania and Ghosts 'n Goblins, but with a character all its own. Far from boulder-like stoicism or ceramic fragility, Shadow of the Ninja promises something uniquely slick within the subgenre. Pirouetting off of well-timed stabs, up ledges and over bullets, tossing chains at range before closing in to melt foes down with fiery slashes, the player's vast moveset becomes expressive amid carefully-constructed chaos. So many tiny considerations toward risk and reward stack up beautifully, from heat-of-the-moment menu navigation to deliberately-calibrated recovery animations. Who better than Tengo to marry the ghost of a beat 'em up to the shell of an arcade platformer?But you should know beforehand that it won't easily surrender its Ninja fantasy. The controls take some learning, enemies won't generously wait for you to practice your wall-running technique, Game Over screens can feel tedious, but it shouldn't take long to grasp the basics, and the ensuing domino effect of acquiring and honing each discovered skill is as satisfying as they come. It's too soon to judge whether Shadow of the Ninja stands toe to toe with the great Classics of Committed Action, but if you aren't sold by the unbelievable charm and volume of its animation or its rewarding expansion of ancient platforming concepts, then I might suggest considering another hobby in this life.

_childDocuments_.review: The magic hasn't died...Natsume made great games on the NES and later on the SNES. The soundtrack, graphics and gameplay were always top-notch. Now they're back again, with the artists and developers who worked on the original Shadow of the Ninja, and they've done it again. It's the most beautiful pixel art arcade action game you'll ever see. The music has been updated and harks back to the original with a modern arrangement without being afraid to pay homage to the past. And the gameplay is like classic Japanese games, with super-quality game design that shows that there are no old or dated games, but rather games that are well-made or not.I highly recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this up on a whim because of a few people I follow recommending it, not really looking too much into what it was about, so you can imagine how surprised I was when it turned out to be a Tengo Project developed remake and of a game I've never heard of.First off, the game's presentation is incredible, from it's sprite work, environments, music, but if you've played their other remakes, this should not be a surprise that they can breathe new life into an old title while still feeling like it's a game from that time.I'll admit there are sections in this game that are downright frustrating, so it's funny seeing how other people approach it from their own playthroughs and realizing that the game's mechanics are important to learn. I bring this up not only because you need to know them to actually progress, but also to not make the game more difficult for you which I did when I kept forgetting the kunai chain easily made so many frustrating enemy placements a cake walk, as well as movement options that keep you outta harm's way. It's definitely a game that takes some time getting used to and much more enjoyable when you do, but it's worth it if you love these kinda games.Onto my criticisms of the game, one being that it would've been helpful to players to learn the game's mechanics organically in the actual game, but instead you have to read the manual just to learn that you can hover to get past a large gap or even wall running, which one of the bosses has an attack that you need to wall run to get out of. Another thing that I was not a fan of, was the fact that if you jump to an edge and hang, you cannot just climb up normally and have to jump forward, which is awful if the enemy is so close to the edge and doesn't give you any room. And finally, the game's autosave feature, which doesn't even keep your progress if you complete a few stages, pause and return to the main menu. It's baffling that it doesn't keep your progress, but when you get a game over and return to the main title, it does at that point.With all that said, it's still a game that's worth your time, a little rough around some edges, but if you love those kinds of side scrolling platformers, especially the work of Tengo Project in recent years, it's definitely worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is for those on the fence after hearing about the controls.Compared to the NES game, this one is less Ninja Gaiden styled and more like arcade action platformers like Strider, Bionic Commando and Makaimura (Ghosts 'n Goblins). The closest pure console comparison is classic Castlevania, down to the pronounced combat focus.As such, the controls are heavy and high commitment, and might feel weird if you only played more tradicional platformers like Mario, but they are tight and you will get them to feel responsive in no time (I recommend a way to force disable vsync, though, to make them just that slightly better).It is short like an arcade game, but just like one, it is incredibly fun to endlessly replay and map out your routes. Try going for a deathless run (I sure will)!Easily one of my favorite platformers on Steam, the more deliberate type is incredibly rare to come across these days, because, as you might get from the other reviews, most people aren't used to or straight up won't like this type of game. But if it looks interesting and you are willing to go outside your confort zone, it is a great introduction to this genre.(also, steam glitched and erased a few hours from the total that I spent offline)

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, pretty fun, but very challenging game.The positives: The sprite-work is incredible and the music fits very well. The movement does require some mastering, but is generally satisfying once you get hang of it. There is no tutorial so you have to figure things out yourself, which might not be for everybody, but it is fulfilling nonetheless. The game also has secret paths freshening up the experience. The weapon system is interesting in where even when you fail, you can purchase items which can make the level progression faster. Most of the bosses are sort of a puzzle, which at first seem incredibly difficult, but once you figure their secret out, you can beat them pretty easily and are generally satisfying.The negatives:Even though the movement is great, I really dislike the requirement to perform diagonal inputs on a controller, which makes me believe this game is more suitable for keyboard. But the most lacking feature in this game is the level design. All levels make egregious usage of "red light, green light" type of obstacles, where 60% of time you just need to STOP to safely cross the obstacle and the levels loses all of their flow.  Since the game is pretty challenging you just want to get to the part you died and the fact that you have to SIT and WAIT in multiple points make the game a bit of a slog. Also, while the sprite-work is beautiful, I've had a pretty hard time distinguishing what is background and what is foreground, which most of the time resulted in me dying, because I misinterpreted a platform or couldn't easily see my progression path.Also off-screen enemies (especially present in auto-scroller levels) that can hurt you if you are in a bad position is pretty unfair and it requires you to essentially remember the enemy placement which doesn't strike me as an interesting challenge. This game is obviously a passion project. It is trying to replicate the ol' NES era of gaming, but I wish they only brought the good parts of this arcadey genre and left the bad parts in the past.

_childDocuments_.review: While I did play many classic platform games on the NES back in the day, I can't say I remember Shadow Of The Ninja much more than a Ninja Gaiden clone. With Shadow Of The Ninja Reborn however I can say it's a much more than that and actually the game I would have dreamed of for on the SNESFirst off it has awesome SNES level graphics and presentation without the occasional slowdown that would happen on that hardware. Music and sound on a level as high as the NeoGeo arcade games.Gameplay is a mix of Ninja Gaiden and Mega Man. First off you have your ninja sword, 8 way whip chain, and LOTS of Ninja gear items. The game is designed well enough that you can use a combo of Sword/Chain whip to beat most enemies especially if you've played something like Smash Bros. Base sword can deflect/destroy enemy projectiles and can be powered up to launch short range shots. However the actual sword hitbox does more damage which may make you try to rush enemies recklessly.The Chain Whip can be fired in 8 directions while jumping, has a LOT of range, and also a lot of recovery that can leave you open.This is where the ninja tools add another layer because they are pretty unique and need to be experimented for preferences. For example ground spike ONLY become active when they stop rolling after hitting the floor. If an enemy walks over and remains stationary the damages builds up.Switching tools at first can be tricky since it has to be done in real time with no pause menu. But once you get the hang of it I felt like I was playing Mercenaries in RE6 againControls might feel strange at first until you get the games flow. The Ninjas do a bunch of things ninjas do like wall run, hang from ceilings, and spin float to change their jump arcs. Mastering when and how to use your techniques give a great of satisfaction once you understand what to do against your enemies. Games like this are why having a high score use too mean so much in gaming.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is arcade goodness born from the craft of veteran developers.I never played the original Shadow of the Ninja, and I certify that you absolutely do not need to have done it to appreciate this remake. It stands on it own and it stands strong and mature.You can feel from the fine-tuning of each facet of the gameplay that this is not a work of amateurish indie developer trying to imitate the classics and slapping together pretentious pixel art.While many complain that the controls feel unresponsive or not coherent, I have to disagree wholeheartedly. The controls stayed constant and coherent always: what people are actually upset about is the fact that you do not have control over your jump in air (its length and height stays constant) nor your movements can be easily cancelled to avoid damage. This is not an oversight, but a clear design decision. The point of the game is that each of your moves and attacks has a weight and you are committing to it, hence you have to carefully evaluate the situation before giving your character a command.Speaking about attacks, how they were calibrated is also a sign of an expert. You have two basic attacks: a katana slash, to attack left and right, and a kusarigama, to attack in the 8 directions. By collecting a power-up, these weapons get a significant boost: your katana emits a short air slash, while the kusarigama has its hitbox slightly increased. They have distinct properties which you will need to use at their fullest. The katana blocks projectiles and its air slash stacks with the damage of the blade proper, thus using it point-blank on an enemy is the fastest way to deal damage. This is crucial to deal fast with beefy baddies. Meanwhile, the kusarigama offers more flexible attack direction, and its hitbox can multi-hit an enemy, rewarding the player positioning with extra damage.There are consumable weapons (and curatives) which cover niche cases, but are very useful when used in the correct situation. Rummaging through your inventory does not pause the game, hence even selecting your consumable is an action requiring commitment, not to be taken trivially.The game modes consist in Arcade mode, where you can complete the 6 stages one after the other with infinite continue, and Time Attack mode, where you can play a stage beat in arcade mode for your best time. These are solid options, but what is missing is a practice mode where you could play stage sections and bosses in a loop to improve your skills and routing. Time Attack mode can be used for practice, but you have to complete the whole stage in one go, and if you die you have to restart the whole stage.Overall, this is a game proving that also in 2024 arcades can bear exquisite fruits. And this time, without crunching through your quarters.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a certified banger! If you're a veteran platformer player that's beaten your fair share of hard games (Castlevania, Contra, etc) then you'll find a solid game here to learn and master. A few words of warning though:1. This game seems to not want to save your progress if you exit out. You need to quit at the game over screen for it to save your continue file. That's a ridiculous oversight and I hope they fix it.2. The controls have a sort of weighty feel to them, almost like smash bros or something. You can't charge in really fast and rely purely on reaction time. This game punishes spam and greedy play HARD, so you don't want to be wasteful with you're button inputs.Tengo Project really know their stuff when it comes to Arcade gameplay and I look forward to whatever they produce in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Never have I felt so conflicted about a review. It is obvious from the very first moments of stage 1 how much love and care went into this game. the animation,  music, enemy and art design. Beautiful stuff.Then I pressed the Jump button and thought to myself how in the hell could you get one basic thing so wrong? I cant think of a worse Jump button feel ever, its just bizarre. It is probably only like a .5 sec delay but it feels so bad I just couldn't even be bothered once I made it through stage 1. It really is a heart breaker.Imagine if jumping in Megaman felt bad, or how about Ninja Gaiden. Even in the original CastleVania games where you could not control your jump arc it at least felt responsive. The original Nes version of this game didn't feel like this I had to go back and play it to make sure.... This is just depressing. I have never felt so bad about clicking No on a review.

_childDocuments_.review: Tengo Project have done it again.Shadow Of The Ninja Reborn is a remake of an action platformer that originally launched on the NES.I never owned or played the NES game so went in with no nostalgia for the original. I can say from playing the remake that it does feel like a title from back in that era. Very difficult (especially in the first playthrough) but you die, you learn and you repeat. The difficulty may be a bit much for many gamers that don't have patience for this kind of title but it is by no means as hard as a lot of titles from that era. You also have unlimited continues and there are some checkpoints throughout the levels so you don't need to start back at the start of a stage when you die. For your ninja moves you can do a slashing attack with your sword as well as an airborne, downwards pogo stab with it too. You have a ranged, 8-way chain attack as well and both weapons can be powered up. There is also an AOE special move that will cost some health but also devastate most enemies in your vicinity. In addition you can collect ninja skills, many of which are hidden throughout the stages, to add to your arsenal. Collecting and finding all of these will promote repeated playthroughs of the game. These can be health pickups, powerful projectiles, melee weapons etc. Switching between different ninja skills can be done by holding down a button and tapping left and right. I felt that this felt a little archaic and could have easily been improved with a wheel selection where you would hold down a button and then different directions on the controller would allow you to select a different skill quickly.Controls can feel a little cumbersome at times. Sometimes things like jumping and catching a ladder might throw you off. Certain commands feel unnatural as well so take a while to get used to. I have to admit that I played this using an all button controller and it was the first time I ever used one so that would have contributed to some of the mistakes I made during play. Bosses are generally quite epic and you'll have to learn their attack patterns to defeat them. If you have any ninja skills left in your inventory when you beat a boss then you can unlock them in the shop to be used in future playthroughs by customizing your loadout with the points you have earned.I haven't tested co-op yet so can't comment on it but will update the review once I have. Graphically the pixel art is beautiful! If you are at all a fan of pixel art then you'll undoubtedly appreciate what Tengo have delivered. The sprites, some of the animations, the beautiful backgrounds. Details such as the lightning effects, the crashing waves, the rain. It all shines here. The music is also fantastic. I love how they have members of the original team working on the graphics and music here. They really have refined their craft over the decades and it shows.Overall I'd probably give the game a 7/10 but I'd change that to an 8/10 if you are a fan of these types of games from that era (like myself).It's not going to be for everyone but it'll definitely have its audience.

_childDocuments_.review: Meh. It's a nice looking game but the controls are super janky, clunky and obnoxious.Sometimes the characters do exactly what you want them to do, other times, they don't. There's a major delay with animations / button inputs... It gets to the point of frustration in a lot of areas... sometimes you feel like you have total control over what is going on, other times you don't. This is the kind of game where if you make a single mistake, expect to make two or three more immediately afterwards... it's a game that requires perfection to enjoy.The difficulty ramps up to insanely frustrating levels in Stage 4 if you have no healing items... You have to traverse a gauntlet of ridiculous fire hazards and spike traps right off the hop. If you don't have any spare health items, this section could make or break an entire run.... it's just an exercise in frustration.Switching between ninja gear is also a chore, there's a half second delay with everything you do and then the long animations on top of it. The ninja gear is just a gimmick... you're not actually supposed to use any of it. You're meant to horde healing items and use them accordingly. The rest of the gear is mostly held to acquire extra points at the end level scoring screen.This game isn't worth $30... maybe $10 - $15 tops. I would wait for a discount... you're not missing out on much, just a whole lot of autism and memorization. This game is also a far cry from the original... you can speed run the O.G. Shadow of the Ninja on NES in like 15 minutes. "Reborn's" life has been extended to around 45+ minutes just because of the jank controls, stage design and obnoxious enemy placements.There's also a slew of hidden power ups, some of which require insane conditions to acquire. An example of this forces you to keep a platform creation item for an entire stage, without dying, just so you can use it to collect another hidden item in the next stage. You're also forced to play on Hard mode for 100% item completion, as certain items only appear on that mode. This game is fun if you have copious amount of time on your hands to memorize it fully but for someone looking for a quick dose of casual nostalgia, it won't be found here... This game is hard as balls and isn't fun, even after you know what's coming, strictly due to poor controls and clunky game play. Like I stated before, if you make a single mistake, it could cost you everything... and that just sucks and isn't fun at all. Only having a single life and seeing a game over screen just dampens your entire mood honestly.The sound track is banging and the game itself is of the richest 2D eye candy you'll ever feast on but the game play itself is just bleh. Also the save system needs some work. I don't understand why the game only saves your position when you die completely and quit to the main menu from the game over screen. You would figure with a game that is this heavily invested in to how technical the game play is, the developers would learn how to program a proper check point system. If you Alt+F4 this game at any point it will erase all of your progress unless you commit to dying... It's a very unintelligent decision made by the developers IMO.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow of the Ninja - Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: This game is way more than I expected it to be. I used to love Shadow of the Ninja, but it was fairly easy and didn't really hit like Power Blade, Shatterhand, Ninja Gaiden. With Reborn, it's turned into very much its own thing, with rewarding piles of gadgets to mess with and plenty of uses for them (auto crush tentacle robots with the machete, kill stage 3 boss easy with a few caltrops). As you progress you earn the ability to buy items before the game starts by simply keeping them in your inventory til the end of a level, adding some reward for not using healing items and powerful weapons. Death is punishing, because you lose everything but a single power up potion and have to figure out what to do from there - that said, everything has a definite pattern and strategy, and it's up to you to execute. Moves feel weighty, which is a little weird, but just like certain older games (Batman, Castlevania) you had to apply strategy and timing to your moves rather than a Strider-esque button mash.Basically, I SHOULD have known. These guys have done some awesome things with Natsume titles, and man, I hope they keep going, cuz each one is a modern masterpiece with a ton of replay value. The music here rocks, the graphics are a little bit like a chibi Ninja Warriors but clean and pretty.Main complaints... some of the movement is a little weird. The way you wall run is holding the button instead of tapping it. If you hit the top ledge you hang there, but you have to press jump again to get up, which is different than how you swing up overhead platforms. Certain things, like the downward stab and spinning float, aren't immediately apparent, but you need to know them to get around. That's really it. Movement has weight and I like it, cuz little things like manipulating your hang time with kasurigama toss is just another element of gameplay. Absolutely recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Was not a fan of this game. Usually for these games I like going through them again, but for this I will let it be. The game has some issues that made me dislike it. It was a gradual thing where in the beginning I liked it, but as it went on I got more frustrated. I played kind of ♥♥♥♥ at times since I just wanted to bust through.  I will say that the aesthetics and artwork are great. Music is quite good too.  No bugs I noticed also. But now onto the issues.  1) Controls are frustrating.  There are lots of buttons nowadays on modern controllers. No needs to limit them to only 5 buttons plus dpad.  2) Game is slow since it is designed in a way that it makes you kill most enemies.  Enemies also get lots of health.   3) Double jump type move is kind of sort of hidden.  Look in Options - Manual for complete move lists.  Jump. then DOWN + Jump for the second  extender.  Was quite confusing for me for a bit since a couple jumps are JUST possible early on, but then you need the extender type double jump...thing.4) Do not like how the item selection is setup.  All those things could be in their own sections by type and set to buttons. Weird how you have to hold the item selection then use the dpad to scroll through list. And pressing left or right moves the list in the Opposite direction. Also you cannot move while selecting items.5) Most bosses do not have a lot going for them and have a ton of health.6) Game is kind of setup to force you to take damage unless you are expecting what happens next on a lot of parts.  Kind of irritating.7) Really not a fan of how getting up from hanging is done here.  You just press up to move up on the platform if possible, but if you press jump you fall. Cannot count the number of times I would mess that up.8) Game kind of implies there is some kind of item purchasing ability but I could not find that at all. I had found a list of items, but I could not do anything with it.9) After dying constant prompts to upload score.  Just...ask once when the player completes please?

_childDocuments_.review: This game is basically an incredible remaster of  , which was originally released in 1990 for the NES. While the general level design, music and gameplay mechanics of the remaster remained more or less faithful to the original, everything from the graphics, weapons, characters enemies was polished and turned up to eleven. The game is so much upgraded from the original, that it almost feels like a completely different title that was instead released somewhere at the end of the 90's for a 16-Bit console. It sounds, looks and plays really beautifully and gorgeous.You basically control either  or , both textbook examples of videogame ninjas from the 90's. Like in the classic  or  games you run from left to right, slash through hordes of enemies, pick up powerups and weapons, wall-jump yourself through obstacles and face nasty bosses at the end of every stage.Not surprisingly, the difficulty is really brutal and you will die a lot in the many jumping sections and tougher battles with the enemies. But it never gets as difficult or frustrating that it seems impossible or demotivating. A lot of the challenges, like the jumping sections or bosses, all have patterns which you need to memorize and look out for. Plus there are checkpoints scattered throughout all the stages and just before the bosses, which I think is just perfect in terms of fairness.You can play the game locally or online with a friend in Co-Op mode, which is the mode I recommend best. A high degree of coordination is needed to advance in the tougher sections and to split up the scarce items. The game takes about 6 hours to finish, maybe less if you are really skilled.The music, which is a faithful remaster of the original NES OST, is pretty darn good too! Favorite Track: "Demon-ruled Skyscraper" / Stage 3 Theme.To put it in a nutshell: If you fancy a rock-hard Ninja platformer in the tradition of 90's Ninja games with a motivating Co-Op mode, you owe it to yourself to get . In my opinion there is not much to dislike, only some minor annoyances such as some slightly unintuitive control mechanisms (like how to climb up to platforms or edges) and some level design choices in the final stage.For me, that was .

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely polished action platformer. I've heard of the devs TengoProject and their remasters/remakes of classic action titles from their SNES days like Pocky n Rocky or Ninja Warriors but this is my first time playing one for myself. Had some prior experience with the original Shadow of the Ninja on NES, which compared to contemporary action platformers like Ninja Gaiden or Castlevania felt less polished. This remake however, blows the original out of the water and feels like it can compete with some of the best entries in the genre.Mechanically very solid with having interesting trade offs with your character's sword and chain weapons and the maneuverability of the characters feel good once you learn to use air float and wall climb effectively. With only six stages it is not a very long experience but learning the levels to clear them on one attempt I found was very rewarding and added some longevity to the experience. The power up to your weapons feels good when you are able to maintain the power throughout a stage to eviscerate through enemies and I think the inventory system is pretty novel allowing you to store a number of items throughout a run so there's this level of long term item management to consider.As for some criticisms, I do wish the item picks were a bit more fun to use. While there are some that can be useful for making hard parts of the game easier to manage like taking out dangerous enemies from a distance, they never felt quite as useful as say picking up subweapons in a classic Castlevania or Ninja Gaiden so I found myself mostly using the inventory to load up on health items during my runs instead. I think some autoscrolling sections are a bit tedious, with the one in the last level being frustrating as the enemy placement can catch you offgaurd on your first run through of the stage. I also wish that the two playable characters were differentiated more in terms of the abilities or movesets since they feel very similar with only some slight variations on walk and dash speed, though the game was such a finely tuned experience maybe it would have been hard to make a character play differently while balancing for the game to make sure they weren't too over/underpowered.All in all, fantastic entry and definitely recommend for fans of action platformers.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadow of the Ninja - Reborn

_childDocuments_.review: Shadow of the Ninja - Reborn is a recreation of it's NES predecessor of the same name. No longer limited by its 8-bit counterpart, the game has been redeveloped by completely redoing the gameplay, art, animation, and story to a certain degree. The main protagonists have been given a complete redesign as well as many of the enemies are no longer relegated as generic military grunts, but instead as a multitude of various demons diegetic to Japanese folklore. The gameplay has also been heavily modified from the original, with now a much expanded moveset for the player, much larger levels while paying homage to original level designs, additional boss phases, and even 1 entire new stage. The art and animation is phenomenal. It pushes how far and how beautifully done pixel art can be presented, providing fluidity to the motion of the characters with clarity and appeal to the environment, without any of them clashing with or obstructing each other. There wasn't a point in the game where something was particular off or off-putting nor was there a moment where I had to even so much as squint to make out something I needed to see.The music is a lively recreation of the original soundtrack, with vivid rock music that constantly keeps you on your toes as you progress through the levels. There really isn't many soundtracks that are calm or steady, even certain cutscenes or the shop. The trend with Natsume games not having any main menu music still doesn't do it for me though, save for Rocky and Pocky.The gameplay is a mixed bag for me. While the new moveset makes for a more diverse method of platforming and combat, it's a far cry from the original that I prefer more to a certain extent. While the NES version had a much more snappier form of movement, both vertically and horizontally, the Reborn version opted to have the movement feel more organic, meaning every action from jumping to using items, for the sake of feeling natural, has startup frames that are a bit too long to proc, enough that the movement does not flow together, as well as the fact that I have died a multitude of times trying to get out of split-second situations stemming from these additional frames. Unfortunately while the animation is fluid, the movement is most certainly not. In addition to that, many of the commands don't seem to function the way I prefer to, as many of them are inconsistent with each other. For example, if you're hanging off a side ledge, the only way to get up is by jumping rather than pressing up, BUT if you're hanging on to a railing above you, the only way to get up is by pressing up rather than jumping (because if you jump you'll just drop down and fall). On top of that, grabbing onto anything is automatic, meaning if I wanted to jump to a platform above instead, I cannot do so because I need to grab under it first before vaulting over. I have died multiple times due to these issues because I get stuck in a panic. If there were options to tweak how I want to traverse the level, it would make playing the game much better.Regardless of the issues, I stand by my praises for the game. The game is amazing aesthetically, and if you're only looking to playing casually, the game is forgiving enough to get you through the game, adjusting accordingly to the amount of times you falter. A normal run on the first time may take you 1-2 hours (but there is a save system so there's no need to do it all in one sitting). However, if you're a completionist or want to go for high scores, then you'll need absolute understanding of the game's mechanics, otherwise your struggles will be from fighting the controls more than the enemies.

_childDocuments_.review: This is how you do a pixel remake! I was actually not a big fan of the original, but I’m so glad I put my trust again in Tengo Project because this tops all of their excellent previous efforts. The game is challenging, but very fair. If you keep dying on a stage, they gradually give you more boosts to help you through. Exiting the stage instead of continuing will allow you to continue from that stage later which is great. I’m not sure what people are complaining about when it comes to controls. The feeling is very precise and getting good is not as frustrating as many other retro titles. My favorite aspect is definitely the wonderful pixel art. It’s so detailed and well animated. I can’t wait to see what the developer is working on next.

_childDocuments_.review: The perfect homage to a NES Classic. 10/10!When i first heard of Shadow of the Ninja Reborn coming to consoles a PC alike i was completely exited. Stage 4 could be my favorite track so far.Nostalgia: 10 out of 10. most of the elements that made this game so loved and popular are here. enemies, music and gameplay.what i dislike:- Main protagonists cartoonish style. back in the day this game looks more mature. the new style is good but i would like to see DLC skins with classic looks. long time fans deserve it.- The main menu when you are starting the game is so basic. - The subtitles in the intro scene are way too fast to read, please fix.

_childDocuments_.review: Tengo Project knocked it out of the park for me with this one. The original game has always been a favorite of mine, and this one expands on it in some truly refreshing ways. The mechanics and the way they interplay with the level design feels carefully thought out and crafted. This is not baby's first platformer. Challenging but fair, it requires some dedication to learn the ropes, and there is very little room for sloppiness when making your way through the stages. The game will punish you for mistakes, even on normal, until you take the time to learn how it works and improve. Read the couple of pages that are the manual and take five minutes to understand everything you can do. There is more to it than you might think. This is not an experience for the lazy gamer. This is for those who want to push their skills to a higher level and master the mechanics and systems involved. Learning to play this game well is extremely rewarding. The spritework and art direction are fantastic. The music slaps and the stages are well crafted. There is a great deal of replayability in item unlocks, time attack (with leader boards), and hard mode. If you have fond memories of the original, you will be pleased with the great care this version takes to pay homage to its source material, working diligently to grow the formula and ideas of the original game in just about every way.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has incredible stage design and pixel art, probably some of the best I have ever seen. The stages are based on the NES original with some very hefty changes that it's basically brand new areas. There is one additional original stage that was added that the original did not have. The bosses are improved dramatically with environmental damage, additional segments/phases etc. There are 2 separate buttons for sword and chain now and they feel great to use.The item system and controls/movement changed a fair bit to the game's detriment. Hayate feels good to play as, but Kaede's horizontal jump arc covers about 30% less distance, making platforming with her extremely annoying. Her only real benefit is that she runs faster, but it's not worth the tradeoff. Some of the basic controls feel a bit slugglish at times, mainly when ascending/descending platforms and often getting accidental wall clings or drops when you're just trying to jump normally. The jump input makes you drop from a ledge instead of go up it, which feels weird.Despite having an unused face button and 2 shoulder buttons, the game insists on having you stop in place to sift through your item inventory rather than having a dedicated item button and hot swapping while moving. Mega Man X series did hot swapping to great effect; it opens up more creative strategies without slowing down gameplay. On top of this some of the items feel underpowered, primarily the melee ones. They lock you in place while using them and end up doing less DPS than just swinging your sword while also having a smaller hitbox. When your inventory is full and pick up a new item it will replace the last item in your list rather than the one you have equipped. This means that if you want to get rid of a specific item you have to sit there and use up its ammo or pick up items multiple times until the one you want to get rid of drops. I think the items are cool, just implemented poorly.Despite my gripes with the controls and items I still think this game is sick and a lot of fun to play.

_childDocuments_.review: This reimagination (this is just more than a basic remake) is an absolute blast and definitely even better than the original game!Shadow of the NInja Reborn is of course more advanced in terms of visuals and sounds but the gameplay is much quicker, levels are here and there expanded to some degree and playing it just feels great. New enemies are great addition, remade boss fights are super enjoyable and the music, yes, the new version of the original soundtrack is phenomal!  Also the game feels much harder than the original game, which I really like.I did not like the arstyle when I saw the game for the first time. The original more like realistic approach was replaced by chibi characters and bright colorful visuals. Though I still prefer more realistic visuals, while I play I just must appreciate all the nice animations, effects and how colors blend together. While its vibrat and colorful, its still looks grimy and somehow sinister. Especially when I set the scanlitnes to something like 7. Great., it is more than a solid effort. Awesome! 8/10.

name: Broken Sword - Shadow of the Templars: Reforged
detailed_description: Step out onto the streets of Paris in 'Broken Sword - Shadow of the Templars: Reforged', a substantially enhanced version of the multi-award winning, all-time classic adventure. Enjoy a globe-spanning story when intrepid American George Stobbart and fearless journalist Nico Collard are pitched into a gripping adventure, exploring exotic locations, solving ancient mysteries, and thwarting dark conspiracies to discover the arcane secrets of the Knights Templar. Whether it's your first time or you're revisiting a beloved classic, get ready to enjoy the masterful “Broken Sword - Shadow of the Templars: Reforged!” Key Features: Compelling Storyline: Dive into a gripping narrative filled with twists, turns, and unexpected revelations. Join George and Nico as they investigate a trail of mysteries that takes them from the bustling streets of Paris to exotic locales around Europe and the Middle East. Classic Point-and-Click Gameplay: Discover, or rediscover, the joy of classic point-and-click mechanics as you solve puzzles, gather clues, and interact with a colorful cast of characters. Immerse yourself in an intuitive and engaging gameplay experience. Fully Voice Acted: Lose yourself in the game's atmosphere with fully-voiced dialogue and engaging performances bringing a cast of wonderful, colorful characters to life. Challenging Puzzles: Put your intellect to the test with thought-provoking puzzles that require observation, deduction, and creativity to solve. From deciphering codes to manipulating objects, every challenge is a step closer to uncovering the arcane secrets. Reforged Features: 4K Remastered Visuals: Experience the magic of the original game with enhanced high-definition graphics, bringing the picturesque landscapes, detailed characters, and intricate environments to life in beautiful 4K for the first time ever Enhanced Audio: Immerse your ears in the enhanced audio as Revolution delivers the finest, most stunning version of George and Nico's original adventure to date, including the incredible soundtrack from world-acclaimed composer Barrington Pheloung.

_childDocuments_.review: - all about point and click adventuresIs this game a masterpiece? Yes. A masterpiece in 1996, a masterpiece today. It is a remaster of the first part, originally released back in 1996. That was a time when some quite good point and click adventure games were still being released, before the genre fell into a comatose deep sleep for many years after such masterpieces as Gabriel Knight 3, Simon the Sorcerer 3D or Kings Quest VIII. Broken Sword, though, as well as its almost equally good successor Broken Sword 2 - the Smoking Mirror, managed to get pretty much everything right. The setting was exciting, the puzzles were fun, the graphics were really good for the time and the flow of the game was just right - Broken Sword rightly became one of the great cult classics in the genre. Not quite as well-known and popular as Monkey Island, but right behind it in the second row of really good point and click adventures and on almost every best list of the most successful representatives of the genre. You play a mystery thriller. Our hero George Stobbart is actually just an American tourist vacationing in Paris when he is drawn into a murder mystery involving murders, a secret society, a beautiful woman, exotic locations around the world, supernatural forces - not to mention a vicious sheep. Conspiracy theories, ancient artifacts, ciphers, Christian themes, the Knights Templar - and all this years before Dan Brown struck it rich with his novel “The Da Vinci Code” (published in 2003) with a very similar theme. George Stobbart just wanted to drink his espresso in peace in a small Parisian café, perhaps flirt a little with the pretty waitress, when an elderly man with a briefcase enters the café. Shortly afterwards, a clown enters the café, drops his accordion and runs off with the old man's briefcase – and the café  is destroyed seconds later by a bomb explosion. The old man is dead, but the waitress and George are unharmed. After a conversation with the police, George meets Nico for the first time - a photo reporter who actually wanted to meet the old man, who wanted to tell her something... and so begins one of the most iconic adventure series of all time.The gameplay corresponds to a typical point and click adventure game. Clicking on a hotspot with the mouse allows you to manipulate it or view it. Click on a person to talk to them (now with icons), click on an exit to go to another location. Click on items in your inventory to use or examine them. A new feature in Reforged is that certain objects shine silver when they are important for progress. However, you can also deactivate this auxiliary function. And I would strongly advise you to do so, otherwise the game becomes far too easy. Any complete idiot can click on the flashing hotspot to make progress; there is no feeling of having achieved something based on your own comprehension. This is no longer puzzle solving, it's completely unsatisfying - at least for me. If I want to click my way through a game without any challenge, I play a (classic) visual novel. Some of the (more annoying) puzzles during the second half of the story have been simplified and are now far easier to solve, but this wasn't so bad.If you've never played a point and click adventure game before, there's also an in-game tutorial that explains the basics. By pressing “Tab” you can toggle between the original (rather blurry on today's monitors) and the new graphics. The conversations are fully voiced, as are the narrator's comments and the descriptions of the items. The game is fun, even if the plot is of course far-fetched, you can somehow put yourself in George Stobbart's shoes as he tries to solve the mystery of the mysterious bomber and the stolen briefcase. Nico also brings an interesting second main character into play, with whom George ultimately wants to do more than just hold hands. I wouldn't call myself the biggest Broken Sword fanboy of all time, but at least I've played through all parts of the series and see the Knights Templar with different eyes than before I knew the game. On my last trip to Portugal, for example, I couldn't resist visiting the old Templar fortress in Tomar. And when I'm sitting in a street café in Paris, I always keep an eye out for clowns...Broken Sword - Shadow of the Templars: Reforged brings one of the best point and click adventures of all time up to date. This is how you modernize a game from 1996. The reworked graphics look wonderful even in 4K, the controls have been improved, the original voice acting has been digitally reworked, and a solution is integrated into the game. I only have one small problem with the remaster - the original was simply too good. At least in the Director's Cut version, the original is still a fantastic game today, even if the graphics were produced for a 640×480 resolution back then. The Reforged version is essentially the same game - the same fantastic story, the same great game flow, great graphics of course - but you won't even notice that while playing because you remember the original in your head in exactly the same way. Only when you switch to the old graphics while playing (possible at any time) will you notice the difference. My point is that the new Reforged version is a fantastic game and highly recommended if you're looking for a really good point and click adventure - but if you have already played the original, then the (perceived) new features are limited, you simply play the brilliant first part again, fear the clown and fall in love with Nico - just like in 1996.A remastered version of a first-class point and click adventure game with a good story and superbly designed puzzles. With the revised interface, it plays like a contemporary game that can easily keep up with the new releases in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I came here after playing an adventure game called "Crowns and Pawns: Kingdom of Deceit" - a modern adventure game clearly inspired by the old Broken Sword game. Yet, playing both that game and Broken Sword Reforged has reminded me why adventure games today suck - and why the genre is dying. Namely, it's no wonder that modern adventure games don't sell well when they can't hold a candle to games made 30 or more years ago! Go and play any more modern adventure game and compare it Broken Sword - and what you will immediately notice is that the animations in old games were VASTLY superior, more detailed and more immersive. Whenever you are picking an item in Broken Sword or using it - or even just moving from one room to another - you are always rewarded with beautifully drawn, unique animations - whereas in modern games they just recycle one and the same animation over and over again.But it isn't just the animations. It's also the puzzles, the story, the characters, the humor, the writing... - every little piece is superior to modern adventure games! I am writing this as a message to any developer who wants to make a modern adventure game. Play Broken Sword, a game made almost 30 years ago - and if your animations look worse, if your story is worse, if your puzzles are worse, if your characters are worse, if your humor is worse, ... then ask yourself, what on earth are you doing? Broken Sword Reforged should be the golden standard for modern adventure games moving forward! This is how it's done! I want the genre to thrive and I want more games like this, but unfortunately, most modern adventure games can't hold a candle to games made 30 or more years ago!

_childDocuments_.review: As my playthrough ended a tear rolled down my eye. The ending cutscene is the only thing which has been noticably changed, but definitely for the better.Being a Broken Sword super fan since 1997 (playing the demo of BS2) I can from the beginning say... they did it. They remade the original game with updated graphics, just the way that I always wanted.The number of options and ability to disable hints, or even preserve the 16:10 aspect ratio and original font of the text is exemplary. All of the negativities of the horrible "Director's cut" are gone, and the game looks and sound fantastic.It feels amazing to enter a location I've been to 20 times before to see how it has changed. Some areas feel "updated" where others feel completely breathtaking where I have to stop playing - look at the screen and simply think "wow".This is the way the game should have been made from the start, and will forever be the proper way of playing the game from here on.If you never ever played this game there is no reason not to. If you want the original challenge - with less pixel hunting - you have that. If you just want to enjoy a story at a laid back pace - well there's that too.Broken Sword is the best point and click game ever made in my opinion, and should be experienced by gaming enthusiasts and video game history buffs.The story is amazing, with great characters and without going into too much detail, just think Dan Brown's The Da Vinci Code (7 years before the book) and you're all set.

Back in '96 this game made me fall in love with adventure games as a teenager and after the decline of those games, it's great to see a little revival of 2D adventure games over the last few years. _childDocuments_.review: This is the definitive version of Broken Sword; a superb remaster. I would recommend anyone who has not played the game or who wants the best possible version to look at this.First, it's worth saying this game is completely true to the original. The "Director's Cut" game was ok, but it added new story elements and gameplay including a new opening that were jarring alongside the original. It also made cuts and changes to small elements throughout the game that removed some of the charm of the original - for example, some of the short videos like George climbing down into the sewer near the beginning of the game were just cut. They were small changes but they detracted from a classic game that had been lovingly and beautifully crafted in 1996.This version updates everything, and seems to cut nothing significant. All the graphics are gorgeously updated into high resolution. Switching between the original and new graphics (available at any point in game) is a stark reminder of how beautiful and detailed the new graphics are, and the high quality they have reached with this remaster. They have made small but clever changes to the interface to make it more accessible to modern audiences, and versatile for mouse, controller or touch play. It's a hard thing to achieve and they've done it superbly - the game plays perfectly with a mouse, and nothing is lost. They've also added optional hints and help into the interface but the player can choose between the new interface and a "classic" mode without the hints.The only flaw with the game is the audio; in particular the speech. It's clear the makers could not do much to the original speech files for whatever reason (maybe the originals are long gone). If they were faced between a choice of re-record, digitial alter or leave as is I think they made the right choice. It is a little jarring to hear the quality of the original audio, but a re-record would have changed the game too much and I suspect digital altering it would have been inconsistent and noticable. And the voice acting is great as was the case back in 1996 - it would have been a travesty to deviate from that. The music continues to sound superb - likely reflecting the high quality of Barrington Pheloung's work and the clever use of short bursts of music throughout the entire game.I've been playing this game on Linux via Steam and the game launched without any tweaking or problems, and has played flawlessly.Overall, I can strongly and positively recommend this game as the definitive version of Broken Sword: Shadow of the Templars. It's beautiful, and 100% faithful update of the original. You can't mess with such a great game; the Director's Cut while well intentioned was too much. This version is superb - it faithfully updates the graphics, makes tweaks to the interface to keep it playable in a new era and makes optional changes that make the game accessible to both a new generation of more casual gamers as well as lovers of classic point and click.Fantastic work; I'm going to enjoy replaying this classic!

_childDocuments_.review: As a longtime fan of this game, I was excited about this remake. The new visuals look great and show the developers put in some real effort. But for the high price they're asking, I'm really let down by the terrible audio quality. It's bad enough to ruin the whole experience for me.You'd expect a pricey remake to improve everything, but they only seem to have cared about the graphics. The sound problems are everywhere and really annoying. The dialogue sounds muffled, and the volume levels are all over the place. When you're talking to the police officer outside the cafe, you can barely hear anything. Then suddenly, when George talks to himself, it's loud again. I had to rely on subtitles just to follow what was going on.Maybe playing with headphones would make it easier to hear, but it wouldn't fix the muffled, terrible audio quality. I shouldn't have to resort to headphones just to make out what's being said in a game I paid this much money for.What really frustrates me is how easy this would've been to fix. I did a quick test to prove it. I recorded some of the game's dialogue and ran it through Adobe Podcast Enhance. It took me just minutes, and the difference was night and day - it sounded like it was recorded today, not decades ago. They could have fixed the entire game's audio in a couple of days, tops. I don't understand why they didn't do this, especially for a remake that costs this much.I've bought every version of this game - the original, director's cut, remaster, even the Gameboy Advance version. I had high hopes for this one. The new graphics are nice, sure, but the bad audio kept pulling me out of the story.For new players, I think the audio might be a deal-breaker, especially given the price. Even as a big fan, I couldn't get past it.I love the original game, but I can't recommend this version. The mix of shiny new graphics and old, poorly balanced audio just doesn't work, especially for what they're charging. If you already have an older version, just stick with that.It's still a classic game at its core, but this remake just doesn't deliver the full upgrade it should because of all the audio problems that could have been fixed so easily.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game and I'm not complaining... well, maybe a little.Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars is an absolute classic—one of the best point-and-click adventure games ever made. The Broken Sword series is also one of the few I’ve followed closely over the years (Broken Sword: The Angel of Death being the only exception—I never really got into it and haven’t finished it yet).I first played The Shadow of the Templars as a kid back in 1996 and immediately fell in love with its atmosphere, humor, and mystery. While the 2009 Director’s Cut got some harsh backlash by fans, I personally enjoyed the new scenes, even though keeping the originals intact would have been ideal.Now, we’ve got Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars - Reforged, offering 4K Remastered Visuals and Enhanced Audio. To make myself absolutely clear, this is by far the best the game has ever looked or sounded. The visuals, which were always fantastic, now boast an incredible level of detail. Where the original game had some awkward facial expressions or body language, this remaster fixes them brilliantly. There are a few stylistic changes, like swapping the wooden floors of the Musée Crune for stone, which might come down to personal taste, but overall, the visual updates are everything a fan could hope for.However, I’m slightly disappointed in two areas: the sound and the interface. While Barrington Pheloung’s soundtrack sounds amazing and better than ever before, much of the dialogue comes across muffled, and certain consonants—especially "s" and "z"—sound oddly lisped. I understand this is a remaster of a '90s game, but I expected more from modern AI processing. Maybe I'm overestimating its possibilities.As for the interface, it’s fine for traditional mouse or trackpad players, but I’ve grown accustomed to using a controller for point-and-clicks—thanks in part to Return to Monkey Island, which, to me, reinvented the point-and-click interface for consoles. Sadly, Broken Sword: Reforged still relies solely on the old method of controlling the cursor with an analog stick. Given the strides in controller-friendly navigation for point-and-click games in recent years, I was hoping for something more intuitive, especially for a game available on multiple consoles.To anyone who hasn’t played this game before, I recommend it 100%. This is the best version of a great game that’s aged remarkably well. So well indeed, that for those who already own the original, I’d suggest giving it some thought—perhaps wait to see if any updates improve the audio or for a potential price drop.

_childDocuments_.review: Broken Sword really is an absolute classic game, and I’m so grateful for the developers to have done such a beautifully faithful remaster here. This game looks pretty much how I felt that it looked like in my head, and then you switch over to the old graphics and it’s amazing how much has improved here (and how much better it previously looking in my head). Despite some of the very reductive comments I’ve seen online, this absolutely is not a simple AI upscale and import, and if you look at what’s available here, you’ll be able to see that. I’m sure one step of the process often does use some AI, but you can clearly see so much detail and effort made to make the art look so much more detailed while in keeping with the vision. This is how a remaster should be. This is the standard I’d love to see in other classic point and click remasters too.If you haven’t played this classic game, and you have any interest in this type of game, I’d urge you to give this a go, I can guarantee you won’t regret it.On a side note: there’s a lot of options here for hints etc which is super nice. You can turn it all off, or have a bit of that depending on if you seem stuck, and honestly that’s fantastic because who wants to keep googling hints or walkthroughs every time you get stuck?

_childDocuments_.review: A makeover of a legendary point&click adventure game. It ditches the often maligned Director's Cut changes (more mechanical puzzles, extra chapters played as Nico) - though they could make a return in some form later (an alternative new game mode or a separate Nico campaign, perhaps). It felt like a good way of experiencing the story as either a newcomer or a fan of the original game.It's fine but it feels like more work could - or should - have been done, especially with sound. Voice lines still swing wildly across a broad range of sound quality and volume; I wonder what stopped the AI being employed more effectively here: unwillingness to tamper with the original too much, budget concerns, or potential legal issues arising from re-generating irl performances? Possibly all three.There are plenty of little imperfections that stand out more with the higher resolution visuals, too, like Duane not moving his lips during some lines, or the toilet brush in Syria now being a more general brush (flat-sided with bristles on one side instead of a round handle with bristles around one end; presumably as a result of AI's misinterpretation of the prompt).I even ran into a bug of sorts I don't recall having seen in my few playthroughs across the various previous versions of the game: you could be talking and exchanging items with Duane while not facing each other and being at least a good few meters apart.I was also disappointed the game didn't come with the soundtrack (at least I didn't see it in the library or in the game's folder) and/or a concept art album, as re-releases of great classics often do.

_childDocuments_.review: The first Broken Sword was one of the first point-and-click games I truly loved and enjoyed because unlike others from its genre at the time that were focusing more on the humor aspect of their stories, Broken Sword was a mix of crime and humor with a dash of Indiana Jones and who as a kid/teenage didn't love Indiana? Ever since then, I've played all Broken Swords games despite their ups and downs, specifically the 4th one. It's a shame the genre is in a dying phase, but it was nice to hear that they were remaking the 1st and continuing development on the franchise with a 6th entry as well. Anyway, is Broken Sword Reforged a faithful remaster/remake? Without a doubt. That's all you need to know. If you never played the series, then this is the best place to start. 👍 +Faithfully remade all the visuals and art+Great cast of characters👎-The voices haven't been re-recorded thus they're of very low qualityNothing has changed from the original as expected, but if you've never played it then the gist is, that you play as George who is casually enjoying his coffee in Paris when all of a sudden he finds himself trapped in a crime/conspiracy that will change his life. Nowadays if you've seen lots of movies and shows, the story won't exactly "wow" you. It's pretty much about the templars, finding a secret cult, treasures, and all that stuff you've seen in Indiana Jones or similar media. What it excels at is its charm, a product of its time, when no one was worried about offending anyone and all they wanted to make was good stories and nothing else. George is a great protagonist, very unique in all the games that I've played. The rest of the characters who will have appearances in future games as well are all pretty good as well, Nico included. Overall even if nostalgia isn't a factor for you regarding Broken Sword, its mystery narrative can still be enjoyable. Story rating: 8.5/10The gameplay has been a bit modernized, in the sense of how the user interface works, however, the puzzles and everything else have remained the same. It's a classic point-and-click adventure game which means you'll have to solve easy to medium type of puzzles that involve combining objects you find in the levels with other items to progress. The beauty of Broken Sword is that, unlike others from its genre, it doesn't have ridiculous logics like placing a cat inside a dog or whatever. I'd say the difficulty is fairly medium.The other aspect of its gameplay is that you'll be engaging in a lot of dialogue, and just like the puzzles, certain dialogues will have to be triggered in order to progress. Not much else can be said about its gameplay, it's simple and effective, and I can't really downvote it for not improving its mechanics since it's not a new game. Gameplay rating: 8/10A bit disappointed regarding the voice-acting because they're of very low quality, as in muffled voices that don't sound very good. It's even more baffling why they haven't re-recorded the voice acting since most of the characters were back in the 5th installment and they could've re-done the voices in the first game. The soundtrack is fine, the game uses a melodic hint system, which plays a small tune whenever you're about to figure a puzzle out or successfully manage to solve one. As for the music quality and all the sound effects, I'm not sure if they were also touched, but they didn't bother me as much as the voice quality. Audio rating: 7/10The pixel art is gone, although you can always switch to it if you desire to, and the whole art of the game has been modernized. The game already looked very pretty for its time and it still looks great even today compared to lots of games in its genre. The modern look feels exactly how my mind remembered the original which means they did a great job at improving all of its visuals while retaining the exact look of the first game. You'll visit a lot of cool places in the game and very rarely will you need to backtrack multiple times to the same scene. The game has been getting patches though I did not encounter any issues with it on day one. Graphics, performance and tech analysis score: 8.5/10A fantastic remake of the first game and a great game to revisit or play for the first time. There's no reason to avoid the game at all. Buy it at any price.

_childDocuments_.review: Guess, it was about time to replay Broken Sword – Shadow of the Templars anyway… A classic from 1996, the original Broken Sword has often been considered one of the best point and click adventure titles. You had one good way of experiencing it (original release played via ScummVM) and one average way (Director’s Cut from 2010). But now there’s a perfect way of enjoying this title, with the new Reforged remastered release.If you are unfamiliar with the Broken Sword franchise, it’s a series of titles made by Revolution Software that center around the adventures of George Stobbart and Nico Collard, who can’t help but constantly get involved with some ancient artefacts and secret societies. These are very much Indiana Jones-like simple adventure stories, that often starts falling apart if you try to analyse them in detail, but remain an exciting journey if you just let them entertain you. With the first title in the series, most notably, being one of the first examples of bringing the Order of Knight Templar into the pop culture, years before The Da Vinci Code and Assassin’s Creed.Similarly to the no less incredible previous title of the studio, Beneath a Steel Sky, Broken Sword builds itself more on “problems” that the players have to solve, rather than on “puzzles”. And because of that, a lot of the clues you must learn are given to you via dialogues, not using items on other items. This is a very character driven game that attempts to feel like a deep investigation into a hidden conspiracy, so you often find yourself following vague leads that often bring you to surprising revelations, rather then linearly following a predictable story. And while the game does falter a bit in the second half, with more and more problems feeling forced and too absurd, it remains fun and intuitive for the most part.Which is something I actually forgot – the way the investigation moves forward often feels natural, despite the fact that there are several completely optional things you can do and several moments where you can tackle the leads in any order you wish. Reforged doesn’t alter anything about this process if you’re playing on the Classic Mode, but if you wish for things to be a bit more streamlined and for the game to nudge you towards next steps, there’s a new Story Mode as well. The highlights for interactive elements return, active only in a certain radius around your pointer. Game now features auto-saves, that are mostly well placed, especially near the spots where you can die. And the enhanced visuals and audio quality are absolutely terrific.Apart from the already mentioned weaker aspects of the second half of the game, the title does have a few rough edges that only a remake could fix. The infamous goat puzzle, for example, is as visually unintuitive as it used to be, despite the concept behind it being very easy to understand. Some of the scene transitions feel too abrupt, with you barely having a chance to register what’s going on, while suddenly finding yourself in a different part of Europe. The caricaturish nature of most characters sometimes feels a bit too much. And it’s a real downer that Nico barely has anything to do in the game. For all of its faults, and they were numerous, at least Director’s Cut tried to give Nico some interesting investigation to do on her own. Those weren’t good, but her presence in the game is very underutilized as is.Nonetheless, Broken Sword – Shadow of the Templars: Reforged doesn’t feel like a new coat of paint on an adventure game that is “of its time”. This game still plays wonderfully and feels like an exciting and wonderfully presented adventure that is as fun to play now as it used to be almost 30 years ago. If you haven’t played this title before or have considered replaying it – Reforged is a great version of the game to grab, so give it a go.

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy new remaster of the 90s point-and-click classic that sends one of the most likable sociopaths in all of gaming history on a globetrotting adventure to stop a worldwide conspiracy. The new version keeps closely to the 1996 original script instead of the changes and additions of the 2009 remastered edition. While I personally never minded the 2009 additions as much as many seemed to do, it is mostly in restoring some of the remasters' changes to the original (like the opening speech) that Reforged greatly improves on the remaster. At the same time, some of the visual and UI updates do work rather well, and it offers the option to switch between the Reforged and the original graphics (though UI elements remain in the updated form). All this makes Reforged, in my opinion, the best currently available version of the game.Pros:- Great characters with (in the German dub) some of my favorite voice work. The main character is - in best adventure game fashion - a cheerfully unrepentant criminal with lots of charm, personality, and witty dialogue. He is joined by a large cast of often eccentric characters. His main antagonist, an international costumed serial killer/assassin, while only sparingly encountered, is often referenced in descriptions of his exploits by other characters. As he seeks out and procures information and disguises himself, it always seemed to me that he was in his own point-and-click adventure, doing as many shady or downright illegal things as our protagonist. The relationship between the leads generally worked really well, .- A truly fun adventure story with a fascinating historical subject matter presented in a way that really stokes your interest and curiosity. Strangely enough, my personal favorite part of the story was always one that went a bit further astray off the main story's path - uncovering the rather melancholic history of the Vasconcellos with their last living descendant. The writing is full of charm and humor. - The game brings you to varied and memorable locations with great character art and background designs. I also generally really like the graphical updates, especially for the characters, though it sometimes seemed like some designs of minor characters became a little less grotesque, a little less distinctive. Similarly, I mostly liked the new background art with few exceptions. Most changes in the environments will likely come down to a matter of taste. The one area that I felt was a clear downgrade was the Villa de Vasconcellos and its gardens, which seemed much cleaner and orderly in the Reforged version, which, to me, took some of the charm away. Though this may just be because of how much I liked this location and its atmosphere back in the day. Still, especially with the ability to seamlessly switch between old and new graphics, it was a delight to see the old story and characters in a faithful new look.- It is hard to rate the difficulty and intuitiveness of puzzles when one remembers at least the more memorable ones from years ago. By and large they are more grounded and seemed more or less logical to me. The difficulty overall tends towards the lower end - so it mostly keeps the story moving. There is a story mode option and a hint system available, though I cannot rate their usefulness.- The UI is generally kept simple and decently intuitive; my biggest problem in the Reforged edition was with a few of the "come hither" movements in bigger scenes. The dialogue interface, which offers some preselected topics (that may need to be unlocked through other actions) and inventory items, keeps the storyline running without getting too bogged down in a myriad of options.- Together with some wonderful music, all these points create a wonderfully engrossing atmosphere and a fun gameplay experience.Cons:- There are some parts of the story that do not flow quite as nicely as they could. Especially the  could have been more developed. - As great as music, envionmental sounds and voice work are, there were some clear audio quality and mixing issues.- At the time of my playthrough, there were still a few minor bugs in the Reforged edition, like the ability to enter the boarded-up café, which led to George changing size as he walked inside the shuttered windows. These problems may have been patched out since then.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't write about Broken Sword - Shadow of the Templars and not be biased, I have a lot of fond memories playing this game back on the original PlayStation with my family and have been a fan of the series ever since. The game had a big influence on the other games I played growing up, it's probably had a bigger part in shaping my sense of humour than I care to admit too.I think the biggest compliment I can give the game is that not only does it look fantastic but it also looks exactly how I remember it. I love the fact you can switch between new and old graphics and that alone shows what a great job they've done updating the game for modern hardware without losing the essence and feel of the original.Design wise the game holds up brilliantly considering its age. A couple of the puzzles are a little obscure (goat) but compared to some of its  contemporaries of the the genre, the majority are well designed. This version also includes a great hints system and settings options that add a number of modern day quality of life improvements that make the game more accessible, if you want to use them.The updated art is great, though some of the dialogue audio has signs of ageing (despite their best efforts to fix this) it wasn't enough to take me out of the experience. I think the game could feel very slow for a lot of newcomers too but, if you're not in a rush to play through it, it's worth taking the time to enjoy the game and the story.I think my favourite aspect of the game though is the writing. It's consistently funny throughout, lines are well delivered and I wanted to make sure I spoke to every character about every item just to hear their sarcastic responses.Oh and just to add - I played through almost the entire game on Steam Deck. At time of writing the Steam page says compatibility is unknown but in the dozen or so hours I played it on there I don't think I came across a single issue - it plays fantastically on Steam Deck.This game isn't going to be for everyone, but I will say if you haven't played the original and have even a passing interest in point and clicks and 13th century conspiracy theories about the Knight's Templar, you should definitely check out this version of the original Broken Sword.If you are a fan of the original this will look and play exactly how you remember it, not how it actually was, which is the best thing to say about a remaster in my opinion.I'm happy to report this version of Broken Sword is fantastic, I hope they  the rest of the series (even the 3D ones) in the same way. It would also be great to have the option to play the Director's Cut content in this game at some point too and, of course, Broken Sword 6 hopefully won't be too far away.

_childDocuments_.review: The art is simply amazing. It looks true to the original and is crystal clear on a 4K monitor. The removal of the Nico sequence, which was added in the Director’s Cut, is a big improvement. That sequence added nothing to the story and didn't feature any interesting puzzles. It never made much sense to me. Another positive change is the removal of the character portraits during dialogues, which had also been introduced in the previous re-release. I generally like this approach in some games, but in this case, it wasn't necessary and the art was quite off.There are a couple of issues, and they both relate to the mouse interface. The controller was treated as the primary input device, even in the PC version, resulting in always-on mouse acceleration, which really detracts from the experience. The cursor also snaps to active hotspots and transforms into a different cursor, and the transition is extremely unpleasant - basically, the cursor jumps a noticeable distance. The original game did have a cursor transformation over hotspots, but there was no snapping, and the transition looked much better. Once again, this seems tailored for the controller. Personally, I believe this game should be played with a mouse on PC, but that’s subjective. What’s not subjective is the fact that they ruined perfectly good mouse controls from a game made in 1996.The mouse issues are a constant annoyance, and combined with the fact that there wasn’t a special price for previous game owners, I find it hard to justify paying €29.99 for a game that reuses everything except the art (aside from a couple of bonus features) from the original, which I already own, along with the Director’s Cut. If I had never played the game before, or at least didn’t already own it on Steam, I would have been happy to pay €29.99. But as it stands, I got a great-looking remaster with downgraded mouse controls, and I had to pay full price for it.But... this is the best game I had played in 1996, and it is still one of the best games I have played in my life even in 2024. Now, if Revolution Software decides to re-release Beneath a Steel Sky with the same quality of image as the Reforged and, hopefully, without mouse acceleration and degraded mouse controls, I would gladly pay €60 for it!
