_childDocuments_.review: It's time to talk to you about a landmark in the point-and-click genre that has left a mark on the genre, Broken Sword: Shadow of the Templars Reforged, which is a well-crafted remake of the classic 1996 point-and-click adventure game from Revolution Software. The original game gained a large portion of its fan base thanks to its immersive story, compelling puzzles, and charming visual style, centered around a conspiracy-filled mystery and historical plot. The 2024 Reforged edition aims to modernize this beloved title while preserving its legacy. The foundation of Broken Sword has always been its rich narrative, and Reforged doesn't change that at all.The story follows George Stobbart, an American tourist in Paris, who becomes embroiled in an ancient conspiracy after witnessing a bombing in a café. With journalist Nico Collard at his side, the two uncover a secret order linked to the Knights Templar. What makes this story stand out, even after all these years, is the way it combines historical intrigue with well-structured suspense. The modern version improves on this strong foundation with minor tweaks to the pacing and some minimal changes to the dialogue.Revolution Software seems to have sought to make the game faster without taking away the charm of the original. Some new scenes and dialogue were added to expand the characters' motivations, giving Nico in particular more depth. The humor, wit and beloved characters remain unchanged, which will delight longtime fans who will find the same sense of enjoyment in the game.The biggest upgrade to Reforged is its visual overhaul. While the original had a cartoony style with hand-drawn graphics that were impressive for its time, the 2024 version recreates that style with high-definition graphics, dynamic lighting, and subtle animations. The streets of Paris and exotic landscapes look more vibrant, and the character models, while remaining faithful to the original design, have been recreated with more detail, offering a modern aesthetic.Revolution Software's attention to detail is evident in the way they have reinvented the environments, maintaining the iconic style of the game. New lighting effects give the scenes a more atmospheric and immersive feel. However, traditional gamers will be happy to know that there is the option to switch the graphics back to the classic style, providing a more authentic retro experience, which is a perfect tribute to old fans.Point-and-click adventure games have a special charm, and Broken Sword has always been at the top of this genre. In Reforged, the core mechanics remain unchanged, but have been slightly expanded to fit modern requirements. The inventory system has been tweaked, making it more intuitive to use, and some puzzles that may have seemed obscure in the original have been redesigned for a smoother experience.Also, the game still relies on a mix of logical puzzles, exploration and dialogue to solve mysteries. None of the puzzles are overly simple, but quality of life improvements, such as hint systems for players who get stuck, ensure that newcomers won't feel overly frustrated. Veterans, on the other hand, will enjoy the challenge, though they probably won't stick around for long due to their familiarity with the flow of the game. Additionally, there are some certain new puzzles added to Reforged that blend smoothly with the rest of the experience. These new challenges, while not numerous, give old players something fresh to deal with. However, the hallmark of the game, namely the puzzles that are inextricably linked to the story, remain as strong as ever.Additionally, one of the strengths of the original Broken Sword was its voice acting, and Reforged retains that quality. Rolf Saxon's original voice as George Stobbart remains, but some lines have been re-recorded for better acoustic quality. Nico's dialogue also sounds clearer, and her character has gained more gravitas thanks to additional recordings for her scene extensions. The game's sound effects have been reworked, and the atmospheric music has been recreated, providing a richer aural experience that complements the game's visual enhancements. Paris comes alive with ambient sounds, whether it's birds chirping in the trees or the distant rumble of the city, adding layers to the immersive experience.In other news, despite the fact that Broken Sword - Shadow of the Templars: Reforged is an excellent revival, it couldn't lack some drawbacks. The new puzzles, while welcome, are fewer than some would expect, especially for a full Reforged release. Some players may find the pace of the first part of the game a little slower compared to the later sections, which remains a remnant of the 90s design.Additionally, while the visual and audio upgrades are excellent, the basic gameplay mechanics may feel outdated for players unfamiliar with the slow pace of point-and-click games. Revolution Software could perhaps modernize other aspects of the game, such as adding more freedom to puzzle solving or offering more dynamic motion controls.Still, despite its many strengths, the pace of the game, especially in the early stages, can feel slow for modern players. The slow progression of the first part, filled with dialogue and investigative scenes, may not appeal to those looking for a more dynamic experience. The lengthy conversations, while important to the plot, can slow down the pace, making the first few hours feel a little time-consuming.Another major problem is the difficulty curve. While many puzzles have been edited to be more understandable, some remain frustratingly obscure or illogical by today's standards. Some include so-called "pixel hunting", where players must click on tiny, nearly invisible objects to progress especially when not playing in the story mode option, which seems outdated for a modern remake. Despite the addition of the hint system, some players may resort to online guides, which reduces the immersive feel.Additionally, while the visual overhaul is nice, it doesn't push the boundaries enough in certain areas. Character movements, while improved, still feel stiff at times, robbing the smoothness one expects from modern adventure games. There are moments where character movement and interaction with the environment feel dated, making the remaster feel more like an aesthetic overhaul than an actual recreation.Finally, the lack of significant new content may disappoint longtime fans. While Reforged introduces a few new puzzles and dialogue, these additions are limited. The game stays true to the original storyline and design, which may seem like a missed opportunity to expand the world or add more modern storytelling elements. For those hoping for significant new plot points or extended adventures with George and Nico, the game may feel repetitive.In conclusion, despite some negatives, Broken Sword - Shadow of the Templars: Reforged is a worthwhile remake that revives one of the greatest point-and-click adventure games for a new generation. However, the slow pace, occasional frustrating puzzles and limited new content mean it's not a perfect experience. Old fans will enjoy the nostalgia trip, and new players will probably appreciate the introduction to this iconic story, but the older design elements and few innovations may not capture everyone's attention. If you're a fan of classic adventures or have fond memories of the original, Reforged is worth your time. However, if you're expecting a major overhaul with significant new content, you may find Reforged a bit poor. Finally, I will say that it is a faithful update that honors its heritage, but doesn't take enough risks to reinvent itself for the modern era and in closing, I personally think that 29.99 Euros is TOO much.Thanks to Gamelab and Revolution Software for trusting me to make this review a reality to the public.Rating 7,5/10

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent remaster. Faithful to the original.Disclaimer: I backed this remaster on Kickstarter, so i may be a bit biased.Important note: This a remaster of the 1996 original and not of the directors cut previously sold on steam. The additional scenes from that version are not in this game (as of the writing of this review) and the intro is restored to the original 1996 version. That being said, the scenes are enhanced very well with lots of more detail. Some slight changes were made to certain scenes, to fix certain continuity errors. The creative director explained some of these in various interviews. They are fine in my opinion.What's really great is that they add lots of options for players to how much hand holding and how many hints they want. This makes it easier for new players, but also allows seasoned veterans of the series to experience the game as it was originally. The music is of much higher quality now, since they had the original HQ tapes to work with. Sadly that was not possible for the voice acting. The low quality voices are very noticeable right from the start. Other than that, it is still the same timeless adventure with George and Nico. A definitive recommend for fans of the original and also for new players who want to experience the Broken Sword series, but are put off by the dated graphics of the original and Directors cut.

_childDocuments_.review: The original game is a timeless classic and it is well preserved and looks good on our modern computers. The script is clear and the cinematic mode provides a very pleasant experience for the text. It is very smooth on the screen if the writing does not disturb the graphic and is on the bottom of the screen. I really like that option. I will not praise the game for its story or the original graphics. We all know and love them who have played it in our youth. It doesn't age, it has not lost anything. The charm of the original is as unbreakable as the original Simon the Sorcerer or Monkey Island. And for that I will always recommend this game. There is a big doubtful point to this version. The new graphics are not handpainted as they claim. I believe the pencil lineart we see in the ads is handdrawn perhaps. It is impossible to tell. However the finished graphics are not. Most of it is clearly generated with AI. I suspect based on the pencil lineart. I can say this with complete confidence as artist and painter and also AI artist. The graphics show all the little mistakes that a human being can not make and all the small perspektive errors that happen with AI and are not present in the original graphics. Do not get me wrong, this has seen a human hand. It is clearly edited and parts of it may even be handpainted. But the bulk of the graphics is not. I do not even say that this is a bad thing. I do not mind taking shortcuts with AI as long as it is done with style and beauty and soul. Unfortunately the reforged graphics of this game are dead and soulless. It lacks all the charm of the original. I must admit, I have seldom seen a graphic that is so lifeless and uninteresting in comparison to the original. What a pity. This could have been great if the artist had been a better painter or prompter or had any kind of feeling for beauty and appael. A game like this deserves better and to reforge graphics a lot of delicasy, love for the original and taste is needed. Another thing that is not okay is that strange help system. When you have run around in circles for two hours and you are still stuck, you can press a button for a hint. That hint will tell you something you already know and is that obvious that anyone playing the game knows it. It will also set you on a cooldown for 5 mins to access the next hint. I cannot speak for you but I feel fooled around and get quite upset when a hint is not helpful. And clearly I am not going to wait another 5 mins to get the next probably useless hint. This is so frustrating. If I am stuck in an adventure game and I decide to get help I'd rather go for an adventure help website that does not include spoiler but hints for specific situations in the game. After my experience these websites are excellent, never tell you to much and never leave you frustrated. Maybe the developer of the hint system in the game should have checked such websites to build a better hint system and also give an option to remove the cooldown. Fazit: If you owe the original game do yourself a favor and use ScummVM to play it. You can experiment with all kinds of settings and filters and have a quite modern experience if you prefer so. It is not worth spending money on this reforged version if you already own the game. If you do not own the original game I suggest waiting for a sale and getting this for a much cheaper price. It will be a great inclusion to your library for about 15 bucks. Paying the full price of 30 bucks is very expensive for such an old game. For that the new graphics should have been outstanding and not just a cheap looking washup of the original.

_childDocuments_.review: This is without a doubt one of the  point and click adventure games of all time and my absolute favourite.Like others have said I've played it countless times, but with this re-imagining I'm taking my time and appreciating all the work that has gone into this reforged version. Just so you know you can change between both old and new versions using tab on the keyboard or the tab/create button on the Steam Deck.The artwork is sublime and stunningly realised in this version with particular mention going to the shadows and light ray effects that were not in the original. What used to be blurred signposts and posters that we could only imagine what was said, can now easily be read and are crystal clear. There was a danger on ruining the feel of the original game in this respect, but they managed to pull if off with aplomb.The game's story is incredibly interesting and revolves around an ordinary American lawyer on holiday in Paris, who gets caught up in an adventure full of murder, laughter and intrigue and whose mystery revolves around the medieval Knights Templar and their hidden treasures.One ♥♥♥♥♥♥ I have though is with the voice quality which has been ripped from the original game and seems somewhat muffled and of a lower quality to the rest of the updates, however this can be forgiven in that the only other way would have been to re-record the lines using different actors which would have made it even worse (I mean Nico for instance has been done by different actresses since and it's never been the same).In conclusion then this was already a masterpiece and this reimagines and updates that for a newer audience. See first-hand how adventure games using the art of hand-drawn animations, used to be made! The Crème de la crème of gaming accoutrement!Now apart from their upcoming Broken Sword - Parzival's Stone, Revolution should reforge Broken Sword 2. This needs to happen! "Quaramonte! Quaramonte!"

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice remaster, but missed a couple opportunities to improve old-timey quirks. As some people mentioned, the audio is pretty bad to the point you immediately notice when the main character starts speaking after each time you start up the game. There are also some LOOOONG-ah animations that need to completely play out in order for the next to start, so sometimes you click at somebody to talk to them, they first play out an animation of putting a piece of wire on the table, the one for caughing which moves a drink right in front of them, they then play an animation to reposition the drink then they pick up their wire and hide it and ONLY THEN you start a conversation. But you first have to stare at them, sometimes for like 30 seconds before they engage with you, it's so annoying.Like I get it, you create a simple finite state machine with queuing to have a complete control of your animations and never reach an unexpected state, but it's 2024 and this could have been fixed espesially for the most egregious cases...Other than that I have no issues and the game is great and the story is pretty good also (though it is still a 90s adventure game so keep that in mind).

_childDocuments_.review: As a point and click obsessive, I will say this is by far the best remastered classic adventure game that I’ve ever played. It is far better than the rework given to The Secret of Monkey Island, better than the rework given to LeChuck’s Revenge, and better than the rework of Full Throttle and Day of the Tentacle as well. As comparative examples, the reimagined art of Secret was a terrible misfire, and the remastered art of Tentacle and Throttle - while faithful to source - did nothing to elevate it.Reforged on the other hand: wow. Faithful to source, yet improved beyond expectation. It is an absolute delight. The redrawn and recoloured scenes are simultaneously better than ever, yet also makes the game world feel as beautiful, detailed and compelling as I nostalgically remember the original to be, playing it on the PlayStation back in 1996. The gameplay still stands up. A good point and click adventure can be a timeless experience perhaps more so than any other genre, and that is certainly true here. I’ve long said this is my #1 of its kind, and unlike so many other games I should have left in rose tinted memory,  it’s a pleasure to be reliving this one in 2024. A must buy. Reward the amazing effort put in by Revolution and play it now. Hopefully we see the sequel get the same treatment.Edit: amazing on Steam Deck.

_childDocuments_.review: Broken Sword Reforged – A Beautifully Nostalgic ReturnBroken Sword Reforged brings players back to the thrilling world of mystery, conspiracy, and ancient secrets, revitalizing the classic adventure with stunning, hand-drawn artwork that enhances its nostalgic charm. From the moment you launch the game, you’re struck by the visual splendor—rich, vibrant landscapes, detailed character animations, and gorgeously crafted European cityscapes that feel like stepping into a living painting.The artwork is nothing short of spectacular. Every frame of Broken Sword Reforged feels like it has been meticulously crafted to respect the legacy of the original game while elevating it for modern audiences. Whether you’re strolling through Parisian streets, visiting glorious stunning Spanish Estates, or uncovering ancient ruins, the visuals provide a stunning backdrop that makes the world come alive. The familiar locations from the original game are more detailed than ever, while new areas fit seamlessly into the established aesthetic.For long-time fans of the series, Broken Sword Reforged hits all the right notes when it comes to nostalgia. The game retains the beloved point-and-click mechanics and puzzle-solving elements that made the original so iconic, while giving them a polished update. Playing as George Stobbart, seeing Nico Collard and familiar characters again feels like reconnecting with old beloved friends, yet their adventure is refreshed by the game’s smooth controls and modern touches. The classic soundtrack has also been beautifully remastered, taking you back to those memorable moments of intrigue and discovery.Broken Sword Reforged is a love letter to fans of the original series, seamlessly blending its gorgeous new artwork with the classic gameplay that sparked countless hours of exploration. It manages to evoke a deep sense of nostalgia while offering something fresh and visually captivating, making it a must-play for veterans and newcomers alike. If you’re looking for a game that perfectly balances history with modern appeal, Broken Sword Reforged is an experience you can’t afford to miss.

_childDocuments_.review: Broken Sword SOTT Reforged is a visually stunning re-release of the beloved classic that updates the visuals, sound design and gameplay mechanics like never before.  Everything has been reworked to modern standards, whilst staying true to the original classic from the early 90s. The addition of the story mode allows newcomers who are not that familiar with point and click puzzle adventures to be provide a slight nudge if they wish to help them along the story. However, those who prefer the traditional classic gameplay with no hot-spots guiding them, that's also an option. The amount of passion and dedication to detail that's poured into the Reforged edition is showcased on every single backdrop. The game not only looks stunning with the beautifully hand drawn and painted objects and sprites, there's also lots of new surprises, with new objects found in the scenery and fixes to some continuity errors from the original, such as the shorter drain pipe which has always bugged creator Charles Cecil, and now has finally addressed it with Reforged. What's also a welcoming addition is the ability to freely switch between both versions, new and old in real time. I found myself frequently switching when entering a new environment to see the improvements and what new objects I could discover. This was like a game in itself, trying to find little easter eggs. From the audio, Broken Sword has never sounded so crisp and clear. Apart form a couple of sounds, everything else is from the original source materiel, but used in an uncompressed format that offers the true quality as it was intended to be heard.All in all, BS SOTT Reforged is the best version of the beloved classic that turned into a full series. As a huge fan, I live not far from revolution and have met Charles myself, and during that time, the team was secretly working on this wonderful reforged edition. Whether your a beloved hardcore fan or a newcomer, Reforged is a game that can be enjoyed due to the updated visuals and game play mechanics. It's like experiencing the game all over again for the first time. A true classic, and the best version of it. 10/10I'm also proud to be part of the kickstarter to help fund this project, and my name can be found in the credits. :)  Thumbs up if you would like Broken Sword 3 next. I do.

_childDocuments_.review: Dream Drop Distance is my favorite game in the series. It's just pure fun, the music is great, it's super silly and whimsical, no one dies or gets trapped in purgatory for all time (for once). They don't hit you with the wacky zany Kingdom Hearts plot until the very end of the game but they do throw it at you all at once and it's a little headache-inducing. Pre-KH3, we all thought the plot of DDD was a bunch of bulls*** that we could just forget about. Post-KH3, we realized DDD contained the most important lore of any game in the series. DDD combined with χ Back Cover set up not only KH3 but all of the games that will come after it. If you don't want to be completely lost, don't skip it. 0.2 Birth by Sleep – A fragmentary passage feels somewhat unnecessary and honestly you can't convince me it's not actually just a tech demo. It does bridge a small gap between Birth By Sleep and KH3, but it easily could have been a short film. χ Back Cover IS a short film. For this reason, I'm recommending buying 2.8 on sale (and I sure didn't pay full price) because it's a package that doesn't feel worth $60. As much as I love and recommend DDD, what Square Enix is charging for these games (remastered handhelds, PS2 games, short films, etc) feels somewhat criminal.

_childDocuments_.review: Kingdom Hearts HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue is the second part of the series recently released on Steam and includes two games and one movie. The first game is , a full remaster of a game originally released for Nintendo 3DS in 2012, which many probably haven't played, and which acts as a bridge between KH2 and 3. The second one is an entire movie, , set before the first game in the series. The latest one, , is set after Birth by Sleep but acts more like a tech demo for Kingdom Hearts 3. Compared to the first pack in the collection, you can see that there's basically only one game included in this package, which unfortunately costs even more than the HD 1.5+2.5 ReMIX collection.Drop Distance HD is the main dish of the collection and features both Sora and Riku while they go through the training to become keyblade masters, immediately following the events of Kingdom Hearts II. They must pass the exam by freeing several worlds still overrun by the Heartless. Compared to previous games, you will visit new Disney worlds, such as those of Tron: Legacy, Fantasia, Hunchback of Notre Dame and more, so it will definitely be a refreshing experience for those who’ve never had the chance to play this game before. Some new characters are also introduced, but they mainly come from , a lesser-known game made by Square Enix and originally released on Nintendo DS. There are certainly other visible changes, such as the graphics, which have been slightly improved with the remaster showing more defined textures, crisp character models and colorful environments. There is also a new combat system known as Flowmotion, which basically improves mobility, speeds up the action and allows for some really cool moves, such as jumping off walls and spinning on poles. The combat system is really fun and you can finally move the camera, so you no longer feel confused in the middle of the action. During combat you will also be assisted by Dream Eaters, colorful creatures that you can create, with different types and skill trees available. They are also helpful for unlocking more skills and passive bonuses for Sora and Riku. It is very important to take care of them by feeding them and completing different activities to increase their experience and receive more benefits. The most important element though, is the Drop system, which allows you to swap between Sora and Riku at any time throughout the game. They both have a time limit and once it reaches zero you will be forced to swap characters, no matter what you are doing. Although the levels explored are basically the same, the perspective is different. Both protagonists face different events and have different quests to complete, which reduces the risk of being bored playing the same world twice. While I like the idea, it can feel a little frustrating to be forced to switch characters in the middle of a quest. Kingdom Hearts X Back Cover is a cinematics movie that tells the story of the Union of the Foretellers and the events that led to the Keyblade War, years before the events seen in the first game of the series. It’s not really fundamental to the whole storyline, unless Kingdom Hearts 3 or the next one has some connection to it somehow. It doesn’t give many answers but it raises more questions and it’s not really that enjoyable either, mainly because characters look more anonymous. However, I have no doubts that fans of the series will watch it anyway, while others may prefer just a quick overview.Finally, Kingdom Hearts 0.2 Birth by Sleep – A Fragmentary Passage is a sequel to both Birth by Sleep and Drop Distance that has you playing as Aqua again, but this time she starts at level 50. It’s a short and dark story that also intertwines with the events narrated in the first Kingdom Hearts but, more importantly, it is a tech demo originally conceived to show what Kingdom Hearts III would have been like in terms of graphics and gameplay. The game is built using the Unreal Engine 4 and there is a clear graphical improvement over the rest of the games, especially when it comes to character models, lightning, reflections and special effects. Gameplay-wise it uses an improved system from the original Birth by Sleep, with the main addition being the ability to unlock cosmetics items for Aqua after completing certain objectives. While 0.2 Birth by Sleep is fun and ties the story to Kingdom Hearts 3, it’s unfortunately a very short experience that many might find disappointing, especially for the price.Similar to the previous compilation, Kingdom Hearts HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue has a number of additions on PC, such as instant loading times, uncapped frame rate (except for cutscenes), support for ultrawide screens. mouse & keyboard as well controller support. The graphical options are still basic though and are a reminder that this is mainly a console port, not a remake or next-gen remaster.Overall, Kingdom Hearts HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue is probably the weakest of the current 3-parts KH collection on PC and certainly has the worst value. Dream Drop Distance HD is a really great and pretty unmissable game, but there is not much else in the package to justify the high price. The Back Cover movie is decent, but not fundamental, while 0.2 Birth by Sleep is wonderful but too short to provide a substantial experience. In my opinion it would have made more sense to add these titles in the Kingdom Hearts III+ReMind compilation, which only contains the game with its DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: Kingdom Hearts 2.8 is a mini collection containing an HD remaster of the 3DS game Dream Drop Distance, as well as containing a mini two hour long experience called 0.2 Fragmentary Passage which serves as a taste of Kingdom Hearts 3 (essentially Kingdom Hearts' version of MGS Ground Zeroes) and a feature length movie that goes over the defunct mobile game. Tested the game on the Steam Deck and it works perfectly with no drops (pun intended) in performance whatsoever, as well as 5 hours of battery life on a single charge without any tweaking to settings.So with that in mind I'm gonna warn you that while it is a fantastic game and the definitive way to play DDD since it's at 60+ FPS in HD and isn't handicapped by 3DS controls, at $60....yeah that's a tough sell. At least wait for a deep discount, or buy the Integrum Masterpiece bundle so you're essentially getting this for free with your purchase of 1.5+2.5 and 3.Also I'm gonna have to lay down some other harsh truths, and that's regarding the "Kingdom Hearts Conundrum™." Before you play Dream Drop Distance, YOU NEED TO PLAY THE OTHER GAMES THAT CAME BEFORE IT. Do not play Dream Drop Distance before playing all the games in 1.5+2.5. The game expects you to know what the hell is going on and who certain characters and lore are as this is a continuation of the story before the big finale in Kingdom Hearts 3. Good news is you don't have to play every single game, you can watch the cutscenes on Youtube and get context for Chain of Memories. But yeah you will need to play 1, 2, and Birth by Sleep in that order for the story to make sense

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very, very interesting... Let's call it "collection", but really, it's one game, one (meaty) demo and one movie.First of all: . This is a direct sequel to those, and you won't understand anything about it without playing those.That said, the answer to the question "Should I buy those" is... you know what this is. It's Kingdom Hearts. The systems are an overall improvement on the BbS Deck system, with added creatures as party members. If you like BbS, you'll probably like this.Another big difference here is the Drop System: Instead of creating one save file for each character, you change your character from time to time (literally: There's a counter, and you're forced to change characters if it goes down to zero). That can be a bit annoying, but there are a few ways around it, so it's not a big deal, just becomes a minor annoyance until you need to grind some specific things.The plot in this is kinda... messy, really. This is where maybe the KH became a bit too overcomplicated for real, with all the Time Travel and possessing going on. Still, if you're invested up to that point, might as well accept this for what it is.The port is also way better than the 1.5+2.5 port: Video quality is better, no crashes, everything ran smoothly for me.In the end, Dream Drop Distance is a decent spin-off, and the decision on playing this all hangs on if you like the series or not: It's essential to play it before III, or most things won't make much sense.As for the rest of the package: The movie recounts the mobile game. It's a bit important for KH3, but nowadays there are alternatives for it. I guess I'm less mad about this not being playable than the other games, at least.The demo is actually very good, with great gameplay, and it has a surprisingly good amount of things to do: A single run may take 2-3 hours, but it is extended by the optional objectives. The way they fit it into the plot is also pretty cool.In the end, this isn't as good value as 1.5+2.5, but if you want to play III, you  to play this before.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the second collection of Kingdom Hearts games on Steam, coming after 1.5+2.5, and directly before 3. As I mentioned in my review of 1.5+2.5, Kingdom Hearts is one of my favorite game franchises, and like the other entries, I had a lot of fun 100%-ing these games as well.Don't start the series with this collection. If you're interested, play the games in order. It's easy to get lost in this series even if you play them in order and pay close attention, so it would be extra difficult using this entry as a starting point.Kingdom Hearts: Dream Drop Distance is a very interesting entry in this series. It uses the command deck system from Birth By Sleep while forcing you to swap between Sora and Riku at regular intervals. It also replaces your party members with Dream Eaters, which are similar to Pokemon, and it's incredibly important that you take care of them because that's where you get your passive abilities.On top of all that, Dream Drop Distance has the most confusing story in the whole series, introducing time travel as a main plot element, taking place in settings that may or may not be the dreams of individuals or worlds, and detailing the villain's convoluted plan for every game in the series so far. And unfortunately, this game is absolutely vital to the plot of Kingdom Hearts 3.Given all these strange elements, it would make sense if this entry was either the best or worst in the series. For me, I think it's one of the weaker entries, but still pretty enjoyable. It helps a lot that the DDD achievements were easier to get than most of the rest of the series, and the Disney worlds might just be the best in the whole series so far. Also, the crossover in Traverse Town was one I loved, since it's a crossover with one of my other all-time favorite games.And then there's the game with the worst title in the series: Kingdom Hearts 0.2 Birth By Sleep: A Fragmentary Passage (at least this was the entry where they started giving the side games numbers to indicate their place in the timeline). I think this game was essentially a tech demo of the Kingdom Hearts 3 engine that was included to add a second playable game in this collection (this game was never released apart from the collection). Actually, despite all that, this might be my favorite entry in the whole series. It follows Aqua, my favorite KH protagonist, and her travels through the Realm of Darkness in the time between Birth By Sleep and Kingdom Hearts 1. The Dark World is a little depressing, but very imaginative, a little surreal, and beautiful. This game is more of a character study than the plot-heavy stories in the rest of the series, and it really only connects to the main story at the end. It only takes about four hours to get through this game. Getting to 100% is a bit more difficult, but still doesn't take too much time. I really love the shorter length of this game, especially after the absolute grind-fest that was Birth By Sleep.This collection also includes Kingdom Hearts Chi Back Cover, which is a cutscene movie that summarizes the important points from that version of the mobile game. I tried to play through KH Union Cross when that was the current version, and if KH Chi was anything like it, then I'm glad to have a good way to skip the game and cut to the relevant story. It takes place in the distant past of the KH world, and sets up characters and plot points that are relevant in the ending of KH3 and, supposedly, beyond. The pace is pretty slow, but the story was interesting enough as background. Unfortunately, I'm not nearly as good at critiquing film as I am at interactive media...Overall, this collection is probably the weakest of the three bundles you can buy on Steam at the moment, but it's still worth playing, and you should still probably just buy and play through the games in the original release order (1.5+2.5, then 2.8, then 3).

_childDocuments_.review: Kingdom Hearts HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue is the second collection in the Kingdom Hearts Integrum Masterpiece, following the Kingdom Hearts -HD 1.5+2.5 ReMIX- collection (jeez, these titles are quite a mouthful).The first collection has a lot of value, mainly because it was actually a compilation of two collections originally released on the PlayStation 3. In total, it included four HD remasters of older Kingdom Hearts titles and two HD cutscene compilation movies from games originally released on the Nintendo DS that were hard to remaster to the same standards as the other four titles.Comparing this second collection to the first one would be unfair, but even on its own, it can barely be called a collection at all, which will be a problem later on. But first, let’s see what is included here, shall we?First, we have Kingdom Hearts Dream Drop Distance HD, which is a full remaster of a title originally released on the Nintendo 3DS. Given this console's unique features, a lot of changes were made to make this title fully playable with a controller, along with other small tweaks to make the game more enjoyable on a bigger screen.Overall, I had a blast with this game. At first, it plays mostly like Birth by Sleep, but it adds a lot more options that make the combat more fluid, fast-paced, and enjoyable. Seriously, gameplay-wise, I think this is only second to the amazing Kingdom Hearts 2, which is no small feat.The biggest addition to this title is the inclusion of Dream Eaters, which are basically the Kingdom Hearts version of Pokémon. They are cute and badass, but more importantly, very useful. Not only can you have two in your party to fight with you, similar to the main titles with Donald and Goofy, but they also unlock new abilities and skills. There are 54 to collect, each with unique stats and personalities, and all have four different moods that affect how they behave in battle. And the cherry on top: you can even pet them!Story-wise, their inclusion feels half-baked, but given how they work, I’m not complaining. The main story is alright. In terms of quality, I think it’s middle-of-the-road. Not bad, but not great either. The original plot is mostly a setup for Kingdom Hearts 3. The Disney worlds are mostly original, and even returning ones feel different. More importantly, they are great, thanks to the richer and more colorful art direction and, of course, a great soundtrack.Something I really appreciate is that while there are two playable characters, Sora and Riku, the game added a system where you are constantly switching between them. It feels weird at first, but this way, it avoids having separate progression in two save files, fixing one of the flaws of Birth by Sleep. This way, your Dream Eaters, skills, and other progressions are shared between them, which is a great quality of life improvement.The two things I didn’t appreciate were the half-baked inclusion of New Game Plus, where only a few things get carried over, and locking Critical Mode behind finishing the game once, something that was always available at the start. Besides that, I think it’s a great title, one that pleasantly surprised me.Next, we have Kingdom Hearts χ Back Cover. Now, I know it appears last in the collection's game selection menu, but I think it’s better if you go with this one next. This one is a movie, and unlike the HD cutscene compilations from the first collection, it’s an actual, original movie, pre-rendered with the Unreal Engine. It takes place many years before the events of the main games and tells the story of the Foretellers, who are like the Keyblade Masters of that time. It’s short (one hour) and I think it helps with some setup for Kingdom Hearts 3 as well, but I enjoyed the story and characters. There are some mobile games that expand much more on this era, and I think they created this movie to cover the essentials for the setup. You don’t have to play those mobile games, but if you’re interested, you can watch a story recap on YouTube to get a better picture.Finally, we have Kingdom Hearts 0.2 Birth by Sleep – A fragmentary passage. This game acts more as a prologue and tech demo for Kingdom Hearts 3 since it’s very short and uses the Unreal Engine as well. And that was the first thing I noticed. So far, the games in this saga have been HD remasters of what you would see on a PlayStation 2. And all of a sudden, you jump to proper, native PlayStation 4 graphics, which was a HUGE leap in comparison. The game is stunningly beautiful and detailed, especially since this was originally released back in 2017.Gameplay is more similar to Kingdom Hearts 2, which is fluid and fun. Your options and progression are understandably more limited, but it still allows you to experiment with the core gameplay. Especially the spell selection—the visual effects look and feel great, especially the stronger versions. The soundtrack is okay, appropriate, but I didn’t feel it was that special.The game still has some fashion rewards that you unlock by completing optional objectives. It also has a New Game Plus and Critical Mode locked behind completing the game once, but here, given the game’s length of only a few hours, it’s more understandable.The story only makes sense after playing Kingdom Hearts Birth by Sleep since it’s a direct continuation as well as a prologue to Kingdom Hearts 3. It’s more personal, but I appreciated it. This game also did one of its jobs properly: making me excited to play Kingdom Hearts 3.So, you can see that everything included in this collection is a setup for Kingdom Hearts 3. Also, calling it a collection is a bit of a stretch. It has an HD remaster and conversion of a 3DS game, an hour-long movie, and a short prologue/tech demo. It feels more like just one game with some bonuses included. But that’s not an issue, especially because I enjoyed everything that’s included here.The issue, however, is the PRICE. This should absolutely NOT cost the price of a full new game, especially when the first collection offers a lot more value and is actually cheaper! This collection is simply overpriced, and I can only recommend it on a big sale or, better yet, if bought as part of the Kingdom Hearts Integrum Masterpiece, which includes everything, even Kingdom Hearts 3.And speaking of issues, please be aware that Dream Drop Distance, the main game in this collection, is basically unplayable on modern AMD RDNA 3 graphics cards. Like in the first collection, it was never fixed on the Epic Games version, and even months after releasing on Steam, it’s still not fixed, which is UNACCEPTABLE. Even the movie is plagued by this issue, making it unwatchable due to constant crashing. Only the prologue/tech demo is unaffected, since it natively runs on the Unreal Engine.And of course, this should only be played after every title in the first collection, given how interconnected the Kingdom Hearts series is. But after playing that, with the right price, and on a compatible graphics card, I can recommend this. I know it’s a lot of caveats, but it’s still a recommendation in the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay. The first game in the storyline is Kingdom Hearts χ which was a free-to-play browser game that came out 11 years after the first game, but then it shut down in 2016. Your quest is to go around collecting Lux particles until you are powerful enough to fight Lord Darkball. Meanwhile in a dream sequence, you are introduced to the master, who is a character that doesn't matter. The master entrusts his prized pupil "Hood Meister" with a mysterious box and sends him into the desert. His other pupils, known as The Five Wise Men then used the Book of Prophecies to go into the future and cast a magic spell, in order to save the world from darkness. Soon afterwards, the Five Wise Men turn on each other because of a cat, plunging their armies into conflict and consequently ending the entire world. It's a browser game so obviously it's gonna be a little light on the story. Thankfully, they released a tie-in movie four years later on the Kingdom Hearts 2.8 Collection called "Kingdom Hearts χ Back Cover" which explains everything. See? Now it all makes sense!The next game is Kingdom Hearts Birth By Sleep which was released on the PSP three years prior to Kingdom Hearts χ. You play as Ventus, who is actually one half of an all-powerful Keyblade called the χ-blade. He is manipulated by the Sith Lord, Xehanort, who wishes to combine him with his counterpart Vanitas so that he can unlock Kingdom Hearts and start an apocalyptic Keyblade War. In order to become young again, Xehanort takes this guy's body but fails but becomes young anyway, then his memory is erased and he is found by Ansem the Wise, before the game even started. Okay? Meanwhile, Ventus is engaged in a metaphysical battle against it's other half who seeks to control him from within his own arm. The battle is lost but at the last second, he shoots his heart power into the Zone of the Enders where Sora absorbs his light ball into himself, which leads into Kingdom Hearts 1.5 Final Mix.You play as Sora, Goofy and Donald Duck as they attempt to save the Seven Disney Princesses, each who represent a shard of the χ-blade, which is comprised of twenty total shards in total and isn't made by merging THOSE GUYS anymore because that game was FAKE and actually, an elaborate dream sequence had by Tigger. Turns out Sora's friend, Riku, is actually possessed by Ansem, who is actually Xehanort that got transformed into a Shadow Man three hundred years ago. Not to be confused with Ansem the Wise, who was a different guy and he's dead now, but not actually okay? In order to defeat Ansem, Sora has to unlock his own heart with the Keyblade which in turn, creates a clone of himself called Roxas.Now, this is where Kingdom Hearts 358/2 Days for the Nintendo DS comes in. Roxas is recruited by Xemnas into the Council of Shadows, whose goal is to summon Kingdom Hearts, which is a video game for the PlayStation 2. He then falls into a coma setting the stage for Kingdom Hearts: Chain of Memories for the Game Boy Advance. During this, there was also a third game playing out called Kingdom Hearts 0.2 Birth by Sleep - A Fragmentary Passage for the PlayStation 4. You see, there are now five different versions of the main character Sora. The fourth being and imperfect replica of the third version, Roxas and the fifth, Data-Sora who was created by Mickey Mouse in a phone game called Kingdom Hearts coded.However, we find out during an introductory sequence in Kingdom Hearts 2 that Roxas was merely the video game persona of Sora who was unwittingly trapped inside of a computer simulation. It is then revealed that Xemnas is actually Ansem, who is actually one of two evil Xehanort clones, neither of which are that Ansem who is now referred to as "DiZ". On top of this, there is also a third Xehanort clone called Xenodouglas, who is a younger version from an alternate timeline. He then conspires with his own self to go back in time and create a second Council of Shadows consisting of 13 different Xehanort clones which when merged, would recreate the χ-blade, which could then be used to unlock the mysterious box, re-summoning the master, who is actually the ultimate puppeteer and true antagonist of the entire series, Pumbaa from The Lion King. _childDocuments_.review: Coming from both a fan and a completionist: This game is a toss-up. I'll be reviewing each game seperately.___________________________KH: DDDHo boy.Alright, so, as a game, Dream Drop Distance is...alright. Some notable things to consider right off the bat:Plot-wise:If you're new to the series and this is your first time reaching this point in the plot, things are going to go WAY over your head. Inception. Confusion. Darkness within darkness nonsense. It WILL get confusing, and you might need some help towards the end. Otherwise, a good game! It's been (mostly) well preserved from the 3DS and PS4 eras and is a complete and whole experience that leads up to, and builds hype for, Kingdom Hearts 3.Gameplay-wise:Yikes. Notice how I mentioned it was (mostly) well preserved? This is where we tackle that issue.Some notable bugs from the 3DS and PS4 eras are still here, both good AND bad. Some good ones include being able to enter and immediately exit the spirit minigames for free points/affinity/EXP, as well as the bug in Flick Rush that allows you to use a defending number in combination with an attack for 25+ higher numbers on the attack.Bad bugs that have stuck around aren't exactly bugs in the traditional sense - Nightmares will occasionally spawn when you're not near the area, (unintentionally) run very far away from the player, and occasional crashing if the game has been running for multiple hours.AOE flowmotion and balloon spells are still obnoxiously overpowered and can easily hand-hold you through the entire game on critical mode. Special portals (which all need to be completed for multiple achievements) are very RNG based and can take multiple drops to get them all. (Took me just over 70 character swaps to finish them all.) Nightmares can either be minor annoyances or CC you into hell and back with ridiculously long and frequent stun mechanics. (Freeze, knockout, and non-reactable follow up damage being the most prominent offenders.)But with all this being said, it's still a solid KH game. If you're looking for a more balanced experience for this title and don't want to just plow through it, stick to these rules:- Remove the "Kick Dive" flowmotion from the command menu- Remove the "Shock Dive" flowmotion from the command menu- Do NOT use any balloon spellsAnd that's it! I personally ran an entire run of the game on critical with these self-imposed rules and found it to be a MUCH more balanced experience. (Or don't! I'm not your dad.)___________________________KH: BbS (aFP)This was alright!Joked about constantly for being the "KH3 tech demo", Fragmentary Passage provides a little more insight into what Aqua was up to after the original Birth by Sleep. There hasn't been any notable bugs, and some objectives can be a little time-consuming, but there was nothing overly annoying or amazing about this game in particular. Just note though, if you plan on 100%'ing this title specifically, you might need a guide to look up specific locations for objectives. This can be done without a guide, of course. I find that an initial playthrough followed by a guided one is best. Also, note: If you want to try and beat the superboss, good luck! There's recognizable patterns and it might take you awhile, but you'll get it eventually!___________________________KH: UXA solid recreation of all major story-beats from Union X. This isn't a game, but instead an HD 3D remaster of all the important cut scenes. If you're interested in this product JUST for this, I'd recommend you look up a youtube playlist instead.IN CONCLUSION:Is this a worthy purchase?Only if you *know* you want this game / to experience these games. (Or if you're a first-timer for the series!) It can be fun, but also infuriating if you accidentally get knocked out halfway through an area.Are the games good?In terms of handling? Mostly. DDD has some issues on occasion with the camera, but that's about it. In terms of value? Again, you might want to be a fan of the series if you plan on getting this.Is it worth completing these games 100%?Absolutely not. No KH game is ever worth 100%'ing, but there's also a level of deep satisfaction when doing so. Complete it as you would normally. Look up guides if you want to 100%.Would I buy this again?Sure! DDD was a childhood favorite and I love to play with the spirits on occasion. Despite the flaws, I can't help but love this series and these games.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll recommend this for Dream Drop Distance, although it is most definitely overpriced for what's offered in the package, especially compared to the first collection which is an infinitely better deal. For sure wait for a sale on this one if you're not buying the whole Integrum Masterpiece (you should be doing this instead).Kingdom Hearts Dream Drop Distance fixes a lot of what I disliked about Birth By Sleep. In place of the 3 characters that all had separate progression and forced you to play the story 3 times over, you just have Sora and Riku, and while they do have to each go through the worlds separately, they actually share what's important, Abilities, Dream Eaters, Items, and Equips. The maps they play are mostly the same, but with different routes that you play through, and in some cases, entirely different areas altogether, which is nice. The Flowmotion system is an enjoyable expansion to the movement system and the maps accommodate for it, being much more wide open, vertical, and platforming oriented. It eliminates the challenge of a lot of potentially cool platforming with how you can basically infinitely keep air, but it's fun to fly around maps and explore looking for hidden treasures. The effect is has on combat can be questionable though, there's a lot of times where you'll want to dodge or jump out of the way of an attack just to trigger a Flowmotion animation and eat a hit instead. The combat is overall a much better experience than BBS, it shares a lot of the same systems in the Deck, but without the annoying Form changes that accompanied every move in the previous game, and enemies aren't nearly as annoying with long strings of death combos or bizarre defense jumps that make things exceedingly tough to kill from one area to the next. The Dream Eater system is fun, it's a little creature raiser minigame that lets you fight alongside former enemies and utilize their abilities and attributes, while they aren't nearly as good as Donald and Goofy, they're at least better than having nothing at all like in BBS. I don't mind the Drop system either, it could potentially get in the way during a long boss fight or enemy encounter, but jumping in and out of characters makes for a mostly enjoyable experience.0.2 A fragmentary passage is... something. It's only a few hours and very obviously a tech demo for Kingdom Hearts 3, but it doesn't really feel good to play. You play as Aqua in this one, sans Ventus or Terra, and most Birth By Sleep mechanics are here, minus the Deck system, which really leaves a lot to be desired as you only have your basic moveset that's given to you and nothing else through the game (minus one form change that you unlock about halfway through). I get that the developers probably didn't want you managing too much in a few hour long experience, but with things like the Wardrobe system in place, I feel like they could have done something gameplay related instead of just throwing some cosmetics at you and calling it a day. Aqua feels really strange to control on the ground, where all the previous games had very snappy movement, there's a strange step delay whenever you turn too sharply, and it feels really bad moving around and getting where you want to go. The combat however is neat for what little is on display, spells have elemental effects and can interact with enemies in cool ways and can trigger powered up super attack versions of themselves if you use them often in an encounter, and the form change system is integrated much better than BBS, and you now manually trigger them instead of them happening automatically. The problem is that there's so little of it and everything else. There's something like 6 basic enemy types and 4 bosses in the whole game, and even being as short as it is, the variety gets old fast, some of the enemy types are downright obnoxious with their homing projectiles, and the big heartless blob bosses have poor tells for some of their attacks, leading to some frustrating fights.The movie that was included seems pretty asinine. It seems like it covers a story that's only halfway over, you get some character drama from some new faces who you don't really care about at all, and then it's over, leaving you with a bunch of mysteries and questions that will probably be answered in 3.

_childDocuments_.review: Dont buy unless you really want to play every KH game. Compared to the 1.5 + 2.5 remix, where you got 2 numbered titles, this is lacking in content.DDD - 5/10The story of is bland and filled with unnecessary and poorly explained retcons which will hopefully be reined in for KH3. The world design is the best since KH1, but the Flowmotion system ruins any feeling of exploration or platforming challenge, with some exceptions like the 2nd to last world. The combat is slightly better than BBS because there are less sections where you do chip damage, though this may just be due to commands like Balloonra doing 2-3x the damage of other commands and significantly more than basic combos. Bosses also have less one shot combos and once more and second chance are also easier to get without using a guide thanks to the Dream Eaters. All the new systems are slightly less frustrating than in BBS but still subpar when compared to numbered entries. The drop system is bad, its either completely avoidable using Drop-Me-Not's or it puts a time limit on bosses when you are under-leveled (if you drop out of a multi-phase boss you will be returned to that phase when you drop again). The command deck system in BBS and DDD is terrible, often resulting in a few commands being overpowered and the others useless, and feels more restrictive in its attempt to streamline the numbered titles command menu. This game is also the only port to suffer from frame drops for some reason.0.2 is okay, but it truly is just a tech demo for KH3. The retcon is unobtrusive and the combat and level design are mostly a return to form.Back Cover is a much better attempt at a prequel than BBS. The time period chosen is more appropriate and actually has bearing on the world building of the KH series past like the Keyblade War and the true nature of Kingdom Hearts. Also, it finally returns to the KH 1-2 approach in leaving somethings up to imagination. This return to intriguing setups, like the Organization in CoM, is a good sign, though I haven't seen anything else from KHUx so its possible that game ruins this sense of intrigue I'm describing.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, the era of Kingdom Hearts where the devs constantly teased its fans about a 3rd entry into the series. This collection is hard to recommend, because its overpriced for just one game, a tech demo, and an hour long feature ad for a cellphone game thats been shutdown. However, theres enough here that I believe warrants a purchase for anyone whose into the series.Dream Drop Distance: I initially hated this title when it first came out. I thought the story jumped the shark big time, and Young Xehanort is the worst addition to the series, an utterly worthless joke of a villain that takes himself way too seriously for a series thats convoluted and full of Disney characters. The Dream Eater system feels like a cheap attempt at being a Pokemon trainer, which feels more like a chore to raise this cotton candy just to get Curaga and second chance...The lack of secret bosses was also a let down, aside from one whose is eh...not that fun. However, its grown on me the more I play it, and its really not that bad. The Disney worlds are hilariously empty and devoid of life, and are waaaaay to big, but the later worlds offer some good old fashion Disney comedy that redeems it somewhat. Plus, unlike Birth By Sleep that had two bland protagonists and a decent one (Aqua), this game has Sora and Riku, two well developed and likeable heroes who we see grow throughout the series (Kairi didn't make the cut, she's a girl like Aqua, so Nomura had no interest in her). Still a fun game that I recommend...only on Proud mode though. DO NOT, play this game on critical mode. Theres a reason why none of the big wig YouTubers ever touch this game, cause all you can do on this game mode is spam balloons and hope you don't get one shot by cotton candy monsters and bosses who belong in the trash can. Still, I'd give it pass.0.2 A fragmentary passage: Basically a tech demo for Kingdom Hearts 3 that would come out less than 2 years later. It's short, but sweet enough. You play as Aqua, the only good part of Birth By Sleep as she wanders through the realm of Darkness. The combat is a step up from the last few titles, and showcases the potential of how Kingdom Hearts 3 would have fun gameplay. The story is okay, Aqua gets her moment to shine for albeit, even though the bosses are pretty underwhelming (Aside from phantom Aqua), and the director thought the Demon tower/Tide was such an excellent boss, that he'd over use the sh*t out of it in Kingdom Hearts 3!... Still, I liked the story up until Mickey shows up, then its back to Aqua just struggling to kill the final boss, and Mickey leaving her behind and not bringing her up again until 10 years later in the story...our Disney hero everyone!!!Like Dream Drop Distance, I give this a recommendation. I especially like the wardrobe accessories you can unlock for Aqua by doing challenges! Shame it didn't make a reappearance for Kingdom Hearts 3. However, like DDD, DO NOT play this game on critical mode. Its designed so badly, that fans are delusional to think that the devs made it like Dark Souls. Its not at all a good challenge, just piss poor enemy designs cranked up to 100.  χ Back Cover: An hour long film based on the cellphone games that I never had the chance to play. Nor does anyone after Square shut it down. Even so, its surprisingly a good film that's reminiscent of the board game/movie CLUE!. it features characters who aren't that memorable, except the Master of Masters, the directors self-insert whose this zany yet ominous figure that has plans that will totally be addressed in Kingdom Hearts 4, in the year 2029. Everyone else is meh, but the investigative tone makes it an interesting watch, at least once. Sadly, having to know these characters and plot points is crucial to understanding what happens during Kingdom Hearts 3 and future titles. Overall, a much better film than the ones in 1.5 + 2.5 Remix. Its only an hour long thankfully, and features some pretty good voice acting from the characters.

_childDocuments_.review: Kingdom Hearts 1.2 games (Or 2.8 as it is known) contains Dream Drop Distance the 0.2 KH3 tech demo and a movie. Dream Drop Distance: Dream Drop Distance is an odd one for the series as it has you heading to dream worlds where you battle and team up with dream creatures. You also jump between Sora and Riku progressing Separately through the same worlds. The game also adds flow motion which gives you environmental moves and special attacks and such. The command deck is also back from Birth By Sleep but moves are unlocked differently. The story of DDD is quite the jumbled nonsensical plot up until the end where everything more or less comes together. Most of this seemingly relates to and attempts to tie things up for KH3 to work better on its own. Overall the game is a bit mish-mashed between different games too but this is much more enjoyable to play because of it. Every enemy can be created as an ally and then leveled up and buffed to provide you with buffs and commands. It's really cool and weirdly reminds me of Spectrobes with the bonding system area. The worlds in DDD are also far bigger than anything seen in the series prior (Both in volume and scale) and there appears to have been a lot of work that has gone into them overall. The music and visuals are really strong and even old areas get some nice new areas to accompany them. Overall a lot of care went into the design and composition of the areas. All in all DDD is a great game. 0.2 A fragmentary BBS PassageThis prologue/KH3 tech demo has you take the role of Aqua following the events of BBS and in part leading into KH3 (And tying in elsewhere) Without having played KH3 I can only guess that this was made to show off KH3's engine, mechanics and how it will likely play. I can honestly say the game visually is impressive with environments, enemies and effects (such as magic) looking incredibly flashy. Aqua herself, unfortunately doesn't play as smoothly as other KH characters which is either part of this or just how she plays overall. A major gripe I do have with this is how the cutscenes look. There's something odd about them, I think it's the shading that makes the characters look very plastic-y and more like dated CGI. It's pretty bad to me but when playing the game it's not noticeable. All in all this is a rather short demo at approx 2 hours though it will take more if you gun for all of the objectives and such. There's also not a whole lot to the story and it's not really required to enjoy the later entries as little of note actually happens overall. As for the movie. I have yet to watch it, don't know if I will. All in all this bundle is of less value than the first one (Four games versus 1 and a bit) but DDD is a decent game and the 0.2 section is reasonable. Overall it's not quite worth the full price. Getting it in the bundle or on sale is your best bet.

_childDocuments_.review: This is basically Dream Drop Distance remake and some bonus goodies. Calling this a "collection" is pretty insulting.DDD is modernized version of KH games. It has much bigger maps, but they are mostly empty. There is new "flowmotion" mechanic introduced, which allows you to travel trough the maps very fast. But I did miss smaller KH2-sized locations. This has reimagined deck system from Birth By Sleep and Re:Coded. This time you get skills from befriending dream monsters. I really disliked this system. Especially since you get 1 friendship point per kill, regardless of how hard the kill was. So instead of leveling skill trees faster and faster as you progress it gets slower and slower. You also can't learn all the abilities at once, which I'm fine with. But really, pretty bad system. I guess they wanted to get Pokemon crowd into the game on 3DS.The game has 2 protagonists that switch places based on convoluted drop system. At first you don't get it, then you abuse it. To me it felt like an attempt to fix 3 protagonists idea from Birth By Sleep... There is an attempt to connect it to the storytelling, but overall I was not a fan. But at least you share most of the stuff between both characters, so progression is much smoother.This mostly focuses mostly on new, unexplored worlds. But second set of worlds is not based on unique Disney movies, and instead focuses on Mickey-related specials. It also has characters from , but it's criminal that they didn't get their own world or anything. I guess it's the same treatment as FF characters, but still.World traversal minigame in DDD is pretty short and not very offensive, but I feel like it was made with 3D presentation in mind. Lack of depth perception seems to make it worse. But it's ok.Overall I like the system in this game much less than previous games. Link system is cumbersome. Sora's side is awful, Riku's side is OK, as it works like form changes. Flowmotion attacks are OP in this game, but they get repetitive. Because I can just use best skills in my deck, and I don't have to craft new ones, the battle becomes repetitive, as I use the best skills over and over again.I'd say DDD is mid 7/10.X Back Cover: n/a. Just compilation of CG movies from mobile game. They look good, and they introduce completely new arc into the series. Which you won't see much of in KH3. But still I suggest getting familiar with this story, as there ARE references to it in KH3.Birth By Sleep - A Fragmentary Passage: This is paid demo for KH3. A taste of KH3. I think it uses the same engine. You get to play 1 world as Aqua, and it takes about as much time as usual world. But there are some pretty cool and flashy things happening here. Very worth playing, and really enjoyable. Also, it's pretty dense content wise. I'd say 8/10. You can spend a bit of time with this doing challenges. If you want.

_childDocuments_.review: RUINING A MEMORABLE JOURNEYI mentioned in my last KH HD -1.5+2.5 ReMIX- review that KH2 is the end of the first saga and BBS is the start of a new saga. I was wrong. Looks like the writers are not letting go of KH1 and instead found a way to shoehorn stuff in order to make the main players from the last saga be involved in this new saga. The last saga I'm referring to is KH1, ReCOM, KH2, and Days, which in my opinion is THE Kingdom Hearts story, and whatever comes after is just an alternate, very bad fan fiction, BBS included.This collection is not a good starting place for newcomers and also not for fans for how bad the story is. This collection has three games which is;Kingdom Hearts Dream Drop DistanceKingdom Hearts 0.2 Birth By Sleep -A Fragmentary Passage-Kingdom Hearts X Back Cover (movie)The story bridges BBS to KH3, hence the title 'Final Chapter Prologue' being a prologue and having important story stuff for KH3. The story is a complete mess. I mentioned in my last review that 'characters are just doing stuff' most of the time. I failed to pick the correct words but what I meant was the writers making stuff up as the story goes along. This new big story introduces a lot of new retcons and inconsistencies with TIME TRAVEL BAYBEE.  At first I don't know how to feel about KINGDOM HEARTS DREAM DROP DISTANCE because it is the first time a game made me feel peak confusion. Sora and Riku are now tasked with unlocking Seven Sleeping Keyholes to become masters and unlock the Power of Waking. Ima be honest, I struggled to even type out or explain whatever comes after that. Something about dreams, alternate worlds, and time travel. I don't think the story is worth experiencing because it actively ruined KH for me, hence why I'm accepting the story from this point on as bad fan fiction.I will say the gameplay of DDD is fun. Despite being a N3DS game, this game manages to feel like a PS2 game, or more precisely having KH2's gameplay vibes. Flowmotion offers some new additions in combat and also you have Spirits which are like Monstie-likes or Pokemon-likes to help you in your party. This is the most free flowing KH I've ever played. There's also a Drop System. Other than having an unfortunate name reminding me to drop the game, the Drop System is a unique take of handling multiple protagonists in a game. It's basically a time limit you have to play as Sora and Riku and you will change when the time limit ends EVEN IN BOSS FIGHTS. The next game is KINGDOM HEARTS 0.2 BIRTH BY SLEEP -A FRAGMENTARY PASSAGE- which is a sequel to KH Birth By Sleep. The name of the game, although horrendeus, make sense because although it is a new KH game, it is more of a tech demo for KH taking only 2 hours. The story continues the journey of Aqua in the Dark World. The story here is also kinda bad but I found it quite enjoyable seeing it as a fan fiction at this point. Good enough for me to not spoil the twist at the end. The gameplay is similar to KH3 and for a 2 hour game, the content is satisfactory.KINGDOM HEARTS X BACK COVER is a movie adapting a mobile game and is a prequel taking place very far in the past. This is what I expected BBS to be honestly, and for that I found the story to be quite interesting. The movie only takes one hour and mostly feature characters arguing and spouting important KH bits for KH3. I will say I kinda expected more since although a prequel, it felt like watching a prologue. Oh wait, maybe that's why its called Final Chapter Prologue.I'm recommending this despite the awful story since it is still a video game. This collection made me not hype for KH3 and not caring at all for whatever story they are planning there, because there is no plan. The games from KH1 - KH2 are still the real canon for me and I'm waiting for this fan fiction to end so that they can start a new fresh story. Overall, a passable fan fiction.3/5

_childDocuments_.review: Kingdom Hearts HD II.8 Final Chapter Prologue is a considerable step down in quality and quantity from the last collection. Containing only one game, one movie, and the prologue of KH III, it remains the same price on most systems as it's sister games and that is a crying shame. For 60 dollars you get less than the last collection in value and in time well spent.Kingdom Hearts Dream Drop Distance isn't a bad game by any means. It isn't much of a good game either, but it gets the job done from front to back. There is nothing inherently unplayable about this game, but it feels like every decision and new mechanic introduced in this game is extremely half-assed.DDD takes place after Kingdom Hearts II and tells a story of Riku and Sora going for their Mark of Mastery. It is a training arc through and through, but in the KH way of tying excessive amounts of lore to everything. It is a confusing story, but it works in the game's favor. I've always wanted a return to the surreal elements of the second game, and low and behold this game has that in spades. The overall presentation of the game is completely commendable. It may have the best art direction and music in the series and that sounds crazy when you realize that this is the same series that houses Simple and Clean and Castle Oblivion.However, presentation can only carry a game so far, and it only carries it somewhere close to the starting line. I won't be the first or the last to say it, but DDD feels like it takes half a step forward and then trips over itself. DDD's combat is based off the system presented in BbS, with only a few mechanics fixed, and the rest of the problems greatly exacerbated. Melding doesn't exist, instead you use the new Link Spirit system, a pet mechanic used instead of the traditional party system (and imo one of the best things this game adds). Monopoly is replaced with NintenDogs and it feels less clunky than BbS's upgrade system. Since it uses BbS style combat, it carries over the flaw of min-maxxing and metas instead of intriguing choice and customization. Instead of doing a cool combo, you could just chuck balloons at enemies and that works the majority of the time.Flowmotion is the newest mechanic added to this game, and you'll either love it or hate it. Personally I hate it. You can't combo any of your moves into Flowmo and it ironically kills the flow of combat. It trivializes the already boring levels of this game, and it definitely needs to be toned down. Not to mention that most of the bosses are built AROUND Flowmo, meaning that most of the time you are using these easy button commands instead of using real strategy.KH 0.2 is the demo of Kingdom Hearts III and I enjoyed it for the two hours I played it. You get to take control of Aqua again, and for Aqua super fans like myself that's really cool. It is one of the most emotionally charged moments in the series, and the glimpses of KH III's level design and combat philosophies have me hyped for that game. I walked away from 0.2 with two things in mind. One: I really want Aqua to have a full game. Two: This shouldn't have been locked behind a $60 package. It's telling when the most entertainment I got from this package were the cutscenes and two hours of gameplay.

name: Eden Genesis
detailed_description: Eden Genesis is a platform game focused on fast-paced trials, quick reflexes, and a rich story by the same dev team responsible for Aeterna Noctis. Take control of Leah, a young cyborg lady, and overcome challenging trials to liberate her corrupted mind! A cyberpunk adventure In the not-so-distant future, corporations rule the world providing ways of increasing the physical and intellectual capabilities of the common folk, at a high price... Those who wear cybernetic implants are doomed. Their lifetime is coming to an end in a matter of time, but luckily for them, there may still be hope. The biggest tech conglomerate just announced a promising solution for this terrible disease! You play as Leah, a young cyborg lady who joins this experimental treatment to find a cure for what is killing augmented people. Overcome the trials to unlock your full mind potential and eliminate the corruption born from the implants that are destroying your neurons. Game mechanics Fast-paced gameplay - Eden Genesis offers a wide world full of trials that require anticipation, quick reflexes, and nerves of steel. These sections contain both environmental and enemy hazards, besides frantic platforming puzzles. Players must overcome them to cure the illness suffered by the protagonist. Responsive controls - The game features an intuitive level design for the players to enjoy precise movement controls. As you become more skilled and Leah liberates more neuron links, Eden Genesis allows you to get even faster completion times every time you enter a trial. In a game with such scale and platforming, responsive controls are a must-have, allowing precise movement and combat. A balanced platformer - While any player will be able to reach the end of the game and complete the main story and numerous secondary phases, it is true that Eden Genesis offers some extra content for demanding players. Many of the trials are optional, and these offer a level of difficulty that only the most experienced will be able to overcome. However, the main playable and exploration core is designed to be accessible to all players. Deep story - Eden Genesis features a stunning plot including philosophic themes and debates about what makes us humans and the limits of science and technology. As every good cyberpunk story does, Eden Genesis makes the player question reality, and have uncertainty about the future. Futuristic setting - The world of Eden Genesis presents a future in which technological megacorporations dominate every aspect of everyday life. Neon lights and cybernetic implants are the protagonists of a unique 2D artistic design, which gives life to an immersive cyberpunk universe.
