_childDocuments_.review: When I saw Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure for the first time I knew I had to play it. Not only did I like how it looked, but the gameplay was very interesting and unique. I was so excited when a demo was released for it and, after playing the demo, I was excited to play the full game. So, how did Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure fare after the first chapter?Arranger follows a young woman named Jemma who has been dying to get out of the stuffy walls of her hometown. Jemma never felt like she really belonged, partly due to being the only one not born within the walls and mostly due to her unique ability to shift the floor around her, which we know she shares with her late mother. Some don’t mind, but some do find it annoying and can’t wait until she leaves. When we jump into the story, Jemma is finally ready to leave her hometown. After doing some last minute tasks, saying goodbye to everyone (even if it’s someone that dislikes her), finding out the situation around the antagonistic force known as Static is worse than anyone thought, and maybe getting kicked out even though it actually wasn’t her fault this time; she finally takes a step outside and her adventure officially starts. Finally being able to have all of her senses take in the Wilderness, meet new people and help them, and find answers to the questions she’s been wondering about.Overall, I think Arranger’s story is pretty good. It felt a bit too obvious it was sending you from Point A to Point B and the game can be a bit too on the nose, but I was interested in the world and the questions Jemma set out to search for. I was also not expecting the revelation and the last area of the game to be what it ended up being.Arranger’s gameplay is actually really unique. Instead of walking around like you normally would, Jemma has the weird ability of shifting, or arranging, the world around her instead. To Jemma, or at least to us the player, the world is made up of a grid of tiles. She can only move in the cardinal directions tile by tile. Not only that, but when she does move, everything that happens to be in that column or row moves with her. Even more interesting is that if you’re at the end of a column or row you can loop around to the other end, which is very helpful for traveling and in puzzles. Not everything will move along with Jemma though, as certain objects or people will have an aura around them indicating that it’s immovable or static (which definitely plays into them most likely being covered in Static). Jemma won’t be able to move past them, nor will she be able to move if there’s an object hitting it when you’re trying to move. The movement system is easy to get the hang of, and I’d say easy to master too, and the various puzzles you’ll run across all throughout the game builds on this movement system. You don’t have inventory, so you move things with you and have to figure out how to position it as you’re traveling and when you get to where it needs to go.The puzzles here more or less challenges you to figure out a way to get an item in position so the path ahead can be open for you to pass through (or loop into). However, it’s not as easy as you think. There’s immovable objects, the layout of the location can work against you, there might be a time aspect like being on a time/move limit, and it can be quite hard to work around having to get multiple objects to stay where they are while also positioning yourself. There are some more mechanics that are added, like the surprise you’ll get when water comes into play, but trust me. I may not have explained it that well, but the puzzles here can be trickier than you think and will surprise you with how many ideas they came up with to keep this game fresh. I have to say that my favorite puzzles were the Static Beasts boss puzzles, which mimic bosses having multiple phases by having the puzzle get harder each time you land a successful hit.There’s even some side content you can do in the form of optional actions and conversations, and side puzzles and temples that are basically side quests in Arrangers. Each Wilderness area has three side puzzle areas you can find and complete, which will open an eye on this weird arch, and doing all three will open up the temple and give you some additional lore.If you couldn’t tell, I loved the gameplay of Arrangers. It’s really unique and I ended up liking having to think about how I’m moving. I loved how you could zip around if the layout allowed it and I found the puzzle difficulty to be perfect where you know what you need to do, but still need to take some time to figure out how to achieve it. Not to mention that Arranger manages to keep the puzzles interesting and fresh by adding something new; and since it always builds upon the game’s foundation of Jemma’s unique movement, you instantly know what to do. Even the optional side content has a unique aspect to its puzzles. I also do think it helps that the game felt like it was the perfect length (or at least to me it was).Honestly, I don’t think there are any negatives against Arranger, or at least none that don’t feel like they’re personal nitpicks. Like, I feel the ending of Arranger was missing Jemma going back to her hometown, the final boss could have been more than it was (though I personally don’t mind as I was already satisfied), and the amount of missable achievements (thought the skip puzzles assist option does make it easier on a second playthrough).To wrap this up, I do want to mention that the music here is absolutely wonderful and I loved the art style and direction they went for the game. The art style works well both in the overworld and in the art pieces and I loved the direction they went with how the game would look. It was a great idea to put a focus on the tiles, having sparse and needed details in the overworld, and have the bigger details shown in the artwork that surrounds the edges of the world’s grid. It does a great job in putting the emphasis on the tiles without drawing away focus as it gives you a sense of the world. I also really liked how cutscenes were handled; being a series of images that perfectly displayed what happened without dialogue and layering over itself which creates some interesting visuals.I knew I would really enjoy Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure and I’m so happy to say that I did. I actually enjoyed it more than I thought I would. The developers did an amazing job not only making a unique puzzle game, but also bringing the world to life. Aside from some personal nitpicks and wanting some more from the ending, I loved everything about Arranger. The story and writing is great, I loved the art direction and music, loved how unique this game was and how it made me think about how I was moving around, loved the puzzles and how the game manages to keep it fresh by adding something new, the puzzle difficulty was perfect, and I especially loved the boss battles. Plus, this game felt like it was the perfect length, to me at least, as it could have easily overstayed its welcome. I enjoyed Arranger so much I’m even going into a second playthrough to grab the achievements I missed.For me, Arranger was damn near perfect and I would definitely recommend checking it out. Especially if you’re planning on doing everything the game has to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: A puzzle game like no other! If you love puzzle games but are tired of common puzzles then this is the game for you, I had so much fun working my way through all the different areas (there is so much you can miss if you don't look hard enough) the story is intriguing and left me wanting to know more but had a satisfying end.I am super appreciative to have been sent this game from the devs <3
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool game!  The puzzles are interesting and varied.  The art is fantastic.  The developers are super responsive in the forums.  The only negative, and it's a pretty big one, is that there is no way to reset areas, puzzles, or screens, so you can start over with everything in their original places.  I understand the difficulty in implementing this, because items can be moved almost anywhere, and to reset them would be difficult to program I'm sure.However, because there is no way to reset areas, you can lock yourself out of completing achievements with no way to ever fix it and you will never get that achievement except to restart a new game to do it the right way this time.  There have already a few soft locks in the main game that the developers had to fix, but they fix them quickly.  However, with the open-ended nature of this game, I can imagine there could be a LOT of people locking themselves into situations that they cannot proceed out of.I hope the developers can come up with some kind of way to reset areas.  The game is a lot of fun, though, given this pretty big exception.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna give this a positive rating because it's really well put together, with some nice puzzles, not too easy, not too hard, but the story clashes in a way that stops me from unreservedly recommending it. It's like something out of a children's book, and while I usually enjoy the upbeat and optimistic kind of story, this one feels like too much of a morality tale. It has lots of characters and dialogue in it, but they all dance to the same tune. It just has no spice to it. It's like solving a sudoku book over a glass of milk: pleasant enough, but ultimately not very satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure is like wrapping yourself in a pastel-colored blanket while a lo-fi soundtrack whispers sweet nothings in your ear. It's a relaxing escape into a world that feels like an Instagram filter come to life. The art direction is stunning, with soft colors and charming visuals that make you forget you’re supposed to be stressed about real life.The game’s storyline, centered around changing the status quo, is decent, but who’s really here for the plot? I skipped most of the dialogue, focusing instead on the pretty colors and soothing music. The humor is self-aware and millennial, which is either charming or cringe-worthy, depending on your tolerance for irony.The tile puzzles are engaging without being mind-bending. They’re perfect for when you want to feel smart without sacrificing your sanity. Not every game needs to be a FromSoftware challenge, and Arranger understands that. It's aimed at younger gamers, but it’s also a delightful break for anyone looking for a less intense gaming experience.With hidden achievements for completionists and a vibe that screams relaxation, this indie gem is worth supporting. Buy it for the soundtrack alone—you deserve a game that doesn’t make you question your life choices!
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Polish over puzzles, which is fine. It's nice to have a game you can breeze through, but it's a shame with how fun the arranger mechanics are that it remains very easy throughout. A lot of puzzle potential in this.Also keep in mind that the story of this "Role-Puzzling Adventure" is more quirky Young Adult novel than anything i was expecting, fine just not for me.The only major criticism is this: How about a chapter select when you beat the game? For the sake of quality of life and because I'm not going to play the same thing again just to get some missable achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure is an incredibly cute tile-based movement puzzler. It features a beautiful art style making up diverse biomes, characters, and objects. Each biome introduces a new gimmick to your movement tactics which makes the game always feel fresh. It's challenging enough that it gets you thinking but not challenging enough that it will stump you. It's quite simple yet subtly complex. There's a fair amount of dialogue. In most games of this type it could be a nuisance but in Arranger it's pretty well written and lightheartedly funny and heartwarming. It tells a feel-good story about always moving forward and having the courage to try new things, meet new people, and explore new worlds. Arranger amounts to a wonderfully cozy game that will stimulate your mind without frustrating it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: A lukewarm recommandation.The game is good. The puzzle mechanics are very smartly designed, the game looks good, it sounds nice.However, it is way too short. It took me 5 hours to complete with all the side content (but not all secrets), and it feels like playing a series of tutorials for very cool mechanics with only a few semi-challenging puzzles. There's never a big payout where everything you've learned comes together. You don't get the "ah-ha!" moments that come from struggling with a challenging puzzle for a while. Even the optional content is too straightforward. It will leave you wanting more.The story is the exact cliché of "pretentious indie game". The writing is not great, but at least it's not annoying, you can just speed through reading the text. The low amount of content makes it difficult to recommend for the full price, but it's a nice little experience that will be worth picking up on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: I'm posting this as a positive review, because I generally enjoyed my time with Arranger and I think it's a good introduction to the puzzle genre. But I do have some problems with the game and I think it is a case of lost potential, in a large part because of Arranger being too narratively shallow and unchallenging for the sake of approachability.The art style is gorgeous and the flow of puzzles was OK, sometimes great. But somehow, the game as a whole just didn't ever "click" into place. It had a lot of good ideas, however they were scattered across different scenes, separate from each other. No mechanic really built upon what happened before, so there wasn't an interesting mechanical arc, culminating in something really special.And the story just wasn't compelling to me. When I first played the demo, I was sure the story would become much more serious and darker, commenting more deeply on the state of our own world, but ultimately, it never broke out of its awkward comedy and at one point I stopped caring, just skipping all dialogs.(SPOILERS:)To expand on the above paragraph, I think that boradly, the story is about isolation and communication. But my feeling after the first hour of the game was that the story would become about the isolation manifesting itself into monsters and as a disease, so something more grand and philosophical than what was ultimately revealed to be the finale. The main villains fell flat for me, because they went away from this initial set up into something comical and fantastic, not really communicating anything deeper than "the elite is feeding upon the masses", which I didn’t think would be the main lesson of the story as it was building up. The monsters, which were the first face of the evil we encounter, don't really have any real connection to the story (or main villains) after this reveal.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: This cute game was a lot of fun to play with the puzzles progressively becoming more difficult. Thanks to the accessibility option I was able to skip two puzzles I could NOT figure out.The design and look of the game is gorgeous. The soundtrack and sound effects were perfect and in harmony. A great first game from the newly established Furniture & Mattress studio. I am looking forward to whats next from this brilliant team.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed the blend of story, characters, art, and puzzles on display.The puzzles constantly introduce new mechanics with none of them over staying their welcome. Each one brings a new twist on old idea, somehow feeling fresh across the entire 8+ hour game (including all the side quests). As someone who has played a ton of sokoban titles I was still delightfully surprised by many of the ideas on display.I for one adore the narrative and characters. Much like Carto, I found the way they interwove the game mechanics into the story to be wonderfully cohesive. Sure, it's not trying to write about any incredibly complex human conflicts. However I think it cleverly talks about many issues that we as people continue to face. The message to embrace change and diversity is sorely needed still.If you are looking for a cute, clever, and thoughtful lil romp I highly recommend this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: A solid and concise puzzle game about moving rows/columns of the world to fit various situations.  It took me a bit under 5 hours to 100% the game.I find the title a bit ironic though, since I'd often leave areas in a significantly messier state than when I entered.  But given the central mechanic of the game, that is basically to be expected :D
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: I'm pretty early on, but so far I like it. It is relatively "puzzle-lite", so if you're looking for super hard puzzles then maybe you'll be disappointed. But it's quite charming, has lovely art and music, and it definitely leans fully into the movement gimmick.(UPDATE after a few more hours:) I'd say that I still stand by my earlier statements. I do think it gets a bit trickier as it goes on, but the game is still mostly focused on keeping you in a flow state rather than having you get stuck on a puzzle for 30 minutes. I think some of the story is a bit over-written, but there are occasional parts where I did find it humorous. It's also fairly lightweight in the story and you can just tap through it if you really don't like it and just look at the quest log for what to do next.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really charming and adventuresome game. The art is lovely, and the use of putting comic-like panels in the background makes the space come alive. The puzzles are not particularly challenging so far, but they come at a really nice cadence that makes it feel like you're an adventurer overcoming obstacles. They are also interesting and don't repeat themselves.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Having picked up the game following my enjoyment of the demo, the 2 hours spent exploring post-demo content have already brought joy and delight. While the game hasn't been as difficult as others in the genre, I've enjoyed working through expanded and unexpected mechanics building off of the core sliding mechanic. If you enjoy puzzle games, I can suggest this one to you.Edit: I've now finished the game. The new mechanics and optional puzzles towards the late game are also great. About 6 hours in all :)
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: I learned of this game through the artist, Dave Hellman. Well, he and everyone else on the team really knocked this one out of the park. One of the most jaw-droppingly beautiful games I've ever looked at, with great sound design, music, and an extremely catchy puzzle mechanic that hooked me immediately. Highly, highly recommended, even though I'm just now getting out of the tutorial area.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Easy recommendation. Fun puzzles with plenty of fresh ideas, but these aren't mind-melters. It's a pretty breezy puzzle game. That's not to say the puzzles are trivial. They will require thinking and puzzling, they just aren't very difficult.The art style is great and nothing I've seen before. The vignettes off to the side add (often literal, but always figurative) depth to scene and transform weaving paths of squares into sweeping hikes and staircases. It's a really ingenious way to add more character to a world made up of a grid and it worked really well for me.The optional objectives are also fun. Some are more difficult (but still not too hard) puzzle sequences, often with novel mechanics, and most are "mess around with this interesting thing in the world and discover a fun outcome" type of puzzles. Once I got the "Feeling Antsy" achievement, I knew the game was special.The story is inspirational and nice to have in a game otherwise so focused on puzzles.Great addition to any puzzler's library.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, lightweight, story-driven spin on the sokoban-like genre, with a lot of heart. I beat it in a single day. There's not a lot of side material, and the puzzles were never especially difficult, nor especially many, but each set of puzzles plays with the core concept in a clever new way, and leaves you wondering what else could be done. I'd love to see an expansion with some meatier puzzles. the lush and breezy artwork and cheerful, self-aware storytelling carry it through its roughly 5-6 hour runtime.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: A very original game in which its premise is, at the same time, its main fault. The basics of the game are so restrictive that it makes it hard to go deep into its own mechanics. Despite that, the short length of the game allows players to explore the rigid gameplay style to its core, and it never gets old.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Arranger is visually stunning and a fun, casual puzzle game! The simple, yet versatile puzzle mechanic (shifting tiles) felt fresh and easy to catch onto. It was simple to use controls-wise, but contained a wide variety of interesting puzzles! I enjoyed that it made the boss fights essentially turn-based (with no health bar for Jemma), adding to the casual, cozy feel.In my opinion, the one downside was the story. It didn't have much depth; the writing felt on-the-nose, telling a very moralized message without subtlety. The story begins with delicious mystery, but the conclusion (and final fight) felt anticlimactic and a bit shallow.Despite this downside, I still wanted to spend hours in the world! The art style was not only gorgeous, but matched the tone perfectly and made for a cute, cozy, and varied land to explore. I loved the comic-like panels that showed up in the background and foreground to illustrate close-up story elements. Really clever and well done! Jemma's facial expressions were so perfect, too.I was excited for this game as soon as I saw the trailer and played the demo, and I'm so glad I got to experience it!! I would love to see more games like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: The definition of elegance in a puzzle game. The game never strays from its core concept, and yet every level feels fresh. Each new mechanic is simple and straightforward, and every puzzle solution involves simply understanding the mechanics for all they are--rather than elaborate procedures that require a ton of trial-and-error gameplay.I found that similar puzzle games like Baba Is You eventually became crushingly difficult, with later levels that required long and intricate procedures. Not so here. The experience stayed at a Miyamoto-esque "just difficult enough" level.Graphics were very cute and worked in context. Music was superb, and reminded me of Michael Hedges or Willy Porter.Though I'm a fan of story-heavy games, I found the dialogue to be deeply tedious. It was the game's only shortcoming.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Lightweight narrative puzzle game that took me about 6 hours. I had fun, but experienced puzzle gamers will find little to challenge them. Although the puzzles can sometimes be clever, the game doesn't explore its mechanics in any real depth. On the other hand, the visuals are charming and the quippy, whimsical style, which could easily have been cringe, lands well thanks to solid writing. Soft recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Arranger's strong point is its original gameplay, which throws us into a giant puzzle where even simple movements have to be carefully weighted. Although there are not a lot of graphical assets, the style and quality of the graphics is high and they are very much in line with the game's setting.Arranger also has important social messages. These include the manipulation of people by the media and the isolation of people by technology. However, we would have liked to see more complex storytelling and a longer main story to convey such important messages.Read the full review:
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game with amazing design and beautiful art, as well as music. In the beginning, I wondered if core puzzle gameplay was appropriate for an adventure game. What if we got stuck somewhere? But after a few hours in the game, I see the level designs are very smart and hard enough to enjoy easily (except the final puzzle, I think). I wish they had something on the game like teleporting to another area (is it in the game? or did I miss it?) and the last auto-save game before going to the last area so I can return to that point to discover more.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - If you like puzzlers with fresh ideas that won’t melt your brain but still give you a decent challenge it’s for you!Superb game! One of the best puzzlers on the market. Level of complexity is just perfect. It’s hard enough to make you feel smart and give a sens of the accomplishment but at the same time you won’t be stuck for hours doing random moves in hope it will magically work. Also the variety is here. Sure almost whole game is based on sliding blocks but there are really clever, new ways to make each part different and fresh. And I’m not talking about new mechanic in each “region” it’s more than that. There are small bits of new stuff all over the game. When it comes to presentation my favorite thing are pictures around the “board” that were showing how world around the character looks like. It really made world feel more interesting than just a top down layout for puzzles. Story is simple and hmmm cheesy. On one hand it touches a serious topic but on the other it doesn’t treat it too seriously. Somehow it felt perfect for the game and I was even interesting how it will sort out in the end. It took me almost 9h to finish it with all optional content (without using guides). In my book it’s perfect as it didn’t overstay its welcome but I feel content with what I’ve got. If I would need to complain on something I would go with too much talking in some places. Some dialogues where there for dad jokes only and didn’t really add much to the story or world building and slowed down the pacing. Also on steam deck characters were a little bit fuzzy. I’m guessing game wasn’t prepared for resolution below FullHD. To sum it up in my personal ranking I think it will go above Inside and Cocoon. I hope there will be a sequel or at least a DLC.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Each puzzle was rewarding, and the art throughout was gorgeous. The temples were SO clever! Keep an eye out for some hidden puzzles.. I loved hanging out with Jemma as she helped out this whacky cast of characters. I'll be thinking about Mr. Help for a looong time. Definitely recommend for anyone that's interested in a fresh take on the sokoban puzzles!
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: This game is phenomenal. It features beautiful art, witty and fun dialogue, good music, and most importantly, novel, addictive puzzle mechanics that scratch an itch that the Adventure of Lolo games cultivated in my youth.This is the type of gameplay that can seep into your dreams, much like Tetris. Or at least it did mine. The main quest runs a satisfying length. i thought the replay would be limited, but i had a lot of fun replaying two more times to get all the achievements.Which brings me to my two biggest wishes; a map, and a series of standalone challenge rooms for once you've mastered the game.i can see myself coming back to try and speed run/complete with minimal steps.Overall highly recommended, and i cant wait to see what Furniture and Mattress does next. (And yes, that jingle is still stuck in my head).
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: If you are worried that this puzzle game is too hard, fear not!I beat the game and solved all the optional puzzles without using online guides or in-game assist mode that lets you skip most puzzles, unlike most other puzzle games i have played where i often have to consult guides multiple times about halfway into the game. (I did read the achievement guide for achievements)Also the art is cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Arranger is a nice and short puzzle game adventure, it got a simple story that still got me a few chuckles and very nice art to look at. It's pretty simple overall and I would have liked the puzzles to go a little harder exploring the mechanics but I still had a pretty good time going through it, pretty chill game !
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Arranger is a game that focuses on its weird world and story, filled with philosophical ideas and deep metaphors. I love it (so far). The puzzles are not hard, as many reviewers have noticed, but if all you look for in puzzles is challenge or epiphany you are missing out because puzzles may be just about presenting interesting new ideas to you and this is also a very worthwhile experience that I can share with more people.THANK YOU to the creators of this game for the wonderful art, world, story and fun gameplay ideas. I'll update my review as I approach the end of the game (won't be soon because I'm busy and I love the fact that the game is allegedly short).
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: This was a fun puzzle game with a charming story that left me wanting for a lot more, unfortunately to it's detriment. The puzzle mechanic of sliding the tiles you "walk" on is very fun and the puzzles developed using this mechanic felt very fun. The only trouble I ever ran into was sometimes the puzzle presented didn't clearly communicate what it wanted you to do. But that only happened twice through my playthrough of the game. The two other things I wished I had was some sort of map I could pull up as the beginning of the game felt confusing in terms of navigating the world. But this ended up not being a big problem as the game is short and you're funneled down a pretty linear path. The second thing would be if there was some way to reset puzzles. That said, I never found myself in a position where I needed it and everything was solvable. The music and artwork is charming and I generally liked the characters, albeit the writing is fairly simple. The overall concept and ideas presented were interesting with the "arrangers" and "static". I did wish that there was more, both to learn more about the characters and the setting in general. It felt like quite a few plot threads were teased and left unresolved. I was just left wanting a bit more. If you're a fan of puzzle games, I think this was worth it. I purchased this while it was on a 10% sale and I do wish it was on more of a sale as the 6 hours I put into this game went by very fast. That said, I had fun and I don't regret my purchase, I just wish I had more.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Clever, unique, and charming, if a bit short and on the easy side.  Mechanics are fairly separated into their own areas, there's never really that moment where things really all come together to use everything you've learned.Also I saw someone call the story "pretentious" and the most it is trying to say is step outside your boundaries a bit and don't be afraid of change.  I think they're putting something in the Mtn Dew these days.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: probably the main "core" mechanic of the game is not just moving the entire line of tiles, but wrapping. i guess it's not  novel, but it breathes enough fresh air into the classic sokoban formula and is used consistently. i'd say some of the additional mechanics were probably not necessary, and it feels like there's too many of them, while most are underexplored and are never used together. some of them are a bit non-obvious (like followers, particularly when combined with those of other people), and some just don't make any sense in the setting (like fishing).don't be discouraged by people saying it's "too easy". people will say that about most puzzle games, except maybe those that are known to be meme-hard. the puzzles are fine. yes, they don't cross the pain threshold, but they do require some thinking, and some are properly elaborate, like the boss ones.i didn't care much about the story (tbf,  few games made me care about their story), but i'm still going to give the story a big + just for not being woke. i was afraid that a certain woke plot twist was going to happen, but it didn't. overall it might be a bit too didactic, but not in a woke way.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Arranger is peak video games !The central mechanic is easy to grasp but very layered, and the game constantly throws new puzzle elements at you.I really liked the pacing too, whenever i started to get tired of the puzzles, there came a story segment, and vice versa.The game'll last you 6 to 8 hours (there are optional, missable puzzles) but every minute of that time will be spent discovering new characters, new mechanics and new lovingly crafted environments. Sonic was right, i do want shorter games
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended. This is a very stylish puzzle game about sliding blocks. Cute story, tricky but not brainbending puzzles, but its art and music that clearly stands out here. Played through in a couple of sittings, never got stuck on a puzzle for more than a few minutes, but had some good "a-ha" moments when you figure out a clever sequence.Definitely worth your time and money.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely charming game, with a meaningful story that also gives a lot of laughs, as well as a puzzle system that adds on plenty of very interesting new mechanics as the game goes on. I honestly feel like these mechanics could be explored in greater depth, so am hoping for a little expansion sometime down the line that'll do so :)
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and quick. Super clean and clever puzzles that don't overstay their welcome. The game keeps going on and before you know it you've beaten it! Addictive and calming. The story is good, though some character lines are a bit cheesy but not egregiously so. The art is so damn good as well as the music and sound effects. Highly, highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

_childDocuments_.review:
Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure follows the story of Jemma, a small-town misfit on a journey of self-discovery. Venturing out beyond her stiflingly cozy confines, she finds an inspiring world - but also one ruled by fear, and a strange, immovable 'static' force.

Can she disrupt a culture of stagnation, and find a place to fit into it?

Gameplay takes place on a unique, interconnected 'grid' that spans the entire world, snappily uniting movement, exploration, and combat. Anything on the same row or column as Jemma moves when she moves, and can 'loop' around the edge of the grid - creating both a playful sense of chaos, and a regular stream of small, thoughtful puzzles that twist and play with the central mechanic.
_childDocuments_.name: Arranger: A Role-Puzzling Adventure

name: Citadelum
detailed_description: Defy the Gods of the Pantheon or follow their will. Become the master of oh so many lives and destiny of so few in this twist to the genre face to face with the old deities. Build your settlement. Gather and refine resources from forests and quarries, breed animals, grow vegetables, fish and make wine, so you can keep your population healthy and fed. Improve your buildings and ensure water supply with aqueducts. Welcome citizens to your village as artisans, farmers, carpenters... or train them to join your legions in different units. Towers and walls will protect your village from barbarian attacks, while it grows into a magnificent city. Expand. Explore the world map, free villages under siege and experience the power of the most advanced armies of the era: the legion, engaging in tactical auto-battle combat. Once the territory is secured, you can set trade routes, import exotic resources and scale up your economy. Send out your explorers to find a collection of mythological objects that will help you in your expansion and complete missions for the Senate. Honour. Rise to the pantheon and gain the favor of the gods. Build temples, make offerings so they will grant you gifts. But beware, because gods behave in a capricious and ruthless manner; worship one of them and you may suffer the wrath of another. Interaction with deities allows a non linear, replayable narrative, full of mythical encounters. Prepare to be amazed when they come down to earth and help you, or tremble with fear if they punish your people. City Building, evolved. Citadelum presents a unique three layered gameplay, based in city building core mechanics, strategic expansion and commerce, and the role of the gods. You will find different missions, artifacts and challenges in every playthrough.

short_description: Citadelum is a city builder set in legendary Ancient Rome. Build your own settlement, gather resources and evolve it into a magnificent city. Explore the world, trade and lead your mighty legions in epic tactical battles. Earn the favor of the Gods or challenge them, if you dare.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game. Specially if you are a fan of "Zeus Master Of Olympus". I was a big fan of old games like "Zeus Master of Olympus", "Caesar", "Pharaoh".And this is the only game, that brings back all these games to life. You can call it "Zeus: Master of Olympus 2, The Rome Edition.With up-to-date graphics and fun mechanics its a "Gem" to those, who appreciate these types of games.I have noticed big improvements from a demo and can say that Indie developer "Abylight Barcelona" have a passion and made this with a heart, not like majority AAA developers who aim just for a quick buck.Look, this game is now just 20 euros and it is owesome.Have realistic expectations and do not compare it to Manor Lords. For me its a 10/10 (This was made for the fans of an old Sierra strategy games).If you know developer - "Impressions Games" this is the closest you can get.-Review update-Overall, after playing it more. I have just one big concern about the game.Its not in early access. This game is by no means perfect and I do not like the unlimited resources, so I have hope that developers will put some work to make this gem more polished.

_childDocuments_.review: The TRVE Caesar 5.  Sort of.Mechanically it does everything that Caesar did but modernized. It even has world map interactions, similar to Caesar 2 (though not as deep.)One thing this game lacks is the personality of the Sierra games. No clicking on your civs for random bits of dialogue. No school children running through the streets as soon as you place a school. Those games had so much charm, Citadelvm is sort of straight laced in this respect and the lack of that 90's Sierra charm is noticeable. Still a fun game for city builder diehards.

_childDocuments_.review: I will just start where I am disappointed. There is a huge disparity in graphics. Next to beautifully modeled and well-stylized architecture, you have absolutely ugly trees. The models of gods, either on the streets or in the pantheon, are simply awful and stand out in a bad way.The city-building mechanics have a very good ratio between beauty-building, functionality, and planning, thanks to well-thought-out effect radiuses and good complexity increment in tiers and at the end of first three missions I ended up with a settlements I could easily call pretty. I do feel that this game is more oriented towards beautybuilding, logistical challange second.I was a little bit underwhelmed with the food production chains, specifically the tiny farms—they're just unfitting and I think  field tiling is today a must for city builders.Combat is super fun! No, really, this is the type of combat I want in city builders, where it is more about building up an army rather than controlling it. And as a bonus, I get to watch the little fellas fight.The religion mechanics are the best I have seen in a long time—super engaging and fun to interact with, with a decent impact on the city.Overworld map is fun and I like the visualisation of roads and merchant caravans (which actually travel the distance).The pricing of this game is absolutely well set and this is 20eur fait and square.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is fun to play. Developers need to re-balance the triggered events. Your city will be fine until you generate an army. Then it's 1 solider = 1 fire/collapse. And the Gods aren't going to be cool with you picking just one. They move into the punishment disposition like snot off a metal doorknob. Also, please add something I can do about the rampant murder. Trade is smooth. Combat is Rock-Paper-Scissors style. Warehouses, Granaries, etc have AOE. Markets pull from anywhere, also covers AOE. City design flows well. Menus, UI, all okay. My only criticism is the very real need for triggered events balancing.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Yes, this hits all the checkboxes for me to be a (little) masterpiece.At its core, this is a new and modern version of the classic and extremely influential city-builder Caesar (Impressions, 1992). Caesar was, basically, just the megahit Sim City (Maxis, 1989) with a historical scenario. Caesar was also the foundation not only for a series of sequels (Caesar 2-4, Pharaoh, Zeus, Emperor), but also for dozens of other historical city-builders, especially during the last few years. You are the major of a town during Ancient Rome. You order where housing should be built, you instruct the construction crew to build factories, you decide where the next fire station will be built. Everything has to be connected to the main building, the forum, by a road, and everything needs access to fresh water. As soon as these conditions are met, settlers will come to live in the town and factories will begin to produce goods. Mine stone and ore, harvest crops. Build warehouses to store everything. While Sim City just had money as a resource, you need over 30 different goods in Citadelum, a bit like in games like The Settlers. The production cycles are important. Keep the population fed with food and happy with a tavern (or an arena for the gladiators), collect money in a tax office, improve health with a doctor, build a few temples for your most important gods. If everything works as intended, it is a joy to watch your city. If something does not work, you will get large warning signs and everything will detoriate if you do not set corrective measures. Build strong walls like in Castles (Interplay, 1992) and employ an army with various units like in a RTS game. Combat is simpler, though. There are 10 missions to play, but you can also just play in sandbox mode or use the editor to set up your own scenario.Complex but fun historical city-builder. The only problem with the game is that I cannot stop to play.

_childDocuments_.review: This game makes me really happy when I play it! It's definitely shifting those dopamine levers in my brain.In 1998, during the golden era of PC gaming, Sierra Studios released a city builder named "Caesar III". I've been patiently waiting for someone to create a worthy successor. I played the Citadelum demo during a Steam festival, so I knew that this game was fantastic.The supply chain in Citadelum is slightly deeper - having a fishing hut isn't enough to supply fish to your populace, you also need to build a fishmonger ( to turn the fish into fillets ). The same idea exists with a pig farm - you need a butchery, to carve up the piggy-wigs. You need a winery, to turn grapes from a farm, into an alcoholic beverage.There are a lot of food types, and you have to meet the needs of both the lower and upper classes.You need to explore surrounding lands, in order to open up possible trade routes.There are about 10 missions in the campaign, with another 9 or so workshop map scenarios, created by players.I'm trying to pace myself, and complete a map a day, in order to revel in the content.I may or may not update this review, since it is a first impressions review.

_childDocuments_.review: --------------------------------Disclaimer : Auto-Traduction from French--------------------------------Honestly, a very solid foundation, but it's hard to stay in the flow and play for several hours due to the gameplay. I really hope the developers will update it and not leave it as is: there are many unfinished ideas. In the end, I would prefer they remove unnecessary game mechanics to better implement the core gameplay.Being a big fan of Caesar, and since the game is clearly a more modern take on it, I allow myself to compare it to its predecessor:# The Positives:- Modernized graphics, which are more than sufficient for a city builder in my opinion.- The addition of construction materials and the production chain system (Anno).- The zone of influence for each building (Anno).- Real-time battles.# The Negatives:- Choosing the number of workers per production building    - Reduces the city's expansion: where you could duplicate the building, you just increase the number of employees in the first one.    - Reduces space management: when needs increase, the number of buildings doesn’t really grow.    - Less visual: you have to click on the building or display an "employee" filter to know your production capacity.    > I understand the game design choice, but I find it less "fun" in the end—it feels less like a city builder and more like micromanaging buildings.- Choosing the number of workers per service building (engineers, firefighters)    - I didn’t really understand the purpose or reasoning behind this mechanic: you have to wait for an incident (fire, etc.) or display filters every 10 minutes to see if employees are missing.    > In the end, you just end up assigning many workers when you first create the building to avoid having to check or change it later.- The maps are not suited to the challenges:    - The maps are (intentionally?) too large: the city doesn’t expand much, there’s no space management challenge or need to make choices about demolishing or moving buildings.    - Too many resources: there’s no difficult decision about the starting location or placing extraction buildings (everything can be done remotely).    > This will probably be resolved with community-created maps.- No maximum distance between production buildings:    - No challenge of city sprawl: resources far away? No problem, just build a road and a warehouse, and the issue is resolved.    - No penalties or bonuses for city placement: you can build anywhere, and it doesn’t make a difference.    > Caesar introduced the challenge of workforce access, which forced you to think about where to place farms and mines.- Economy:    - There’s not really a challenge because a class of wealthy houses pays high taxes without complicated needs: trading becomes unnecessary to build up treasury, so why sell resources?    - No stock management: you can produce in quantity and from anywhere without managing the impacts on your city.- War: battles take place on a separate map    - No pressure to defend your buildings: there’s no strategy to defend your city based on the type of attack, no area to sacrifice in order to win the battle.    - No connection with the city: it’s a separate game within the game, but the layout or urban planning decisions don’t affect the battle (being close to a map edge, placing a resource near a frequent attack zone, etc.).- Local attacks:    - "Barbarians" attack the city, but they "pop" randomly, with no real coherence regarding the region, topography, or defenses. I don’t really see what they add to the game—it discourages exploration just to avoid raising the danger meter too quickly. In the end, I find a challenge where an enemy blocks the road to another city on the world map more engaging (mission 2). It forces you to choose between developing the city or allocating resources to the army to unblock a trade route.- Exploration:    - Turn-based: having to regularly move a scout cavalry unit to a new square on the world map doesn’t add much. If we made all the moves in one go, it wouldn’t change anything.    - Scout death (the horse can die if it encounters an enemy): it’s not something the player can anticipate, and our choices don’t make a difference—it will eventually die. Why not add gameplay to this event? (send in your legion even if it’s incomplete, turn back to save the scout, but the enemy approaches your city, etc.)    > In the end, the world map doesn’t add much today. If it were discovered from the start or revealed automatically over time, the result would be the same. Despite this, I remain optimistic about the ideas the developers could implement to create gameplay here: it could become a unique feature of the game.- The Gods:    - Olympus: the "Olympus" view doesn’t add much other than visuals, but it could be replaced with an image or a cinematic at the beginning of the adventure. I just want to skip the cinematic every time we summon a god...    - The buffs: whereas some gods could have interesting beneficial effects early in the game in Caesar 3 (Mars for the first wave of barbarians, Mercury to avoid creating too many farms early on, etc.), Citadelum leaves them on the sidelines.    > In the end, you just end up sacrificing pigs at their temple to satisfy them so you don’t have to deal with it later.- Other:    - It’s hard to distinguish house evolution: there’s very little difference between levels of evolution, which takes away the satisfaction of progressing through levels and reading the needs.    - You can’t display the location of a notification: theft, murder—yes, but where?    - Houses with too much population: you end up adding houses one by one to avoid unemployment, which is quickly punitive. There’s a paradox between the micromanagement of employees in buildings, while on the other hand, you bring in dozens as soon as you place a house.In conclusion, I really hope this is some sort of alpha and that the developers haven’t released it just to abandon it. There’s potential, but too many ideas feel unfinished. If the game stays as is, I won’t be returning to it. I sincerely hope there will be improvements in the future.Good luck to the team! :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game caught my eye since it first resembled the old Impression Games series. In some respect it does, but Citadelum makes things easier while also making other aspects more complicated.A throwback to the later half of Impression Games' city-builders, particularly those featuring deities, Citadelum is a neat game that takes you through the late Roman Republic and into the early Empire period. Unlike Impression Games, you need resources to build structures, requiring you to be cautious in your intial expansions everytime you start a game. Similarly, unlike Caesar 3, you can build your aqueducts in tandem with the roads, something that I took time getting used to.Speaking of gods, the player can make sacrifices to them to earn divine favour & stave off their displeasure. Amusingly, you can even sacrifice your excess populace to do so, a historical anachronism since the ancient Romans abhorred human sacrifice.The Dii Consentes in Citadelum are rendered reasonably well, both in their heavenly screen as well as when they come down to earth. Oddly enough, only four of the 12 major gods are depicted overall. At times, the animation could be better rendered, but no complaints on my part really.Throughout my playthrough, the game has been bug-free, but some of the mechanics are confusing. I can understand when I'm alerted to the fact that the populace emigrates elsewhere due to a lack of festivals or cultural events (bread & circuses), but when they leave to seek jobs elsewhere despite the numerous vacancies? Now that is puzzling.Similarly, the revenue generated from trade & patrician taxing is a bit in the favour of the player. You could set wages at the highest and taxes at the lowest, and you'd still make a profit.The world map is enjoyable to explore, while the military aspect is a more fleshed-out version of Impression Games' titles, though as a city-builder Citadelum is not heavy on that element. At least you can form proper stances before attacking.On the subject of maps, the game's editor (developer Abylight Barcelona deserves a thumbs-up for including it from the get go) is a bit confusing for the layperson. A shame, I would've liked to make my own sandbox map as it were.Elsewhere, some of the UI is a bit inconvenient. For one, it would have been nice to be able to key in values like the number of sacrificial pigs at temples, or the number of troops one wishes to train, instead of having to mash the mouse button repeatedly.Overall, I'm satisfied with Citadelum, especially its pricing, which is quite affordable for my currency. Again, Abylight Barcelona ought to be commended for producing a full game instead of going into Early Access. Lord knows how much they had to spend to do so.I look forward to any potential DLCs for the game, especially ones which allow you to manufacture those goods which are currently only available via trade.

This game brings up my childhood back in better graphics and more improvements.These developers took Zeus and Poseidon, Pharaoh, and Ceasar series pillar concepts and modernized them to our present standards... What a breath of fresh air !I hope they add some content to this especially since they tackled the Roman empire and its mythology/culture. _childDocuments_.review: This game touted itself as the spiritual successor to Caesar III, and the aesthetic is an instant appeal to anyone who are familiar with Sierra's games of old. The game play is nothing revolutionary, and anyone who play these games on a regular basis can grasp it in half an hour, thanks to the very detailed and helpful economy management (one of the better among the genre).However content is thin. Building are easy to manage partly thank to management panel, everything is instant so no need to wait for your decision to take effect etc. There is no wonder to look forward to, so the only thing left is war game, and it is too easy since your city can be defended by watch towers manner by pairs of lone guards. Beyond that game play is simplistic and repetitive.The game is priced fairly, or you can buy it at sale but dont expect too much if you want a deep game. You can experience everything it has to offer ATM in about 6-8 hours if you are veteran of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Allright, I've only just played for a few hours but this one is getting a positive recommendation. I suppose the easiest way to explain this, would be a CEASAR 3 clone, that aims at being very similar to that and perhaps improve it here and there. If that was the goal, well then, success. I think some small level of criticism fits well here. There is little new. Battles now occur on the campaigh map, and they revert to a local battle map (I still havent seen that happen but apparently enemies can also appear at your city and wreck havoc there too, as per the older game). Some YT channels are pointing out that many of those new features get tiresome quickly and I can already see that is going to be the case with some features; for instance you have the same "please the gods or else!" thing, but now there is an 'olympus' UI where you are forced to see one of the gods stand up, run towards the screen, jump at your lap, appear on the city level map and go about wrecking up the place. Ugh... it felt boresome the first time, imagine that going on forever. Jeeez. Bat idea. I would have much prefered this to be a togleable option. Maybe gods maluses could just be made into an option of merely having maluses or ruined buildings here and there. Or whatever. Anyway, a positive point is that the game looks just like and improved version of Caesar 3, instead of trying to be like the eyesore of the later Caesar isntallments. It is square and predictable as an isometric game, but it is actually 3D and you can scroll around the view as you like, A good choice! Feels familiar and nostalgic, but at the same time, practical and good to look at. I will have to play more to decide if I like this more, but insofar I have liked it 'enough', They get extra points for understanding that no one wants a full re-invention of the wheel, just give us "point-five' versions of games we loved and miss, instead of radical new stuff that ends up pleasing nobody - I AM LOOKING AT YOU, VICTORIA 3. Give it a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: Citadelum is a spiritual successor to the old Sierra city building games such as Caesar, Pharaoh, and Zeus: Master of Olympus. On each map you build up an ancient Roman city from the ground up, placing housing, setting up a water supply, food, and eventually building up entertainment and a military. There are a few scenarios to play as missions or as sandbox.This game is NOT like city skylines or other city building titles where you slowly sprawl out over the course of hours. Instead a scenario is like a puzzle, where you build up until you accomplish your goal and then end the scenario. A map took me roughly an hour or two to complete. Citadelum's basic mechanics is honestly much improved over the old titles. The Sierra titles used a "walker" system where buildings would send out walkers who service the surrounding area but it was always super finicky where they went. This game does away with that and just gives buildings area they service, so there is much more certainty. It allows you to build up supply chains more cleanly. There are still a lot of levers to pull to get efficiency and you will need to prioritize certain industries, add to that enemy raids, and there are enough decisions to keep you busy during a run.That said though, where this game fails pretty hard even compared to its predecessors, are the scenarios. Each map offered is basically the same. You have plenty of all resources available, use them to build up to a certain point, the end. They really needed to be a bit more creative than that, like restricting certain buildings or resources so you need to import goods, maybe a time limit, or appeal to a certain god... or just SOMETHING. The variety in the scenarios is HUGELY disappointing, and almost makes me not recommend the game. They do try and make up for it with community scenarios but I never liked that. It shouldn't be up to me to find fun and interesting scenarios for your game. If it isn't fair for me to criticize a game for the bad community content, I am also not going to praise it for good community content.Overall I give this a tepid recommend. Its still a fun core of a game it just really, REALLY, lacks variety. After you master building a city there is not much more to see as the game will never test anything else. Luckily that is still 10+ hours of good content, but I did expect more.

_childDocuments_.review: I would have given this game a thumbs up after I played for about 10 hours or so. Playing longer made the game start to become monotonous. You built basically the same city in every region. The parts that increase the difficulty are when and how yo get raided. So once you rush guards, which are usually more than capable of handling the assault, it becomes trivial and you end up building the same simple production chains over and over again. Once demand increases you just pop down more. As long as you have a collection depot in the area it doesn't matter where. So there is no need to even think about a production chain. Forester on one side of the map, wood cutter on the other side, furniture maker somewhere else. As long as there is a warehouse nearby it doesn't matter. It is about as entry level as it gets as a city builder. Far less complicated then games out 30 years ago. depending on perspective, may not be bad to some, but I'd like to have to at least consider what I'm doing when putting it together. The appeasement of the gods is pretty easy too once you get enough pigs to sacrifice. You can hold festivals, but the only one I used was Mars's to help with troop training.World map play is the worst. I was hoping to have a bit more interaction with the other cities, maybe even dominate them in some way, you know Veni Vidi Vici, but they are there for only trade, which unless there is a specific mission goal, is completely unnecessary. You get some much more from taxing your patricians that it's trivial. The other bad part is you have to explore to find these cities, which opens you up to more raids. The smarter thing to do is wait till you have everything in line with food and material production, then explore. which leads to the last part, the battles. I didn't come into the thing expecting total war, but what was provided is ridiculous. If you have bigger numbers there is not much you can do to lose. There is also no benefit from strategy. Want to slam that cavalry into that occupied opponents flank? Go ahead. Will it matter? No. You can just run everyone straight into everyone else and that's about it. Sure you can maneuver around if you want, but it's not going to effect the outcome. Then you better save before hand because no matter how stacked you are, there is a bug that makes the basic enemy (Not some hero unit) destroy your army. I have 60 infantry, 60, archer, 40 Cavalry, and 4 Centurions get all but destroyed but 18 enemy archers.After about ten hours I found it tedious. I actually thought for a while "well probably still early access, plenty of time to cook." But nope, full release. You're not missing anything by passing.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay.  It tries to be Caesar III for the modern era but comes off as a pale imitator instead of capturing or improving the foundation that made Caesar III and all-time classic.  The "campaign" is just a series of disjointed missions, combat is disconnected from your settlement, and the game devolves into more of an efficiency puzzle for simpletons than a city-builder.  Religion is okay but nothing groundbreaking.  The trading system doesn't feel as organic as Caesar III either.  Was hoping for more of an empire builder which this is not.  Despite looking decent, what's under the hood isn't impressive, Caesar III is still the champ.  I'm only going thumbs down because if you want this experience in a more polished, integrated and engaging package with admittedly dated graphics, Caesar III is easily your best option.  If you want a better looking more bare bones and clunky experience pick this up on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: This review focuses solely on the technical optimization of the game. The gameplay itself is enjoyable, and I appreciate the combination of city-building with 4X elements (even if simplified, it's still engaging).This isn't a negative review, but at this point, it's a "DO NOT RECOMMEND" or "Be warned." The game runs poorly and heavily strains the GPU. There’s no granularity in the video settings—just HIGH, MEDIUM, and LOW options, which don’t cater well to everyone. Several posts in the Steam forums echo similar issues.On LOW settings (with no AA), the game is playable, but any attempt to switch to MEDIUM or HIGH results in sluggish performance and GPU overheating.I will update my recommendation if the developers address this problem. It may stem from the Unity engine, but regardless, providing more granular graphics settings is essential for a better player experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This city builder presents a shiny exterior reminiscent of classic Impressions Games/Sierra titles like Caesar, Pharaoh, Zeus, and Emperor, but ultimately feels like a simplistic mobile version of those classics. The game-play is rudimentary, and after just a few missions, you'll unlock all the features, losing any sense of progression or challenge.In contrast to games like Caesar III, where each mission offers a real incentive to continue, this title lacks engaging challenges in its campaign. The sandbox mode is equally uninspired. While you can choose your starting city, the location doesn’t impact game-play significantly—you're free to grow any crop, access all resources, and max out buildings without effort. This lack of variety means the game quickly becomes monotonous, regardless of the map you select.Trade and interaction with other cities are minimal since you have access to everything you need from the start. This eliminates the complexity of managing resources or establishing trade routes, a core element that made the classic Sierra games compelling. The thrill of balancing population, managing logistics, production, and diplomacy is notably absent or underdeveloped here.The game also misses the charm and personality of the classic titles. There are no quirky dialogues from citizens or unique building designs—most structures look bland and similar, making it hard to distinguish between them at a glance. Elements like fishing boats and animated marketplaces or quarries, which added life to earlier games, are missing or completely superficial. Key information overlays, such as crime rates or economic details, are also lacking, reducing your ability to manage your city effectively.Logistically, the game struggles as well. Once neighborhoods reach the highest level, market traders often fail to deliver goods to citizens, leading to frustration and housing downgrades. Options for setting limits on warehouses and granaries are missing.Military mechanics feel nearly nonexistent. Unlike Caesar III, Zeus, or Emperor, your army can’t be deployed and micromanaged within your city to defend it from attacks. With simplistic enemy encounters, defending your city becomes tedious rather than exciting. You can deploy your army on the global map for quick battles, but these encounters lack challenge and yield little reward.The global map offers opportunities for exploration and trade, but again, the value of trade is minimal, and unlike Zeus or Emperor, you can’t conquer neighboring cities. This limits strategic depth and undermines the military aspect of the game.In summary, this game falls short of the expectations set by classic city builders like Caesar III, Zeus, and Pharaoh. While it might be worth picking up on sale for a few dollars if you're looking for something to pass the time, there are far superior options available, especially among the classic titles.
_childDocuments_.name: Citadelum

_childDocuments_.review: In short - Anno and Civ had a Unity-based baby that's beautiful but missing a few genes. 7.5/10.You have your traditional map view to develop a city in, and a region map which plays out Civ-style to explore neighbouring territories.  In your city, you start by building a forum.  Don't let this dictate your city design unless you want it to however, as it is largely useless.  Unlike town centers in something like Age of Empires, the forum just sits there.  It can act as storage, but you don't really need it to when warehouses and granaries are cheap to build.  This then invalidates it for anything more than a decorative piece.Like Anno, you have a range of roads and decorative pieces to jazz up your city of two building types - plebeians and patricians.  These buildings upgrade visually and monetarily (yay, more taxes!) depending on their needs being met, one of which being zone desirability.  There are entertainment buildings where you train actors and hold plays to improve general happiness but that in itself is not a metric - you have prestige.  The more prestige you have, the more decorations you unlock.  Pop-ups on the upper-right of the screen tell you what you are missing lifestyle-wise, such as religion or entertainment, as it causes people to leave if not in adequate supply.  Food and other resources can be toggled to show a + and - metric along the top of the screen and is customisable, which is useful.The game can be quite easy on normal settings, so harder settings are advised.  In my 3 hours of play time with normal difficulty settings I've almost maxed plebeians and patricians, so be advised that the depth and duration to get to end goals is not quite of the Anno length, and I experienced no challenge in combat situations.  It falls into the sort of Age of Empires flow where, once you identify a good starting pattern, you can play rather quickly with little need for variation.For food, you have small orchards, not sprawling Anno-esque farm plots with acres to farm.  You assign farms, mines (next to small rock features), and production buildings a maximum of 4 workers and can set the hiring priority.  You can also pause the mine, however this will not unassign the workers; you need to remove them so they go back into your hiring pool for shifting to other buildings.  Production buildings range from food types to meet plebeian and patrician needs through to armor, swords, and bows for military use.  Fire stations require water through aqueducts and a reservoir and I have yet to see a working purpose for a well, since it was not used to put out a fire.For military, you can create guards for protection around your city to reduce crime and deter raiders.  You also build a recruitment center to recruit soldiers, which you can then train in a separate building to become a footsoldier, archer, or cavalryman (buildings are per type).  Centurions are also available to lead your armies, but I have yet to require them, so I have not tried those.  These units are then used in your main military campaigns in the region map.Combat is a general click-and-drag to create a formation on the land.  AI charges head on without much forethought.  You can place formations around landmarks such as forests to flank the enemy but the AI does not handle it well, sometimes splitting the flanking formation around the landmark and reducing the strength of the flank itself.  Example - a small forest was between myself and an enemy and positioned in the center-right of the map.  5 archers waited near the middle of the forest edge with the intent to run around and shoot from the side once the enemy was engaged.  Instead, three did so, and two ran the other way around to join other soldiers in the main direction of attack.In a way, combat feels like Endless Space in its early days - you make an array of units and try to make them work to their best advantage, but it's largely a slugfest with manic charging.  Soldier beats Cavalryman, which beats Archer, which beats Soldier.  This seems a little strange to me, but what do I know?Graphically, it's fit for purpose but won't blow you away.  Being a Unity game there are not many settings to adjust, and the highest settings are still sketchy, but good enough to enjoy if graphics are not your focus of a game.  Sound is the same - it works and draws you into the atmosphere, but isn't of the likes of Andrew Hulshult or Austin Wintory.Replay value is high due to the nature of the game.  You can test different army configurations, play sandbox mode and experience missions, create mods and your own maps, download community maps, and so on.So, why 7.5/10?  Despite some of the rough edges, it's fun.  The game itself is fun and has enough content for the price tag.  The graphics and sound work as needed.  The city building content that is provided is fun, even if the combat is lackluster.  Modding and community files give the game extended life and possible depth of scenarios and, given the historical setting, I'd wager there will be a lot of content to come from the community as it can be rather passionate.  If you take that away and rate it purely on the core game itself, I'd say 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw the Prologue version of Citadelum on Steam and immediately got Caesar II / III and Pharaoh vibes from the videos and screenshots. I loved those games back in the day, that's why I gave Citadelum a chance. And boy, it has been a long time since a game has taken so much of my time...Citadelum comes with a 10 mission campaign provided by the developers, following along with the Rise of the Roman Empire. Well, some part of that rise, at least. The missions increase in difficulty and it's fun to build up your city every mission, each time going just a little bigger than the last. After you finish a mission, you can continue playing with that city or start a sandbox game in the same map with custom settings to increase or lower difficulty.You will provide your citizens with different and ever increasing requirements, trade for goods or extra income and defend your settlement against enemy raiders. Plenty of enemy armies await you to defeat while testing your perfect battle strategies. The game itself is 'bugfree' (at least, I haven't witnessed any more since the last stable release). No unexpected behaviour, no strange side effects. Now, for all the good that Citadelum already is, there is room for improvement as well. I think more content or challenges can be added to improve replayability for instance. There could also be improvements in terms of mission objectives and game play elements to better match the storyline.But, development isn't done yet. Yes, the 1.0 version was released just now, but developers are not done yet. At launch time, one of the developers proudly said "It's been an amazing journey. And I can assure the best is just to come." And I believe him.Here's why. I've taken part in the beta test and have had direct contact with fellow testers and Abylight staff. During the feedback process, they have responded quickly and with respect towards all opinions. All reports were read, discussed and, if possible or desired, fixed within a (couple of) days. I think this is a great sign that Abylight is committed to Citadelum. They want this game to resonate with the players. To achieve this, developers will have to be open to feedback from the community. And so far, they are.Long story short: Citadelum shows amazing promise. The current state of the game already has me spending many hours playing, building and fighting. And I am confident that future updates and the community generated content will keep pulling me back in.

_childDocuments_.review: Close, but no cigar.Really, it is almost there. But what we have is the classic situation of a game not being quiet sure what it wants to be.Citadelum has a lot of good ideas. I really like the idea that you are in control of a city that is part of a much larger map. You can trade with other cities, there are enemy armies that need to be dealt with, there's the occasional find of a special relic that you can gift to one god or another... The idea really is great, but it's really not a lot of fun.Trade is completely inconsequential for anything but a handful of campaign missions. Buy some stuff you don't have (or need) on your own map from town A and send it to B. It is beyond meh.The armies on the map need to be dealt with lest they attack your own town. I like that. But your choices beforehand (compostion of your army) and actions during combat are pretty much inconsequential as well. I am a strategist, but this is the first game where not touching my units at all actually yielded better results. Moreover, it's best not to explore at all. An undiscovered army is an army that does not threaten your settlement. Finding a relic is super exciting! For all of about 3 minutes. After that you realize that appeasing the gods with festivals is easier and safer than raising armies to deal with discovered enemy armies.If you do explore, then your town turns into a soldier factory. Really, that is its sole purpose. To keep up with demand for (churn of) soldiers on the larger maps, you will probably have 4 or 5 barracks just to pump out infantry. It's fast, but not much fun. It's about the same fun as manually collecting gems from all of your buildings in a mobile game every 5 minutes.Once you have found the town you need to trade with, it's best not to explore at all. Which means pretty much everything on the map is absolutely meh.That leaves us to the city building. From an angle, the building graphics are super detailed and a true triumph. It's really amazing to see people go into buildings and walk around there. But for some reason the developers chose to use drab browns for the roofs of every building. And guess what you are staring at the entire you are in the game? You guessed.Other than beautification, there are no adjency bonuses, though there are area of effect. 80% of the buildings have a 3x3 grid, so that is what you will build. A grape farm has the exact same layout and size as the grain farm. A single tree is enough to get 100% production for your lumberjacks. Production chains are never longer than 1 step (grapes to wine, fish to filets), and providing your citizens with everything they need is a breeze. And once you have reached around 800 citizens, there is basically no incentive to go any further. My guess is that once most people get really bored with this game when their defensive walls are in place, enough money is coming in, and they have reached an economical equilibrium.The ideas are there. The bones are there. But this game just lacks soul and purpose.
