_childDocuments_.review: This game has a very good foundation. I love the concept and it definitely has the potential to become a classic. My biggest concern is the lack of content and a very weak endgame. It also becomes very easy once you've played your first round.This game could go viral if it included features like legions attacking the base when they get close enough, more resources (like Garum!), and a wider variety of buildings. We don't even have a senate!  There's so much potential here, and even without major game mechanic changes, they could add a lot. The God system is lovley and really well implemented. Though they should have more benifits and harder punishments. Considering how important the gods were back in the ancient roman times it makes a lot of sense how big of a role they play in this game and its very rare that it such a system is so well implemented in the game like it does in citadelum.The developers have a choice: abandon it and wonder why player numbers stay low, or add content and potentially create a classic. It's very rare to find a game with such a well-rounded foundation these days, and they should absolutely build upon it!

The game is very polished. There are only 10 or so missions in the base game, but the devs (or early access players?_ seem to have made the first batch of "community" content with another 10 missions, and one of seems to have multiple parts. _childDocuments_.review: First, the good! Because Ancient Roman city builder Citadelum certainly has some fun ideas:  It refreshingly explores a lesser tread period of Roman history—the immediate aftermath of Ceasar’s senatorial assassination and the chaotic power vacuum that followed as Gaius Octavius (Ceasar’s adopted son) returns to Rome to enact his dead father's revenge. Now... will you get to  any of that in Citadelum? No. But we’ll unpack that problem in a minute. Citadelum injects an otherwise by-the-book ancient civilization builder with a touch of the divine in a really fun way! Jupiter, Neptune, Mars, Apollo—all the major Roman deity equivalents party atop their Pantheon as you toil away far below. As you toil, keep an eye on each god’s favor meter—max it out by honoring a god at their temple or devoting relics you find during your explorations to them, and they’ll hop off their celestial perch to shower your settlement with a god-specific boon. However, let the favor meter dip into the red, and you might find yourself with a very pissed off Jupiter on your hands. (First time this happened to me, he blew up school and then a hospital lol.) And finally, Citadelum sports a no frills combat simulator that, while far from perfect, is more entertaining than I’ve seen in many city builders (*cough Builders of Greece cough*) and it adds a healthy dose of violence to the otherwise methodical act of economy management. Now, at this point, if you’re thinking to yourself, “Uh oh... we’re only a minute in and he's already transitioning from The Good?” then buckle up, because the remainder of Citadelum ranges from o-kay to oh-my goodness, what year is it?  Speaking of... the visuals. Woof. Citadelum’s color palette comes in dull shades of brown and green, the foliage looks stiff and copy/pasted, buildings are virtually indistinguishable making it hard as heck to navigate your city, there’s no day/night cycle, and the only weather effect is “cloud,” and water is really, really sparkly to an almost distracting degree. Zoom in a little closer and you’ll see that the complexity of citizen animations in Citadelum is a downgrade from the developer’s prior work in One Military Camp, which is a shame because the exposable building layout effect in Citadelum had potential to give us a fun peek into everyday Roman life. As is, it’s pretty plain.  Oh, and did I mention the gods look like they were rendered in Unreal Engine 2? Yikes. But even if ♥♥♥♥-adelum looks like a ten-year-old turd, I’d still recommend it to fans of the genre if I found the gameplay compelling. Alas, herein lies Citadelum’s greatest failing in that it sets itself during one of if not the most compelling era in ancient human history and then refuses to let you do anything fun with it. Instead of, for example, building up an economy and then marshalling Octavius’s forces to conquer his way to the senate, each mission instead starts you off with a short text-based history lesson and then gives you a detached list of objectives like level up five houses or send 150 silk back to Rome. Each subsequent “mission” (if you can call them that) then just gives you a slightly harder set of objectives and fewer starting resources. And so, Citadelum’s core gameplay loop remains almost identical throughout—you’ll place your forum, build some mines and lumber mills (that never expire, by the way), sow some fields, build more houses, allocate workers to and from positions as needed, tier up your city and build the unlocked buildings, and then begin prioritizing whatever it is the objectives list wants this time. Meanwhile, you’ll be clicking scouts through a tedious exploration mini-game before they inevitably stumble upon and are killed by an enemy legion. Depending on the mission, you might then have to rally troops (who take a  long time to arm) and kill your way through said enemy legion, as they’re blocking the neighbor city with the resource you need to trade for in order to, you guessed it, complete one of those arbitrary objectives from earlier.  And yet! I think I’ve somehow saved the absolute worst for last. Because through some strange series of design decisions, Citadelum seems to have cut out what could have been its most redeeming feature. You know, the coolest part of Ancient Rome? Gladiators!  I was shocked last month—after having followed Citadelum’s development all year—to get a “NEW GAME ANNOUNCEMENT” email from the publisher saying that  would come out in 2024 right after Citadelum as a  game. I don’t know what the ♥♥♥♥ happened here, but gladiatorial management is a fun idea that should’ve definitely just been part of the Citadelum base game, or at the very least a DLC update down the road.  In conclusion, Citadelum disappointed me. It has a few fun ideas, but fails to leverage them into a compelling and replayable overall experience. I’ve yet to see a price announcement, but... I wouldn’t recommend it for anything north of $15 USD. So, I’m giving Citadelum a rough aggregate MEGA score of 2.22/5 (full scoring breakdown from "Plot" to "Sound" available in the video review), but, as always, I’m more than happy to answer any questions you have about the game or my review. Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: I am pretty happy with the few hours i put into this.Now i never played Ceasar games, but i have played CivCity Rome... which for all purposes this is a better game than that ever will be.I enjoy the general simplicity, food is easy to manage and you do not need much of anything to support a large city, which is nice, i personally do not mind simpler games.Bassically you build workshops/farms/other to gain resources, you need people for said workshops so you build houses, but wait all of that needs salaries, money to be paid, so you build another type of houses that need more than those houses and those houses you only Tax, which gives you back money. Its relatively simple, just build buildings when you need them, periodically increase the ammount when your population is really large and that is it. There is also automatic upgrading of houses which means they have more people/get taxed more, that ussualy just means more resources but you also need to make things more appealing such as putting down decorations, its not too picky about it although some Ranges might seem a bit short, its nothing like CivCity Rome which required you to have your entire city planned in your head due to how short ranges are here, plus once you realise that Storage houses can be accesed from any distance so you can safely keep them far away from houses, its not that bad.The big downside is Religion, the Gods in this are picky, in fact ill highlight, the Tutorial of this game is bad, i have advanced past the point of tutorial multiple times that it stopped giving me tips [since it goes in a specific order rather than being dynamic] so at a point i got hit by God's being picky, and the game only told me about how to manage gods after i had suffered multiple of my buildings being destroyed.The gods system needs some changes, they are a bit picky and pleasing them requires putting down a bit of resources... only for that to only slightly apease them.Combat is basic, not that it needs to be complex, you just make units, then in battles you make formations and - just have more units than the enemy and generally you will win.The only actual downgrade from CivCity Rome are people themselves. In this game you can look inside buildings and watch your people work, that is nice not many games do it. However in CC Rome every single Person had its own house, its own work scheduel, and houses Dynamically changed, every resources was GRAPHICALLY represented in the house, and people interacted with the buildings. Now obviously this game is much larger than CivCity, but it would have been nice to see bit more of a connection, especelly since things like people in Theater appear out of thin air, rather than seeing people go to acting school, then going to a theater, and also going home when their its their free time, but again, this game is much larger so that might be more complex.Overall i am pretty happy, no issues though performance does get a bit stuttery on a large city, overall pretty simple but very fun game, its worth the asking price imho.

_childDocuments_.review: ------------------What is Citadelum?------------------Citadelum is a grid-based, Roman city builder game where you manage resources, trade with neighbouring cities and battle enemy armies on the map. Similar to one of my old favourites, the classic Imperium Romanum Gold Edition.----------Game Types----------Choose between Campaign or Sandbox Mode. It also has a Map Editor for those who want to make their own campaign.--------------------Campaign Mode Screen--------------------You choose between several missions from Easy to Hard difficulty. Each Campaign has a checklist of tasks you must complete. Examples like (Send 300 Wheat to Rome, Discover 3 cities on the map, defeat 2 armies, Increase desirability of 4 plebian Houses to level 6 etc.) You get the jist.------------------Building your City------------------ You start off with having to pick a place on the map to build your forum, preferably near water, fertile soil, rocks and ore etc.. Then you start building homes for your citizens, there are 2 types of houses.. - Plebian houses, are simple buildings, these house your workers which you need to staff your industry buildings, farms, storage, maintenance etc.- Patrician houses are different, they provide cash for your settlement; build a tax office near them and they will give you money.You have to provide both houses with basic needs, Plebs need wheat and clean water, Patricians need clean water, watermelons and cabbage. Increasing the desirability by placing fancy statues, hedges, fountains etc. near their houses? Increases the size of the house giving you more workers in Pleb houses and providing more in taxes from your Patrician houses, houses can upgrade up to 6 levels, the highest levels require theatres, arenas, baths, doctors and a whole array of meats and vegetables etc. to keep them happy, but reward you with maximum workers and tax payers.Houses require.. - A road connecting to your forum.- Aqueducts to provide fresh drinking water.- Maintenance buildings like a Fire Station and Engineer Building to stop buildings setting on fire and collapsing.- Guard Houses to reduce crime.- A Market to provide them with food with the buildings that make and store food and wares.- Avoid putting certain buildings that reduce desirability too close to your houses.- Provide Entertainment, Religious etc. Buildings to keep your pops happy and unlock next level homes.- Desirability objects that improve desirability, upgrading your houses and their capacity. -------------------Keep the Gods happy-------------------As your city progresses, you must build Temples to the gods and offer them sacrifices and festivals to honour them.There are 6 Gods that MUST be appeased, Minerva, Ceres, Jupiter, Mars, Apollo and Pluto.You will go through the game filling their happiness bar; if you make them happy? They will offer their blessing which is basically a buff to a certain part of your city; but if you neglect them? They will appear in your city and destroy select buildings they represent. Examples, Mars, God of War will grant you instant soldiers, but will destroy your barracks, stables and archery buildings if you anger him. Ceres is the Goddess of Fertility, appease her and she will fill your farms with produce, anger her and she will destroy those farms.When a God lashes out, their mood bar resets to neutral and slowly starts decreasing back to angry again if you continue to neglect them.---------------------Beware the Barbarians---------------------Your settlement eventually will be attacked by barbarian raiders, they will burn down several of your buildings before dispersing.You have to build recruitment centres, weapons buildings, watchtowers and have them manned by guards to fend them off.On the campaign map, you send explorers to venture the map, unlocking new territories.. You either discover new land, a new city to trade with, relics that grant happiness buffs to the god you choose, or you'll uncover a barbarian army (Losing your explorer in the process). There is a bar in the top right that shows you the intensity of barbarian raids, the higher the bar? The more barbarians raid your city.Wiping out armies reduce the bar, reducing the intervals between invasions, but there is always a 20% that just invade no matter if you wipe out all armies on the map.-------Battles-------Once you've built the military infrastructure, you can recruit 4 types of Roman Soldier.They fight in a Rock, Paper, Scissors type way.- Infantry, good against Cavalry, weak against Archers.- Archers, good against Infantry, weak against Cavalry.- Cavalry, good against Archers, weak against Infantry.- Centurion, single support unit that buffs the troops. You choose what units to use, strategically place them on the battlefield, make them aggressive or defensive and move the units towards the enemy.Certain areas of the map are blocked by barbarians requiring an army to remove them. Some need to be defeated in order to progress the campaign.----------Conclusion----------It's a pretty little city builder and it's quite challenging to play, misplacing buildings or forgetting a certain need could sew chaos into your city. Has a wonderful Soundtrack that captures the Roman feel.Problem solving when something in your city goes wrong is always a fun little Brain teaser.. That is.. Until you figure out exploits, like building loads of Pig Farms to spam the Gods with sacrifices to activate buffs.You can recruit yourself an army without even needing to build infrastructure to arm your recruits, just their barracks; simply keep spamming Mars with 19 Pig sacrifices and you'll have an army in no time.Same exploit applies to filling your farms with endless produce with Ceres, keeping people constantly happy with Jupiter, or filling your coffers with gold from Pluto. Spoils the game when you get to the level that you can unlock the Pig Farm, all plain sailing from there.It's battle system is a simplified version of Songs of Syxx, not on par with it.The way Imperium Romanum does it's war mechanics is way better and more satisfying than Citadelum.The User Interface for battles needs serious improvement, you can't click on the unit you want to move when they are all clumped together in battle, causing many casualties.I've played much better City Builders than this, I don't think I will ever play this game again now that I've completed all the campaigns.There are better City Builders out there. Imperium Romanum is way better and it came out in 2008, grab a copy on GOG or Steam for £7.99 (Grab it 7 hour after posting this for 50% off £3.99 on GOG)This game gets a 'Meh!" rating from me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game transported me to a black hole where I easily spent 6 hours building a small sized city in sandbox mode. I’m excited to get into the real gameplay soon. I’ve never played Caesar that people are comparing this to but to me it feels like a hybrid between age of empires and anno. The mechanics are polished and easy to learn. I love the little details put into the game like the inside view of the buildings. I hope to see additional production chains and building types as well as more levels/classes in future updates or DLC. My one pain point with this game is actually with the camera, which needs to zoom out much further to be able to easily see your city sections. Overall, highly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a good city builder (I haven't played Ceasar but I have played Zeus a lot so I will talk more from the perspective of the latter).I will mostly point out the things I find lacking or that could be better. The game could see a lot more quality-of-life improvements.- Markets seem a little slow/weak. If you build full households in their radius, they do not seem to feed the households fast enough. They should be operating at 100% within their coverage! That is what the coverage should mean- The game lacks macro economic sliders/controls. In Zeus you can just reduce your workforce with an easy Up/down slider to say "all/most, some/very little" in here, you have to manually toggle up every workplace to go up to 4. Either let us set defaults or to control this at a large scale. The economy screens are not great to be honest and I don't use them much- Immigration is suuuper slow. When I build a ton of housing, I wouldn't get them filled even by when I would get through the entire mission- Granary/Storehouses also seem a little inefficient. My farms often are plagued by "this is holding all the resources it can" icons, even though there is an empty storage place within radius. It honestly sucks that storage needs to be so close to the materials. In Zeus, it didn't matter how close you are storage, they would just deliver it anywhere.- Can we get the bars for the Gods to be visible at all times, or pop up when they are almost red? Having to hover over to check each one can be inconvenient. Also, clicking on a god should zoom you over to the temple, so you're not scrambling to find where the temple of a particular god is- Visual clarity on buildings is not great. I know I keep touting Zeus, but that game delivers so much more information at a glance because the buildings are far more distinct and colorful. I  can instantly know if my houses are at max level, what kind of farm I'm looking at, etc. It's a lot harder here.I'll like the game more if it's smoothed out.

_childDocuments_.review: As a passionate fan of citybuilders, I can highlight many positive points that I have seen in my hours of play:- The campaign is varied and is very well if you want to go following a bit of the history. In addition the tutorial explains everything in detail but leaving you free to advance at your own pace.- The sandbox mode is excellent: you can customize the game and for example play without enemy attacks to build the city peacefully.- What I see more potential but I have not yet been able to test is the part of creating maps and missions and upload them to Steam Workshop. I have already subscribed to some of the maps that have been uploaded and they offer totally different things to the campaign. In short, it is a game to spend all the hours in the world.

_childDocuments_.review: Citadelum is a faithful modern take on the classic city builders Caesar, Zeus, Pharaoh, etc. The smooth control scheme, detailed feedback and management, and graphics are welcome updates. It also utilizes a global resource pool which prevents the economy from getting too bogged down. It scratches the city building itch for me.Unfortunately it doesn't have the charming sense of humor that I loved in Zeus. Citadelum plays it very straight. It also is lacking the giant capstone projects; temples are cheap and are built instantly.I have a couple easy wins to suggest. There should be a sound effect that plays at the start of each day, as I am often sitting around with zero money until taxes are collected. I guess it could be even better if taxes are collected continuously. The second thing is that the city level notifications are actually startling and disruptive. I always scream in surprise when they pop up and it even cancels the item I was placing at the time.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like it, but sadly it is quite boring and repetetive. The pseudo rts style battles are mostly "fake".I should have refunded when i could, but as I said I really wanted to give it a chance and forced myself to play the "campaign".It should be rated as mediocre, so i need to give it a negative review - overall rather as "very positive" is not justified..
_childDocuments_.name: Citadelum

_childDocuments_.review: Citadelum is a cozy Roman city-builder in which you have to produce different resources, make sure your citizens see their needs fulfilled and engage in war and trade, while making sure to please the gods. Or it should be. Sadly, the result is a bit mixed.The basis for the game is great, it works well and I find the art cute. And the music, oh, the music is fantastic! However, the game has a big problem: the lack of challenge and consequence make the game repetitive and unsatisfying to some degree. More info about this on .Nevertheless, Citadelum has a lot of potential and I still recommend the game. Just take into account that it won't offer complex challenges and that it may turn repetitive soon. But I hope the developers can keep improving the game, because it can truly become a masterpiece and I'll be here for it!

_childDocuments_.review: Recommend: Yes, but I do have some issues with the game. Overall I enjoyed the game, but there are a few things that just seem to fall short. If you are looking for a city builder game, this one does an okay job, but I would recommend Nebuchadnezzar for a better experience.  Campaign: The campaign has about 10 maps or so and each map has about five victory conditions. Once you finish the conditions, you are prompted to move on to the next map or continue playing. To me this system falls short and feels unfinished. Having the conditions play out over "steps" and adding more conditions would have improved the campaign. Also, having the player play a map, move to a different map and then go back to that map later in the campaign would have made the campaign feel more complete. Money: The money is more or less irrelevant after you get your basic setup in place. On the "Hard" maps, I would run out of funds, but a 5k grant would give me just the boost I needed to get over the hump and then money did not matter. Gods: The gods don't really have an impact on gameplay. If you ignore the gods, which I did for the first part of the building process, they would get mad and hop down to your city and cause a little damage. Usually they would destroy four or so buildings and then off they go. The other gods "angry" meter would then reset and they would not be an issue for a bit.

Gods mechanics are fun, depending on the level of the city maintaing their needs can get to You.One thing I'm not the fan of is the soundtrack. It's quite generic, and gets borring quickly.Otherwise very good game!

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game as stated by many reviewers. Nothing to add here, other than that I would like more content, a good campaign like in Pharaoh and Zeus is desperately needed (yes I played user content) and an extra zoom level on the city would really be nice. _childDocuments_.review: Caesar resurrectedWell, if you do like the classic Caesar games series you might like this one too. It plays very similar and allows you to build an ancient Roman city to your liking. Roads, water, food, baths, culture and entertainment have to be managed and your city has to be fortified and defended. There are lots of farms, raw materials and trade shops to run. The Plebeians do the work and have to be paid, while the Patricians do pay the taxes. Your city is alive and its denizens do go to the public baths, temples and theaters. The Olympic Gods are a bit too flippant depicted and by the time you can call on their favors they don't help you much...There is also a world map on which you do explore, trade and fight. Although it is heresy to call a formation of 200 men a Roman Legion...It is a new indie game and therefore has some childhood illnesses like bug or poor balancing but the core is good and should be made better over time by the developers. If you have to quarry marble is to be questioned but olive oil and Rome are inseparable. We need to plant olive groves. And the Romans die use the public baths nude of course. Even if the Pope does not allow it afterwards... I would give the game an 8 out of 10.
_childDocuments_.name: Citadelum

_childDocuments_.review: A city builder and economic sim set in ancient Rome, this is reminiscent of Impressions Games' PC classic 'Caesar' series. 'Citadelum' is a breath of fresh air. A 360-degree camera, building interiors, excellent music, a pantheon of Gods to appease or infuriate, exploration, trade, and the list continues. I've yet to encounter any bugs. Everything works the way I want it to. This reminds me of the level of quality you used to be able to expect from PC games. It's absolutely magnificent.
_childDocuments_.name: Citadelum

_childDocuments_.review: The game is well made, but it's way too hectic for me. I prefer a little more relaxing style. This feels like a constant disaster simulator. Some of this may be because I'm playing it for the first time and not as efficient as I could be, but it's just non-stop. There doesn't feel like there's any chance to catch your breath. You are non-stop building housing because the moment you build one house people start moving in. Of course, this means you need all the other services people want.But this is more of a "me problem" than anything. The game seems very good, and I'll continue to play it off and on and maybe I'll click with it later. I don't want to give a thumbs down. It seems fine for people who like this style of play.
_childDocuments_.name: Citadelum

_childDocuments_.review: A curious case: most indie games are launched in EA nowadays; this one was not but it should have been. Some parts are not finished at all; patches were promised - we'll see.It is playable, of course; not optimized  (quite a few people seem to have problems with overheating) but I encountered no real bugs or CTDs so far. Some other points:- I like the graphics: crisp, just my type and the main reason why I bought the game. You can look inside a house; a nice idea but with a problem: exteriors change after a house is upgraded but interiors never do - once you've seen one you've seen all. Forum looks the same from start to finish - a real mistake. Maps are kind of samey (I haven't tried the user-made ones yet).- Gods are also a nice addition. At first I was disappointed that there are only six of them, but then I had enough problems with this bunch to stop complaining. (At least I understand now why Romans turned christian in the end.) I do miss Venus but since there is no sex in the game she would be redundant. - All of them act as dei ex machina but that's to be expected, I guess.- Production chains are OK but nothing new there. Some more or less curious details like onion (etc.) orchards (one learns something new every day) and stone cutters making bricks  (OK, stone bricks, but they are not called that); no real brickworks at all - Romans would be baffled.- Finances: think of yourself as a Roman Jeff Bezos and you'll be fine. Also, export everything you can and import nothing, unless you absolutely have to. No real dynamics there.- Warfare: not a Total War game, of course, but even the rock-paper-scissors system does not work ATM.- Lacks most of the charm and wit of Impressions games on which it is obviously based.Hard to decide. If you haven't played Impressions games you should try them first. If you are searching for a serious simulation you should take a look at Grand Ages Rome (not perfect either) or wait for Pax Augusta (which might be really good but will probably take years to complete). Citadelum sort of covers the middle ground; I will recommend it but beware of all the caveats.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a city builder that has some limiting factors that could frustrate some players.  Is it fun for casual game play sure but if you are expecting a Caesar III revamp this isn't it.It's will limit your population growth so if you hate games that prevent you from doing things fast this game isn't for you.  You can have every other resource but you are going to wait for ever to fill that population cap. And god forbid if you have one unemployed citizen.  This game will remind you of your mistake of not having a job for him set up a hour before he comes in every 5 secs. I haven't traded much with other cities because I usually get everything I need in the map and money isn't an issue because tax dollars easy to fill the coffers.

_childDocuments_.review: This brings me back to Caesar II in the fondest possible way. A game which I just wasn't old enough to fully comprehend the full complexity of but could appreciate the visuals, ambiance, and pacing. All those are elements are here in spades. I never played C3 so maybe there was some improvement to the battle system over C2, but the combat/military arm of Citadelum is way more enjoyable than my memories. I will say my number one sticking point is the Area of Effect UI while placing a building is identical to the buildings having already been placed making it difficult to figure out where one is needed, esp as you can't zoom out too far imo. That's the only thing that really bothers me repeatedly... zooming further out would be dope too.Smooth flow & pacing, just frantic enough. Although I'm still yet to complete the campaign so it definitely hasn't reached peak urgency, which I think is a good thing. Works well on the Steam Deck too. Although at one point after a loong play session and after a quick burst of development to my settlement, she began to chug slower and slower then locked up where I had to hard reset. Set to Proton 7-35 after that and no problems so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Citadelum

_childDocuments_.review: I find this to be a very catchy game. I thought it was a revamped version of Caesar or similar games, but it has enough new features to make it its own thing. If you're a fan of the Roman era, you'll love this.I think there is some room for improvement, with more features, maps, and scenarios to be added. Relying on the creator community is fine, but the game could use some fresh content once every few months, at least.
_childDocuments_.name: Citadelum

_childDocuments_.review: I had the opportunity to test this game before its official rrelease and all I can say is : that's a great indie game in the line of Caesar III. The game is very clean and polished for a release (no game-breaking bugs, good optimization and cute graphics). battles can be played in real-time (similar to total war though in a smaller scale) and gods can roam trough the streets if summoned after rituals and festivals, providing boons or ires depending of their resent toward your people.And the ice on top of the cake : I'm often very sharp with the game devs and direct so this means a lot :Abylight Barcelona devs are good guys, reactive, open-minded, they listen to their community and those things must be highlighted. It's a quality very few devs can claim to have today.Both of their games (citadelum and One Military Camp) deserve to be in the city-builder aficionados library.Keep going that way Abylight !
_childDocuments_.name: Citadelum

_childDocuments_.review: Its an okayish Roman Anno Clone with lots of potential.Gameplay is fun and I enjoy it not being overcomplex as the later Stages (and DLCs) for the other mentioned game, BUT Citadelum needs some more of everything. For 20 bucks, its fine, but still feels like Early Access. We'll see if it grows.Not necessarly more/oovercomplex, but wider, or like getting another population tier.Nevertheless, at the current state I'd rate it 6/10 "Buy it because you're in general a fan of the rome topic or city builders" because of:The Market mechanic sucks. Let the people GET their stuff from the markets. Not let market traders bring stuff to the single houses - too many houses in the influence area of a market? Those plebejans starve... The patricians do not develop besides all needed goods are overproduced and similar slightly sketchy stuff.It needs some shortcut keys - half the interface feels quite copied from Anno anyways, so it sucks that there is no keys for roads, warehouses, houses and so on.It needs upgrades for fire stations and the architect to enlarge their range, maybe for other buildings too.It needs an option to set good limits for warehouses and granaries, currently it's on/off only AND the buildings need precious workforce to collect AND deliver.Sliders in the trade view... srsly... Just let us type numbers.The gods need to demand festivities, in form of a pop-up, maybe even like a choice "Two gods demand..." with buffs in one area and debuffs in another, even ZEUS from 2000 did that more... immersing.The campaign is presented very rudimentary and boring, after half the second "tutorial" mission, I went to sandbox.Main question is: How far does Citadelum evolve before A117 drops, will it keep fans for its very own charme and beautiful details (love looking into the buildings) as well as the quite small scale... Or will it be abondoned and vanish.
_childDocuments_.name: Citadelum

_childDocuments_.review: I was one of the privileged few who had the opportunity to play Citadelum in advance and without restrictions. Over 2 weeks, totaling 50 hours, I enjoyed this surprising game that captivated me every evening after work.I left my suggestions and pointed out some bugs and inconsistencies—as expected, but I had no major issues, and the game ran smoothly on my PC without any CTD (crash to desktop) incidents. With every suggestion I made on Discord, there was always a response from the developers, seeking perfection while staying true to the project’s initial vision. I increasingly prefer indie game developers for this very reason: their closeness to the community and their tireless pursuit of perfection and the joy of playing and enjoying the game.Although this game already offers many delightful and addictive elements (in a good way), which fully justifies its purchase, the developers are committed to continuing the development with new buildings, new challenges, and improvements to the current mission editor.With the continuous development of the mission editor, it will be possible to extend the life of the game and, consequently, provide additional hours of enjoyment.For those who loved Caesar III in the past, as well as its current mods, you will surely feel at home and relive those good and addictive times. I’m reliving them now, and I thank the developers for Citadelum.Expect new missions from me and the entire Citadelum fan community in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: == amazing , 5 truly jesters gave me fake jester icons , It seems like you enjoy racial chaos and distorting history; you're indeed a jester . please give me more , let me know how many of you , dont let me down . =====================================================================================The game isn’t difficult to play. It features a retro gameplay style based on old-school city-building simulation games, which has been simplified. The AI logic in the game is much better, and the details of the buildings, interiors, and city dynamics are very well done. The recruitment system for military units, in particular, is not as complex as in older games. I highly recommend purchasing this game.However, despite this, I would still give it a negative review. The studio isn’t a large or even mid-sized one, and I believe a studio of this scale and status, working on a game with this theme, wouldn’t fully attract the attention or exploitation of a company like SweetBaby.Although in the later period of the Roman Empire, due to its policies, there were instances of Black citizens, the situation portrayed in the game—where 50% of the population is Black and the other 50% is White, with the streets filled with a chaotic or balanced mix of races—is far from historical reality. There is no clear historical evidence that Black soldiers served in the Roman army. In the game’s Italian peninsula map, the entire city is Black. The Roman Empire was a maritime power surrounding the Mediterranean, and it never advanced deep into central or southern Africa. Additionally, starting from the mid-3rd century, the "barbarization" of Roman soldiers reached 75%, but even then, these soldiers were still from other European ethnic groups, not African. During both the Roman Empire and Western Roman Empire periods, the majority of the military was still made up of people from the European continent. So where did all these Black soldiers come from? This is truly laughable. screenshot hereI must say that this studio's inexplicable pandering to DEI (Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion) by distorting racial history is the greatest insult to both history and mythological systems. Can I crudely and stereotypically interpret this as Westerners enjoying distorting their own history and taking pride in it?For example, take Relic, the studio that develops RTS games. In their games, they would rather insert Black soldiers, who sacrificed themselves in the fight against fascism, as mere appendages in all-White units than actually study and restore the real military organization of Black soldiers in the U.S. Army during World War II. They also refuse to accurately respect and represent them in the game.Who are the true beneficiaries of diversity? This is a laughable and ironic question.

_childDocuments_.review: Gaming on Linux: This game runs out of the Box using Proton on my Arch. For me it looks like Platinum status in this regards. I could not find anything that is not just working as expected. % out of 5 for the technical experinece.The first two campaign missons are kind of a tutorial that helps you to understand the game mechanics. That's nice. I like, that the campaign missons are embeded in a historical context and not pure fantasy. However the campaign itself unfortunately lacks a bit a comprehensive story.I would have hoped for an epic story about the rise and fall of rome. More a 3 out of 5.The city builder part itslef is until now very soft and easy going. So far no real chalenge for somebody experienced in the genre, I miss a little bit the puzzeling etc e.g from Anno. The production chains are nice but could have little more depth/compexity. Again a 3 out of 5.The battle part looks a on the first sight somewhatt like total war but gives you little to no control about the units. Its more a less just about placing the units on a map and press the play button. I couldn't figure out how to gain more control. This is more 2 out of 5 for me.Just a little more on this side, e.g. similar to "Centurion: Defender of Rome" and I would be happy.Bottom line I had hoped for a mixture of the good ol Cesar games and a game called "Centurion: Defender of Rome" from about the same time. While Cesar was more about the city building, centurion was about help rome to expand. It was a nice strategic battel simulator with a focus on conquering what was later called the roman emprie.I can still recommend the game, but I think at the moment there are a lot of unused opportunites and potential to create a realy great game out of the solid fundament.If the devs are reading here: I would be really nice to exchnage the texture of the default plaster (level 2 street, bottom texture of the forum) to something nicer looking. _childDocuments_.review: tl;dr, 7/10. It'll satisfy your Caesar III urge, just don't go in looking for a complex and granular city building experience.The best word I can use to describe Citadelum is 'formulaic'. City design is going to be pretty much the same from mission to mission and you'll do pretty much the exact same sequence of actions to achieve pretty much the exact same results with only a small amount of variation. The game desperately needs some sort of system in place to funnel your resources and give you a reason to really specialize, such as the need to establish complex trade systems like you had to in the Impressions Series. Or building monuments, those were always great fun.This isn't to say the game is BAD. It looks pretty, it plays smoothly, and it's genuinely fun to build up your city. You won't run into any sudden difficulty cliffs. It's a very good 'pick up and play' sort of game. I just wish there was more to do, and more long-term goals to work towards.Combat is basic but it gets the job done. Exploration could use an automation option.

_childDocuments_.review: Citadelum is an exceptional city-building game. If you're a fan of the Caesar series, you'll feel right at home here. The game offers a perfect blend of fun, relaxation, and strategy, making it an enjoyable experience for both casual players and seasoned fans of the genre.The city management mechanics are solid, with a great balance between resource gathering, building, and expanding your settlement into a magnificent Roman city. The game also shines with its stunning graphics, bringing the beauty of Ancient Rome to life in a way that feels immersive and rich in detail.In addition to the city-building aspect, Citadelum also offers tactical battles and a dynamic world to explore. The option to lead your legions into epic confrontations adds an exciting layer of strategy. You can also interact with the Gods, earning their favor—or challenging them if you're feeling bold!Overall, Citadelum is a fantastic game for anyone who loves city builders and Roman history. It's relaxing, visually impressive, and packed with depth, making it a must-play for fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a basic Roman city builder. It is priced accordingly, and from a small set of devs. Played as such, it's a gem for those who enjoyed the Caesar games. Its limitations are very clear from early on - there is next to no progression. You will get access to everything very quickly, and if I were to take a guess, the roadmap for the gameplay probably had much more development of the mechanics. For example, the army can only be used on the regional map, not on the city map, where you need guards instead. It leads to armies rampaging through the city when there is in theory an entire legion there.The gods are a nice addition, but limited in that they are either happy or angry. There's no politics between them. You don't have to sacrifice one's favour for another. Throw some money at them and they will come down and give you some superficial rewards.The regional map is a nice addition, but the battles are simple. Just get a huge army and throw them at them. There's no tactics. The formations are pointless - again, this was clearly going to be further developed, but they ran out of time/money.So, this is a long way from perfect, and it's basic and it's old school. BUT... it's fun for a few hours, and it's worth my money in the hope they can develop Citadelum 2 and do more with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Citadelum

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent game that really harks back to the legendary Caesar 3.The main praise goes to the dynamic production, which is fun, and the variety of productions (there could even be more!) available.The battles have interesting mechanics, but I suggest improvements in the movement of troops, which sometimes go in directions that are not in battle.The God system is also well balanced.Exploring the map is another positive point.As for negative points, I think the game deserved better graphics. This is something to think about for a sequel to the game.The campaign is very short, but the community map system (this was a great goal by the developers) partly makes up for the lack of more episodes to play.The game is also quite square, which is fine, it reflects a classic. But since the release of Manor Lords, I feel that making the city more organic would appeal more to a city builder player.Finally, I want to congratulate you on the initiative. The game really is fun. It's worth the price and I recommend it to everyone on Steam.For those of you who read to the end, give me a gift. :)

You must do the missions on the campaign so each time you need to plan differently for different goals. Also, there are some battles you need to do when discovering the map outside your city and if you don’t fight the enemies, they attack you, so you need to prepare an army and guard your city with city defenses and city guards. The battles itself are not like total war of course, but they are pleasant and fun.Another thing you can is play the sandbox mode where you don’t have objectives and just do your city as you wish, and I also had some good time on it. O sandbox mode I spent more time on visuals and decorating the city and I enjoyed it a lot.I can recommend this game for casual players like me, because I enjoyed every aspect of it, from planning, to resource management, to the battles and decorating but I believe that for veteran players that play a lot of city builders this game will be easy.The upcoming free dlc is also a pleasant thing since there is nothing to do after the main campaign besides the sandbox.

Combat does leave much to be desired in term of sending troops out to fight enemy armies as its mostly automated movement and requires little player interaction.

name: Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord
detailed_description: The horns sound, the ravens gather. An empire is torn by civil war. Beyond its borders, new kingdoms rise. Gird on your sword, don your armour, summon your followers and ride forth to win glory on the battlefields of Calradia. Establish your hegemony and create a new world out of the ashes of the old. Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord is the eagerly awaited sequel to the critically acclaimed medieval combat simulator and role-playing game, Mount & Blade: Warband. Create and develop a character that matches your play style as you explore, raid and conquer your way across a vast medieval sandbox where no two playthroughs are the same. Raise armies, engage in politics, trade, craft weapons, recruit companions and manage your fiefdom as you attempt to establish your clan among the nobility of Calradia. Command and fight alongside your troops in first- or third-person in huge real-time battles using Mount & Blade’s deep but intuitive skill-based directional combat system. Put your combat prowess to the test against players from all over the world in multi-player PvP, including ranked matchmaking and casual game modes, or host your own server with the Mount & Blade II: Dedicated Server files. Customise the game to experience an entirely different adventure using the Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord - Modding Kit and share your creations with others through Steam Workshop.

_childDocuments_.review: To be frank, I'm very torn on whether to recommend the game. Because it IS in early access and because I have faith the developers WILL turn it into a worthwhile game, I will go ahead and recommend.Here is the main issue - in it's current state, it is a graphically polished yet resoundingly hollow copy of Warband. Quest variety is not there. Earning renown is an absolute chore (+3 renown for winning a tournament? Really?)The map topography feels very odd and clustered with mountains and rivers.Combat is definitely more difficult, but as others have said, it turns into a slog of whack everything that isn't you.Combat AI is improved, I had a fun tournament experience with some 1 on 1s. But Campaign AI feels lackluster.Item variety from trading is broken and nonsensical at times with notably few options.I have 95% confidence it will become the game we want it to become. That 5% doubt is just the sheer disbelief that I have become bored after only one day when this sequel was in development for almost a decade. Still, I believe the developers will listen to the community and make it the game we believe it can be.DEVELOPERS - please take notes about what made Diplomacy, Floris, etc. Warband mods so popular. We want meaningful depth.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to maintain a positive tone, but it's undeniable that this game is essentially dead—it's not just dead, it's buried. It's disheartening to witness how this game, especially after the success of Warband, has turned into a ghost town.If you're new to the Mount and Blade series, you can give Bannerlord a shot, but don't set your expectations too high for developer support. At this point, the only hope for revitalizing the game lies with modders.Sad day for gamers.

_childDocuments_.review: I have at this point put 42 hours into this game and I will say while it was a lot of fun, I wont be playing again until full release. I still give a thumbs up because the combat is amazing and the game aesthetically looks really nice and has some good lore potential behind it. Right now there is just an unplayable broken mechanics that 40-50 hours in will end your campaign, and that is the entire taking over of the map by a single faction thus ending your game, or making it really boring. I would love to see a civil war mechanic or an alliance mechanic for smaller kingdoms to team up on an encroaching super power, but until that happens I have to stop playing for a bit. I would say get the game if you're okay with trying it out for curiosity and some of its better mechanics. Overall I just think this game needs more time which makes sense since its early access but I really hope their main priority right now is rebalancing power between factions so one doesn't end up dominating the entire map so easily. I have high hopes though and hope it'll be closer to potential in another year or so!

_childDocuments_.review: After many years of waiting for a great successor of M&B: Warband - I am disappointed. Developers have lost their sense of whats good for the game and whats not. Endless development with no hope of it ever becoming a title we have all been waiting for. Why do they keep updating multiplayer with meaningless updates? Cheers? MVP system? Skins? Who ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cares? Why arent they focusing entirely on singleplayer untill the official release?2022: its even worse - every minor update breaks most of the mods so you cant even play without crashing every 15 minutes. Very fun game indeed.Combat AI without mods is complete ♥♥♥♥. Siege towers? - well, devs prefer to work on mvp and competetive system in a dead multiplayer rather than fixing core mechanics in singleplayer. Again, modders are repairing those issues where it becomes ridiculous when this game is unplayable (atleast for me) without mods.Shame. Dont get me wrong, its still a good game, but I expected more from TaleWorlds. If you are ready for whacky AI, unfinished singleplayer with endless and meaningless slaughtering hundreds of brainless meatbags OR downloading tens of mods (through third-party websites because workshop is still not implemented) that make this game bearable after 10 hours - go ahead and buy it, you will have fun for sure. For now I would wait and see if the final release (if we will see one in the next year) will be anything better than this. I still have hope for TW to make use of this great opportunity for possibly the best game in this genre.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Warband with lipstick smeared poorly on it's beautiful face.From the old Papyrus font to the UI, there's nothing new. They've even recycled the quests, and made it less obvious where things are than the first game.A lot of the features are dumbed down.And bugs. Bugs everywhere. Holy crap. Enjoy your entire empire getting stuck running into a town to chase an enemy with 1 unit (themselves) for eternity, until they also run out of food and turn into 1-unit armies.Then there's the siege bugs which are going to be nasty to solve - units that get pushed below the ground, or are surrounded so thickly by troops that you can't end the battle.LET'S BE REAL: If you played M&B1 enough to be bored of it, you'll find nothing in M&B2 to interest you. 10 years of dev work to essentially reskin models.Even worse, low graphic settings look worse than M&B1 and for some players (according to the discord) it's still SLOWER than M&B1. Jeez.Don't buy if: - you got enough out of M&B1. There's nothing new to see here. - you have an mid tier computer, you won't be able to run it. - you expect a polished game. Some early-access games have at worst some weird edge-case bugs. This one's riddled with them.

_childDocuments_.review: This is game is in a very odd place. The game is not finished at all - it is certainly early access.4.5/5 Graphically - This game is marvelous what you see is a beautifully animated and well designed world, at any moment especially during war you can feel like you are actually watching a movie more than playing a game.2.5/5 Controls - I'm throwing some shade at the game here, I miss lock on and between this and kingdom come I'm starting to see that developers are moving towards how to make controls as confused as they can. I at times feel I could enjoy the game more if I was looking at the game rather than at four arrows or trying to shift my mouse so as to block in the correct direction. I just feel like the controls are taking away from the game more than they are adding to it. The only saving grace for the controls is the large scale combat which has a learning curve but not to the extent that it inhibits me from seeing what is actually happening on screen and being taken for a ride on how amazing the game is. The current combat system is really distracting but the war controls are spot on. 5/5 Game Play - There are about 50 hours of game play before you get bored and 150 before you accomplish anything grand and another 100 of that before you get close to beating the game. Is it grindy HELL YES, is it doable... certainly. BannerLord suffers here but I'm giving it a perfect score only because its early access. There is a game here, with loads of content but it feels like there could be more - things are missing it feels like at each level of the game.By level of the game I mean that the game really transitions into different things as you play. One second you are a clan leader basically being nomadic, then you are strong enough that someone might want you in their kingdom or you can try to make your own. Finally you get to Empire and so on... but some things are just missing - such as looking for a Lord to parley - sometimes these lords simply disappear. So while the game is saying they are in a city you cannot find them in that city and they never leave so you can speak with them.5/5 The experience - The music, lighting and world building in this game are all what saves everything else. If it wasn't for the combat being utterly distracting and repulsive I'd simply say this was a good game without the experience but with the experience this is a great game.Overall - 4/5

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed SOME of the game. But I gave up on actually completing a campaign. I progressed to the point where it was just mine and one other kingdom. After that I lost interest in finishing. Understand that I haven't cheated in a game since I was a little kid. I don't like cheating because it completely kills the sense of accomplishment and success for me. But this game, it pretty much forces you to cheat if you want a "fair" playing field. Where to even begin? Vassals leaving your kingdom - You need clans to join your kingdom if you want any hope of conquering the other factions. Without them your kingdom is weak and will get demolished by factions with a stronger military force(more clans). You slave away to build your charm skill and raise your relation with nobles so that you can convince clans to join your side. Only for them to leave at random for no reason at all regardless of whether or not you have high relation with them. This breaks the game imo. Recruiting Clans - This is 50/50 from what I saw. Some clans will join you just be convincing them. But other times they will want a substantial amount of denars to convince them EVEN AFTER winning the mini convincing game. This is impossible to manage when you don't have many fiefs and aren't making enough money. And again, they will just leave at random, causing you to waste money on them. War Declaration - Its nonsense. Before you have any hope of building a strong enough military force, other factions will declare war on you and your tiny little army of a few clans will get ravaged without a drop of sweat falling off your enemies. Every fief you worked hard for will get taken from you and your kingdom will be fiefless. And paying denars to make peace is a waste of time. As you play the game they seem to want more and more amounts of it to actually make peace. Its rediculus and also game breaking. It was at this moment that I actually started cheating, practically spamming  the "declare peace" command every 5 minutes because I kept going broke from it.Execution of Nobles - So you wanna give up trying to be nice and "convincing" clans to join your kingdom? Now you wanna throw away the nice guy persona and start chopping off heads as a plan B to even the odds of your kingdom vs others? Guess what, this is massive trap that will pretty much ruin you in the long term. Pretty much every noble will hate you and never join you. Speaking of hating you, raiding villages is also a trap. Easy supplies sure, but the villagers will hate you causing you to miss out on a buttload of recruits for your army. These negatives that I mentioned pretty much forced me to cheat. I really don't see how anyone can actually create a kingdom and conquer the map WITHOUT using atleast some cheats. Or maybe I'm just not big brain enough to figure it out? Aside from all that, the combat is amazing. I liked the sieging and the massive 1000+ battles. Formations actually seem to matter. I've managed to overcome massive odds from just good positioning and formation. This is a major plus and my eyes were glued to my screen in pretty much every battle I was in. I don't think this game is worth the price tag though. I would go as far to say it IS a complete game content wise. But there are way too many game breaking problems I had with it on a mechanical side. If you want to play this game, I highly suggest you download the mod that lets you access the admin commands. You will need them.....Alot

_childDocuments_.review: This is a first impressions review on launch.Massive fan of the series but very disappointed so far. Hope my explaination inspries change, because all the aspects they have improved are excellent and well done.Bit of background:2200 hours in Warband almost all of it spent in multiplayer, the thing that has kept me playing for so long is the incredibly easy to learn but hard to master combat mechanics, which have always been consistant.The point:As of right now everything that made warband such a rewarding and addictive experiece in its combat system, no longer exists.Compared to warband the melee combat is spammy, inconsistant, weightless/floaty and the best tactic seems to be take the longest fastest weapon available and spam attacks while moving backwards.After hitting someone once there seems very little they can do to stop subsequent attacks and the best bet is to spam back just in case you miss and then the shoe is on the other foot.The walk speed is so high compared to warband so weapon length is effectivly reduced and judging weapon distance is much harder. This and swings sometimes seem to not register, clearly passing through the target more often than is acceptable, single and multiplayer so its not the servers.Glancing blows or bounces at min and max ranges seems all to common, takes 5 hits on average with a 2h.So far its been way harder to control attack and block directions but I dont know whats changed there.Fighting multiple people effectivly has been made near on impossible because of these mechanical differences, mobbing someone is the best way to take someone out and there is no longer alot you can do about it.The shield bash is nice but that and the kick seems to be even harder to land and less useful than in warband.Feints seem pointless as you just lose the speed advantage when spamming someone.Chambers are so fast subsequently that they are rarely ever blocked but are also incredibly inconsistant to pull of.Suggestions:Slow down the combat and movement, make attacks and block much more deliberate, ideally put Warband's combat into the game and start from there but honestly that combat system is perfection imo, feint spamming might look a little funny but no more so than bannerlord in its current state.Also not a fan of the new equipment system because now everyone just looks identical with less variety of equipment to use, don't know what was wrong with CS GO style of equipment system they had, especially when you're not utilising vast variety of armour and weapons in the game.Praise:So far its all just a shame because all other aspects seemed to have gotten the time care and attention they needed.Performance on my ageing machine has been absolultly no problem and graphics have been vastly improved while staying looking the its predecessor.UI and menus lovely and finally brings warband into to modern day.Singleplayer (again minus the combat) has all of the good bits of Warband and the old RPG style has been simplified to the perfect degree without losing any charm and just increases usability and quality of life a bunchTL;DRMelee combat, the focus of the series is vastly inferior to predecessor and personally the only aspect they had to get right and sadly havent. Especially after 8 years of development.Consider copying warbands combat more closely in feel, speed and consistancy mainly.Every aspect other than the combat is a joy and is greatly improved.So far an incredible shame, I hope the devs take on critisism from veteran players.Probably wont keep playin for much longer at this stage.Thanks, Saxon

_childDocuments_.review: Updated 04/2021 - original review below.Single player has gotten a lot fixed since my first review. It is mostly stable and a ton of perks have been added/revamped to be more useful. I would say it is worth buying now if you have been on the fence about it and are interested in SP campaign/mods.----Original review---Firstly: It's in Early Access. I have ran into bugs. Rather than complaining on the forum, I do what I should be doing and report them so they can fix them.I got exactly what I paid for. An Early Access game. Same thing happened with ARK.Now for the actual review:The game runs very well in most places (sieges are a terrible grind fest with low FPS during the wall assault but performance improves once the walls are breached.) I have 60-80 FPS during field battles with a R5 2600X, 16 GB RAM and a 390X Gaming GPU. On an SSD, most maps load in 5-10 seconds. If they don't, it's a bug and gets reported.The game is beautiful. Much in the way of graphical improvements over Warband. Still the same familiar controls on the battlefield makes jumping in easy for veterans.There is a wealth of additions, such as diplomacy, which were modded into Warband but a core part of Bannerlord. You can eventually vote for kingdom policies, for example (if you aren't a mercenary in the army.)It is a bit lacking on stuff to do in the early game so far. All I have managed to do is kill 3k looters and tick off half the lords I need to talk to for the main quest by joining their enemy's service (they all walk around with 2-3x the troops I have so I can't just walk up and talk to them now.) But, that's what happens when you get antsy, lol.If you are willing to take the time to submit feedback and go into this KNOWING it is Early Access and there WILL BE BUGS (you have no excuse - it literally says all that on the detail page) then I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. I really do. There is nothing else like it on the market except the first game in the series, which is over 10 years old at this point. And yet... When you defeat a female commander on the battlefield and take her captive, your character has two dialog choices: "You are my prisoner now!" and "You are not a warrior. I will let you go." But when you capture a male commander, you get "You are my prisoner now!" and "You fought well. You are free to go." WTF Taleworlds? Clearly the female commanders are warriors... they are out there in armor commanding troops and sticking swords into their enemies. So why, oh why, must the player character treat them like they aren't? Even when the player character is also female? Just... why?I can't recommend this game because of the casual misogyny. Yeah, I get that it's a medieval setting. But it's also a *fantasy* setting. If we can have crossbowmen facing off against Roman-style legionnaires, and if our armies never die from disease or exposure, and if we don't have to feed our horses, and if we can lead 1,000 troops through the desert with no water supply, then why do you think we need "realism" in the form of misogyny? It just doesn't make any sense, and it makes the game less fun to play for those of us who aren't jerks.And yeah, I get the irony that I'm cool with lopping people's heads off in game, but I draw the line at misogyny. It's my review. Deal with it. Also, have you played your own multiplayer? You have a sexism problem in your multiplayer scene. Maybe stuff like this is part of why. Maybe that's not ok. Maybe that's a reason that those of us who are sick of sandwich jokes and attack helicopter jokes shouldn't spend money on your game.One bright point... TaleWorlds did release modding tools recently. I'll be modding the dialog. It just seems so unnecessary that I should have to.

Which will push you to eventually not want to be apart of the faction, to create your own.Marriage, the wives and husbands in this game are abundant, but alot of them have really crap skills or just bad personalities which narrows it down to a couple of wives/husbands. You work your way through getting to know them and raising your reputation with them, until they finally like you and you ask the lord of their clan for her/his hand in marriage, then all of a sudden their reputation for you is set back to 0 with very shallow dialogue choices, as if they now hate you.Another important note on the marriage system is, when your having children with your partner, there is no option to just outright have sex with them, basically your partner is just for playing board games with or making them run settlements / armies. It takes 2 weeks of being together with your partner to finally get the chance of receiving a notification of having a baby.There is no option to become assimilated with a clan if you are a female and in the Sturgian Race that can make your husband look weak from a roleplay perspective. Similar to joining a kingdom you should have the option to join your husbands/wife's clan. If you just want to backseat and not worry about leading a whole clan.All in all, I am disappointed in TaleWorlds and I have played for over 600 hours.So suffice to say this is an accurate review.

_childDocuments_.review: SUMMARY: This review is based purely on the state of the game at Early Access, and not on promised future updates, fixes or game changes. I will be changing this review as the game goes on in development.I will start by saying that Bannerlord is constantly improving, constantly being worked upon(at the time of writing this, the developers are putting out daily updates) and definitely heading in the right direction. It's not there yet, though.Features the game introduces and improves upon include a new, beautiful Calradia, a streamlined and more detailed UI, permadeath, greatly improved battle commands, siege weapons and destructible objects, truly interesting and divergent factions, and improved trade mechanics, to name just a few. Personally, one of my favourite new features is the clan system, in particular the dynasty aspect. Having my son/daughter avenge their father's pointless death seems like it would be a lot of fun.From a performance standpoint, the game has a number of bugs that are decreasing with every daily patch. I have a pretty ancient i5, 8GB of RAM and a GTX 970 and this game runs perfectly smooth on high, at least. That's not a brag, i'm just poor and can't afford an upgrade. I have had no crashes to speak of, so can't comment on that. I guess I am lucky (this setup seems bombproof...)The reason I can't recommend this game right now is because it essentially completes itself. You end up with a steamrolling/snowballing faction that obliterates everyone else, and more or less unites Calradia without you ever having influenced it at all. At least, that has been my experience across multiple games. From what I gather, others are experiencing it as well.This sort of ruins the point of the game for me. No matter how big my army is, it's virtually impossible to turn the tide after this happens, and most certainly makes the game pretty dull for me to play.I hope this gets sorted soon, and I can come back and recommend Bannerlord. Because I do love it, no matter it's flaws.PROS:- Much improved graphics over Warband- Interesting new trade mechanics- A clan and faction system that seems both streamlined and expanded- More organised combat and siege battlesCONS:- AI could be improved- Excessive loading screens- Steamroll of doomRating: (5/10)
_childDocuments_.name: Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. I've played every one of them since they've come out. The graphics have heavily been updated since the previous games and it looks amazing. The motions are smoother; I could go on forever about everything I love about this game. So I'll just give my critiques:1. I liked the old point system better... it's so hard to level up in this game, but it's clever, i guess.2. (See update at the bottom) The looter/raider mechanic sucks. This is the most important, in my opinion. There are several thousands walking around the game, more common than other war parties, traders, and villagers combined. You get captured by one group of looters and escape, then 3 seconds later another group picks you up, takes your gear and a huge percentage of your money. I've spent probably 3 of my 20 hours playing in captivity. My biggest pet peeve about the whole thing is raiding their bases. Utterly ridiculous. I roll up with 81 soldiers and try to attack a hideout, with all my most capable soldiers at the top of my list, and it only allows me to bring a 6-8 mix of soldiers, usually more recruits than veteran soldiers. This makes attacking hideouts with 20+ bandits (which is all of them) not fun, because you have to keep throwing your soldiers at them, retreating, then re-attacking. If I'm going to attack a bandit hideout, I want all of my soldiers or a fair fight... I don't want to sacrifice 50 of them to chip away at a large bandit army that my could have easily crushed. If you retreat a bunch of times, the game starts to glitch and will drop you a distance away from the hideout.3. There's a lot of dialogue that TaleWorlds forgot to add. I spoke to Nadea at my castle and all she said was "(Default into for famous player, Will try to make sure that does not occur)" and I spoke to a follower at a tavern and it said "(Generic NPC intro).That being said, I still love it. It was released with only minimal errors, and it's still in early access. It's very challenging.Update: There is a mod on Nexus called "Hideout Player Party Limit Removed." It fixes my number 2 issue.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game and this franchise. I was willing to excuse so many crashes, bugs, and unfinished aspects of the game since it fell under the purview of "Early Access". First I will acknowledge what has gone well, and ultimately why my review is negative.The singleplayer has come a long way, and I have sunk hundreds of hours into it from first EA release to full launch and after. Kudos to TW for that. Developing anything must have been hard during the Covid years, and they kept pushing through. Multiplayer is a hot mess. Crashing servers (literally after every round or every other round) is the main cause of death to multiplayer. The mp is actually a lot of fun WHEN and IF it works, which is very rarely. I understand that they are working on this problem, but my response is ultimately what leads to the negative review:Why was THIS the full release? Why not just keep it under EA until some of these huge issues were fixed? The last patch to come out was 1.9, why not just keep going? The game is clearly not done, so don't market it as such. TW has been very very clear that fixes and patches will continue to come which is reassuring to a degree, but it does make me wonder what was so special about 1.9.1 that it went to full release? A very strange development philosophy is ultimately why I am leaving a negative review. Game simply is not ready to be full release, and ignoring a problem does not make it disappear.EDIT: I am looking forward to changing this review when/if TW releases a finished product. This game has amazing potential.

_childDocuments_.review: I have had over 100 hours of good fun with this game (mostly with heavy amount of modding to get it to a state I truly enjoy), worth hmmm $25-$35 or so on sale. So a very tentative thumbs up, i guess. However, there are some very important things to know before I endorse buying it.1:The game has been 'released' for almost 3 years now, after 2 years in early access. Normally, this is a huge pro and shows forward consistent development and a full product for sale. Buuuuut, the game, as it is right now in mid 2024, is functionally the same as it was in like 2021 early access. There several core areas of the game that are simply unfinished or missing. Right now, in May 2014, the last 'update' was 3 months ago, but that was simple bug fixes(and mod breaks, *sigh*), the last ACTUAL update was in December, 5 months ago, and even it was quite meager. This is a really concerningly slow and bad pace of updates that make me believe truly that this product will not reach its actual end of development or fully realized potential. Its honestly a bit baffling to me, someone with zero game design experience. Maybe just bad scaffolding/planning or tech debt?2: Modding is, honestly, 100% required to get this game into a good state. Like I said, there are too many missing features and areas that are dramatically undercooked or underutilized. So expect a lot of work before having fun.3: Modding is not nearly as easy and developer enabled as it should be considering the history of this series. The bug fix updates wreak havoc on mods, the process of troubleshooting mods and getting them all to work well together is a bit miserable. This is a catastrophic design oversight in my opinion; from conception this game was always going to thrive on the modding community like the first game.4: While this latest version has much better tutorial that it used to, it really doesn't give you any direction or nearly enough knowledge about how to progress or achieve much of anything. You will be looking ♥♥♥♥ up. You will be googling weird things. This not a flaw necessarily but you should know this before buying.5: Even with many great mods, balance is really powerfully out of whack. Short of modifying game files yourself (i had to, mods simply didnt cover what is needed) you are going to have a hard time making multiple character builds feel equally strong or useful.

_childDocuments_.review: I've written and re-written this review three times. I did not like Bannerlord at first. If you enjoyed Warband, give it a shot. It takes a bit longer to get the hang of, but change is good in this case. Instead of just rolling past looters and random bands, I'll still fight them because they give my lower level troops meaningful xp. The diplomacy is much more interesting (and much less of a pain in the ass) than WB. The first time I got grated a city, I spent 100 diplomacy and did not expect to get it. When I was granted it, I was overjoyed and caught myself literally dancing a jig. There is a bit more of a learning curve than Warband (which is why I did not like it at first), but really honestly it is a better game. If you never played Warband, then it is a competent, fun, medieval, single player, open world RPG/RTS/squad-based game that's worth double the price. Also, the developer is updating pretty regularly.
