_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna be honest. My hype died down dramatically about a year ago. Even removed Bannerlord from my wishlist at one point. But today, I can happily say that so far, despite a few hiccups, Bannerlord is everything I wanted it to be.First off, minor issues I've come across so far. Had one crash during the tutorial bandit camp fight, one loading screen that took waaaaay too long to do anything, and a LOT of performance hits. Thankfully, most performance issues cleared up after jumping in the graphics settings (too impatient to set it up first thing). Still some minor frame rate hiccups, but overall running fairly smooth.I like how the skills page has been completely revamped. Horse archer AI takes a few cues from some Warband mods, they now skirmish properly. I highly recommend turning down AI combat difficulty, otherwise it can get very overwhelming. Also, everything is a lot more dangerous than in Warband in the early game. Looters and common bandits can pack a punch if your not expecting it. The smithing is pretty cool, but you are gonna have to invest some time into it to really get anything out of it. Accompanying warlords is much better now. Can now directly attach your forces to the main host. Gone are the obnoxious "scout these 3 places", and "go get x cattle" tasks when out on the march. The rest I still need some time to figure out, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥... Taleworlds sure didn't give up, It was I who lost faith. This could have easily been another Duke Nukem, but they delivered. I bow my head to thee, and offer an entire inventory's worth of butter as penance.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: It is a good game and TaleWorlds did not disappoint with the next game in the series. Early Access doesn't mean an unfinished product in this case. The modding community, if they are anything like they were with warband, will release some amazing community content that will bring you back to this game for years.Mount & Blade then the following M&B Warband are 2 of my favorite games. These were the games that truly opened my eyes to what a strong modding community can do for a game and its lifespan. As well as what a committed and passionate team can do for a games development.Bannerlords still feels like Mount & Blade, it still feels like its roots. They added some cool new features like the ragdoll physics (excellent by the way) and reworked the UI and siege battles (also excellent). They also made combat just... more satisfying, I don't know if its the cool ragdoll physics where when you shoot an arrow into someone's head their head snaps back before they fall or if they tweaked the sounds and motions of combat but it's working none the less.Now I was very skeptical when they released this as early access. I had been waiting for the game for years and when I saw early access I was expecting an unfinished product. I am sure they intend to add more throughout their early access phase. However the base game is there and playable with a story line to follow if you want so I wouldn't let early access dissuade you in this case.I haven't tried multiplayer yet but have high hopes considering where warband left us.Finally the modding, modding=replay value. TaleWorlds Entertainment and the modding community for the original game as well as Warband taught me this. I would be shocked if Bannerlord's community didn't keep the tradition going.EDIT: I forgot to mention 1 big issue, performance. This isn't an issue with the normal day to day and it can look quite beautiful on a moderately built PC. When you get into a siege your computer will take a nose dive though. I can run a siege at 300 bodies on low settings. I would absolutely love to see that number go up, even without an increase in graphics quality. If TaleWorlds can do both...? Well I don't know what I'll do but it'll be with a spring in my step that's for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: I quite enjoyed M&B Warband, especially with the Viking Conquest Reforged mechanics.Now, after playing more, i can say that i still would not recommend this game in its current state.-Mainly, that it is overpriced for an early access title with 50 € for less content than M&B Warband.-It has less functions than Viking Conquest Reforged or vanilla M&B Warband.Silly yet good example of missing stuff:as of the 17 of April, the combat log will still remind you of the fact that THERE IS NO TEXT/TEMPLATE to display HITS ON A SHIELD ON CHARACTERS BACKS.No neat little log entry about relative velocity, damage done and absorbed.Just a small error text about that issue in the log.A little something which was integrated into M&B Warband from the start.-Tournaments are bring your own armor, which means that you will get utterly wasted till you get some actually good armor.And that the unit types with good armor are almost always winning.Bandit Hideout quests are still very challenging for non-melee focused players.The amount of enemies to defeat with a limited party size in the mission is difficult.But the scripted "Boss meet" sqeuence at the end of it, with the MC forced into hugging range,  is the main problem.----Currently, the developers balance and fix many things and often.Which is WHAT HAPPENS DURING EARLY ACCESS.I repeat: Fixes and balancing are what DEFINES AN EARLY ACCESS period.Contrary to other reviews, the developers doing their best to make the game more playable, fixing bugs and balance issues is what should be expected in early access.The developers of this game are doing a good job at that, no question!At the same time, the expectation about what early access should be is distorted by too many other "early access" titles  on Steam not doing that.Thus bugs and unbalanced features are "okay" since the Devs will(should) fix them.Especially in a early access title.--Yet, after the 20% off discount is gone, the game is overpriced for the content in early access.Thus not recommended.--Also, some other missing things:No spearwall that makes people brace their pikes.Horse Archers are still the bane of any army without em.No private hideout mechanic like in Viking Conquest.No ship combat stuff. (Minor issue.)Enemy and Allied Soldier pathfinding and combat reactions are still wonky and similar to prequel.Plenty of other popular mod mechanics for M&W Warband are not included in Bannerlord, despite often being Quality of Life enhancements as well as the prequel being around ...ten years old at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: Now that the bulk that of the crashes and corrupt save issues have been fixed I am changing my recommendation from no to yes.In it's current early access state, Bannerlord very much feels like an early access game, which is leaps and bounds beyond the state it was released in at launch a week ago. At launch, in order to avoid crashes basically meant avoiding playing the game in general as everything from quests to combat could cause a crash. And if you weren't maintaining multiple save files, those crashes could result in save file that was no longer playable. Add to that after only 2 or 3 days, nearly everyone was encountering corrupt save issues and having to start over. The game felt very much like an alpha version.However, the devs have been outstandingly diligent with providing daily patches this last week, fixing dozens of crashes and all of the corrupt save issues that I had encountered (which was 3). Given how long it took them to get this game to early access in the first place I was VERY surprised at how quickly they were able to put out patches to fix major issues.The game is still missing some planned features but could definitely pass as an unpolished final product and provides more than enough content and features for tons of playtime. And now that the major bugs are getting under control, I expect to see devs shifting work back to features and polish and see more great new features roll out before the final release.

_childDocuments_.review: For now it's a no. The single player experience hasn't changed much since Warband and most changes they've made are not for good. What hasn't changed? The music. Same awful, cheap music they had in Warband (with one or two new ones). Same boring tune during walking around the map; makes you feel like playing some really old or low-budget game; no improvement on that whatsoever.Combat-wise: some attack moves look nicer and they've introduced directional blocking with shields. You get nicer tools to control your army's movement and positioning on the battlefield but sometimes it's a bit tricky to use while being engaged in melee as clicking causes units to move.In terms of economy, they've changed the way workshops work. You cannot buy cheap raw materials and drop them off at your workshop. Instead, the workshop has to automatically buy the goods. This means carpenters are probably the only workshop worth building. The workshop don't make as much gold as in Warband.Skills and level progression: first five levels are easy to gain and then it becomes slow grinding to the next one. Perks you get for levelling up are not always worth all the effort and the number of skill points you need to get to level up on higher levels is just ridiculous. Levelling up a clan is also a very slow process.Weapons: weapon choice seems to be somewhat poorer than in Warband and seems very basic. Crosbows are rare and there's only few types. And while you can easily get some better arrows, better crossbow bolts are simply non-existent.Balance: some kingdoms seem to be much stronger than others. To the point that by day 442 the map is dominated by two factions. _childDocuments_.review: Oh boy, here I go writing another negative review for a game I used to enjoy because, apparently, game developers got together and decided 2023 was the year to see how many terrible ideas they could cram into their games.Anyway...Yes, I would've recommended this game at 1.0, and would probably recommend you rollback and play that version of the game if you do end up buying it. My reasons:- The game has an encyclopedia feature that lets you track the Kings, Lords, Ladies, and potential Companions in the game. It was a useful tool to use primarily because companions (aka Wanderers) are randomly generated at the start of a new game, so you could see if you had any decent recruits to pick from at the start of the game. Well, somebody at TaleWorlds apparently decided it needed to be turned into a Pokedex, but you know, terrible. So now they've introduced a "Fog of War" feature that blanks out all the entries in the encyclopedia until you "discover" each person in the world. I don't know who this is for, since all the Lords, Ladies and Kings are pretty much the same across playthroughs, the only ones affected by this are Wanderers and Leaders that are spawned in during the game (in rebel cities), of course they'll probably be killed off before you even meet them, but whatever, I guess. So now, if you want to know if you have any decent companion recruits you have to basically chase them down to see if they're worth it, because while the encyclopedia does tell you where they were last seen, they'll still randomly teleport to different cities at random times. Meaning you could run all the way across the map to find a companion in one city, just to get there and find out they've teleported to a city back on the other side of the map you started on.- Sieges have become an absolute nightmare. Originally, defending sieges against NPCs played out similar to the older M&B games: Attackers start the siege, prepare siege weapons (siege towers, battering rams, trebuchets, etc.) while defenders prepare their own defenses (crossbow turrets and catapults), attack the castle and either win or get beat back, combat ends, and you immediately get ready for the next round of combat where you fight the attacker's army minus the troops you took out already. It was a fun, sometimes challenging, sometimes frustrating, mechanic and it usually could take around an hour (real-time) to beat back the 1,000 to 1,400 man armies at your doorstep.Not anymore.Now, after beating back the first wave of attacks, the attacking army will fall back to their camp, regroup and rebuild all their siege equipment. This might not sound bad, but it's important to note that the majority of the enemies army will be taken out by siege weapons, and siege weapons don't kill troops anymore.Read that again. Siege weapons don't kill troops.Meaning, of the 300~500 troops you fought off, you most likely only killed 20~50, so while the attackers are regrouping and rebuilding, all the wounded troops are getting healed, so you'll have to fight them again in the next fight. On top of that, the attackers army can be reinforced by additional recruits, so even if you do manage to take out half their 1,200 man army, there's nothing stopping another 1,200 man army from coming along and joining the siege between fights.So basically, battles that use to take around a real-world hour to fight can take hours or even days to finish. I don't know about you, but I have a life outside of video games, so spending an real-world days trying to defend one castle is not something I can get invested in...Continuing with how much sieges have been made unbearable, you need a decent engineering skill to prepare defenses (again, catapults and crossbow turrets) during a siege, but failing that, you at least had some basic resources to fall back on, namely refill stations for your arrows and crossbow bolts. Not anymore, because whether or not they spawn will depend on the level of the wall around the city/castle you're defending. So if the owner of the city/castle you're defending hasn't been maintaining it, you're basically SOL because, while you can still build catapults and turrets, simple things like lining the walls and towers with extra quivers is apparently an impossible task without a major architectural overhaul of the defenses.One final point on sieges I want to bring up is the fact that when the attackers did launch they're attack, there was a prep moment before the battle started where defenders could familiarize themselves with the layout of the wall, where the breach points are, where the defenses are (you get four defensive weapons that spawn in fixed locations, but what weapon spawns in what location is completely random), where you're character starts, and where the attacker's siege weapons are. Well, apparently some players complained that clicking a button to start the battle was so overwhelming that TaleWorlds decided the best course of action was to get rid of that feature completely. So now the battle starts with you having little to no knowledge of where you are, where anything is, or how to get anywhere.This all in the last few updates since 1.0, I mean, there're still boatloads of issues with the game that haven't been fixed. AI is still a buggy mess, mounted archer will charge straight into enemy spearmen like they're heavy cavalry and die, foot troops will completely ignore enemies that are stabbing them to death to try and chase after some random jerk on a horse, the guys in charge of reloading catapults won't be able to pathfind between the catapults and piles of ammo so they end up getting stuck inside the catapult, and you'll see individual lords surround enemy siege camps and do nothing. Because while, collectively, they have more than enough soldiers to fight the attackers, individually none of them have enough to want to try, so they sit just outside the aggro radius of the attackers where, even if you try to fight the attackers, they'll be too far away to join the battle on your side.Okay, so I had a couple more issues with sieges... my bad...These are just the major issues I've encountered, there's more, but then it starts to get into nitpicking and most of you haven't read half of this review anyway so I won't get into it. This isn't a terrible game, like I said, if you do get it, roll it back to an earlier version. But I just can't recommend it as it is. But hey, maybe that'll change someday.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game, but also not too different from thew last. Sieges primarily, saw a huge improvement, from the original narrow path of doom. Now there are siege engines on both sides to damage both the castle and the invading troops. There are also rams, siege towers, and ladders to give the attackers a real chance. The overall game AI is improved, but still wonky at times. Sometimes they are super smart, and sometimes super... silly. Looters are now snipers, make no mistake. They all throw rocks better than archers shoot arrows. Better in both accuracy and precision. Armor will not save you from rocks either. Apparently, plate, chain and padded armor all together reduce damage taken from rocks by only a small margin... Shields still nullify damage, thankfully. There is almost no logical way to wield a crossbow without first leveling the skill. Oh, and leadership only really improves if you officially lead an army, not your professional one, even if yours is 4 times as big. Graphics are better, game play is improved, overall fun game, with some bugs and silly discrepancies. Highly recommended when on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Warband (800 hours)! Bannerlord (200 hours) is potentially an awesome successor. Yet it is unfinished and not enjoyable in the vanilla form. It's grindy and lacks original content and very buggy. You can say it is a High-Resolution Warband clone, priced double. Thankfully the modding community build great mods - theoretically augmenting the bare bone gameplay. Sadly the game developers have NO regards for backward compatibility and completely disregard modders. Any mod breaks with EVERY official patch. It is hilarious, but also discourages modders and gamers to enjoy this game. The Launcher is broken and you have to manually fiddle with the Load Order and make manual version checks, which again is always tied to a specific module version and not a minimum version. All because the Devs don't care about backwards compatibility.If it weren't for the sluggish DevOps I would recommend this platform - provided you use mods. But those break constantly and are often abandoned by frustrated modders. As a programmer myself, and without seeing the codebase of bannerlord, it smells to me like untested, ad-hoc and spagetti-code. Which is most likely the reason, why it is unmaintainable and hard to expand.As in early access this all might be understandable or fixable, but now Bannerlord is supposed to be a Full Release... Well not quite finished I would say.If any Bannerlord Dev read this, my advice: Put ALL your resources in supporting the modders. They make your PLATFORM playable and probably can fix the gazillion bugs you have accrued.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing so far. Even with my thousands of hrs spent in the previous M&B games there was still a bit of a learning curve in the new mechanics. Just goes to show how much they improved on their combat as well as everything else perceivable. Yes, as many others I was having stuttering issues, primarily in field battles, even with my prime gaming pc. That being said after about 20 minutes of researching and tweaking I've narrowed it down to a "not really that frustrating" state. Although you can't even hold that against them as this is an early access version, optimization issues are definitely going to be the worst of the crop. Primarily they have been focusing on more game breaking ones, as they well should. For example, the update they just released, fixing game saves becoming entirely corrupt after a certain amount of saves? Uh, yeah I would be pissed if I lost my whole campaign just because I save often, and they already fixed that. I can handle a bit of stuttering in battles here and there for now.So let's delve into the rest here, lets see.. The campaign on literally every point of all aspects has been MAJORLY improved, compared to the older games. I mean, the convenience of all the menus and everything, even down to the hotkeys has been improved. I can literally be in the town menu and save my game at the same time? Uhh hell yeah! That's just one of dozens. Hrm oh yea the use of companions? Majorly improved, you can literally be working on 5 quests at a time if you wish it, while working on your own, and no that's not the limit, just a simple figure. In the older games you didn't have much use for companions other than having military badasses, folks who upped your party skills for you, and.. didn't really see much else until you became a Faction leader yourself. In this your companions begin aiding you and your 'Clan' right after you get your first one (which really should be within the first half hr to get one).Ah one of my favorites other than the combat is the new Leveling and skill system. It may seem to take long at first, but if you prioritize your new focus points correctly, and sparingly, it speeds up considerably. Also that whole new system really seems to allow you to more direct your focus on what you want to do. I mean, before it was too simple like "oh i need more money" (rinse repeat money making things) or "oh I need more troops" (rinse repeat troop gathering and training) etc.. With this new system it's like, "oh well if I want to level this, then I need to do this, and while doing that I could be trying to level these other 3+ things." Or could be like "oh I need money, I'm gonna do tournaments, but while doing those tournaments and traveling between them I need to be working on these other 7 things, while making money on the way". And really with all those aspects, and you trying to focus on so many things (and no its not overwhelming) you'll get side tracked just as you would in Skyrim or something. That to me adds a lot of fun into a game, when you plan something out, but while going on your personally set goal you get side tracked and aren't even planning anymore. Rather than doing the same redundant ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ over and over again.. which to me is one of the #1 killers of any game. This is coming from a guys who still play OSRS lmao, and the epitome of that game is pretty much redundancy.I could go on and talk about more points but.. Idk if people are even gonna read this. That being said, if you have any specific questions on the game, just ask and I will thoroughly answer. I highly recommend this game, I mean cmon guys we've been waiting 7-12 yrs for it (depending on how you view that). Get hackin and slashin!

_childDocuments_.review: This is not what anyone hoped for with the sequel to Warband. The balance within the game is incredibly broken, as looters are an incredible threat to beginner level characters. Your character, regardless of its skill or level, appears to always been slower, less skilled, less dexterous, less healthy than the lower levels of A.I. When the tutorial is hinges on your mandatory "Headman's Troops" to lift all the weight, and you still take an hour or more to finish it due to you dying over and over again, there is an indication the balance of the player vs the ai is broken. This isn't even taking into consideration the unfinished nature of everything other than combat. Diplomacy is broken, town management is based around money and food, workshops are completely hands off, characters are bland, after 5 missions you have done them all, gangsters and leaders have no impact. I loved warband, I put almost 2000 hours into it, tried the mods, played the dlcs. Warband was excellent. This isn't what anyone expected or hoped for. I really want to like this, and I am trying to play it, but it just isn't worth the money or time.

_childDocuments_.review: Mount and Blade II: Bannerlord is a game that offers an immersive medieval roleplaying experience that allows you to play as a lord, merchant, or any other character that comes to mind. The gameplay is great, offering a range of activities and customization options to create a unique experience. However, the game is lacking in diplomacy features, but still manages to be good overall. While there are bugs and jitters present, they are not game-breaking and do not detract from the overall enjoyment of the game. If you're looking for an immersive medieval experience with great gameplay, Mount and Blade II: Bannerlord is worth checking out especially since it keeps getting improved upon.

_childDocuments_.review:
The horns sound, the ravens gather. An empire is torn by civil war. Beyond its borders, new kingdoms rise. Gird on your sword, don your armour, summon your followers and ride forth to win glory on the battlefields of Calradia. Establish your hegemony and create a new world out of the ashes of the old.

Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord is the eagerly awaited sequel to the acclaimed medieval combat simulator and role-playing game Mount & Blade: Warband. Set 200 years before, it expands both the detailed fighting system and the world of Calradia. Bombard mountain fastnesses with siege engines, establish secret criminal empires in the back alleys of cities, or charge into the thick of chaotic battles in your quest for power.

name: Berzerk: Recharged
detailed_description: Chicken, fight like a robot! Evil Otto and his deadly robots are back in this reimagining of the 1980 arcade classic Berzerk. Berzerk: Recharged challenges you to fight your way through a deadly maze filled with waves of menacing, vocal robots. Deft twin-stick control and power-ups are the only way to survive, as you shoot your way through room after room in this never-ending dystopian maze. And don’t forget, Evil Otto may have a smile on his face, but he is deadly and invincible. As with all Recharged games, you can chase a high score in arcade mode, or take on one of the many hand-crafted challenges to test your shooting and dodging skills. If things get too hard, you can always grab a friend to double your firepower in local-co-op. Megan McDuffee’s original soundtrack of sci-fi synths captures the ambiance of a harrowing space station shootout – and a very cool 80s arcade. Key Features Arcade Mode: Survive an endless maze of random rooms that get progressively harder the further you get. You will know when you reach one of the five levels of increased difficulty when the robots change color. Challenge Mode: 20 hand-crafted mazes that deliver unique gameplay challenges. Power Ups: Pick up weapon modifiers including a spread-shot, big shot, or a series-staple railgun. There are also player modifiers for speeding up, a shield, and placeable mines to use against your rude and relentless enemies! Local Co-op: Bring a friend to reach even higher scores in arcade or persevere through the toughest challenges. Leaderboards: Compete in global leaderboards in arcade and challenge modes.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't understand the hate this game is getting. The Atari Recharged series is about making new versions of classic games, not recreating the original exactly as it was. After all, what would be the point in that, when Atari owns and can just release the original? And it's not like this is a new concept, newer "improved" versions of games have been getting made since the early days of the arcades.I have the 2600 version of Berserk, I busted out my cartridge and played a few games as a refresher before I played this. There are a lot of nice improvements over the original here. Firstly, the graphics and sound blow away anything on the 2600. The 2600 was innovative and great for its time, but by today's standards the graphics on the best games look like something a 4 year old drew, and the sound was rudimentary. This new version takes advantage of modern capabilities, without vastly changing the game play. The walls are no longer lethal, which is nice, but some rooms do have laser gates. Touching those will give you damage, but other walls won't. Another improvement is that there are now 4 varied enemy types with different abilities, rather than a room full of the same robot. There are the humanoid drones, which are closest to the original robots. They will move towards you and shoot 1 bullet at a time at you. There are pursuers, which fly towards you and explode. There are turrets, which are stationary but they track you and fire 3 round bursts. And there are crawlers, which don't fire and they only hurt you if they touch you. The 4 enemy types make it more interesting. There are also achievements, such as killing 150 of each type of robot and killing 100 enemies when Otto is in the room, as well as reaching a certain number of rooms. The fact that you don't have "lives," but rather a 5 hit health bar makes reaching certain numbers of rooms easier, as dying and then respawning, restarting the room (as the original did) would break your momentum. I found myself doing some achievement hunting. I got all of the kill ones, the one where you have to kill enemies with Otto in the room was fun. Basically, kill as few enemies as possible before the Evil Beach Ball of Death spawns, then kill what you can and escape or die, depending on whether Otto kills you. The achievement I'm working on now is doing 20 straight rooms without taking damage, the most I've done so far is 12 rooms.As for the game play itself, there are different play modes. You can play Arcade or Missions, though there's no explanation what you're supposed to do in the missions. So, I just play Arcade. You also have different options in Arcade mode to change the difficulty. Yon can start with 1 bar on your health. You can also play without power ups. And, finally, you can play without dash enabled. You can start a game with 1, 2 or all 3 of those enabled. Each one you enable increases your final score by 100%, so you can get 2, 3 or 4 times your final score. I usually play with dash disabled unless I'm doing one of the "reach X number of rooms" achievements, as that's the only time I use the dash.There are some things that are the same as the original. The rooms are still randomly generated, the enemies still change color as you progress. Though, instead of changing as your score increases, they seem to change after a certain number of rooms. And, of course, Otto is still invulnerable and will kill you by touching you, no matter how full your health bar is.Then there are a few things that changed that I'm less than enthusiastic about. Otto no longer gets faster after you kill all of the enemies in a room, his speed stays the same. Having him speed up made it more of a challenge to avoid him. Now it's pretty easy. Also, you can no longer shoot enemy bullets and destroy them, like you can on the 2600 version.So, bottom line, I think this is a fun game. It's a cool time waster. Games can be quick or long, depending on your skill, or lack thereof, and on what spawns in each room. And, at only $10, it's a good deal, like the rest of the Recharged games. (I have them all) I'm not sure how often I'll actually play this one, but it's definitely been entertaining me, so it's worth the money. Or, if you don't think it is, just wait for a half off sale, as they happen fairly regularly.

_childDocuments_.review: Bad by any metric. Sluggish, low-impact dual-joystick shooter with dull enemy design, lifeless powerups, and uninteresting obstacles. As a game with Berzerk written on the front of it, it's somehow even worse. The menacing, robotic speech of the original has been replaced with a guy talking into a vocoder. The characters have an almost cartoon-ish style to them and Evil Otto is turned into a giant beach ball-looking thing that loses all of the quiet menace of the original. Who is this supposed to be for? Feels like something that was developed as an early Xbox Live Arcade game but got rejected for being too dull.Just feels like it misses the point across the board. There's probably a cool way to make a new Berzerk game, but this ain't it.

_childDocuments_.review: Remember fondly playing Berzerk when it first came out. This updated version attempts to capture that spirit with the confined mazes, the invincible Otto and add a few new twists. I'd argue most of the new twists they added negatively impacted the gameplay experience.Take, for example, the utterly dumb bottom 1/8th of the screen that is shadowed and makes it difficult to see enemies. Yeah, cool, they can hide from you, but then you can't even see yourself very well. The developers need an option to turn this off. The original Berzerk was a flat maze and you could see everything. What developer Sneakybox tried to do here actually distracts from gameplay.Dash in Berzerk? Huh? Why add Dash? Part of the fun of Berzerk is that Otto can outrun you. The enemies can eventually outrun you, too. Sure, a dash action can save you, but it's totally unnecessary until deeper in the game, which the vast majority of players will never see. Luckily, the devs offer an option to play with the dash disabled and earn a multiple of your score. That's cool.Some of the powerups are kinda useful, like the shotgun fire, but anything to do with dash is unnecessary (see above). Slowdown? Yeah, that helps with the enemies that fix on you and come after you fast, but by the time you get the powerup, the level is cleared or almost cleared and Otto is coming out. Bottom line: play without powerup, get a 100% multiplier on your score. Another problem: there are only two leaderboards, the single player leaderboard and multiplayer. The single player leaderboard actually covers three different modes: Iron Man, which is one life only, powerups enabled/disabled and dash enabled/disabled. If you run Iron Man mode only, then it's one life, with no powerups and dash and you get 300% boost of score on the same leaderboard. Apparently the developer thinks that score should be shared with others that do not use this mode and the score bonus. IMO, they should have different leaderboards for each configuration/mode. It's more fair to compete that way. It's fine to have one leaderboard with the score multiplier bonus (it isn't their actual score, which is strange, btw) but why not have more leaderboards with all options/configurations? And the leaderboard for multiplayer is local only, so only the player logged in gets credit. That's a bummer for your friend that plays with you, because they get zero credit for being on the leaderboard. This is something that future Recharged titles need to fix. Mutliple Steam users should be able to get credit for a multiplayer session. I get that there would only be a login for the second player when playing remotely, so probably a challenge to incorporate this, but it's a bummer for multiplayer gaming sessions with your friends. The multiplayer Berzerk: Recharged experience is fun.Glitches. Oh my. This feels glitchy in a number of ways. One, what's the deal with zoning between rooms? It's very jarring and not smooth like a game that was created for arcades 40+ years ago?  Another is the fact that when you first zone in, sometimes your character will stall or glitch move into a different part of the screen near the doorway? What? This makes firing at enemies right away unnecessarily difficult. By now, you're probably figuring out all the reasons this game is a thumbs down for me. I'm not going to refund it, because I've kept the other Recharged games, including some that should have been refunded. Buy Asteroids: Recharged or Yar's Revenge: Recharged instead of Berzerk: Recharged, but get them when they are on sale. These games should not cost $9.99. They are $5 and less games, at best. This one needs some more work with updates before it's worth even that. On one hand, glad to see Atari pushing for these updated versions of classic games, but on the other, they need to put more love and time into these than what's being packaged and presented here. We want it to truly represents the gameplay experience those of us loved with the original game with modern update. One comment from a friend who played this with me was "this seems like a mobile game" and that wasn't meant complimentary.  The version I played at launch feels more than a little rushed in the development process.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure what the issue is but there doesn't seem to be any joystick support on the Windows version of this. It's all good to design a game to be mouse-and-keyboard first, but it seems crazy to me not to have a joystick option. Worse, there's no way to remap the controls so you're stuck with WASD and the extra keys of the devs' choosing. The UI is also poorly implemented. There are wonky issues with feedback that make it hard to know if you've properly made a selection.Regarding the game, it's okay. I love the original arcade game but this is essentially an early prototype of Enter the Gungeon and doesn't feel like the original Berzerk. This isn't worth $10, $5 at best. I got it with Humble Bundle so I got my money's worth. Not much to recommend but it's not a "bad" game so if you've got the cash and the time, give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm of a couple minds on Berzerk Recharged.  I hated giving this game a thumbs down, but had no choice.As a simple "shoot anything that moves" games goes, Berzerk Recharged is just fine.  It rapidly gets challenging once you get to the room 20+ and the bullets start flying faster.  I don't mind the twin stick setup as such, though I would've rather had it to where you fired when you pushed the right stick rather than requiring both the right stick and the trigger.   So it does give you a challenge, and it doesn't let you goof off too long before sending Evil Otto after you.But the issues.... The issues with this game might seem minor (one is a little bothersome), but they are part of what made Berzerk Berzerk....  First, the robots don't taunt you throughout the game.   Or at least not in a way that is that audible.  I will occasionally hear the game's attempt at something like "destroy the intruder", but it's so difficult to hear even with the music dialed all the way down.  It's not prominent in the way it was in the arcade version.Second, Evil Otto isn't quite the threat that he was in the arcade game.   You see, in the arcade game, he could go through walls and got faster as there were fewer robots on the level.  You couldn't just mess around for long with him on the playfield.  Recharged on the other hand, he can't pass through the walls,  the grin isn't as obvious.   I don't know.   Third, the hitbox on the player is too big.  I had bullets kill my character even though they probably still an arms length from my character.  Makes it difficult to judge how close I can let the bullets pass by in tighter spots.Finally, if you perished, the original would show you getting electrified and the robots gloat "Down with the humanoid, down with the intruder".   Recharged, you're stuck with flashing immediately to game over on the fatal hit.Again, if this game didn't have the Berzerk name attached to it, I would've scored it a recommend, but Recharged just doesn't feel right when compared to its predecessors
_childDocuments_.name: Berzerk: Recharged

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the previous nine Recharged games (though wish they had the dip switch settings of the originals), but man, I pretty much had a visceral dislike of this one.  I've never uninstalled a game so fast before.  Twice in less than half an hour of play-time.  I gave it a third try the next day and disliked it less, but still ended up uninstalling it.  It feels so generic and is too different from the original to trigger any sort of nostalgia.  Definitely watch a video or two before you buy this.  The other Recharged games are basically the originals with “more” and/or power-ups, but this one changed things all over the board.  The overall speed is way faster than the original, which necessitated twin-stick controls (though you still have a fire button).  It has way more bullets on the screen and quick homing enemies practically from the word Go, an isometric viewpoint that is surprisingly difficult for me to parse, significantly less voice samples compared to the original (which might be the biggest crime of all), and modifiers which only make the game more difficult.  They could at least have given the equivalent of Missile Commands' Calm modifier so you could have pacing closer to the original.  Maybe if it had the control scheme of Robotron 64 I would have liked it.  In any event, I find myself among the haters, and the only reason I’m not returning it is because I bought it as part of a Recharged bundle sale.  The biggest downer might be that going forward I’m not going to buy any Recharged titles before I have a chance to really look into them, including seeing how the reviews shake out.

_childDocuments_.review: REVIEW #95Berzerk: Recharged----------As I write this, Steam user reviews for Berzerk: Recharged are closely split between positive and negative. Being a fan of both the arcade and Atari console versions of the original Berzerk game, the feedback from other players almost deterred me from trying this title out until I took time to read what was being said. It seems like many are turned off based on nostalgia-fueled expectations and how this game failed to meet them versus the actual quality of what's presented here.In light of this, let me start with this disclaimer: if you're expecting an almost-exact replica of Berzerk with maybe just a shiny coat of paint on top, you will not find what you're looking for here. However, if an action game that takes the themes and gameplay elements of the arcade classic and works with them just enough to be similar to the source material but also manage to feel like a unique experience AND still be a heck of a lot of fun to play sounds interesting to you, then I encourage you to give Berzerk: Recharged a try.With that out of the way, let's get a bit more into the nitty gritty of what's offered here.Berzerk: Recharged is a top-down(ish) twin-stick shooter with 2 variations: arcade mode and challenge mode. In both variations, players must navigate a maze full of robotic adversaries and environmental hazards with the goal being obtaining the highest score that they can. Challenge mode has 20 preset maze configurations, whereas arcade mode randomly generates a maze layout every time and continues endlessly until the player runs out of health. The players and some of the robot enemies can shoot projectiles, and the game can often feel like a bullet-hell title, which makes gameplay feel tense and fast-paced. There's also a time-based score multiplier which gives the player incentive to keep moving if they want to quickly rack up points. Power-ups and a dash ability are included, but disabling these features (as well as the player's health bar) will result in hefty scoring bonuses being added to a game's final total.Presentation-wise, Berzerk: Recharged is okay. There's nothing offensive or subpar as far as sound design or graphics are concerned. In fact, the bright color scheme works well with the game's sense of style, and everything animates well. However, there are some odd design choices here. For example, the robotic voice samples are very low in the overall sound mix, which makes it often hard to tell what's being said. Also, the protagonist looks like Ronald McDonald going out on Halloween as a space cowboy, an impression that's especially due to the character's red/yellow/white/black color palette. That isn't a deal-breaker by any means, but it's a bit distracting and certainly looks out of place from the rest of the game. Also, while I don't exactly count this as a major negative, the general presentation of the game did sometimes feel weirdly like I was playing an Original Xbox Live Arcade title, which not all players might vibe with.Technically, while bugs have been reported by other Steam users, Berzerk: Recharged has been running almost rock-solid for me (except for one minor glitch that causes Evil Otto's face to vertically invert sometimes). Controlling the main character also feels smooth and responsive, especially with an Xbox One controller.In the end, what really works for Berzerk: Recharged is how it plays, and it feels to me like an addictive arcade-style shooter that I definitely would've been pumping plenty of quarters into if I found it in an arcade in the '80s. It took me all of 10 minutes to decide that I really like this addition to Atari's Recharged series, and if the trailer and screenshots on the store page interest you, then I suggest picking this one up.NOTE: local co-op is available but was not evaluated for this review.

_childDocuments_.review: This plays like if berzerk was a flash game! The designs are terrible, controls are wonky and there a few bugs that need correcting. I *LOVE* the original berzerk and still play my same copy I got as a kid. This is a insult to to the source material. Where is the heart and soul that the Arcade version or hell the atari 26k version had? None of that is there. Someone seen the source material and put modern stank on it and with blur\bloom effects, added a mission mode without even implementing the foreboding and ominous atmosphere of the original and just for THAT alone and the aformention issues I have. I have to give it a thumbs down. So far that's 2 recharges I don't like, the other being "yar's revenge".

Plugged in a mouse but the aiming is insane. Its like aiming with a mouse for MIssle Command (For this game, thats very bad) The orig used a joystick. _childDocuments_.review: Ok, I'm going to say outright. This is not a bad game, but it's also not a great one.Whatever you do, DO NOT BUY THIS AT FULL PRICE. Don't buy it at a slight discount either, buy it as part of the bundle or wait until they finally do a good discount.If what you want is straight forward twin-stick shooting, this game delivers. The dash and the powerups don't really add much but the game plays just fine. However, it doesn't have enough content to justify it's 10 dollar price tag. You've got a very basic arcade mode and some missions. That's it. They really should have added a port of the original arcade or Atari 2600 game as a mode, it's a shame that they didn't because as far as I can tell Berzerk hasn't been ported to modern PCs or consoles yet. I think the only way you can play it is through emulationWhile I don't think the game looks ugly, the graphics are pretty bland and generic. Also, hearing "fight like a robot" every 2 seconds in an 80s arcade game is funny, for a game released in 2023 it's lazy and repetitive. It would not have taken much more effort to have the robots say a few more things. It's odd that of all things they decided should stay true to the original, that's the part they picked. I know the majority of this review has sounded negative but again, it's not BAD it's just not as good as it could have been. If you get it cheap or get it as a gift it's a cute, simple game to kill some time with. It's honestly refreshing to play an overhead shooter that doesn't have a ton of complex mechanics, a story mode, or meta progression. Sometimes you just wanna shoot stuff until you lose. And for that reason, I think i'll be picking this one back up from time to time.Lastly, here's a message to the devs: It's not too late, you can add a port of the original Berzerk in an update! Either that or you could add some kind of mode that's nearly 1 to 1 to the original. It'd be easy to do but would add a lot of value to this release. Please consider it!!!

_childDocuments_.name: Berzerk: Recharged

_childDocuments_.review: This is another solid entry in the Recharged series, though I've never played the original Berzerk and can't say how it compares.For this game, you go from room to room fighting robots. You have a laser gun and a dash ability, and-- if you stay in a room too long-- a bigger robot, Evil Otto, will show up and attack you. Evil Otto is invincible, and will kill you on contact.The arcade mode is apparently endless, so you just play to see how far you can get, while the game also offers the usual mission levels we see in the Recharged series. While the mission levels in other games have tended to have varied goals, in this one you are only tasked with killing all the robots on each level.I liked it, and finished all the achievements. I definitely recommend it if you've enjoyed past entries in the Recharged series, and I hope they will make some more.
_childDocuments_.name: Berzerk: Recharged

_childDocuments_.review: I have a very fond memory of Berzerk on the Atari 2600. The sound effects were pretty cool, as well as the death animation. Evil Otto was terrifying to me as a 6-year-old. This recharged version is nice remake in my opinion. It plays a bit differently than the old version, but it's good. I recommend this game, because it is very fun. This remake was way overdue.
_childDocuments_.name: Berzerk: Recharged

_childDocuments_.review: Have liked the other recharged games.Not this one.  Controls feel clumsy and what is going on with the walls.  Why can some bots and shots move through some walls and not others?  I feel this is some sort of aesthetic thing and not a clipping issue.  Anyway - it is incredibly distracting when a shot or bot goes right through a wall to nail you.Hard pass unless they fix the walls and the clunk.Oh and the bots need to talk more with different voices ... like the original did ... 40 years ago.Evil Otto is pretty cute though.
_childDocuments_.name: Berzerk: Recharged

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Berzerk since the 2600 days, one of my favorite Atari games. With that said I have no issue with this new version. Fun fast gameplay, 2 players option, good music, feels just like any other conversion of the Recharged series. I don't understand the hate for it, not sure what other fans were expecting. If I had the opportunity to play both versions back in the 80s, the Recharged version would've be my favorite. I recommend it, if you're not a purist you will enjoy ir.
_childDocuments_.name: Berzerk: Recharged

_childDocuments_.review: Not the best of the Recharged games. I've enjoyed almost all of the new recharged series, but this one missed the mark.The dual stick/press button to shoot just doesn't feel "right" for Berzerk, the controls feel loose and the pacing of the game is off.Good Thing is the Original Berzerk still holds up and is quite playable. So the fundamentals of a Recharged 2 game would be achievable.  Give this one a pass unless they retool the game and control scheme.Maybe remove the push button to fire and just map to the 2nd stick? Then slow the pace by about 10% for the character speed to add some drama to the chase.
_childDocuments_.name: Berzerk: Recharged

_childDocuments_.review: This is not the way to update a classic. Boring and uninspired. I usually like the recharged games, but not this one. The perspective is weird and the type of artwork just does not fit the game. The trademark robot-taunting is also missing which is an unforgivable omission. The solid concepts of the original game are barely visible in this remake.
_childDocuments_.name: Berzerk: Recharged

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough one to go either way on but, taking everything into consideration, I lean  towards no.Berzerk is an icon in video games, one of the first if not the first to feature digitized speech. It's what made the original so fantastic. Goving it the Recharged treatment here ultimately makes it feel like just another game. It looks fone but, like many of the other negative reviews, I don't like how the bottom of the screen is partially obscured by the layout. Sound is where this really fails-the robot speech of the original is all but gone. Evil Otto still speaks but in a low monotonous tone you can barely hear over the music-and the music isn't that good. You should have a controller to play as this is now a twin-stick shooter, the controls are fine and they added power-ups but the default layout is clubky and can't be changed. They also added a bunch of challenges and local multiplayer but there isn't much replay value here, wven with achievements.If they at least put the original robot voices back, or put in the original (it wasn't an Atari game though) this would be a better port, and it's not a bad game but as is I can't recommend it as much as I like the Recharged series. It's just missing those little things that made the original an icon. Wait until it goes on a 50% off sale to buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Berzerk: Recharged

_childDocuments_.review: This is not Berzerk, but it is what Berzerk would look like if it were made in modern day (which is exactly the point of the recharged series). It's a fun twin stick shooter that sticks with the theme of Berzerk, but changes the gameplay from being slow and methodical to something faster and bullet-hell-ish. Some of Berzerk's (and even Frenzy's) mechanics aren't present until later levels (including electric and destructable walls), which is a fair trade to help newcomers / seasoned players adapt to the new gameplay style. Lives are trade out for Health, and Dashes and Power-ups are added into the mix to work with the more frenzied nature of the game. It's not exactly Berzerk, but it's fun.A lot of reviews on this game are from when the game launched, where it had some issues, notably in the audio department (Robot taunts were hard to hear, and indications that the player was hit were subdued, hampering the health system). An update has since been released to fix some of these issues, and the game is a lot better because of those changes.
_childDocuments_.name: Berzerk: Recharged

_childDocuments_.review:
In this reimagining of the 1980 arcade classic, Berzerk: Recharged challenges you to fight your way through a deadly maze filled with waves of menacing, vocal robots. Deft twin-stick control and power-ups are the only way to survive, as you shoot your way through room after room in this never-ending dystopian maze. And don't forget, Evil Otto may have a smile on his face, but he is deadly and invincible. 

As with all Recharged games, you can chase a high score in arcade mode, or take on one of the many challenges the design team has hand-crafted to test your shooting and dodging skills. If things get too hard, you can always grab a friend to double your firepower in local co-op.
_childDocuments_.name: Berzerk: Recharged

name: Life Eater
detailed_description: Our Next Game About the Game Life Eater is a horror fantasy kidnapping simulator. Play as a modern-day druid living in suburbia, holding down a dead-end job to pay for your true vocation: conducting the annual ritual that keeps the world from ending. To delay the end of the world, you must sacrifice a number of specific - but vaguely-described - human beings every year. Use a video editing-inspired interface to discover the story of your victims' lives, one schedule block at a time. Pry into the most intimate details of your targets' schedules, and when the time is right: abduct them before the authorities can find your lair. Time is short and your list of names is long. Choose your options wisely... and pray that the dark god you serve is even real. Features: Use an innovative 'timeline' interface for a new kind of analog horror game. Get to know the unsuspecting targets of your town, intimately. Replayable blend of authored and generated stories. Fully voiced story mode featuring Xalavier Nelson Jr. and Jarret Griffis. Original atmospheric soundscape from David Mason, the composer of DREDGE. An additional Endless mode, featuring decades of procedurally-generated targets.

_childDocuments_.review: A very special game for horror lovers and all those who love dark stories. You play as a kidnapper/serial killer who stalks his victims for a cruel and hungry god.In terms of gameplay, this means that you're given prospective victims and a description of who your god wants. For example, you may be asked to find a victim who is unemployed. Then, using all sorts of unsavory tactics, you spy on the prospects to collect evidence on who matches the desired description, all while managing time limits and suspicion.These systems work great on their own. They're compelling and satisfying puzzles to solve by their own right, but they also do a great job of making you complicit in what the main character is doing. The vibes here are awful, and to combine that with the "hell yeah!" feeling of solving a tricky puzzle lends to a very unique and compelling effect.In between each puzzle, you're given cutscenes that show what the protagonist is going through during all of this. Once again, we have just terrible vibes and wonderful creative decisions coming together to make something truly brilliant. The protagonist's doubt and shame and pathetic loneliness are all on stark display in these scenes, and they illustrate a man who is practically begging to fail or be proven wrong.The premise of this game is undoubtedly GROSS, but the game itself does not indulge in its own edginess. This is not a "Hatred" scenario. It is smart, careful, and thoughtful in a way that left me blown away.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: It is entirely possible to finish the main story of this game and 100% it in the process within 2 hours and request a refund.  I'm choosing not to request that.This game isn't anything mind-blowing, but there is definitely a lot of passion and hard work put into it.  You play a man who examines the schedules and lifestyles of multiple potential targets in order to deduce the one he believes he is supposed to sacrifice to a malicious god that threatens to destroy the world.  Upon doing so, you use the information you've gathered in order to correctly complete the sacrificial ritual.  Rinse and repeat.That premise alone is interesting and the gameplay loop is actually pretty challenging.  But honestly, what I really appreciated the most was the voice acting.  There are only two speaking characters; the protagonist and his unfortunate captive.  In spite of there only being these two very limited speaking roles, the voice actors held absolutely nothing back in bringing them to life.  Especially in the scene preceding the final main story sacrifice.So yeah, I'd say 15 bucks well-spent.  I'm not gonna keep playing it, but it will stay in my library out of appreciation for what was created.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: A short game, 2-3 hours, and kind of a first draft of a proper gameplay loop with some pretty clunker hard fail states that nonetheless is still an absorbing play, and a nice little story. Bravo for a novel concept and game mechanic; I would love to see a more developed follow-up on the "timeline stalker" genre.I think my main criticism is that the voyeurism and nastiness is indulged lightly but then kept at arm's reach in order to tell a story which doesn't really connect with the gameplay. It's a traditional puzzler that way, where we beat the current setup in order to be shown the next little bit of story. Together they're more than the sum of their parts, but both components feel like they could be stronger. Generally I admire the line it treads, writing wise. On the other hand, is there really any "tasteful" way to handle a game where you're a serial killer? Like Dexter, it is kind of a "have your cake and eat it too" conceit, but let's not serve too much cake; serving the dark god is both something that allows the audience to stomach what follows but while also more or less ducking a lot of the baggage that comes with the subject matter. I appreciate it isn't too nasty, but then, maybe something a little more outré... maybe being deeply inappropriate is the only way to honestly interrogate our love of violence in videogames. Maybe a game that had a little more muscle in the gameplay loop, flinched away from the subject matter less.I understand not doing that in order to tell a nice little story but Johnny never rings true, despite a very nice vocal performance. The "I don't want to see..." scene is unmotivated, unsupported in the story. I understand what it points at but it comes off here like a sort of anime style visual flair that was chosen as an image (a fine way to work) without putting in the work to make it land properly. Both characters are barely sketched in, and if I'm to play through the puzzles in order to get more story, I think the story needs to work harder at being dramatically structured. Many of the scenes don't have recognizable human motivations; the dark god business both feels as though it ducks much of the nastiness of the subject as much as it elides any kind of grounded depiction of mental illness, or really any of the psychology connected to this subject.I don't know. I liked it, I'm still thinking about it, which are two good signs. Maybe I'll come back and present my thoughts in a more coherent form later. I applaud what feels like potentially its own micro genre, and hope others follow in its place. Thanks for making the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: I ended up refunding this game, you'll know pretty quickly if it's your thing or not. However, I still think it's a great game, and worth a shot if the concept sounds intriguing to you.The story and art is phenomenal, no way around it. The little bit that I saw had me wanting more, and it immediately hooks you. It's melancholic, abstract, and beautiful. So too is the narration. It's absolutely wonderful, and fits the main character extremely well. The protagonist sounds truly broken, and in a delivery you'd expect of a film, not a game.That being said, I bounced hard off the gameplay. It didn't click with me, and by the third mission I accepted it wasn't my thing. That's not to say it's bad: the timeline resource-management system is a fun idea. But that novelty made it difficult to approach, and I wasn't able to pick it up.Is Life Eater worth your time? Probably, I'd recommend you give it a go if you like the concept. It has a lot of great ideas. It just didn't land for me personally.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not usually very big on shorter games, but this one was very good. I haven't tried the Endless Mode, but as for the story mode, it has a good story, a nice art style, and fun puzzle(?) gameplay. You shouldn't get stuck for too long on something, but some of the "years" can be tricky to figure out at first, but the game isn't too punishing in letting you retry after failing.tl;dr Definitely recommend it if you like shorter puzzle-y games with a story.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to drop a negative review and I wish there was an option between thumbs up or down.  If you see this game for a few bucks on sale it's probably worth it if you are interested in the premise.  I was really digging it for the first couple of hours, up to the point that I realized the mechanics introduced at the beginning are really all there is to this game.  I wish they had done something more interesting with the victims as the game progressed, but it's 90% the same thing over and over with each schedule until you get lucky and pick out maybe a clue or two that's unique to the level at which point it's pretty obvious what to do.  The one level that I had to play a few times to finish I feel was more due to an ambiguity in the way the clues are labeled by the game than an ambiguity that fit the narrative.  Even for the more mundane parts of each potential victims schedule I feel like the game could have served the story's conceit of a conflicted main character better by writing more actual characters as the victims (through unique items in the schedule) rather then making them feel like random dice rolls.  Good concept, but underdeveloped.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: It probably says a lot about me that I didn't find this as a horror game so much as a tragedy. Every target is fated to a gruesome death, where they are stalked like beasts, found and taken once the hunter knows enough about them, and dissected until finally stabbed in their beating heart. The player plays as the protagonist but in a way they also do as Johnny; much like Sherlock and Holmes, you're both the lead and his captive audience of one.The gameplay itself is interesting, once you get used to how to manipulate detection and time management. It's weirdly satisfying to, through only two actions and one hour off the timer, get three potential targets down to the one you need. My only problem is the amount of time in the later levels/years; while I could usually pin down the correct target, I would run out of time figuring out how sure I was or I wouldn't actually see much of the narrative interplay between the possible targets and how they related to each other.I'm sure Endless Mode will tack on some more hours to my playtime once it releases, but the four hours I spent on the story mode were well spent.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: Watched manlybadasshero play this, and thumbing up his video does not show enough support to the people that made this happen, so I want to engage by buying the game and leaving a review.Great voice acting. Great soundtrack, and every track is great and mood and scene appropriate. Tense, emotional, and tragic game from start to finish. The game-play itself isn't riveting, but it also much easier to digest if you absorb the mechanics piece-by-piece and take your time (no pun intended).
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: I really flip flop between recommending and not recommending with this one, on the one hand the art is beautiful and the idea is amazing, really good flavour, but there's just not enough, the gameplay has too little to it. With later levels having no way to increase the difficulty except add more useless information to the person's schedule, each level is essentially one logic puzzle and the busy work to find out the important parts. There is very little strategy and it gets stale quickly. The story could save it but it's super predictable, has very little interactivity(one choice at the end) and doesn't flow very well (the game is set over the course of years, but their conversations feel more akin to being weeks apart, with basic questions coming up in year 8)All of this could be forgiven since I did enjoy the two hours I had with it, but unfortunately the price drags it down, it is way too short for the price and isn't the unforgettable experience that would justify such a big price to time ratio. Overall I'd only pick it up on a good sale or if you really have money to burn.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: Life Eater is a great premise that is disappointingly not backed up by logical mechanics or interesting storytelling.I was hoping for a rotten gut-punch of playing a voyeuristic stalker simulator, but after an hour-or-so of getting hammered over the head with how randomized the stalking methods are, I settled into just selecting by the time the method takes over all else. It no longer mattered that it wouldn't make sense to pay a data broker to unlock what I expect to be the target's commute time or send a phishing sext to find out that the target is asleep. All that mattered was getting the intimacy percentage up and memorizing the  same 5 traits to pass the quiz/ritual at the end. The random generation of names and vague avatars for the targets also undercuts getting to know them in way that I feel really deflates the entire game. Anything that could make the targets feel more real would make such huge strides towards dragging you into some intentionally bad vibes.Overall, I really want a version of this game that is built into a larger stalker/serial killer simulator or a version that is a more authored and confident linear experience with written characters and logical stalking methods that result in events that make sense.P.S. - Being able to fail the ritual is an odd decision. Other games have gotten away with keeping whether your actions were "correct" vague until the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: I really love the idea of this game, the story and art are great and I love the whole idea of it. I really wanted to love it, but the gameplay proved to be frustratingly vague. I appreciate that it doesn't hold your hand and wants you to figure things out yourself, but there's a complete lack of feedback as to what you're doing wrong. I tried many times, failing for no reason I could discern. Checking with guides only made it more frustrating as I knew I was doing things right and going after the correct target, but was still failing for some reason. I'd love to enjoy this game and see everything it has to offer, but I'm not going to sit there and brute force the same level, hoping the game decides I got the right target this time.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: This game broke into my home, pushed my wife to the floor, kicked me in the gut, and spit in my dinner.And I thanked it.SERIOUS REVIEW STARTS HERE-In all legitimacy, this game was absolutely stunning all the way through. I never leave reviews usually, but I HAD to for this one. It lacks story compared to what I'm used to (usually an RPG player), but I find this a good thing actually. The gameplay mechanics require a lot of focus, and Life Eater does a fantastic job of giving you enough story to be invested + hooked whilst allowing your brain space for gameplay. The plot that is there is also generally steady and doesn't take any wild turns out of nowhere.Having said this, the story and characters I feel do not suffer (much, anyway). I do wish we had more with Zimforth and Ralph, that maybe we could have gotten more backstory. Johnny too, oh man, I love Johnny so much. And the dynamic with Ralph and Johnny, while I feel is a bit sparse and at time unrealistic, *wow* is all I have to say. It's so good. Both of them live in my brain rent free. You have to play and find out for yourself.Thank you Markiplier for making me find this game yesterday, it's already one of my favourite games to date.I beat it in one sitting. I will absolutely do it again.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: I'm reviewing this to get it out there. Even the tutorial has a really stellar performance from the lead actor and the gameplay loop has me hooked. The game's a reasonable price and the writing is, as is usual for Strange Scaffold games, top-notch. This needs to get more attention and better reviews than it's getting from larger outlets. Stellar idea wrapped up in a great scenario with great performances. Get in here!
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, it isn't a poorly made game, and the story is gross (in a good way) but isn't self indulgent like a lot of other games of this kind (think things like Hatred or Postal). It tells a story of a serial killer who is sacrificing people to a god that may or may not exist. It is told in short snippets between puzzles and never puts itself in a scenario where you're ever "rooting", so to speak, for the main character.However, I just honestly think the puzzles are okay. Maybe it didn't really jive for me, but I found the back and forth between balancing your sus meter, decoding who to abduct, and the mini "quiz" of sorts at the end to be not an entirely satisfying loop. There were situations where I'd figure out who to abduct but then fail the actual little quiz at the end because I missed a small key detail somewhere (note that a limited amount of hours for each puzzle means a little bit of it is left to luck choosing the right box). Obviously a bit of a skill issue in ways, but there were definitely situations where I was seemingly correct but still lost a strike anyway (i.e. in Year 7 you were tasked with finding someone w/ a second job. I was able to choose who i believe was correct, but when I'd make the choice where they live alone, it'd always be wrong even though there were no open sections on the person's schedule when they weren't working that weren't marked "alone".)I also think for 15 dollars I would like just a little bit more polish around what does exist, because I think the very boxy presentation makes the game feel a bit more like a 2000s era flash game than something released in 2024. All in all, I don't really think I can recommend this at the price its at, but if you are able to pick it up for a small discount and want a pretty uncomfortable and unforgiving puzzler with themes not often explored in this sort of genre then I'd give it a go.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay loop was engaging and enjoyable for me but feels a bit underdeveloped. A lot of it is very much guess work but the game usually gives you enough time to look for the right areas. You get some small hints on what kind of victim you have to go for and based on that you snoop around their schedule to figure out if they are the one or not. For example you might need to find someone who is a loner without friends so you look at their weekends to see if they hang out with anyone or not.After that you need to do a ritual on your target, this includes breaking ribs, removing a lung etc. Knowing what to do here is answered by how well you know your victim. Do they have kids? What is their haircolor? So even if you figure out your target quickly, it might be worth snooping on them a bit more to answer these questions. My main issue with this is is that these questions are always the same, so you know what to look for. It would be interesting if these were randomized or changed per chapter to keep the player on their toes. In short the game has a great concept and I enjoyed it a lot. It was a bit too easy i'd say and some more variety would be great. The game is also quite short so for that I find the price quite steep. Get on a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: Such an amazing and underrated game, I cannot recommend it enough.Incredible art, Beautiful story, Unique time management game mechanics, Unique theme, Good voice acting, Absolutely incredible ending too.The final choice at the end was built up so perfectly that I genuinely agonised over the choice, and the game was challenging enough to keep my interest but not make me rage. The attention to detail is just amazing too, all the neighbours have detailed (sometimes scandalous) inner lives that you uncover, some of which interacting and crossing over with one another's. There are only ten set levels, but there is also an endless mode.My only critique is a personal bias, the ending is incredibly open ended and leaves you with many questions and I'm far too nosy to leave it there, I'm extremely curious and if there is a sequel game I'd buy it immediately. But that is a personal opinion rather than a analytical critique.
_childDocuments_.name: Life Eater

_childDocuments_.review: Little tidbit before the review that does not matter to the game in the slightest: It caps itself at around 30 fps. If you're a fps slut... What the ♥♥♥♥ are you doing looking at this and not the next $80 slop I mean C.O.D. game?I would recommend you play this game blind, as it is best experienced that way. I am very glad that I did. I suggest you scroll past this review if you don't want spoilers.The stories that you can piece together using the information that you uncover within the lives of the people that you don't even know are interesting on occasion. You can learn a lot about them. I managed to grow emotional connections to these people, people who are no more to us than menu options. You don't get to see what these people look like. You don't get anything more than basic information even though you learn so much about them.I felt pain for the dying old man. He was already on his death bed, and yet learning that the lives that his wife and daughter were living were so peaceful made it hurt me.I felt enraged against the person being cheated on.I felt sadness for Ralph. Both endings, one bittersweet, the other just bitter, were very good. The bitter one left me feeling emotionally unfulfilled. And that's a good thing. It should make you not feel anything, and if you do feel something from it, it should be sadness. The ending that I find to be better leaves you questioning if everything is going to be okay, if, even though Johnny got a renewed chance at life. Will he even be allowed to use it?"I love you, Johnny."..."Do it, Ralph."That hit me hard. I don't know why. But that part hit me.Thank you to everyone who developed this game. I loved this.
