_childDocuments_.review: Really is a mixed bag. Its a great game with execellent writing and combat. There's no bugs as far as I can tell. 50 dollars is kinda crazy for a ported game with no remaster let alone they don't have ultrawide support for cutscenes (you can add it with a mod). Game is insanely unoptimized. Get it on sale if you can.
_childDocuments_.name: Red Dead Redemption

_childDocuments_.review: Finally, after a long wait, one of the true gems of my childhood can be experienced on the pc for the first time. But charging 50€/$ for a port of a 14 year old game, with minimal adjustments and graphical touches is ridiculous. The hefty price tag would be reasonable for a proper remaster, but for a port, it's just greedy. Although, If you've never played it before, you'll get your money's worth with its brilliant open world, characters and rich story. Overall I would recommend waiting for a sale if you have played the game before.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited more years to finally be able to play this game with mouse and keyboard than I was old back when I played the original PS3 release. Still a great game.Sure a proper remaster or even a remake would have been much nicer but the game still holds up quite well even with the old textures. Gone are the days of a 640p@30FPS performance. The game now shines in new splendor and is rendered in up to 4K with a framerate as smooth as butter. The game also now supports ultrawide aspect ratios (21:9) in gameplay, however in cutscenes black bars will appear on the sides.I'd say the game is worth its price tag of 50$, but I can see why it isn't for some people. For me personally, one of my favourite games of my childhood now finally arrived on PC after 14 years.In the short time I played for now, I got the impression of really good port with great controls and optimization.

_childDocuments_.review: "Some trees flourish, others die. Some cattle grow strong, others are taken by wolves. Some men are born rich enough and dumb enough to enjoy their lives. Ain't nothing fair" Every time I replay the first Red Dead Redemption I always have the same fear, that I'm not going to enjoy it as much as I used to. I've replayed this game a minimum of once a year every year for the past 13 years of my life, so it would be fair if by this point there was some semblance of burnout encroaching upon my love for this game. However, after playing RDR on PC I can happily and thankfully say this is still my favourite game of all time. I'm not going to spoil anything here, because RDR is one of those pieces of art that you just have to experience. Some of the finest writing in all of fiction, a western epic fit for the big screen, accompanied by one of the most diverse and likable casts in modern gaming, going hand in hand with a massive and lively open world for you to get lost in, makes for a masterpiece in not only game design but storytelling. RDR isn't just my favourite game of all time, it's one of my favourite pieces of fiction of all time. Bravo to everyone involved in bringing this game to PC, it was certainly long overdue. Overall - 10 / 10

_childDocuments_.review: This review is not about the quality of the game but rather the price for what you get. What you receive for $50 USD is a port of a game that released 14 years ago and it's DLC expansion. While it is nice to have this game freed from console limitations, it is quite literally just a port of the PS3/X360 version with FSR and DLSS added in, which shouldn't be necessary since it's so old and adding those into a game is so easy that modders do it on release day for some games. You still get muddy textures, weird audio, NPCs getting stuck on terrain during story missions, etc.On the performance end, everything seems fine. I'm using a 3060 so I'd expect it to run well, which it did. The Steam Deck seemed to struggle with some higher settings, even with FSR on Ultra Performance.This is a great game and deserves a proper remaster and maybe the modding community will really transform this game into the remaster it deserves. Please wait to pick this up until it's on sale for $30 which is a way more reasonable price. If you bought this like I did, I implore you (heh) to refund and wait until the price drops.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first time playing Red Dead Redemption, and I’m having an absolute blast! The game is a lot of fun, with great mechanics, engaging combat, and a captivating story. The world Rockstar created really makes you feel like you’re right in the middle of the Old West, and I’ve been enjoying every moment of it.That said, I do have to mention that the $50 price tag for this 14-year-old port feels a bit steep. I’m glad it’s finally available on PC, and I really don’t mind that it's not a full remake—I'm just happy to be playing it at all. But $50 for a game that’s over a decade old is hard to justify. I think Rockstar could have priced it more reasonably, especially considering there aren’t many upgrades to the visuals or features.Even with that in mind, I’m still really enjoying the game. If you haven’t played it before, it’s definitely worth picking up, just maybe wait for a sale if the price feels too high.

_childDocuments_.review: It has taken 14 years, but we can finally play this great piece of gaming history on PC. The port is good and the game looks crisp, and comes with the bells and whistles you want on PC. It's obviously a little strange playing this after the sequel, even though RDR2 is a prequel story wise. The story ''continues'' quite well, and you can tell they took care to get RDR2 to line up to this game. Gameplay wise the two games play almost the same (ride around, take cover, shoot), but in some ways it's a little rough to go back in time because RDR2 is so vast and immersive, i can get lost in it in ways i can't really do here. I found myself fast travelling a lot to go to quests instead of taking my time in the world and riding everywhere. But that's what a sequel is supposed to do, it improved on this game in many ways, and saying it went the extra mile is putting it very lightly.RDR has a fairly straightforward story that shines because of the great cast of characters and the dialogue between them. RDR and RDR2 are both majorly influenced by western movies, but RDR has more of the goofy spaghetti western elements, more cartoony characters, but still plenty of dark moments, especially in the Mexican chapter.RDR2 is one of the most majestic games ever made, and it couldn't have been possible without this paving the way and being a legendary hit in its own right. Highly recommend checking it out once it hits a sale, if only because of its age.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, glad to have it on steam after all these years. Two major issues though. First, the price is too damn high. Secondly, it requires the third party Rockstar launcher and account.Let me give you an idea of how that went:During installation on my steam deck, I encountered some issues while logging into the launcher (beyond not remembering my account details from ~4 years ago).On my first attempt it threw out an error relating to Steam and required me to restart the launcher. Easy enough. Then I got another error relating to an internet connection problem, and to restart again. During this restart it hard crashed the Deck and I had to power it back on.I then realized that I was trying to install the launcher at the exact moment of steam's weekly Tuesday maintenance. No problem, I just had to wait five minutes and try again. At this point I had to give up and reset my password, so it send a code to my email, I got on my phone to reset the password, and finally logged in. And then it forced me to verify my email. So I got my phone again, found the email, entered the code, and then FINALLY I was in!And then it forced me to PERMANENTLY link my Steam and Rockstar accounts. Guess that means there's no family sharing! Plus it's entirely possible I had two accounts for both my old and new emails, sure hope I didn't use the wrong one. (In addition, I hear that if you lose access to your Rockstar account you are no longer able to play any of the Rockstar games you own on Steam thanks to the "permanent" part I mentioned).Now I have successfully launched the game. What a great and very necessary process! There's no multiplayer, so there's especially no reason for an external account.It would be nice for the game to actually just launch when I press the launch button.It was also a bit of an extra hassle on Deck since you have to use the steam button+trackpad to actually interact with the launcher/installer with a cursor. No controller support there.Time for Valve to crack down on 3rd party launchers. Won't change this review to positive until then.

_childDocuments_.review: The setting and storyline of RDR is its saving grace. Obviously, this game is great and allowed Rockstar to take the Red Dead title and create a series of RPG games set in Reconstruction America.PROS:-Great storyline; characters are alive and believable, and their personalities and outfits embody a time past. Honorable mention to the incredible voice actor of Seth Briars (Kevin Glikmann) who is easily the most unique and hilarious character in the game.-Setting, graphics, and atmosphere are amazing. Simply riding your horse and turning your system up can be enjoyable. A lot of thought was put into ensuring that all elements of various desert biomes were captured: (Gaptooth Ridge - Mojave Desert; Cholla Springs - Sonoran Desert; Hennigans Stead - Montana & Dakotas; Diez Coronas - Utah; Perdido - Chihuahua; Punta Orgullo - Sonoran Desert). Except for West Elizabeth area, the locations seem to be spread out in a way where they aren't too far away that riding there would take far too long, or too close where the wilderness feeling isn't there. Seems that all New Austin and Nuevo Paraiso locations are balanced well. I wish there was more weather variation, but that's more of an opinion of mine. Wildlife adds some texture to the game, but are only interacted with while completing certain challenges or wilderness challenges (both optional). Sound design is notable, except for all weapon sound design. -There are other smaller aspect of RDR that are fun and worth noting, such as playing poker and exploring non-essential locations, like Tumbleweed and Silent Stead. CONS:-Worth the money, but not worth the time to 100% everything, as the redundancy of practically everything you do in the game makes the gameplay feel like a never-ending fever dream. -Not one gun in the game sounds "alive". Only the bolt action rifle and double-action revolver "feel" like they're doing anything. All other guns - including mounted guns - sound like plastic BB guns. Overall sound design is exceptional - only the firearm sounds and depth are in the shallow end of the pool.-West Elizabeth areas feel empty and small, almost like a second thought. Being tucked into the North-East armpit of the map kind of confirms this, as getting there can only be achieved by riding through Hennigan's Stead (easily the least interesting area of the game), only to come upon the "great" plans (smaller than Cholla Springs) and the Tall Trees, a forest area that isn't big enough. -Missions are fun but only for the purpose of being a player in a great story. The actual mechanics of the storyline )i.e., playing the missions) is redundant. This is something that Rockstar is known for: they seemingly create the main character's movement and capabilities first, then program the missions around what the player can do, instead of offering something unique in the missions that cannot be done outside of the missions. The same issue spans across all Rockstar titles.-Horse mechanics are alright, although there are aspects about the horse movements that are purely moronic: the auto-jump function, shying away from cliff edges, sharp turning while holding still, running away when whistled-for). -Character movements. All of them. Everything about the movements feels like a cutscene. Saving your game, getting on the horse, getting off the horse, playing poker, player horseshoes (lol), riding a horse, hitching a horse, running, picking plants, taking 3 business days to open the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ treasure chests during the treasure hunter challenges, climbing ladders, pulling out the rope, looting corpses, fast-travelling, talking to Nigel West Dickens, hogtying victims, picking up hogtied victims, putting hogtied victims on your horses back (all 3 tend to happen back-to-back; the last one sometimes happens while your whistled-for horse is running away from you), skinning an animal, falling from a height and laying on the ground for a century before finally recovering your wits. Need I go on? Practically everything you do in this game is basically a mini cutscene and un-streamlines the gameplay. -Challenges are empty, boring, and produce and empty reward that cannot be enjoyed, as by the time any challenge is fully complete, the end of the game is nearing or has passed. Why would I want to wear an expert hunter outfit which gives me extra animal parts when skinning an animal, after I've already spent 3 hours of gameplay watching cutscenes of my main character skinning all these animals to begin with? Literally useless rewards.tl;drBuy the game because it's fun, and offers a great story experience. Choppy movements and redundant actions leech some of the fun but overall, RDR is video game gold.

_childDocuments_.review: If you’ve ever wanted to experience the thrill of being a cowboy without the risk of getting shot or having to learn how to ride a horse, Red Dead Redemption is the game for you! This sprawling open-world adventure has everything: breathtaking landscapes, gripping story lines, and enough chaos to make a tumbleweed blush.First off, the horses. Oh, those magnificent creatures! They’re either the most loyal companions you could ask for or the world’s worst GPS. One minute you're galloping through a sunlit prairie, and the next, your trusty steed decides to reenact a scene from Bambi and takes a nosedive off a cliff. Thanks, buddy! I really wanted to experience the ‘falling with style’ aspect of cowboy life!And let’s talk about the characters. From the lovable misfits to the mustache-twirling villains, each one is more eccentric than the last. I mean, who doesn’t want to spend time with a gang of outlaws who seem to have taken one too many hits to the head? You’ll find yourself laughing out loud as you try to decipher whether they’re plotting a heist or just trying to remember where they left their horses.Then there’s the wildlife! If you thought hunting a bear was challenging, try avoiding it when it decides you look like a snack. Nothing quite like being chased by a grizzly while desperately trying to remember which button does the “run for your life” animation. Spoiler: it's the same button that prompts you to take a selfie with a cactus.Lastly, the side quests! They range from helping strangers to getting into bizarre duels that feel like they were scripted by a group of caffeinated raccoons. Each mission is a delightful blend of chaos and comedy, where you might end up accidentally saving the day or becoming the town’s most notorious outlaw—often within the same ten minutes.In conclusion, Red Dead Redemption is a delightful roller coaster of laughter, mishaps, and cowboy hats. Just remember: when life gives you lemons, find a horse, ride into the sunset, and definitely avoid any cliffs. Happy trails!

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played RDR2 first then RDR1 I enjoyed this game, but for different reasons. RDR2 is a very slow and realistic game that heavily focuses on subtle music and a dramatic story with deep characters. On the other hand, RDR1 is a fast pace and cartoony game that focuses on bombastic cowboy music and a comparatively simple story full of one-note (but interesting enough) characters. Is this a bad thing? No. Just don't go into RDR1 expecting RDR2 besides a continuation in the story. Besides that, it's like comparing apples to oranges. I recommend this game, BUT if you are deciding which game to play first I'd recommend RDR2 over this due to it having more content and being earlier in the timeline. For those curious, I had about 12 hours in the game when I completed the story mode. However I didn't touch most of the side-modes or stranger missions. Although being a shorter game with less content, I think Undead Nightmare will stay in my mind longer than the main story did. It only took about 6 hours to beat, but it was still enjoyable for what it is. It's a what-if scenario where a zombie outbreak happens right before the end of the main story. Zombie games can often mesh together, but I feel UN is very distinct due to it being set in the wild west as well as sprinkling in of mythical creatures. RDR1 already had a less serious story and cast, but UN really leans into the comedy and it works well with the set-up. Additionally, characters from the main story get more screen time in this what-if scenario which I really appreciated as it fleshed them out a bit more. The gameplay loop of saving all the towns while completing story missions is basic, but this with the more linear structure of traversing the open-world had me appreciate the map more than I ever had in the base game. It also led to me doing all of the entertaining sidequests (albeit there are very few of them in this mode). It'd be a disservice to play the story mode but skip out on Undead Nightmare.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, $50 is steep & honestly a bit ridiculous for a port of a 14 year old game. To me, owning Red Dead Redemption on PC is an investment into the future of modding for this title if that's what you're interested in, as I certainly am.  For those concerned about the lack of multiplayer, modders will likely bring it back by the end of the year in their own way.  The headless zombie bug from the PS3 / X360 versions of this title is patched out, making the Undead Nightmare DLC playable & enjoyable.  On the terms of emulation, playing a port of a game designed specifically for PC on PC has always had a better feel to it than running a console port through an emulator.  Here, Rockstar Games has given players certain graphical & other optimization settings that are meant to be experienced on the PC port.  On modern systems, the game looks great, performs well & definitely has a unique feel with keyboard & mouse supported for the first time.Above all, Red Dead Redemption is an true masterpiece of a game, a story unique in its own about grit, hardship, loss & the early concepts of the all important American Dream which seem all but obtainable in modern times.  No other piece of media gives a rich & fulfilling taste of the Old West in the United States like RDR does.  Not even to mention the effect this game has had on a generation.  The nostalgia factor with this title is like no other.Buy now, buy later or wait for sale, it's up to personal preference, just make sure you play it at least once.

_childDocuments_.review: For years now, I have been eagerly checking whether there were any new rumours or official announcements for a full PC release of Red Dead Redemption...And I'm happy to say that this is a very good port. Really, as far as ports go, this is pretty much as apt as it can be -- a simple yet perfect translation to PC and nothing more.I had an absolute blast exploring the world, soaking in the story, and engaging myself in the gameplay loop.As someone that played the sequel before the original, it can definitely be felt that this is an earlier iteration. It's a little clunky at times, not quite as refined as it later would be, but still never much of a detriment to the overall experience.My only real complaint is that the crouching feels really delayed, and the cover-system felt rather unrefined.Both America and Mexico have been such a delight to ride and explore through. The vast landscapes with incredible vistas can truly be felt, especially when sprinkled throughout with an endless variety of different points of interest.But what I found especially enthralling was how well the game still looks to this day. Beyond the foilage lacking true ambient occlusion; the overall game still looks incredible to this day. The world is nicely detailed, textures are surprisingly high quality for the time, character animations look really smooth, and the sky-box especially blew me away.The game's story was full of excitement and thrill, and I found it an absolute pleasure to dig myself in.The characters were really lively and full of personality, I came to find a lot of joy in just listening to all their witty and well-written dialogue.I do think that it feels a little stretched and poorly paced for a short section a little after the middle of the main-campaign. But it comes to regain its composure not long after, luckily.Undead Nightmare is a perfect remix of the main-campaign's experience, and was a really worthwhile escapade after the initial story-line.It can almost be perceived as an entirely different game, for it overhauls so much of the core main experience, and cramps it with an endless variety of twists and turns. It's rather short when compared to the main-campaign, but every minute spent has been really fulfilling.It lacks much of that coherent long-form story-line of which the main-campaign presented, for it instead has you re-encountering most friends and foes from the main-game, except now under the pressure of a zombie infection. Almost feels like an act of fan-service, and I simply adored it.As a heads-up, both campaigns are punctuated with the occasional technical glitch and such, but it's never reaching anything actively detrimental.If you've ever played a Rockstar game before then you know what you're in for. It's certainly a few fine tiers above a Bethesda game, as it's most often without much of an actual hindrance to gameplay.Though not without error, Red Dead Redemption has been such a gratifying and enjoyable experience for me to delve into.While I've now finished both campaigns, I'll likely return a few times more for some fun completionist stuff.I'm really glad I finally got the chance to enjoy and beat this game. It's been a really nice pleasure.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely worth the price of admission, I can't wait to finish this story, I never completed it on consoles (PS3 or XBOX 360. _childDocuments_.review: Definitely my favourite Rockstar game, by far. I remember counting the days for this to release back in 2010 when I was in school. The story isn't spelled out to you, John's backstory is elusive, and the game knew how to keep your mind on his past as you played his present. In fact, John’s story was so intriguing that the game’s successor was a prequel that fleshed out little lines of dialogue in the first Red Dead Redemption.This game understands the time period its based in and explores the complexities of the United States and Mexico in 1911 delicately but with a hint of exaggeration and satire that felt well done. Much in the same fashion as Grand Theft Auto, Red Dead Redemption is a satire on reality, albeit a much more toned-down version. The ideas and concepts in the game are not spelled out to you but are present. It’s a complicated rendition of the old-west and its characters are equally complicated and well embroiled in the circumstances from which their world affords.  For all intents and purposes, I prefer this over the second game. I preferred not knowing John’s backstory, it was intriguing, and it allowed my imagination to run wild. Knowing it actually dampened my experience. Furthermore, I believe this game is just a superior product. I feel the characters were better written and the art style went in a better direction. It feels less cartoonish without sacrificing the humour, whereas the prequel feels cartoonish especially when it sacrifices the humour. This Red Dead Redemption is also less clunky and isn’t teeming with excess the world over. It’s a game, plain and simple. It doesn’t waste your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine this, it's the year 2010, Blockbuster for the most part is still around, Game Informer is still at it's peak, and I am roughly 9 years old. Around this time I was painstakingly awaiting the release of the then unreleased Red Dead Redemption, a game that to my knowledge was just going to be a follow-up to the 2004 classic, Red Dead Revolver, and boy was I shocked at how much that statement was hollow. I know what you're wondering, why the stupid backstory, to put it simply, when I was a kid, I was far too stupid to fully appreciate and understand just how grounded and nuanced it was compared to it's predecessor. Now in 2024, Redemption has hit the PC market with the help of Double Eleven, and can I say that after the launch of the GTA Definitive Edition it's relieving seeing a port that not only works (even though there much to be said about that "Edition"), but feels like it's been completely left unaltered, which is surprising since this game is now three console generations old, but regardless feels just as good as it did back in 2010, which really gives me hope for more future collaborations between these guys and Rockstar, they know what their doing, although it is a shame that the Multiplayer couldn't be salvaged or the CO-OP campaign but that's fine since I believe more people would be interested in the main story and it's expansion.To summarize both sections of this package, Red Dead Redemption on it's own still holds up, especially after 14 years, the story for the most part seems far more anxious, with stakes being high all throughout, I say this since RDR2 is a prequel to this game and if you are someone who only played RDR2 would may be in for a surprise at how much this game doesn't try to be an immersive sim like RDR2, it's the perfect middle ground for an experience that wants you to explore and have fun without the burden of these almost unnecessarily drawn out additions from the second, although skinning animals may be a little tedious with the same three animations playing out depending on the size of the animal. Some people may be gutted at the lack of customization that was seen in the second but I actually like the outfits in this since they work as a greater incentive to interact with the game worlds side activities, and I found myself enjoying the game far more this time around at the age of 25, because it's a great demonstration of positive reinforcement, since these outfits provide buffs and perks, with some seeming solely situational, and even if that's true it's a nice little payoff for exploring and interacting with a world that's actively hostile.As for Undead Nightmare,  I must just be old but for what it's worth it's a fun little addition, even if it feels like a bi-product of the zombie craze of the late 2000s to early 2010s, it's a relatively short expansion, not to the point where it feels like a waste of time, because it's certainly fun, a nice little distraction from the more realistic main story.Overall with the argument being made that a 14 years old game is not worth 49.99 being somewhat valid, I will say that you will get your money's worth with RDR, whether you buy it at full price or on a discount, it's certainly a game that's stood the test of time, being a smash hit that left a lot of young and old gamers in 2010 cry, feeling a sense of fulfillment that was almost unprecedented at the time, I will say that it would be cool to see the multiplayer skins for Revolver be included as costumes, or Double Eleven and Rockstar can repurpose them for a Revolver remaster, which I would like to see, especially if it's handled by Double Eleven

_childDocuments_.review: It's solid. It's always been an amazing game and really ties into RDR2 with many background tidbits if you pay attention. Like, read the first available newspaper, for instance. The story is one of the best, a very grounded campaign with great characters, a few goofy characters, all memorable, and fantastic dialogue. There's a few mini games like Horseshoes, poker, five finger fillet etc. They're all good, typical Rockstar minigames. The world is the real masterpiece here though. It's just amazing and truly beautiful. You'll be fully immersed and get to visit South of the border into Mexico mid-way through. Unlike RDR2. The hunting was much improved in RDR2, but it's here too. The price of $50 is really my only sticking point. If you've never played it before? Maybe, maybe it's worth it if you have no other game to play currently. But really, I'd probably just wait for sale. $50 is a bit expensive for a minimal effort port a decade and a half later.Performance is great. I haven't had any bugs except 1 NPC falling through the ground. It's literally Xbox 360 Red Dead 1 ported over with a few new features. DLSS/DLAA (native DLSS, no upscaling), Reflex+. 4k. 144 fps. FSR 3 frame generation (lol what?) and increased foliage, level of detail and shadow options. Shadow softening (CHSS) etc. That's pretty much about it though. Literally, nothing else. I was hoping for a skin animation skip button, and maybe an option for sprinting to not require repeatedly pressing a button, but no such luck. Hopefully modders will get on that. It runs well. I can max out at 1440p, DLAA, 75 fps at about 75% gpu usage with a 2070 Super and Ryzen 3700x.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm so glad this masterpiece finally came to PC.  It's well worth playing and everyone on PC who has never played this game should play it 100%!  I'm just disappointed that after 14 years it's only a port.  This game really, really, really needed a good remaster.  The textures, lighting, and geometry all need updated.  I think Rock Star really missed out on a great opportunity here. I also think $50 for a port is asking too much.  $20-$30 would have been more reasonable.  $50 for a good remaster would have been more appropriate.

They also did a good job with porting it to PC, but I'd say the game is much better with controller. I actually used controller for most of the horse riding, then used MnK for shooting. Up to you though. My only real issue is the keybinds with MnK. They don't allow you to do double keybinds, but they have double keybinds set. Makes it awkward to change bindings.

_childDocuments_.review: Red Dead Redemption is an incredibly enjoyable game, and its story ties beautifully into Red Dead Redemption 2. Playing this after experiencing the prequel adds an extra layer of appreciation for the characters and events.However, it's clear that this is an older game compared to its successor. The physics and graphics, while decent for their time, feel a bit dated by today's standards. That said, the core gameplay and storytelling remain engaging, making it a must-play for fans of the series.If you can overlook the aging visuals, you'll find a game that's still worth experiencing for its narrative and connection to the larger Red Dead universe.

_childDocuments_.review: By all appearances, this seems to be a perfect launch of the original on the PC. I have had no issues with launching the game or bugs or anything. Just a smoothly running game with practically no load times because it’s a 2010 game running on a 2024 gaming PC. When I beat RDR 2 a few years ago it really made me want to go right into RDR 1 to continue the story but I could not be bothered to bust out my old 360 and play it on that and I was hoping there was news of a remaster or PC port on the horizon but there was nothing at the time. Obviously, this is exactly what I wanted short of a remaster which would be great too (I mean, Rockstar remade half the map of RDR 1 inside of RDR 2 as practically a throwaway for fun for you to just run around in at the end of RDR 2… it wouldn’t take much more to finish it out with the Mexico side of the map, but the reanimation of all the cut scenes and stuff would be where the real time consuming work would be) but a PC port is fine with me. In all honesty, this game set to Ultra graphics setting looks great even to this day. Obviously, it is not on RDR 2’s level, but it can still be commended for how good it looks. Also, it is super commendable that this is simply a PC port and yet doesn’t have some bloated 50 GB space requirement. Just 12 GB which is very reasonable for a 14-year-old game. I think the $50 price tag is asking too much considering that that is almost the same as RDR 2 when not on sale, this game is 14 years old, and isn’t a remaster at all, just a plain PC port, but still, I love both games so much and the opportunity to seamlessly jump from RDR 2 to RDR 1 that it is worth the price for me at least. If in about a year or so it goes for 50% off on a Steam sale then it will be absolutely worth it for anyone though. Overall great game and appears to be a slam dunk of a PC port without issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Really feel like making a review for this game because it's aged surprisingly well and I think you should all play it. Let's start with the elephant in the room, The 60 Dollar US price ( I payed 80 CAD!), While I do think its way too expensive, The main game took me 24 hours and the Undead Nightmare DLC took me 4 (I took extra long because I wanted the 100%) And I thought it was worth it, Most 60 Dollar games end at the 5-6 hour mark, And you get triple that here.MAIN GAME: I played this game for the first time when I was 11 and I enjoyed it, But not enough to call it a top 5 game of all time, Now I cam say safely it is a top 5 game of all time, The aiming and horse riding is so fluent on computer it is a whole other experience, The story is amazing and really depressing, While still keeping in funny characters. One problem with the story is there is a lot of filler, But as soon as you finish Bonnie's missions it's mostly gone. Also most of you are fans of the sequel (Or Prequel I should say), Which improves apon most things, But your still going to be sad when the game is over because it's so funCOMPLETION: I enjoyed this game a lot when I was younger and wanted to 100% it, It was surprisingly fun to complete, So was Undead nightmare. Big problem with most Rockstar games is there are some gambling based achievements, Which might make a few people mad( I am horrible at poker so shoutout to my buddy for helping me out, I ended up using his tricks to redo the achievement because I felt like I cheated). 100% Took me 75 hours and I was pretty quick.COMPLAINTS: There are a couple, Sometimes when calling your horse over to you, They spawn on top of a mountain and walk off to get to you, WHICH THEN KILLS THEM IMMEDIATELY!  Sometimes your horse just dies when sliding down a hill. This even happens with the Horses of the apocalypse, Which are immune to damage. Also the world can feel very empty, Random events do most of the time spawn and make it more fun, But you get screwed sometimes and end up riding to a place with no much interaction. NONE OF THESE ARE BIG PROBLEMSFINAL VERDICT: Fun, Amazing characters and antagonists, Does not get very boring and is just a great game all around, If you are a fan of RDR2 and want to play the sequel to the amazing story, I recommend you buy this ASAP. If you are tight on money then wait for a discount, And if your like me and want to replay it (My Original copy broke but it might be a problem with my console, So I just bought the PC version) it's really up to you. If this is your first Red Dead experience, You most likely will enjoy it! 9.4/10 and 10/10 port

_childDocuments_.review: The worst thing people have to say about this game is the price. It's definitely an odd choice for Rockstar to be charging fifty for a game this old. However, in my mind personally this game is fully worth it to me. There's so many things that make RDR an all time classic. In terms of gameplay, it still feels incredibly crisp and satisfying. Outside of occasional horse control, everything feels very responsive and could honestly be mistaken for a third person shooter releasing today. Gun variety is great. The shooting mechanics are classic rockstar third person and I highly recommend playing the game in expert targeting mode just for a slightly more challenging experience. The shootout set pieces of the game are honestly incredibly iconic and stick out more in my mind than a large number of the fights in RDR2. Locations and environments really feel unique, the loneliness of Tumbleweed, the excitement of attacking El Presidio or Torquemada, the snowy desolation of Dutch's snow fort. There are just so many classic locales that really emulate the vibe Rockstar was aiming for with this game. I think they were also able to handcraft these places better just due to the smaller size of the map. No two places in the game ever feel very samey. They especially worked hard to craft that vibe of Western loneliness and isolation. Plus the setting combined with the musical score is just mindbogglingly atmospheric.Obviously aside from the difference in map, all the core mechanics you would recognize from RDR2 started here and still feel exciting. The mini games are all fantastic and can be fun time sinks, especially Liar's Dice. Horse breaking and finding the rare horses of the map is incredibly exciting. There's definitely less of an emphasis on buying a good horse and more so finding one. Really everything about the core gameplay is stellar, the only complaint you can really lodge is that some of the initial story missions are relatively slow with low stakes objectives. Story and characters truly are the real value in this game though. RDR1 was Rockstar's first complex and deep character focused story. Everyone you meet, including strangers for side missions, are really thought out and unique characterizations of western tropes or early industrial age inventors. Nigel West Dickens, Seth, and Irish are all incredibly memorable, and for me the second act Mexico characters involved are all standouts with entertaining lines or motivations and slight complexities. RDR2 was definitely more focused on the gang and defining them as compared to most of the random characters you'll meet for missions along the way. And above all else, John truly gets to shine here. Arthur is a fantastic character and rivals John in every way. But there's something about John's maturity in this game and his attitudes towards the other people he meets that really gets me. The ending of his story especially was the first time I ever cried at a video game before. You really feel for John in this one and he's a fantastic main character. While I am disappointed that multiplayer was not included. It was certainly a gem for it's time, and I hope it'll come back. *There was nothing more enjoyable than riding a buffalo and jousting a friend on the tall trees bridge, or playing multiplayer liars dice.* I think what's included here is exceptionally worth your value in terms of time you can get out of it. Undead Nightmare alone is easily more expansive and exciting than 3/4 of the DLC released for games today. It was a true overhaul and really let the combat of the game shine. Plus finding cryptids and the horses of the apocalypse is an experience that's never left my mind years later. It's not the deepest story of all time, but it's truly one of the best expansions released for any game ever. To wrap it up. This is still one of the best games Rockstar has ever released to this day. It runs fantastic on the PC port and if you decide to buy it, it's definitely worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Red Dead Redemption is an incredible game that feels like stepping into the Old West. The story is powerful and makes you care deeply about John Marston and his past. The world is beautiful, detailed, and full of things to explore, from wide-open plains to small, dusty towns. You can hunt, ride horses, and even just sit back and watch the sunset—it all feels real.The gameplay is smooth, with exciting shootouts and missions that keep you engaged. The random events and side quests make every playthrough feel unique and fresh. It’s easy to lose hours just exploring, meeting characters, and uncovering secrets.Overall, Red Dead Redemption is a must-play for anyone who loves a good story and an immersive world. Even though the games is old,  it’s one of those games that stays with you long after you’ve finished.

I bought this game because it's a story that is worth remembering, and it's a game worth memorializing. It might not have the mechanics or gameplay depth of Red Dead Redemption 2, but people who argue this will conveniently ignore that other games at the same era of release such as Mass Effect 2, Halo: Reach and Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood also did not have the same depth as you see in modern video games today. These same people would also be reasonable to admit that such games were designed for consoles in mind, and not necessarily meant to take advantage of the open and limitless potential of the PC platform at the time. I want to reiterate, however: I agree that the $50 price tag is somewhat uncanny for a game this old. Wait for sale.As for myself, I think this will be a fine addition to my collection.

_childDocuments_.review: Nostalgia can be a fickle thing. You can love a game, and have fond memories of it through the years, only to come back to it later, especially after sequels, and find it doesn't hold up as well as you thought. Red Dead Redemption is a game most at risk of that. Released in 2010 for PS3 and Xbox 360, Rockstar never seemed to consider a PC release, a decision made all the more strange when Red Dead Redemption 2 came to PC in 2019. Better late than never though. I haven't played the game since the original 360 release, and I am delighted to say the game is still as great as it was when I first played it. Sure, it's dated when compared to RDR 2 or any other open-world game released in the last 5 years, but it's not an ugly game. The Old West vistas - mountains, canyons, frontier towns, deserts - still catch your breath, there's moments when you're roaming on your horse and the sun light just catches on things, rocks and cacti, or you're chasing bandits through canyons as deer panic to get out of the way and you think,"Wow, this is still a beautiful game."The gameplay is essentially GTA in the Old West, a decent length main story with some short side missions and a sprinkling of activities like poker, blackjack, horseshoes and five finger fillets. You can also run simple jobs in towns to get money for horses, clothes and weapons although you'll get more than enough from doing the main story. The narrative is not as epic in scope compared to its successor, and lacks the seriousness that made that story so acclaimed, but RDR's plot still a lot of fun and John Marston was Rockstar's best character until Arthur Morgan came along in RDR2.The port is good. I had a steady 50-60 fps at high settings on my Steam Deck, although there was the occasional stutter in towns. On my PC - GeForce 3080, Intel i5 12600K - I get a solid 144 fps at 4K with DLSS, every setting maxed. You might argue a 14 year old game should be able to do that anyway. I bet you can't say that of many games with the scope of Red Dead Redemption. High fps support continues to be rare for console ports even with new games released now.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start out by saying I absolutely loved RDR2, this sequel is not RDR2.  It's almost as though Rockstar said "screw it, good enough". The game is a bit glitchy going from running smooth to bugging out to where John Marston is suddenly moving like a tweeker bouncing all over the screen.  The graphics also get a bit glitchy after a little bit of game play, characters appearing behind themselves and moving independent of the forward image (though I took too much cough syrup at first).  I'm not entirely supporting the lack of modification you can do to the weapons, purchasing new clothing, haircuts, and facial grooming.  I don't regret buying the game, just wish they would have spent a little more time polishing the end product prior to release.  Truthfully, I would have been thrilled with RDR2 and an expansion pack for the John Marston missions, would have saved Rockstar time and hassle.

_childDocuments_.review: If you, like me, missed out on the original *Red Dead Redemption*, this new PC port is a fantastic way to finally experience it. It’s also interesting to notice the early versions of systems that would later evolve in *GTA V*—like the weapon wheel, checkpoint system, and even horse races. For instance, in this game, the weapon wheel doesn’t slow down time while you’re using it, which feels different compared to more modern Rockstar games.The graphics hold up surprisingly well, but the NPCs show the game’s age. They don’t feel as lively or reactive as characters in today’s games, and the loot system isn’t as expansive as what we saw in *Red Dead Redemption 2*. That said, *Red Dead Redemption* is a genuine classic, and this PC port does it justice.

_childDocuments_.review: As a devoted fan of Red Dead Redemption II—my all-time favorite game—venturing into the original Red Dead Redemption on PC was an extraordinary experience. Having never played the first game before this recent release, I can confidently say it has far surpassed my expectations.From the moment I began, nostalgia washed over me. Witnessing familiar characters in their older years was a captivating journey. It added a rich layer of depth to the story, allowing me to connect the dots between their pasts and the events of RDR2. Dutch, the silver-tongued figure from RDR2, was particularly poignant. It’s bittersweet to see how he has evolved (or perhaps devolved) into a character with little left to say in the first game's narrative. His haunting presence prompted deep reflection on the themes of loyalty and disillusionment that resonate throughout both titles. Observing his decline added emotional weight, enhancing my appreciation for both games.And the music—oh, the music! The classic Western sounds are mesmerizing. Each note draws you deeper into the world, echoing the landscapes and the tumultuous lives of the characters. The score beautifully complements the stunning visuals, creating a symphony that elevates the entire experience. The melodies feel timeless, evoking a sense of adventure and nostalgia that perfectly captures the spirit of the Wild West. I found myself humming the tunes long after I’d put the game down, each piece woven into the fabric of my memories.Playing Red Dead Redemption now, especially with the advancements of the PC port, is nothing short of remarkable. I can only imagine how blown away I would have been had I experienced this game at launch. Even by today’s standards, the graphics and gameplay hold up incredibly well. The attention to detail in the environments—ranging from dusty plains to bustling towns—creates an immersive world that feels alive. The fluidity of character movements and the intricacy of animations make every moment engaging. Whether riding through vast landscapes or engaging in intense shootouts, the experience is nothing short of exhilarating.The storytelling remains a hallmark of the series, with each mission and side quest weaving together a rich tapestry of life in the Old West. The characters are vividly portrayed, each with their own motivations and complexities. The dialogues are sharp, and the interactions feel genuine, making it easy to become emotionally invested in their journeys. It’s a testament to the developers’ mastery of narrative that I found myself deeply immersed in this world, even knowing the ultimate fates of many characters.This latest edition not only brings the classic back into the limelight but also enhances it for a new generation of gamers. The combination of storytelling, character development, and an evocative soundtrack has made my experience unforgettable. If you loved RDR2, you owe it to yourself to dive into Red Dead Redemption. It’s a beautifully crafted masterpiece that feels just as relevant today as it did over a decade ago. Bravo to the developers for this incredible port!

_childDocuments_.review: Quite simply, one of the greatest games ever produced.RDR1 has aged well, and is still a game more than worth putting some hours in. Sure, we can quibble about the small size of its open world, the lack of extra games within games, side quests, activities, compared to modern games. But that's because the open world game paradigm shifted when this masterpiece came out, and it still remains a benchmark of how to make an open world open and alive. Graphics wise, the visuals still look good. Game controls can take a moment to adjust to, again because you're going back in time in terms of responsiveness and refinement, but they're nowhere near as janky as other games of that era are if played today. Overall, the transfer to PC is seamless, and the game works equally well on controller or mouse and keyboard. The story? Well, it just feels good to walk in John Marston's boots again. Personally speaking, I prefer RDR1 to 2 in a lot of ways. Let's be completely clear, RDR2 is a far superior game in every way, and storywise there's few games that have that quality to its writing and acting. But where Red Dead 2 is an Oscar Winning legitimate drama, Red Dead 1 is a blockbuster popcorn crunching action movie. If RD2 is Unforgiven, Shane, or Once Upon a Time in the West, RD1 is The Magnificent Seven, They Call Me Trinity, or Rio Bravo. It's simply more fun being John than Arthur.

_childDocuments_.review: While very late to the platform, Red Dead Redemption on PC is a perfectly done port and is definitely still worthy of all of its praise 14 years later.I had not played Red Dead Redemption since it launched on the PlayStation 3, and I have been awaiting a PC port as long as everyone else, and I am so happy to finally have it in my possession. The game performs exactly as I remembered it, with even less glitches surprisingly, and the higher resolution & smoother framerate offered a great bonus. I think Double Eleven did a great job at optimizing the game and implementing great quality-of-life bonuses for modern technology. I wish this had landed in my lap sooner, but I am so happy it can finally be properly played this way. It is remarkable having an aging Rockstar Games title on PC without mods and community fixes being required to play the game. Some of my favorite Rockstar titles were utterly unplayable without silent patches and custom configs, which I think is inexcusable in the current day. Even some slightly later titles like Grand Theft Auto IV are infamously chuggy and unoptimized on newer machines, so this particular port was such a blast of fresh air. I would be okay with Double Eleven porting and optimizing any other Rockstar titles that suffered similar fates, it just works right out of the metaphorical box this time.Aside from my technical woes finally being answered, Red Dead Redemption is still one of the most worthwhile single player experiences of its generation, so you would definitely be doing yourself a favor by trying it out. The following Red Dead Redemption 2 achieved such a high fame, deservedly so as I gush about it every chance I can, and while people gladly spend hundreds of hours getting lost in that game, I think you would be doing a disservice by skipping out on the former. I also think it should be played before Red Dead Redemption 2 as the rest of the world played it. The story unfolds in a great way regardless of the order you play them in, but I feel like it is better to see where the journey started for players. While it is nowhere near as detailed and immersive as the 2nd game, Red Dead Redemption is a very engaging experience from just the story alone. Even knowing what happens, I still get wrapped up in the plot and wish it never ended. I won't recap it here, so I'll just say the bare basics of being a former outlaw running around the wild west in the style of a Grand Theft Auto game should really sell you on this game and let you know if you think you'll enjoy it. That description is what sold me on the game in 2010 and I never regretted giving it my attention.The controls felt very smooth on an XBox controller for me, and everything functioned exactly as I remembered. Nothing felt unfair or frustrating, sometimes you are overloaded with instructions in the upper-right corner, but if you're invested in the game you'll know what you're doing. The combat is very fast and snappy, the world is massive for the time and surprisingly never dull in your travels, the music is great in the background, the humor lands despite being quite on-the-nose in the typical Rockstar fashion, and the storytelling & characters stand tall with some of the best in the Western genre. The only really frustrating aspects never fell on this port but rather on the design of these Red Dead games overall, and that is just a bit of luck you need to complete certain challenges and stats. You're going to need some to locate certain animals or complete gambling challenges if you are chasing a completionist achievements like I did. That can definitely be pretty time consuming if the cards aren't in your favor for a while.The inclusion of the zombie Western chaos, Undead Nightmare, is such a nice bonus to be included in this game, as well as all of the DLC content from Game-of-the-Year editions from years ago, it's nice not missing out on those. I had actually never played Undead Nightmare before this port, and finally doing so was very worth it. The gameplay shift of a zombie apocalypse with far different priorities, as well as the characters and humor flipped on its head throughout was such a nice surprise. It felt like a custom conversion mod with fully voiced cutscenes, and I don't mean that in a bad way at all. It's so awesome to me that Rockstar took one of their big open world games and twisted it into a nearly entirely different game, it feels unreal and I would love for that to be done more often across the industry. The whole add-on has the attitude of a schlocky B movie and I wouldn't have wanted it any other way. I laughed at all of the circumstances and I had a ton of fun playing with the new mechanics and weapons.The absence of any multiplayer elements from the original version is a big hindrance. Much like the repackaging of Grand Theft Auto IV, it's only a detriment in my opinion. I doubt it is that hard for Rockstar to provide the services to allow these older games to keep those game modes. I may be completely ignorant, or maybe they just don't want to deal with the logistics and upkeep, but it would have been nice to have those servers. Also the price is definitely way too high for a game this old. I would say anything above $20 at most is gouging, and I understand I am contributing to the problem since I played and reviewed it, but I agree with others that it is just way too much and I want to warn people to not be irrational like me. I would definitely wait for a sale or for the base price to start dropping.Overall, Red Dead Redemption on PC is a great port. It scratched so much nostalgia and fond memories for me, and it's a much more complete experience now that you can play both Red Dead Redemption games on the same platform, as well as the Undead Nightmare DLC. It really is the port I dreamed of for so long, and I am excited to see what kind of mods and crazy things people make with a more accessible official copy like this. I'm very glad with how smooth and bug-free this release is. I wish the multiplayer was included, and the price is ridiculous, but if you can justify the purchase and are a fan of Red Dead Redemption 2, I definitely think this is worth your time. I hope Double Eleven is kept on board to finally port other titles or fix other old floundering Rockstar games.

I'm definitely not a graphics/performance expert. I am quite content to put everything at low and crank a steady fps in any game I play, but here I have it on ultra and the only setting i changed was motion blur and it's running a steady 120 at 1440p. My pc is aging towards upper midrange at this point.Anyways, aside from the launcher, I have nothing but good things to say so far. _childDocuments_.review: Let's get the first thing out of the way, the price is too steep. There's no getting away from that and if you aren't desperate to play it now and can wait a few months then pick it up on sale. It's a shame and worrying that Rockstar feels justified in charging this.HOWEVER, if you can swallow that price point what you are getting is one of the greatest games of all time with one of the greatest expansions of all time. It's truly one of the most special gaming experiences you can have. This native PC port of Red Dead Redemption(still can't believe I'm saying that) has all the settings you would want from a good pc port such as numerous graphical and framerate tweaks as well as more modern upscaling and frame generation settings. This runs buttery smooth at ultra settings at 144fps on my PC and just looks fantastic for a game that's coming up 15 years old soon. It also runs at a solid 60fps at high settings on my steam deck OLED. As much as you can say "So it should run well for such an old game" true but in 2024 would you be surprised if any game came out an unoptimised mess? but no on a technical level, it's pretty much flawless.Overall thoughts are, whether you get this now or wait for a sale(definitely justified if you feel that way) you absolutely won't be disappointed in the product you are getting, this is a REALLY good native pc port of Red Dead Redemption 1. Some might be disappointed it's not a full-on remaster but my honest opinion is, would it be nice? yeah, especially for the price. Does this game need a full-on remaster? no, it still looks and plays extremely well. Whether it's now or on a sale, absolutely buy this game it genuinely is a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: The original Red Dead Redemption remains a unique, weird and violent artifact of the Xbox 360 era of gaming. If you've never played the original game, Red Dead II's tale of the "death of the wild west," gives way to the world and events of this game:The Wild West is dead, and John Marston is here to pick at its bones. This is an entirely different kind of tragedy. The game's tone is far closer to Grand Theft Auto's glib cynicism, but it's heightened by the unblinking casual cruelty of this more desolate corner of the West. There's an uncanny mood of quirky weirdness, gothic moodiness and spiritual decay to this experience that's absent in the sequel. This is a very different beast, and it stands apart very well from RDRII on its own quite well. The story is still a masterpiece, the gameplay is still very much of the Xbox 360 era (but feels sharper than ever on MKB), and the settings here look better than ever. This game absolutely looks, plays and feels it's age --but given how superb it always was, I actually enjoy how perfectly preserved of an experience this is. Double-Eleven knocked this port out of the park.Speaking of perfect preservation, the wildest criminality on display here is Rockstar pricing this exactly the same as they did when it hit the shelves in 2011. Is it worth it? Sure. But it's no less raw a deal than any John Marston makes in this game.This is still a must-own for any self-respecting gentleman's Steam library.

_childDocuments_.review: 14 years later, finally, Red Dead Redemption on PC.  Took me 48 hours to get all the achievements.  My rating: 9 out of 10.Despite RDR being a 2010 game, it mostly plays like a modern game. Yeah, 2010 games are considered old now. It’s actually fast paced than RDR2, overall movement is faster, and you can camp in the wild then teleport to anywhere.But the graphics keep reminding me, this is still a 2010 game.The combat actually feels the same as RDR2. Dead-eye, mark, headshot. The story is better after playing RDR2, everything makes more sense now. I really like the story in Mexico more. But overall, it feels short compared to RDR2, especially latter missions that involve Dutch. I really like the Undead Nightmare DLC, it makes me wonder what if RDR2 gets a single player story DLC. But Rockstar has changed, they get greedy, they only care about monkey making online mode, despite RDR2’s online mode being a huge failure.100% RDR is less painful than RDR2, but still, there are many hunting and collectibles that are RNG based, it’s annoying running around for half an hour just to find 8 snakes.The biggest problem is  the price, for a 14 years old game that Rockstar refuses to put on PC. 50 USD is too expensive, a lot of newer, better looking, more content packed games cost less than 50 USD. Just as I said before, Rockstar has changed, it gets greedy.In conclusion, RDR is a fun game, worth playing in 2024 on PC. but right now, it’s overpriced on STEAM.

_childDocuments_.review: Where to begin.I cannot overstate my love for this game, and it releasing on PC exactly around the time I started gaming on Steam feels so unbelievably fitting.I first got Red Dead Redemption for the PS3 for Christmas aged 11. This game very quickly became the primary game that I played from then until the age of 20. I amassed thousands of hours playing this game on many different saves. I even befriended Rob Wiethoff on Facebook about 11 years ago and spoke to him on numerous occasions. Looking back I was a very annoying young kid and he was very generous with his time, I have nothing but kind words to say about Rob. The Polygon video 'Finding John Marston' is essential viewing.When RDR2 came out, I simply couldn't attach myself to it the same way I did with this game. Nothing was ever going to live up to the first in my eyes. I spent hours a week on the Red Dead Wiki, watching videos (I deeply miss RDR videos from c.2010 being easy to find) and listening to the soundtrack. Red Dead Redemption made an indelible mark on my soul and is truly one of the most formative parts of my early years.The story of this game has quite possibly the greatest video game writing of all time. Take your favourite spaghetti western movie, add Rockstar's unrivalled ability to create emotionally developed and deeply interesting characters and you are left with one of the single greatest western stories in media.The greatest part of this story was the way you gradually learned more and more about John Marston's past life, something that players who started with RDR2 don't get to experience in the same way. After all these years of playing, John feels like an old friend.Even relatively small characters (Amos, Herbert Moon, Eli & Jonah are some of my favourites) are well acted and thoughtfully placed within the greater scope of the story. Dutch Van der Linde is a truly despicable character in this game, and Edgar Ross will leave you with a lasting hatred. The ending of this game had me in tears as a young boy, and when I played RDR2 the ending felt like a poor copy that you saw coming a mile off.The world...In my opinion, the most meticulously crafted world video games have to offer. RDR2, despite being visually gorgeous, is in my mind, lacking in character. Nothing about that game says 'Western' to me. This game on the other hand perfectly captures the feel of the Wild West in its dying days. There are picturesque green hills and snow in West Elizabeth (Tall trees being my absolute favourite location), deserted towns like Tumbleweed that feel as though they are haunted (if you know you know, those were the golden days on YouTube...) and the absolutely stunning Mexico. I've spent hundreds of hours just walking around, soaking up the atmosphere, listening to NPCs go about their days. You will never get tired of exploring this absolute love letter to the Wild West.I have very clearly laid out my Red Dead Redemption biases already so forgive me for saying that this is the single greatest soundtrack of all time. 'Born Unto Trouble' is seriously my favourite piece of music. Ashtar Commands' 'Daedman's Gun' is absolutely soul destroying when you first hear it. I spent many hours as a young kid listening to that song staring up at the ceiling as I laid in bed. Jose Gonzales has become an artist I really enjoy due to his feature in this game. Without spoilers, the moment 'Far Away' plays is one of the most iconic moments in gaming, and Jamie Lidell's 'Compass' manages to compliment the game perfectly despite not sounding stylistically uniform to the rest of the music in the game. The ambient whistles that play are haunting and sound straight out of the Ennio Morricone songbook, I've whistled some of them almost every day for over 10 years.That brings me to the side activities. LIARS DICE. Liars Dice is the single greatest game of all time. Blackjack is always brilliant and although In am atrocious at poker, I will spend days of my life playing these games over at Thieves Landing. Night watches at MacFarlane's Ranch, although repetitive, are always good ways to kill time. Bounties are a constant stream of action.Undead Nightmare is a product of a bygone era. DLCs like that simply aren't made anymore. the entire aesthetic of the game are turned on its head, and Rockstar even created a brilliant horror Rockabilly soundtrack to go along with it.The lack of multiplayer is definitely a minus, especially being priced what it is. Online was very simple but fun, picking your character from the many people who show up in the story, and consisted of free roam and various mini games like death matches, capture game modes, races and co-op missions. As a kid, me and my childhood friend would spend hours creating our own stories and games in the open world.To conclude...Most of my love for this game is deeply rooted in nostalgia. It is woven into the very fabric of my life. However playing it again has only cemented my love for it. It holds up so well. I can't promise this will be the life changing experience it was for me, but at least it is a beautifully made Western that is packed with action, emotion and endless replayability. I look forward to another decade of playing Red Dead Redemption.

_childDocuments_.review: The champions of double-dipping strike again. Rockstar Games is infamous for failing to introduce any product they release to the PC platform in anything that could be mistaken for a fair and timely manner. But here it is. After 14 years they have finally mustered up the energy to... pawn the task off to a third party developer that no one recognizes. What could go wrong there?Not much evidently. This port is very good. Performance is above average in my opinion, considering how this game hasn't been able to be emulated in 14 years and here I am playing a port without dropping below 60fps on a lower middle range GPU. The only things that really stand out as subpar are texture quality and audio compression. But this a consequence of the games age.  $50 is egregious, but what may be absurd to one person may seem fair to another. I would wait for a sale on this one, just on the principle of how Rockstar treats PC users alone. If you're wondering what I mean by that, then look at the release timeline for GTA V and know that they're gonna do the same thing with every major release in the future. I purchased it knowing I will get $50 worth of time out of it and I can typically count the amount of full price games I purchase in a years time on one hand, so that's enough for me to justify it.Other than the price tag, there's is nothing to complain about here. Double Eleven did a great job and it's the same old Red Dead Redemption. The game is a pinnacle moment in video game history, and since it's almost old enough to be drafted into the US military, I don't feel the need to explain why.

_childDocuments_.review: Red Dead Redemption (RDR), developed by Rockstar Games and released in 2010, is a landmark in video game history, revered for its storytelling, atmosphere, and immersion. Set in the early 20th century American frontier, it follows former outlaw John Marston’s quest to rescue his family by capturing his old gang members. RDR is more than just a western-themed game; it redefined the open-world genre, exploring complex themes of morality, redemption, and the passing of an era. Here’s an in-depth look at its significance across storytelling, gameplay, cultural impact, and the genre itself.1. Narrative Depth and Emotional ImpactAt its core, Red Dead Redemption presents a deeply emotional and layered story, unlike most other games of its time. John Marston, a reformed outlaw, is blackmailed by federal agents who hold his family hostage, pushing him to hunt down his former gang members. This setup provides a narrative arc that is both personal and poignant, as Marston is continually forced to reckon with his past sins and the violence that defined his previous life.The characters in RDR are compelling and complex. Marston, who tries to be honorable and just but finds himself dragged back into a violent lifestyle, represents a tragic figure trying to escape his past. The supporting characters, including former gang leader Dutch van der Linde, showcase the fading American frontier and the inevitable intrusion of government and civilization into the wild. This narrative exploration of redemption and regret is rarely tackled with such maturity in games, and it influenced the narrative depth seen in future titles across the gaming industry.2. A Breakthrough in Open-World Game DesignRDR’s open-world design set a new benchmark for realism and interaction. Rockstar Games took a massive leap from the more caricatured style of Grand Theft Auto to create a world that feels authentic and alive, rather than just fun and chaotic. The world of New Austin, the fictional American-Mexican border, isn’t just a backdrop; it’s a character in itself, with ecosystems, realistic wildlife, and unpredictable weather cycles. NPCs go about their daily routines independently, and random events, such as ambushes or strangers needing help, create a sense of life beyond the player’s control.The level of immersion found in RDR encouraged players to explore not just because they wanted to finish objectives, but because the world was a joy to experience. Activities like hunting, horseback riding, and poker added to this immersion and set a standard that other open-world games would strive to replicate. RDR also took steps to blend gameplay and storytelling: missions felt like natural extensions of Marston’s story rather than isolated objectives. This immersive, seamless integration became a model that influenced major franchises like The Witcher and Assassin’s Creed.3. Thematic Exploration and Social CommentaryRDR doesn’t shy away from engaging with complex themes. It offers a nuanced take on the fading American frontier and critiques the often-romanticized notion of the Wild West. The game presents a sobering portrayal of the conflicts of that era—law versus outlaw, civilization versus nature, and progress versus freedom. Marston’s journey is set against the backdrop of rapid modernization and the encroaching power of government, law enforcement, and technology, which bring both progress and oppression.The portrayal of Native American characters, though controversial, reflects the era’s tension and complexities. While some aspects of this representation could have benefited from a more sensitive approach, it still contributed to conversations about race and justice. RDR’s narrative sheds light on how myths of the “Old West” often overlook the harsh realities and injustices faced by marginalized groups. This introspective and critical perspective allowed RDR to transcend gaming conventions and position itself as a legitimate piece of cultural commentary, elevating the medium as a storytelling platform.4. Technical Achievements and Cinematic ExcellenceRDR’s technical accomplishments were groundbreaking for 2010. The game’s world was not only massive but also artistically crafted with a cinematographic eye. Rockstar used techniques reminiscent of Western films, from John Ford’s sweeping landscapes to Sergio Leone’s tense close-ups, to capture the mood and essence of the Wild West. The soundtrack, composed by Bill Elm and Woody Jackson, uses atmospheric, sparse instrumentation to echo the desolation and tension of the frontier. Each musical cue was crafted to reflect Marston’s journey and emotions, creating an iconic soundscape.Moreover, the integration of motion capture allowed for authentic character expressions and gestures, which heightened the emotional impact of interactions and cutscenes. While other games focused on flashy mechanics or graphics, RDR concentrated on creating a cohesive, grounded experience. The game’s approach to cinematography influenced later titles, such as The Last of Us, which similarly used realistic motion capture and camera work to tell mature, emotionally complex stories.5. Legacy and Influence on Gaming CultureThe success of Red Dead Redemption not only solidified Rockstar Games as a powerhouse in narrative-driven games but also redefined expectations for open-world gaming. Games following RDR began to adopt more nuanced storytelling, character-driven narratives, and meticulously detailed environments. RDR’s DNA can be traced in countless games released since, from The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, which built on the open-world storytelling structure, to Horizon Zero Dawn, which borrowed RDR’s approach to environmental storytelling.RDR’s influence extended beyond mechanics; it shifted public perception of video games as a storytelling medium. The game’s mature themes, cinematic direction, and emotional weight demonstrated that video games could rival the narrative complexity of film and literature. Players who might have previously dismissed games as simplistic or juvenile found themselves drawn to the emotional depth and historical richness of RDR, making it a game that bridged audiences across demographics.6. The Impact of Red Dead Redemption 2 and Continued LegacyThe release of Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018 further solidified the series’ place in gaming history. Acting as a prequel, RDR2 deepened the story and characters introduced in the first game while pushing technical boundaries even further. The success of RDR2 brought renewed attention to RDR, with players revisiting the original or experiencing it for the first time. This continuity helped to cement RDR’s place in gaming culture as one of the greatest franchises of all time.The legacy of RDR continues to influence open-world games today. Players expect richer worlds, more complex characters, and narratives that demand emotional investment. Games like Cyberpunk 2077 and Ghost of Tsushima owe a significant debt to RDR’s pioneering approach to blending story and gameplay. Rockstar Games’ commitment to authenticity, emotional storytelling, and immersive environments has set a standard that continues to challenge and inspire game developers.ConclusionIn sum, Red Dead Redemption was a watershed moment in gaming history, proving that video games can serve as powerful tools for storytelling, exploration, and cultural commentary. Its immersive world, complex characters, and emotional resonance provided an experience unlike any other, capturing the hearts and minds of players worldwide. RDR did not merely entertain; it engaged, challenged, and moved players, leaving an indelible mark on the gaming landscape. Over a decade later, Red Dead Redemption remains an essential experience for gamers and continues to influence the evolution of open-world storytelling. For its contributions to the gaming industry and the art of storytelling, Red Dead Redemption will forever be remembered
