_childDocuments_.review: The story of Red Dead Redemption takes 15-20 hours to complete. The Undead Nightmare expansion introduces a zombie-themed storyline, adding another 6-10 hours. However, completionists aiming to explore every side quest, challenge, and achievement can expect up to 50 hours of gameplay.The gameplay blends structured mission-based objectives with an open-world design, creating a believable Western experience. You control John Marston in a third-person perspective, navigating one of the best Old West presentations in gaming, spanning deserts, plains, towns, and rugged mountains. Movement on horseback is the essential method of transportation, offering a sense of scale but also playing a strategic role in pursuits, battles, and general traversal. Horses have a stamina system, and the mechanics reward finding a balance and bonding with faster or more resilient mounts. Combat is an integral mechanic of the gameplay, featuring a blend of cover-based gunfighting, melee, and horseback shooting.The signature Dead Eye targeting system allows players to slow down time to mark targets or execute precise shots, adding a cinematic feel to gunfights while providing room for strategic planning, and is extremely useful in more challenging encounters. The weapon variety is extensive, with revolvers, rifles, shotguns, and throwing knives that reflect the Wild West setting. Each weapon type has distinct handling, range, and reload times, impacting the approach and strategy. In between missions, random events keep the gameplay and the world dynamic. Random encounters with bandits, animals, or distressed travelers can lead to mini-objectives or optional challenges, such as helping citizens, hunting, or chasing criminals.Additionally, an honor system tracks moral actions, influencing NPC behavior and impacting prices and interactions in towns. Side activities such as gambling, duels, and various types of hunting offer meaningful diversions that feed into the economy and provide additional depth. The gameplay pace is rather planned and pre-defined, emphasizing realism and carefully setting up the atmosphere for various things. Fast travel options are available but limited, encouraging players to experience the world and its varied environments firsthand. As you progress, you unlock new areas, facing harsher climates and more aggressive opponents, which gradually scales difficulty and variety in gameplay.Visually, the game is remarkable for its time, and certain aspects hold up nicely even today. The open world is a dynamic landscape, with sweeping deserts, lush forests, and rugged mountains, all rendered with impressive detail. With the increased render distances of the PC version, at times it truly feels like a modern game that came out not some few years ago. Lighting and weather effects are superb, adding atmosphere to every time of day—from vibrant sunsets casting golden shades to stormy skies rolling across the plains. The user interface is sleek and obscure, the HUD fades into the background nicely, and the minimalistic approach helps keep the focus on exploration uninterrupted.While the audio design is certainly limited by modern standards, it does a job of portraying and getting across the original vision. Nature sounds—the calls of distant coyotes, rustling grass, and whistling winds—are well-designed, creating a believable natural environment. Gunfire is punchy and impactful, adding to the weight and realism of combat. The voice acting is excellent, as expected from a Rockstar production, with characters voiced by a cast that brings genuine emotion to the story. The soundtrack is a pack of subtle, mood, and action-driven pieces that perfectly capture the low tone and Western setting.RDR1 is an open-world action-adventure game set in the late 19th century, during the decline of the American Wild West, where the country is transitioning from the wild frontier to a more modern, law-abiding society. The story and the narrative follow John Marston, a former outlaw, as he travels through a vast old-west world, encountering different characters in small towns and untamed wilderness. During the story, Marston, forced to do so by the government, tracks down his old gang members in exchange for his and his family's safety.The narrative explores themes of redemption, loyalty, and the clash between law and crime. The game centers around exploration, combat (including gunfights and horseback riding), and completing missions that advance the story. The missions and side quests also feature various activities like hunting, bounty hunting, duels, and so on. The dynamic world feels alive, with changing weather, wildlife, and spontaneous events. In addition to its emotional narrative, the game delivers an immersive adventure that captures the spirit of the Old West, blending action with thoughtful storytelling and open-world freedom.The PC version builds on the original foundation, with some small but evident improvements. Even though these upgrades do not drastically change the visual outcome, the improvements that did make it to the PC are welcome. The most notable improvement on PC is the extended render distance, making it visually the best version to experience the game. However, the rest of the graphical presentation is unchanged, so you'll still see some pop-ins with distant objects and shadow draw-ins. The game now has an unlocked frame rate, capped at 144 fps—a solid improvement, although some PC players might want more, so an uncapped option would be welcome here. Modern anti-aliasing options, FSR Native AA and DLSS DLAA, are present.A more widely used and recognized method, TAA, is missing, which limits visual smoothness since the FSR and DLSS options have drawbacks, although less noticeable when compared to newer and graphically modern game releases. Still, these modern AA options are better than what would otherwise be available. Even though many hate TAA for its blurry appearance, its temporal stability is worth it as a much cheaper (performance-wise) solution compared to cross-vendor compatible FSR Native AA which is much worse and less temporally stable to my eye compared to anything TAA does in other games. DLSS runs on dedicated hardware, so DLAA is much more performant. Options to turn the AA off or opt for the original FXAA method are available.The CPU requirements are high and excessive, even considering the render distance improvements, especially evident in more dense areas, but is a trade-off we have to live with considering the aging technology. On the GPU side, it runs smoothly and should run well across most graphics card models, so graphics performance shouldn't be a big worry. In general, the look remains authentic to the original release, which, in my view, is important, as any other way would've been disrespectful to the original work. Considering the year the game was released, this "revamped" PC release will not run on the hardware from its time, at least not optimally, due to increased CPU demand alone. But hey, at least it isn't a stutter fest due to the broken shader compilation most modern games ship with.The PC release of Red Dead Redemption is a prime example of how a classic/retro game should be treated for the modern day. A few clever enhancements can go a long way, allowing newcomers and long-time fans to experience the game in its finest form yet. The pricing of this release is the most discussed point, and while it's nice to have such a game finally available on the PC, a price tag of 50 EUR is too much, even for a classic of this caliber.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite game from the previous generation. It was the game that made me buy a PS3 back in 2011. I strongly believe it is one of the best games ever made. But let's not dwell on my sweet teenage memories and talk about the final product that R* has delivered:The story is amazingly well-written. The music is right on point. The dialogues are superb. The tone of the game is unmatched, delivering a dark and gloomy experience that truly reflects what the Wild West must have been. Adventuring alone in the desert feels creepy, and there is always an eerie feeling to it, which the spaghetti western music harmonizes with perfectly.The game was developed during the last good years of single-player games, where if you wanted to unlock something, you had to complete challenges to obtain it. Microtransactions were, thankfully, non-existent. Speaking of unlocking, the game has a deep outfit system. As mentioned before, you can unlock outfits by completing engaging challenges, and most of the outfits give you some kind of advantage. You can cheat at poker with a carefully tailored suit. You can improve your aim by shooting with one eye blinded. You can dress up as a rival gang member and go unnoticed. This is an amazing feature that I’ve longed for and haven't seen in any other game besides the Hitman and MGS series.This last point, combined with the honor and fame systems, gives the feeling that you can influence the world around you, which is incredibly immersive and always feels alive.But why am I giving a negative review, then? Well, I think that R* needs a wake-up call. They have been making quite a lot of mistakes lately, and they can’t still think that their reputation is untouchable. This delivery is unacceptable. Held up against the highest standards (as it should be for this company), it falls quite short of the mark. It is the exact same game that came out 14 years ago. Textures, animations, sounds, and gameplay have been delivered unmodified. This is a 14-year-old game priced like every other brand-new AAA title. They haven’t put a single drop of love into the re-release of the games that put them in the position they’re in now. I know this is not a remake nor a remaster; it’s just a straight port. But, for god's sake, you could've spent some time refining some animations, redoing some textures, and polishing the audio.I normally don’t mind about graphics and textures, but the gameplay is weakened by animations that sometimes lack continuity. You can’t shoot and duck, or run and take cover. You have to stop playing one animation to start another one. I don’t understand why this is still a thing, since they had this solved back in GTA IV. Of course, this wasn’t that big of an issue back then. But we've come a long way in terms of animations and movement feel. Speaking of movement and feel, riding a horse with a keyboard feels non-responsive and straight-up weird. I had to plug in a controller to optimize the experience, then go back to KBM when in need of unholstering.Missing QOL Features: If you want to switch from the base game to the DLC, you have to quit to the main menu. This was inconvenient 14 years ago but bearable. Today, it’s unfathomable.Performance is terrible. Regardless of the frame rate you choose, you will experience screen tearing. I haven’t found a way to make it run smoothly despite having high fps.Back in 2011, I had a blast with Multiplayer Mode. It was pure fun. You could play the typical multiplayer activities like shoot-outs, team deathmatches, horse races, you name it. And every item was unlocked through leveling up. No microtransactions, no life-consuming mindless grinding. It was perfect. Of course, now it’s nowhere to be seen. No surprises there, seeing how they never cared about RDR2’s MM and let it bleed to death.You can’t live off the past. You can’t keep feeding off the love that we held for the games and experiences that you gave us. It’s high time to put players before shareholders. Companies around you are losing their reputation, and there is no coming back from that."People don’t forget; nothing gets forgiven."

_childDocuments_.review: Red Dead Redemption is one of the most anticipated game to finally come to PC.So, this is not a remake or a remaster, just a simple port with a few minor improvements nothing major, yet even without a complete overhaul, Red Dead Redemption remains intact on PC, delivering one of the most captivating and authentic Western experiences in gaming history. ( alongside Red Dead Redemption 2 of course :) )Like I said, this is not a remake or a remaster, but this game holds up impressively well. Though textures aren't quite up to modern standards, the overall artistic direction and sheer depth of the environments keep the experience immersive.Though the port hasn't introduced new gameplay mechanics, Red Dead Redemption still stands out for its fluid, satisfyingopen-world exploration, narrative-driven missions, and dynamic events that add enjoyment to the gameplay. The Dead Eye mechanic, where time slows down to allow for precise targeting, is one of the game’s most iconic features and feels even more natural on PC with a mouse and keyboard.For a port, especially one that's over 14 years old, 50 euros feels like devs are asking too much from fans. A more reasonable price would make this an easy 10/10 recommendation, but as it stands, it’s a steep cost for what’s basically the same game on older consoles. I pre-purchased it, and while I’m happy to play it, I can’t help but feel it would’ve been a fairer deal with a lower price...While some may be disappointed by the lack of a full remake or remaster, this PC release of Red Dead Redemption is still a journey worth visiting or (revisiting) for others :)In the end, Red Dead Redemption on PC is a dream come true, and I’m happy to recommend it with pleasure <39/10

_childDocuments_.review: After being edged for 14 years, Rockstar finally gave it to us! John Marston's original adventures on the American frontier and Mexico on PC. One of the greatest games of all time freed from its console prison by the fine folks at Double Eleven. You guys ROCK!Set a few years after the events of the Epilogue in Red Dead Redemption 2, John Marston's past catches up to him and he must now face the consequences of his actions. Hunting down the relics of the old west in an attempt to bring civilization to the last frontier of America. It's a masterful tale of Redemption powered by great acting performances and Rockstar's unmistakable writing. To top it all of, the fantastic soundtrack that is a staple of Red Dead.Whether it's bounty hunting or meeting strangers on the road, the frontier is a harsh and beautiful sandbox. This was THE game at the time, which transferred what you love about movies such as "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" into the videogame world. While its predecessor, Red Dead Revolver, had delved into the old west, Redemption was THE one, which proved games set in that period can be truly incredible. Activities such as treasure hunting, horse riding and poker are only few of the things that will get you to say yeeehaw in no time!The PC port of Red Dead Redemption is amazing. It runs on a vast range of machines and the entry barrier is very low, anyone with a PC made in the last 10 years can probably run this game and get great performance. The only thing I wish was different was the DirectX version. It uses 12 instead of 11, which I don't think is necessary for such an old game. Double Eleven (which also made the Switch and PS4 port last year) have done a great job with optimizing for PC and I hope Rockstar works with them again in the future.The zombie horror-themed expansion to Red Dead Redemption is also on PC. What would happen if none of the events of the main story ever happened and John was just chilling in his ranch? Well why not a zombie apocalypse? Tasked with finding a cure for his family, John will partake in a whole manner of crazy quests. It's another example of how an expansion for a game SHOULD look like.While its price tag of $50 can be steep, this version of Red Dead Redemption is the best one to play now. It runs and looks great, you can use a better input system in keyboard and mouse and you can bump your resolution to heights never seen before. If you are someone's who's never played the game, I'd recommend picking it up at this price tag unless you have a console and like controllers. If you do, you can just pick up a second hand copy cheaper and play it on the Xbox 360. Whatever you do, this is one of the best games of all time and you should definitely play it and its successor at least once.

Then they email you a code for each of those devices as some kind of perverse extra bonus prize for giving them your hard earned money.It’s a disgraceful way to treat your customers.Other issues caused by the launcher is the disablement of Steam cloud support forcing the player to rely on Rockster’s own buggy alternative which occasionally results in conflicting game saves. It’s a shame this bare bones port doesn’t include a menu that shows you real time comparison screenshots as you toggle graphical settings on and off. It’s also lamentable that there isn’t the same benchmarking feature that is available on RDR2. Finally, why didn’t Rockstar make a Steam graphical preset? It’s a lazy job, if not a rushed one. _childDocuments_.review: Red Dead Redemption 2 is in my top five games of all time and it's a special game for me. Since I played it in 2020, I've wanted to play Red Dead Redemption 1 and see where would John's story go. I didn't have a console until a year ago, I never got the chance to play it. So, thank you Rockstar Games for releasing this game on PC after all this time. I got to play Red Dead Redemption 1 for the first time without any spoilers, but sadly I can't say I liked it a lot. Overall, it seems overrated, much like GTA IV, from what I can say based on the high review scores. Allow me to explain why.The storyline in Red Dead Redemption 1 begins with a really interesting premise: John Marston, an outlaw, seeks to retire by hunting down his old gang members we know from Red Dead 2. Instead of delving deep into John's past or even the complex relationships of characters, 90% of those missions involve John doing favors for people who really do nothing in return, making the overall story of the game feel more like a series of chores than any type of redemption arc. I wished to see Jack spend time with his family and  We are literally an errand boy for the whole game. John Marston is likable, but not even comparable to Arthur as a display of character presentation. When it comes to the side characters, most of them are flat and boring, exaggerated Wild West stereotypes, not really contributing to the overall story in a meaningful way. They all make John risk his life multiple times and do errands for little to no help at all and then disappear. While in Red Dead Redemption 2, side characters had depth, histories, and personalities; here, you can't find that. The story has the filler feeling except for the last 5% of the game for most of the time, really sad. This is a dealbreaker for me.Another letdown The biggest letdown in Red Dead Redemption 1 is without any doubt its mission structure. While I didn't expect Red Dead 2 level mission variety, I hoped not to see GTA 4 mission design here. There's really no creativity in missions at all; after some time, they start to feel more like chores since there is no story motivation in place as well. "But what do you expect to do in 1900s wild west?" You may ask. Well, that's Rockstar's job to find out. Even if you can't find new stuff for the player to do, presentation could make those repetitive missions much better, like in Red Dead Redemption 2. "The Final Mission in RDR2", "A Quiet Time", The Poker Boat Mission, "The Hot-Air Balloon Mission", "Mansion Mission", "Heists", "Guarma"... The list goes on with these amazing and vastly different missions. If there is a will, there is a way to greatly present these -ride horse, kill people- scenarios in RDR1. GTA: San Andreas, a game 6 years older than RDR1, and has more variety and freedom in its missions. Another disappointment regarding Red Dead Redemption 1 is simply how empty its open world feels. That is, the map itself is big and does a fine job of visually evoking the Wild West, but there's really not much to do in it. The towns in it are small, there are no landmarks in the world so everywhere looks identical. A visually stunning world at times yet otherwise so lifeless and unexciting that exploration seems like it really was such a missed opportunity. Graphics look pretty good though, they enhanced the visuals a little bit for this release.One of the things that really hit me playing Red Dead Redemption 1 was how actually similar it all really felt to GTA IV in its overall design flaws. Just like GTA IV, RDR 1 often falls into repetitive and boring gameplay loops. Both tell a journey of one character, yet fattens it out with a lot of tedious, repetitive missions that don't change much from the start to finish of the game. Much like GTA IV with Niko Bellic, John Marston spends most of his time doing favors and chores for people who rarely add real depth to the main plot. Both games also share similar mission structure and game design. Both games feel overrated for me compared to Rockstar's other masterpieces like Red Dead Redemption 2 and Grand Theft Auto V.  Overall, Red Dead Redemption is a high quality with its gameplay, physics, animation quality, graphics, voice acting, sound design, etc. But I can't say I recommend it since the story is meaningless, the missions are super boring and generic, and the world feels just so empty and lifeless compared to other Rockstar titles. Rockstar reached another level with Grand Theft Auto V and Red Dead Redemption 2. Those games proved that Rockstar is the best in the industry. Since 2013, I have been waiting with insane hype and expectations for their next masterpiece: Grand Theft Auto VI. See you next year, dear Rockstar. I can’t wait to experience the new best game of all time.Follow My

Need to get somewhere fast? Ride a horse. Need to get somewhere slightly slower but with style? Ride a horse. Need to apologize for accidentally running over five NPCs? _childDocuments_.review: its hard to come down too hard on this game for being overpriced. it IS overpriced, this game is 14 years old. Fallout New Vegas came out the same year and has been 10 bucks for like 10 years. Even with the remaster work, this is a 30 dollar game max.what else though? i mean this is literally Rockstar's tightest game--takes everything necessary from GTA 4 and wraps it in some of the best Western fiction written, bar none, while removing almost all the fluff--theres still plenty of minigames to engage with, and you can even cheat at poker with the right outfit, but theres no social meters to maintain, no superfluous skills to upgrade, and very few meaningless side missions--even the ones that are like "pick 10 flowers" are for a guy who believes the rotting corpse of his wife is still alive and talking to him.John Marston is reformed from his criminal past, and starting very soon after Red Dead Redemption 2's epilogue, he is conscripted by FIB (FBI) Agents Ross (yes, that Ross from RDR2) and Fordham to hunt down surviving members of the Van Der Linde Gang, starting with Bill Williamson and Javier Esquella. Unlike RDR2, which tends to plod along at a very contemplative pace and directs you a little too much, RDR1 is a much more game-ass set of missions, that still have a very unique and excellent sense of immersion. John will help a rancher with ranch stuff, the local US Marshal take out the Walton Gang (seen in RDR2 if you go to New Austin), help a snake oil salesman rip off rubes, do some horse racing, cross the border into Mexico, and fight both sides of its revolution.The ending is brilliant and its use of licensed music rivals Vice City despite being ONLY ONE SONG. Jose Gonzolez's Far Away is one of those moments in gaming you will never forget. It's regular soundtrack is solid and complementary, albeit sparse, and John's iconic theme is still iconic. The only drawbacks to this game are created by RDR2's existence. While some connections are amazing, like Sister, later Mother Superior Calderon, who was able to council Arthur through his death and later council John, Uncle--the gang's layabout drunk who ended up helping John build his house and watches over Abigail and Jack while John's away, or the Stranger, a fellow who claims to be connected to John through the death of Jenny, the girl who was killed during the Blackwater Ferry job. However, theres no significant mention of Arthur, or most of the supporting cast from RDR2, especially those featured in the epilogue, like Charles or Sadie. Mechanics like hunting can feel lacking and features like first person are oddly missed. John can't swim. Play Hardcore to make it feel a little closer to its sequel with permadeath horses, less deadeye and health, etc.pro tip: if you need to cross the map but theres not like a marker to travel to, stick a waypoint on the map and set up a campsite--you can fast travel directly to your custom marker from a camp

_childDocuments_.review: I originally played and completed this on the Xbox 360 back in 2010/2011, so I was overjoyed to hear that it was finally getting ported over to Steam. Naturally, I got the game on release and have now 100% the game and got all of the achievements. This is one of my favourite games of all time; great characters, compelling story, amazing soundtrack and a vast, open world with lots of exploring and fun to be had, both on the main story as well as Undead Nightmare. Game mechanics are still good too. If you just play the main story and do nothing else, you could get it finished within 20 hours or less. However, if you're looking to 100% to game and get all of the achievements, you can easily sink between 50 to 80 hours (depending on how good/quick you are, I guess!). I completed this game fully in 75 hours and they were 75 hours well spent. It really is a beautiful game, just like RDR2 is also beautiful. Although this version of Red Dead Redemption doesn't have Red Dead Online, it didn't bother me at all as I don't care for the online aspect of this game and only wanted to play Single Player. The question everyone seems to be asking is "Is RDR1 worth the price?". The answer to that question depends entirely on the individual. For me, it was well worth £39.99. It's a solid game and an all time favourite of mine and I thought the price was reasonable. Before this game came out, I had only just finished getting all of the achievements on RDR2 so I was in a massive Red Dead mood and wanted this game on release, so I was going to buy it no matter the cost. However, if you aren't a huge Red Dead fan or have no attachment to the franchise and are quite happy to wait for a sale, then do so! Whether you pay full price or not, you'll still be getting a really good game.

_childDocuments_.name: Red Dead Redemption

_childDocuments_.review: Fourteen years later, and this game is still an absolute masterpiece. I played Red Dead Redemption on the PlayStation 3 when it was brand new, and I can safely say it has been Beautifully ported to PC with little to no bugs. _childDocuments_.name: Red Dead Redemption

_childDocuments_.review: While I do prefer the prequel story of RDR2 more than this game's story, this game is still really fun and engaging. _childDocuments_.name: Red Dead Redemption

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely stellar port. The game has never looked or ran this good. There are more visual improvements than I expected with greatly enhanced level of detail, draw distance, shadow quality and anti aliasing with support to DLAA and smooth shadows as well as HDR. It looks gorgeous and plays like a dream.One of the best games of all time.Never mind its 14 years since the original release. this still, by far, the best game being released on Steam in 2024.
_childDocuments_.name: Red Dead Redemption

_childDocuments_.review: For a Rockstar PC Port it's surprisingly good, most launch with bad performance and bugs, even today GTA 4's Episodes of Liberty City is basically unplayable, and RDR2 suffers from massive stuttering due to it not running well with modern CPU's. I can say with RDR 1 managed to complete it and Undead Nightmare with only one bug during a mission in Mexico. but it runs well.If you're debating whether to spend the 40 quid, think of it this way, you're probably gonna put at least 25 hours into it if you plan on beating both the game and the DLC. And if it's your first time playing through it you'll probably get around 40 or so hours and have a good first experience
_childDocuments_.name: Red Dead Redemption

_childDocuments_.review: ABOUT THE GAME ITSELF:Red Dead Redemption is one of the best video games ever created. Surpassed by its sequel and maybe a handful of other games. John Marston is a great character and going through his story is a real treat. They just do not make games like this anymore.A MUST PLAY!ABOUT THE PORT:This is an excellent port of Red Dead Redemption!Runs smooth as eggs and looks great in 4K!Everything you love is here, the classic story and Undead Nightmare.No multiplayer for this version, which is kind of a bummer, but you will love playing through RDR all over again with these improvements.First timer? This is a great way to experience the game for the first time.Hands down cannot recommend this game enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Red Dead Redemption

_childDocuments_.review: I have not played this game since my childhood but now 14 years later I can finally replay it almost like for the first time on PC.Positives:1. Audio design2. Open world design3. Interesting Characters4. Dynamic story with many layers5. Content filled experience6. Well-paced game.Negatives:1. Main story can feel dragged on at times by telling the player to go to one place, just for the protagonist to be unable to find what they're looking for and being told to go to another place. _childDocuments_.review: In a world where, 2K VC and FC card packs are sold 10s of dollars, this 14 years old masterpiece is worth every penny.I've originally played this on my PS3 and bought the game to see if the magic is still there or I'm riding on the waves of nostalgia (specially after RDR2).I'm happy to report the obvious , this masterpiece is timeless and  a great port.The story, the characters, the environment and the atmosphere are something that very few were able to create in this industry.It's easily worth the full price in my book, Partner.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a PC guy, I've never owned a console of any kind. That said obviously I never got to play this game until now. I have played RDR2 and it is solidly ranked as my favorite game of all time. I wish I could have played this game 14 years ago, I probably would have been much more impressed. Don't get me wrong, I'm about half way through as of this writing and I am enjoying the game a lot. It's just that after playing RDR2, as expected, this one is underwhelming. I've seen a few claims that RDR1 is better than RDR2. I respectfully have to disagree. Besides the obvious graphical differences I think RDR2 has a better story, better protagonist, better supporting characters, better game play, more challenging missions and more attention to detail. I should also add that this game was clearly meant to be played with a controller. Game play with mouse and keyboard is not nearly as smooth as in RDR2 especially when riding the horses.  All that said this game still gets a positive score from me and will be ranked close to the top of my all time favorites list. It was obviously ahead of it's time when it came out and it set the groundwork for the makings of my favorite game.Update on my review after completing the game: RDR1 tried to make me cry but failed.... RDR2 tried to make me cry and succeeded more than once. Nuf said. Not sure if I'm going to bother with Undead Nightmare or not. Of got other more interesting games to play.

Also, the game has only been out for like, a day as of writing this, and theres already mods for it (besides forty million lame Reshade mods), so it'll be fun to see where it goes. _childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite games of all time, finally on PC! Before today, the only way to play this game above 30 fps was to buy a ps5 and get the ps4 version to play bc. Not any longer. Strangely, the game doesn't let you go completely frameless, but it caps it at 144. That may bother some, I am cool with it. I love playing it above 100 fps, and using a mouse instead of a controller for aiming really helps.There are options to change it so you can just hold shift instead of tapping when on your horse, which is how I recommend. My only big negative is as of right now, the game does not notice my two mouse buttons on the side. That is very rare for me to see a game not support it, but even more rare when it's a large dev like Rock*.For the most part, so far, this is a very competent port, and for the $50, I expect that. But I want them to fix the small detail of no recognizing mamba's mouses control, and that probably means other brands as well, if not all. I will edit if they change it, my score is still a plus regardless. It's one of my favorite games of all time. And to be able to play it how I want now, it makes this even better than before. I wish multiplayer was here, but instead we do have a very solid DLC, Undead Nightmare. I am excited to go into that as well, with mouse and keyboard. It was fun but on console, it was too difficult to have to get only headshots unless you set the aiming to casual, especially because ammo was more scarce than in the campaign. Now, I will be able to play that game with manual aiming like the original campaign. I knew people who liked the DLC more, heh. I am a fan of both but prefer the campaign, but find the DLC to be one of the better DLCs to release with a game.

_childDocuments_.review: I only ever played Red Dead 2 because I haven't owned a console since the PS2 days, and came into this game blind without knowing much about it. I won't have much commentary about the porting quality other than I had no problems with the port, it looks like they took care with scaling the graphics or whatever, and this port was NOTHING like the disastrous GTA games where so many assets were out of place or completely awful looking. In short, this port is just fine!Most peoples complaints about this game are that $50 is a lot to ask for a port of a 15 year old game, so if that matters to you then it matters to you but I felt fine with my purchase.Red Dead 1: I was excited to the adventures of John Marston and the rest of the gang. As previously mentioned I came into this game after playing Red Dead 2 a LOT and... I kinda wished I was playing Red Dead 2 instead. The world of Red Dead 1 is much smaller, and the camping and physics are very limited at this point. I Kept playing the game for the story, but eventually I did get used to the scaled back gameplay and found myself enjoying everything, but still wishing I could cook meat, or use my herbs. I found all my different types of herbs and meat I collected to be JUST for the purpose of selling and no further tinkering required. As far as the missions and story go, I rather enjoyed the scaled down production because it felt like it was easier to remember characters since there were fewer of them, and just generally easier to follow the plot. Help 3 people through multiple missions, achieve the regional goal, move on to the next area, rinse and repeat 3 times.Gambling and challenges are back and I was surprised to see them in there, I really had fun with that. So even though everything is scaled down, if you want to recapture some of that time consuming and ludicrous challenges that RDR2 set you up for, this is an option here as well and I did my best to get as many challenges as I could before I got bored, and enjoyed myself. I have yet to beat Red Dead Undead, I'll update my review when that time comes, but as of now I feel fully fine with this game and how it turned out, and enjoyed my time in it. I'm not sure if I will come back to it because I'd rather be playing Red Dead 2. Hmm, that should be a bumper sticker

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent port.After the ps4 port of this game was kind of meh, I was kind of worried we'd be treated to the same kind of minimal effort on pc. Well, to my surprise it's more than I was expecting; up to 144fps support, frame gen (ok?), dlaa (very nice), and hdr. The latter is kind of a game changer since this was one of the most washed out games in history imo. Now colors pop like never before, depending on if your display supports it, and the quality of said display of course. Above 60fps support is also eye opening, and something I did not at all expect after the ps4/5 version was capped at 60.As for price, that's the one thing that's pretty negative I'd say. _childDocuments_.review: We finally have the original masterpiece RDR on PC and it's one of the best ports I've ever experienced. Keep in mind, however, that this is a , not a remake. It's the original game engine with modern features implemented, such as FSR, and significantly improved visuals. That being said, I'm able to get a constant 75 FPS on a laptop from 2016, with absolutely no hiccups or lag, on maximum settings. Runs buttery smooth. You could probably run this on a potato. That being said, don't expect this to be RDR 2, as it's quite different, more "arcade" and less realistic. There's also some jank with facial animations but other than that, I have no complaints. Rockstar made a wise decision in not changing anything too much. You essentially get the original game with an updated coat of paint. Just understand that going in.
_childDocuments_.name: Red Dead Redemption

_childDocuments_.review: A good port for one of my favorite games—if not my absolute favorite. It's nice to finally have it on PC so I can enjoy one of the games I played as a kid without having to play it on a switch or through other means. The only problem I have with it is the pricing. The improvements don't justify the price tag. If you've never played this game before or you're just wanting to have it on PC, I recommend waiting until it goes on sale. It's a great story that holds up even after 14 years. I definitely think anyone who has or wants to play RDR2 at some point should play this game as well!

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing port for an amazing game. This isn't my first time playing RDR1, I played it to death on the Xbox 360 and went out of my way to 100% it over a decade ago and I will do it again on PC. I was worried this port would be a mess like the GTA Trilogy was but thankfully they did an amazing job here. I've only experienced one small bug so far. (Stay away from Goats in Undead Nightmare lol)It runs very well as it should for an old title, they went out of their way to add extra PC features, such as: HDR, DLSS / FSR, up to 144hz support, 21:9 Widescreen support, Modding support and since it's on DX12, you can mod in Frame Generation easily. The shadow quality, view distance and foliage have been drastically improved compared to their console versions. If you're able to emulate RDR1 on PC like I am, this is still worth purchasing. This is by far the best way to experience RDR1. That said, I do think the price tag is a bit much for such an old game and it's a shame there's no multiplayer as it was pretty fun to play back in the day. Highly recommend!

Mouse 4-5 *thumbs* are not mappable so like me your g502 is a 3 button mouse unless you remap keys using your mouse software aka lghub for me. I had some stuttering issues in the opening town on a reload of a save *I walked out of town without doing the scripted scene* I'm on a 5800x3d/32gb of b-die and a 7900gre. It took Rockstar far, FAR too long to port this to PC but its an excellent port nonetheless, definitely could've been a lot worse and less faithful knowing Rockstar.The game itself is perfect, almost all missions are total bangers with excellent combat sections that are brutal and impactful and none of the filler missions that fluff up the playtime in the sequel. _childDocuments_.name: Red Dead Redemption

_childDocuments_.review: So the game itself is as great as ever but if you've already played it on Xbox, PlayStation, Switch, or emulation, (and most PC players have at this point...) this game is not worth $50 at all. It does have some nice graphical upgrades like long draw distances on grass, higher quality fonts, weapon and map icons, native support for up to 144fps and ultrawide (albeit with pillarboxed cutscenes). Playing with keyboard and mouse is nice, but outside of combat, the controls are pretty awkward so you'll still want a controller nearby, namely for the minigames (poker, liar's dice, blackjack).This is probably the best way to play RDR1 now, but not as this price point. This game should have only been $30 max, and if you've already played the game before, I wouldn't bother at $50 and just wait for a sale cause ultimately, this is the exact same 14 year old game you can get for under $10 on an Xbox 360 and that version includes multiplayer which was gutted from the PC version.

Now with this great first part, I can deffinetly finish the second. This freaking series is like a movie!I just love it!

_childDocuments_.name: Red Dead Redemption

_childDocuments_.review: Red Dead Redemption 1 is a prequel game to the game called Red Dead Redemption 2. RDR2 was released in 2018 and since 6 years have passed Rockstar had much time to improve both the graphics and both the core gameplay elements. When I started this game I couldnt wait to continue the story from where we left off. I was so happy when I saw that Arthur Morgan made a full recovery since the events of RDR2. I was also happy when I was reunited with my most beloved original gang members. I always wanted to know what will Sadie, Charles, Trelawny, and all the others do after the gang break up and I was thrilled to meet them. As I said earlier 6 years have passed since the release of the 2nd game and it really shows. Graphics are greatly improved its truly feels next gen and the game benefits heavily of the modern game engines avalaible for Rockstar. I would recommend this game for everyone 10/10. Now I going to start the walking dead crossover DLC. (fingers crossed for a Rick Grimes cameo)

_childDocuments_.review: Developed by Rockstar San Diego, as a follow up to the 2004 hit game Red Dead Revolver, Red Dead Redemption is a Western epic, set at the turn of the 20th century when the lawless and chaotic badlands began to give way to the expanding reach of government and the spread of the Industrial Age.  The story of former outlaw, John Marston, Red Dead Redemption takes players on a great adventure across the American frontier. Utilizing Rockstar's proprietary Rockstar Advanced Game Engine (RAGE), Red Dead Redemption features an open-world environment for players to explore, including frontier towns, rolling prairies teeming with wildlife, and perilous mountain passes - each packed with an endless flow of varied distractions. Along the way, players experience the heat of gunfights and battles, meet a host of unique characters, struggle against the harshness of one of the world’s last remaining wildernesses, and ultimately pick their own precarious path through an epic story about the death of the Wild West and the gunslingers that inhabited it. [Rockstar Games]

Strengthen your bonds and build your party to take down powerful foes and discover the kingdom’s true nature. Key Features: -Go on quests, dungeon dive, & hunt for treasures by day. Choose your actions wisely, time management is key to achieving your goal. -Ride your “gauntlet runner” to faraway dungeons & towns across an expansive world. Discover beautiful landscapes  accompanied by captivating music, immersive UI, & anime cutscenes. -A unique battle system combining turn based & real time action grants strategy & exhilaration at every turn. Party customization through “Archetypes” provides freedom to personalize your adventure. -A mysterious & exciting story unfolds in a world where people must fight their own anxiety. Join the high-stakes Royal Tournament that promises hours of captivating exploration and discovery.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what a journey this game was. Never played an Atlus game before, so this is my first entry from their catalogue.This game just put me back to my childhood when I was enjoying Final Fantasy X for the first time. The sense of a great adventure with a great cast in a profound fantasy world.The great scheme of a story with many twists and turns, with loveable characters with beliefs and fears and  a great pacing which motivates you through the whopping 70-100h campaign. It reminds me a lot of FFX and Avatar The Last Air Bender, cause like these two, it really emphasizes on the journey and the many interactions, development and growth between the characters , that you met thoughout the journey. The micro (story between characters) and the macro (the overarching story) is so well done. Just a note you have to read a lot, not all conversations are voiced. If you don't like that, then it's not your game.The Turn-Based Combat with the Archetypes is well made and the constant new unlocks and enemies, made it enjoyable till the last fight. Though the dungeons are pretty generic and definitely not a highlight. But some designs of the monsters and bosses are really something else and to defeat some of theses bosses, especially on hard mode, required a distinct strategy and clever maneuvers. Experimenting with different archetypes and their synergy is a key factor in the combat system and your defining way to your success through the main story. Also the music is great, especially the combat themes go really hard. Every region feels fresh and make you excited for the next story arcs and the new characters they introduce.Did I mention the Artstyle? Though the technical side and graphic is not really that great for todays standards. The Artstyle pours out of every pore. From the stunning menu and all the little animations to the really great anime cutscenes in important moments, everything is done with so much love, you can really see it in a every corner of the game.The story is a heavy hitter with subjects like Discrimination, Gen*cide, Suic*de and much more it really builds on the question, if we can ever achieve or build a utopia-like world or environment, where everyone can live side by side all equally with the same chances. Though it might sounds like that, it never felt naive cause this game always gives insights from different perspectives and made you think about it and put the discussion for this subject in the forefront.About the characters: almost every one feels fitting in the story and enhances really the experience with their backstory, which you progress through the great bond system. And man, some side characters and their  stories like Alonzo or Brigitta overshadows even some of the main cast.The main villain in the game is a great counter part with his own beliefs and goals and I really like his presence and his clever scheming behind the scenes. But I do feel like the explanation of his driving force for all his decisions and sacrifices, felt a bit forced and rushed towards the end.But enough said, if you wanna dive into a big fantasy world with a profound cast of characters,  a great turn-based combat system with a memorable soundtrack,   outstanding artstyle and a deep conversation about modern subjects and different perspectives about moral and philosophy then this is a no brainer.A very strong GOTY contender.

_childDocuments_.review: It's got Persona DNA but still stands out as its own unique evolution. The fantasy setting and art style are fantastic, the story is intriguing, and the mix of real time and turn based combat is unique. I've seen some people bag on this game for not having Fusion, but honestly it feels really limiting to say this game is better or worse for having a different mechanic. As much as I love other Atlus games, I found the Archtype system refreshing, as well as the ability to change up Archetypes on more than just the protag for different scenarios. It makes gameplay feel customizable in a way a lot of companion RPGs don't. It's still an Atlus game, there's still social links, calendars, and dungeons, but it manages to innovate enough aspects to not feel ultra samey or boring. If you're on the fence, try the demo. It's long for a demo and while it won't give you the best view of the overall story, obviously, it will give you a feel for the atmosphere and gameplay loop to help decide whether it's for you or not.

_childDocuments_.review: A Persona style game for people that don't like Persona games.Whether this reads as a positive or a negative will depend entirely on your opinions on Atlus's prior games in the Persona franchise. The fingerprints and the basic formula are there, but everything is very surface-level and streamlined.Instead of Personas we have Archetypes, similar on the surface, but without any of the personality or uniqueness. In prior games the protagonist would have a selection of hundreds of unique Personas to call upon and collect, giving you all sorts of different combinations to mix and match for your way of going about things, similarly with each of your party members and different combinations of the party composition.With Archetypes, there are a much smaller pool to pull from, and rather than each one having a unique look and 'personality', they are exactly what they say they are, Archetypes. Further, it is not only the protagonist that has the ability to use any Archetype he chooses, but rather everyone in the party can use any Archetype and any equipment. On paper this may seem like a good change, in practice it makes every member of the party completely interchangable. There is no consistent acquiring of new Personas via capturing them in combat or by fusing them, or big changes to your party once new members join. Once you're 4 or 5 hours into the game, you will have acquired most of the archetypes that actually have meaningful differences between them. Instead, the focus is entirely on just battles and dungeon crawling. Further, the social-sim side of the game is almost entirely non-existent. The bonds in place of social links are present but simplified, with the social levels being very short interactions with no meaningful dialogue choices rather than long character focused cutscenes, and with no long stretches of story and character interaction between the dungeons. As said previously, the focus is entirely on getting you back into dungeon crawling and combat as quickly as possible.Lastly, though this is more opinion based than the prior points, the theme is far simpler and less interesting. Gone are the themes of how to deal with death, corruption in authority, and vigilante justice, instead with the far simpler theme that discrimination is unjust. A perfectly serviceable theme, but one with no ambiguity or greyness. The villains are completely villainous and unsympathetic, the heroes are entirely heroic and just. Nothing is wrong with it, but neither is there any room for deeper exploration or discussion. Now, to loop back to the beginning, if you are reading this, and this sounds like the kind of streamlining you would enjoy, or that it has simply cut out the parts of the Persona games that you wanted to skip past anyway, then this game is for you, and consider this review a thumbs up. However, if you enjoy all of the depth and complexities of the Persona games, then Metaphor will come up lacking.

_childDocuments_.review: The rigidity this game has with archetypes is unnecessary and terrible. In the Persona games, when you enter a boss fight and discover their weaknesses, you can switch your active persona in battle to react.In this game? Nothing. You can't switch archetypes. This vastly increases the trial and error by death or quitting where you go in just to figure out what an enemy's weakness is, and then either die or force quit the game to get the ACTUAL archetype setup you need.Devs: WHY? Why in the world can you not, after years of this BS, just reduce the friction here and let me switch archetypes in battle? WHY do you insist on forcing people go to through this force quit garbage?And making this even worse is the lack of ability to escape. What is the point of putting in an ESCAPE feature only to deny it whenever anyone actually needs it? Enough with the trial and error by death to figure out boss weaknesses already. I instantly know the party I have is fruitless, yet can do nothing about it. At the very least, just let me reload a game without force stopping the game.And then this Ho mo  Margo boss fight, a fight that requires very specific skills (the core element spells which only two archetypes have) and a very specific archetype setup, right after another boss fight where you offer no opportunity to save or change archetypes, is just crap icing on a crap cake.You offer this rock-paper-scissors gameplay but then don't offer any mechanisms to adapt. I go into a boss fight not knowing what it is, so I go in guessing rock, and then it turns out that's wrong for the entire fight. But I'm STUCK with rock. The whole gameplay premise is ruined by your shortsighted, unnecessary and thoroughly incompetent rigidity.And if all of this garbage wasn't enough, after you die and force quit, reload, reconfigure your part, finally get the skills and ultimates that will help you hit their weakness and win... you MISS. And if that wasn't infurating enough, you LOSE THE REST OF YOUR TURNS.All this crap is completely out of my control, and I'm tired of having to do boss fights multiple times because I don't want to use a guide to figure out what my party setup should be. All of this is stupid, artificial and completely unnecessary dev design decisions. And I'm done rewarding this unnecessary friction and garbage.PS: Having a skip button without a confirmation on what is actually a cutscene pause button for most games has to be one of the most mind numbingly dumbest design decisions ever to ship. It's like they took feedback on not being able to skip and took it stupidly far in the other direction. I subconsciously hit it to pause a couple of times after a long boss battle only to skip the post-boss cutscene which is absolutely infuriating.What is the big deal about having a confirmation on the skip button? FFS.

_childDocuments_.review: I think I am halfway my first playthrough. I am not an expert of JRPGs and I had never played an Atlus game. Overall I am in love with Metaphor: ReFantazio. Why?- Graphics is nothing special technically, but style and art direction are gorgeous. From menus to camera movements in key scenes to character design to animated cutscenes, everything has an atmosphere between the awe-inspiring and the frightening.- The overall story is engrossing and leaves you wondering what to expect next, even if some minor plot points are predictable. I cannot wait to discover new wonders and see where the story will lead.- The fantasy world and story of the game are metaphors of our modern society with many of its more challenging topics: war vs peace, individualism vs solidarity, conflicts of race and religion, overcoming anxiety and even the role of social media and digital technologies (disguised as magic in the game). The game also contains many cultural references that are quite surprising in this medium, from Hieronymus Bosch's works inspiring the design of "humans" to Thomas More's Utopia (the map which is almost identical to More's Utopia's map, the protagonist who is reading a forbidden book about a utopistic society, even the character of More).- For a non-expert in JRPGs like me, game mechanics are quite complex but the game introduces them progressively and every piece fits nicely, so that you never feel overwhelmed and the level of challenge is just right.- The score is magnificent, every major location has its theme and they linger in your mind all day long;- On my Steam Deck OLED it is just perfect and it's relaxing and engaging at the same time.The only negative aspect I can find in the game is that in the largest dungeons or during some of the major plot events you are practically unable to save or reach a checkpoint for up to 1 hour, so you need to carefully plan your gaming sessions. After all, in-game time management is a main gameplay mechanic, so even from this viewpoint the game is a... metaphor.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10Metaphor: ReFantazio is fantastic. Basically the Persona formula reimagined in a fantasy setting. The game offers everything fans love about Persona—the engaging social elements, layered turn-based combat (which kinda reminds me of techs from crono crusade), and deep, character-driven storytelling. THE GAME IS LITERALLY A METAPHOR. The world is immersive and meticulously crafted, with memorable characters. a lot of the characters are stand-ins for different government concepts or historical figures. The one minor critique: the day transition screen plays the same dialog and video at the start of each day. Adding some variety here could make daily progression feel even more dynamic and immersive. Despite this small issue, Metaphor: ReFantazio is a must-play for Persona fans and fantasy lovers. I'm also an ATLAS shill, so there are probably issues that i'm just ignoring. TL;DR, I had fun, its a great game. and it's not completely cringe.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, as a fan of both Persona and Shin Megami Tensei, I do really love this game so far. Its beautiful, the music is fun despite the battle music making me laugh a little every time i hear it for the first time in a while, and the story seems very interesting so far. Overall I can recommend this game, its challenging and I do really like the press turn system more than I like the Persona combat system. I do have some issues with the game though:1. A strength of Press Turn in SMT games is that you have very good control over what order your party's turn will be based on the position of your demons in your party. its usually Main Character -> Demon in P1 -> Demon in P2 -> Demon in P3. My issue with the implementation of press turn in this game is that each round the starting party member rotates, making it very hard to plan around team builds as you then have to potentially waste press turn icons getting to the team mate you want to start with. Its added complexity that isn't needed, it should let you set a turn order for your party outside of combat.2. The final boss of the first dungeon is overtuned, If you like the Persona games you'll like this game, if you like SMT games you might like this game if you don't mind the social aspect to the game. As a fan of both I do really enjoy this new entry and I'm sure many of you will too.

_childDocuments_.review: Love the game, it might be the long awaited departure from Persona series we needed. While there is no particular disadvantages of Persona, 5 games in the same setting with P5R and P3R feasted its fans back to back. I personally feel like there must be something fresh and different before P6 comes along. And this game is just that.Differentiated enough, some systems even outright better than Persona. The fresh fantasy setting gives so many opportunities for the developers to capitalize on, and they did. The story while still fumed with persona writing all over the place, it is still a gripping story that legitimately both enticing and immersive in its own right. The story itself is a simple focused tale took place in well-developed world, it was getting shoehorn a little but way less than P5. The writing seems to be more adult oriented this time, while I appreciated teen - adult audience targeted writing of Persona, I feel like Metaphor aimed towards something different while keeping the core of the story spinning in that world.The gameplay is brilliant, this is pretty much QoL the game, to the point that I feel "too convenient" sometimes. You can do almost everything spending half of the time require to do in Persona in the terms of setting up your characters/builds. This however, made the game feels a little bit shorter than persona too (but in comparison the lengths are about the same.) But let think about it like this, if a 100 hours+ long game with so many systems to save your time still makes I feel like this game is "too short", it must be one hell of 100 hours they managed to keep you on great time most of the time.The voice acting is amazing! The musics of this game is carrying hard! And it runs great on portable devices too due to its not too steep spec requirement. I still don't know how can this game needs 90+ GB to install, though. One criticism I have on this game is the first three hours of this game kinda "misleading" as the game made you think it going to be more spacey than it really is. _childDocuments_.review: 8.5Metaphor is one of the best JRPGs of 2024.It combines the best aspects of Shin Megami Tensei (combat) and Persona (scheduling).What's good:- The combat is phenomenal. It takes the extra turn system from SMT (grants extra turn when you hit an enemy's weakness) and the persona system (each character is assigned to only one archetype while in battle, even for the protagonist. Archetypes can be changed after battle or get other powers if you rank up the social links of your followers).The battles were so fun that I've never used the auto-battle function and the Synthesis abilities on the long run were far more interesting than I initially thought.- The music overall is good and the battle themes are just perfect, never got tired of them. However, the background music for cities or certain dungeons becomes repetitive, as most of the game plays epic musics, even when the situation doesn't call for such grandiosity.- The world-building is solid, and the medieval-meets-weird theme is a refreshing change for the JRPG genre.- The character models really remind me of Fire Emblem: Three Houses, and some of the music also sounds a bit like FE3H. The outdated graphics also enhance the similiarities.What could've been done better:- The characters feel one-dimensional. They mainly serve to move the plot forward, with personalities based on a single trait (anime tropes). Unfortunately the social links are also affected by this problem. For example, Strohl always says some noble BS and is revolted, Hulkenberg always says some knight BS and likes to eat, Heismay always talks about his son and the other followers are mostly the same thing.The reason as to why I think the characters and social links are weak in this game, is because, 1, they didn't have the time and budget to flesh out the characters, 2, the kill-or-be-killed atmosphere on the continent doesn’t leave much room for them to display more relatable, mundane aspects of their personalities, as Persona does.- The pacing in the beggining is just way too fast, when did they get so attached to Grius to make such a big deal?- The plot had so much potential, but they were never able to do it justice, either by cheaping out in some cutscenes that carried weight in the story or the plot convinience where no one questions the group's actions.And the biggest gripe that I have is that they always think that they're smarter than the antagonist. It drives me crazy that they can be so naive.Summary:If you're a gameplay over story type of person, then it's worth the buy. And if you're an Atlus fan, you've already bought the game without seeing the reviews, like i did.118 hours played (demo time is not added to the game hour count)107 hours full game + and 11 hours demo.

_childDocuments_.review: This game frustrates me. Endlessly. I'd actually be less annoyed with Metaphor: ReFantazio if it completely sucked, if it truly and cleanly ruined fantasy for me. But it does SO many things right, and looks gorgeous doing it. It has engaging combat that meshes Persona and SMT mechanics exquisitely, resulting in turn-based gameplay that precisely as intuitive, fun and rewarding as it needs to be. It feels good to exploit enemy weaknesses for more turns, or evading/repelling/blocking to deny enemy turns. That never gets old. And even if other combat aspects DO get old when you're grinding for hours on end, the game mitigates this by allowing you to "skip" tedious mob killing via the simple over-world combat (abuse the targeting system, it turns said combat into a fun mini-game instead of a frustrating chore).The Archetype system is definitely simpler than systems from other Atlus titles, and the fact that every playable character can use almost every other Archetype might NOT be a plus for some players. Personally, I think the system's great. It feels streamlined, and most in-game quests encourage the experimentation and swapping of Archetypes across characters, which in turn helps keep combat fresh.The core gameplay loop is also fun. There are periods of reprieve where you interact with companions/allies you'd actually care about, stock up on items and gear, explore beautifully realised towns and cities, and improve your Royal Virtues (basically personality traits crucial for a ruler, which help advance companion/ally story lines for extra perks + immersion). Then there are periods of planning your route across the world, travelling in the gauntlet runner to dungeon delve for hours on end, before finally returning to base to do it all over again.And those companions you'd actually care about? You'd care because they're wonderfully voice-acted, each with their own motivations, backstories, and personalities that are either relatable, amusing, engaging or a combination of the three. Their own stories may not necessarily be unique (for example, the fallen noble trope and the ashamed-knight-seeking-redemption trope isn't exactly unmolested territory), but uniqueness was never the defining benchmark for well-written characters.The overall plot/world-building is wonderful too. Not overly convoluted like certain JRPGs can be, though this isn't a simple "protagonist versus the clearly evil antagonist" story either. It's much more nuanced than that, and while some players may rightfully complain that it's not nuanced ENOUGH (perhaps because it doesn't flesh out the political complexities and in-game racism in a way that feels "real"), I found myself anticipating much of the voiced dialogue, and was compelled enough to read a fair bit of the Memorandum a.k.a in-game encyclopedia (something I rarely do).Combine everything mentioned above with an atmospheric soundtrack and an absolutely stunning UI, and what you get is a game that looks and feels good at doing what it does. So WHY is it so frustrating to play?The first couple of hours deepened my immersion, yet tested my patience. It took roughly an HOUR before my first taste of combat (partially my fault, due to chatting with random NPCs), but it's ridiculous that my first encounter with enemies involves just running away. No overworld combat, no turn-based combat. That whole thing makes sense story-wise, but having a Persona 5-style intro where you dive straight into combat before reverting to the story sequence would have done wonders for pacing.And the pacing. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, the pacing. For a game that's fundamentally based on time-limits, with several elements (including playable characters) being essentially time-locked, pacing needs to be almost PERFECT. But it's not, not even close. The biggest downside to the Archetype system stems from this. Because everyone can level almost every other Archetype, playable characters that join late in the story are significantly lacking in overall Archetype levels, which in turns makes you less likely to want to use them unless you don't mind nerfing your team or committing to hours of grind.Then there's the gauntlet runner, your mode of transportation across the world. It's one of the best aspects of the game, but it's fully upgraded version allows you to traverse practically anywhere within an in-game day. I hated that, or rather, I hated that said upgrade came too quickly. Again, pacing. I loved that I had to plan my route if I wanted to visit multiple locations for multiple quests. I loved the extended travels with occasional combat encounters, companion interactions, and making multiple stops for certain points of interest on the map. The game should have dived even deeper into that, added more quests with time limits simultaneously so you had to CHOOSE where to go at the expense of another. It should have made the travel matter more. And it was all trivialised in the name of convenience all too quickly.I wished the mid-game content wasn't as lacking as it was, at least for me. There simply wasn't enough time to enjoy certain characters organically, or to fully immerse myself in the journey across the world.Then there's the dungeons/combat-areas. Yes, it's an overall gorgeous game, not graphically, but artistically. But the vast majority of the dungeons comprise of visually bland corridors, identical and uninspired. The stylistic UI does an extremely good job of distracting from that, but when you're in the same location for a couple hours, you're eventually going to notice.The game is SO close to amazing. SO close. I DO recommend it, but I wish I could do more. I wish I could rave like a crazed fan over how the game gave me MORE of what it does best. The route planning, the timed-quests, the organic character experimentation. But it all ends far too quickly, or paced far too poorly, for me to personally view it as the unparalleled shining gem it could have been.

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 5 is far superior. I was expeting an evolution in combat, but instead the fights  were significantly less entertaining and the game suffers from the worst MP management in all the franchise. I gradually grew tired of this half-turn based combat, and the inability to change archetypes during fights with the protagonist often led to deaths and the need to reload, as picking the wrong archetype could easily ruin an entire battle. The game's message and moral are commendable, and I found the antagonist and his motivations more compelling than the party (except Heismay, I love you little bat). I also appreciated the brutal depiction of the abusive nature of the Euchronia realm. Overall, it's an ok game, but I was expecting much, much more.

_childDocuments_.review: Take Persona, put it into a fantasy setting, and remove being forced to attend school. That's basically what Metaphor is. So far I'm really impressed with it, it is similar to SMT and Persona for sure, but it does enough things differently to feel distinct and stand on its own. The tone is a lot more serious and mature than Persona so far. There isn't a comedy relief moment every 5 minutes to keep it light hearted, they aren't afraid to show you blood and death either. Every character so far feels realistic and authentic to the setting, and nobody is annoying or goofy.It isn't without problems, though pretty minor. Small things like why doesn't your floating sword skateboard make any noise at all? Or your attack animation during real time combat taking longer than the enemy can start and finish their own attack while you are animation locked, leading to some frustration where you'll be spamming the dodge button but cant get away in time. Overall though, all the major things you would want have been nailed. The music is great, the voice acting is stellar, the archetypes system is fantastic with mixing and matching skills from different trees to cover weaknesses, or double down on magic power etc. Your squad composition also determines what 'ultimates' you can use, turns in combat are now more of a currency rather than each person gets 1 turn, then the enemies go, repeat. You can move party members between the front and back row now, missing is devastating because you lose 2 turns now. Combat in general feels more risk/reward than previous atlus games. There's some good challenge here too, I'm playing on normal and a few battles already have been really close calls.
_childDocuments_.name: Metaphor: ReFantazio

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: After finishing the game I can say that... It is great! The character are charming and lovable. The combat (imo) is a complete upgrade from persona's combat both over world & in turn-based combat. The game's story is engaging as it doesn't really slow down (besides the time in between story beats for social stats & bonds) which makes you want to see what happens next. This game is without sugarcoating it is . It has social links (bonds), social stats, and the calendar system. Which are key components to persona, but how it differs is the combat, Metaphor uses SMT's press turn combat which if you played SMT knows that it works well! Over world encounters are instead of hitting an enemy to get a turn advantage, you down the enemies I'll just say "posture" bar to get a turn advantage with an extra befit of stunning the enemy and taking I'll say ~20% of their hp.  Metaphor also improves on persona's social stats element by showing you how far you are away from level up a social stat which is very nice. Another great thing is that you no longer need to use a persona for social links or bonds anymore which is VERY nice please keep this. Also, bonds automatically rank up so you don't need to waste days on bonds if you miss up a dialouge interaction with a bond!Some things that I liked about this game is the archtype system it feels as if instead of making each party member's archtype very niche and make them only able to use one element & very specific buffs & debuffs. It allows all party members not just the protagonist use all archtypes which allows for some real variety to combat. The characters feel less tropey I guess, like there isn't a butt of a joke character or very smart is my only unique quirk character. The music as always is really good. (especially the  themes)Some stuff I didn't like though both major & minor are that the story towards the end gives you a HUGE plot dump. Which I myself don't really like when games do that. So, this maybe minor or major depending on the person. The side dungeons are kinda samey which makes them a bit of a slog to get through sometimes. A bit of a minor critism at least for me, there is very little interactions with other bonds or party members during a character's bond event besides like one notable one.  There is probably more I could say both positive & negative but this review is getting abit too long for my taste. So, if you like persona  you will not regret it. I'm trying to make more a bit serious reviews when finishing with a game. So, this review maybe a bit scuffed.

_childDocuments_.review: Metaphor is a game made by the same people that made Persona 3,4 and 5 but it is an unique experience that stands tall on it's own.Game has 2 major systems that ATLUS games are known for - Daily time management and JRPG style combat. Both of which are improvements from previous games of the development studio. Those systems are generally always either something you like or absolutely hate - it's not going to be a game for everyone.If you are fine with above mentioned though you are in for a ride. This game is an absolute shining pearl in already amazing year for games. It has amazing Art Direction that should age well, insanely good soundtrack, great characters and memorable epic story that is constantly surprising you with it's twists and turns. Metaphor also improves on battle system making it easier to use than Persona it's also much more forgiving in terms of time management. Generally speaking if you never played any ATLUS game because getting mid way into series of 5 games is daunting this one is perfect entry point to check if you like the game play. On the other hand beware that in typical ATLUS fashion game takes over 80 hours to finish. Which also makes it generally good purchase even at full price. Game runs well on steam deck (i have played it exclusively on SD at the time of writing this review) and doesn't have a lot of places where you are unable to save so it's also great game on the go.I fully recommend giving it a shot especially when it's on discount. ATLUS Absolutely cooked with this one.-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Personal note to SEGA... For the love of god remove Denuvo already. Everyone could use those additional frames in game. And in general stop putting that thing in games as it's absolutely pointless and it makes our (people that actually pay for games) life worse.

_childDocuments_.review: My experience thus far can be summed up with one word: "disappointment".When i saw that the game mixed Persona-esque combat with a Final Fantasy-esque story, i was hyped. I am a massive fan of the Persona games and was hoping to experience that same type of game with a more serious story.Unfortunately this game falls flat compared to that series.You get the freedom to pick whatever role combinations you want, but the game still bottlenecks you by inflicting harsh punishments if you pick roles that the developer doesn't want you to pick. Want to bring the Healer role that you leveled up to a Goborn fight? Screw you, they enrage and murder your team! Switch to a role that is still level 1 because you didn't expect to need more than one Knight!The bonding system (which i really like in Persona) also feels dumbed down. Instead of having to work for bond levels by hanging out with your friends and party members, they just throw bond increase events in your lap. I reached bond level 4 with Hulkenberg without ever hanging out with her, because the game told me "okay, you can level up her bond now!".The combat is very dull. I liked the "sneak attack" mechanic at first, but it turns out that running towards an enemy and hoping that they don't turn around gets stale very quickly. This isn't like Persona 5 where you can scope out an enemy's patrol route and engage them when they are off guard; you have to be lucky as enemies will walk in random directions every time they turn around. Then you get into the combat itself and it's just...spamming. Spam whatever attack the enemy is weak against, spam the Knight taunt and heal when needed. This game isn't worth €70 by a LONG shot. Maybe for half that price it would be a good enough game. But i would rather play Persona 5 again over playing whatever this shlock is.

_childDocuments_.review: Metaphor: ReFantazio aims for the depth of Persona but falls short in key areas. While the game is visually appealing, the grind feels more like filler than meaningful progression, and the characters rely too heavily on familiar anime archetypes without the layered development that makes Persona characters memorable. Unlike Persona, where every interaction and system serves the story and character growth, Metaphor’s complexity feels detached from the narrative, making the experience feel flat. If you’re expecting the same level of character-driven immersion as Persona, this might not be it.
