_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - If you've never tried out one of these exceptionally long Atlus RPGs (SMT, Persona, etc.) and want to give one a try, this is it.Gameplay: This dev team, after making three Persona games using the calendar-based system, has finally landed on its delivery with far less of the pacing issues of Personas 3 through 5. Actual turn-based combat borrows from Shin Megami Tensie's "press turn" system, which is easy to understand and allows far more creativity in battles. Fans of the monster collecting of SMT and Persona will be let down, but I found the "Archetype" system to still be engaging (if not a bit stingy at first, but your mileage will vary).Story: Easily one of my favorite narrative hooks in an Atlus game. I found the writing a bit shakey in some areas, but the characters are compelling and the high-fantasy setting a real treat. Major themes lack subtlety in any way, shape or form, but they are compelling and I enjoyed it all from start to finish.Music: this team does not miss. Chief priest of Myojoji Temple Keisuke Honryo is the goat and deserves to reach nirvana.Overall: as someone who has played Persona's 3-5, I can confidently say this dev team has polished this style of RPG to a shine. There's always going to be aspects of the "calendar system" that remain annoying to me personally, but the improvements made with this game give me confidence in this team's ability to address feedback and implement creative solutions.

_childDocuments_.review: If you can get past the fact that this game is in a technically unacceptable state (due to Atlus using the outdated P5 engine, unlike P3R and SMT Vengeance which use Unreal Engine), you'll love everything it has to offer.I shouldn’t have to use a Vulkan injector to get a consistent 60 fps for a game with the graphical fidelity of a PS3 title in 2024. Even with the injector, my system is working far too hard to maintain 60 fps for a game with such low graphical demands. And to be clear, I’m not criticizing the game's graphics—I don’t play these games for visual realism; that's not what they’re about. I play them for their amazing art style. The beauty of games that emphasize art style is that they typically demand very little from your system to run smoothly. Given that context, along with how hyped this game was, at least within the JRPG community, this port feels like a huge '♥♥♥♥ you' to the players.Nihon Falcom, the creator of the Trails series (my beloved—easily one of the best series in video games), unveiled their new custom in-house engine with the latest entry in the Trails series: Trails Through Daybreak. On a side note, the game nailed the real-time action and turn-based combat fluidity before Metaphor—Atlus didn’t do it first, Nihon Falcom did. It blows my mind that a significantly smaller studio with a much lower budget can create an engine that, as far as anime-styled games go, is very technically impressive. The PC port of Daybreak, in particular, far exceeds the expectations of a relatively ‘good’ PC port. This comparison proves there are absolutely no excuses Atlus can make: Tony Stark made Daybreak and its respective engine in a cave, lol. I really hope Atlus fixes Metaphor, because while the game remains playable despite its numerous performance and optimization issues, it’s still completely unacceptable. As long as these issues persist, the system requirements listed on the game's store page are blatantly misleading to any gamer looking to dive into this refreshing experience.Why am I so harsh? Well, it’s because I love Atlus and their games—specifically, the Persona series, which is a testament to the potential video games have as a storytelling medium. But that’s the thing: you can have the best-looking UI, a truly compelling story (which is why I’m here), and a refined combat system, but if you don’t get the fundamental basics right—those essentials that bring all these elements together—the experience for players will never be as impactful as it should be. This, in turn, significantly undermines the hard work of all the creative minds behind this ambitious project.Once I finish the game, I plan to write a full review and provide an update. For now, though, I’m using this space to voice my valid concerns—all of which are technical.

_childDocuments_.review: Metaphor is a beautiful merging of Atlus’ previous work that also manages to go above and beyond its predecessors. Take Persona’s strong character writing, combine it with SMT’s more involved combat, and stuff in a unique, engaging high-fantasy plot. The game is not entirely without flaw, but those problems seem tiny compared to everything Metaphor does right. If Atlus’ other games are generally an 8/10, Metaphor is a 9/10 or more. In my opinion, between Persona and SMT, their biggest weaknesses have been their overarching story. To me, the plots have always been kind of “mehhh” but I stick it through because of the characters or the gameplay, respectively. Metaphor does not suffer from this problem. There is an end goal established early on and everything you do is clearly in service of that goal. There is very little meandering and the story being told is deeply engaging, more so than previous Atlus games. In Altus shedding the pseudo-realism and instead opting for full on fantasy, there are much more interesting stories that get to be told.    Thankfully, your gang isn’t just a bunch of highschoolers anymore. Metaphor’s main party have varied and interesting personalities as well as a significant connection to the main plot. Gone are the days of “uhh I found this guy crying in the street so he’ll be joining us” or half a social link being about bad cooking. There is less "hey we're all friends :D" vibes compared to Persona, and I think that's fitting for the more serious story being told.It’s Persona’s calendar system with SMT’s combat. Then you get to play with the archetype system, which is sort of a middle ground of party customization between the two games. I really like the archetype system, generally speaking. My problem is that, at first, you’re given the illusion of complete freedom in what jobs you give your party, when that’s not totally the case. In the last 10 or so hours of the game, you’re introduced to the cool, final form archetypes for your party members, but you’re only allowed to equip them on their respective party members (not anyone else) AND only before training specific prerequisite archetypes. Essentially, you’re only able to use these cool final forms if you used your party’s “canon” archetypes, so it’s sort of a fake freedom. This wasn’t a problem for me, mostly, but I can see the more “unorthodox” players getting annoyed by this. I think the game moves at a really good pace for the first, like, 45ish hours with how it balanced main story and side content. But the last 15ish hours really dragged at certain points. First they hit you with the “this is our final battle!” and just meta-wise I could tell this obviously wasn’t the end, but I was getting that vibe of  “okay, we’re almost done”. Then they hit you with the “THIS time is the REAL final battle!” and, unsurprisingly, it wasn’t. At a certain point I was like “okay, when’s this game actually over?” So I was feeling a bit tired already, then they hit me with a BIG chunk of calendar time to wrap up all the side content, which was way more time than they’ve given at any other point. It really felt like a long time to not be moving the main story forward. Like, genuinely I was so ready to finish the game that I skipped ALL of  and part of  social links because I was ready to just WRAP THINGS UP. The pacing really just falls off a cliff at the end. The (real) final encounter brought it back for me, but that final stretch was tough. - The OST is great, as usual- I don’t think the game looks all that amazing graphically, but the hand drawn art is beautifulMetaphor is a great game. If you've enjoyed other Atlus games, you'll like this one. If you bounced off of other Atlus games, Metaphor might be the one that gets you. Try to avoid burning out on the final stretch.9/10, GOTY

_childDocuments_.review: ==NO SPOILER REACTION==this is the best iteration of alot of atlus staple mechanics. the story is dramatic fantastical and significantly tonal; while some of the metaphors are kinda obvious the amount of layers and lore to get to that metaphor is really well done. in the same way personas basic friendship themes arent the only function of social links.its best played unspoiled so dim the lights free a few hours in your downtime and listen to the excellent voice work and music, absorb it cause if you half think anything you could easily die. dont worry though its not that hard either. maybe harder than persona even at p3 standards; but its easy to retry fights rewind to the beggining of battles if ya made a mistake or learned something new, its the most fair game and you could overlevel if ya want too. best part is unlike persona 5 you dont always immediately kill enemies youre better than in the overworld- you have to care about their animations now, both your arceitype (its just like jobs in final fantasy) and your party can even gang up on em. when they come back to persona this is the part i hope they transfer over, shadows kinda just have one attack that causes full battles, but you can just start it anytime but have to hit them so a lil bar doesnt fill. adding a bit more reason to play a bit more stealth, its wonderful for when youre leveling that you still have to think and be situationaly aware. Id have a book to write if i gushed about the story plus i dont wanna spoil it. if you even kinda ♥♥♥♥ with persona or the smt franchise youll fit right in if youre just a jrpg type this is the best one in a long time.if you like rpgs this is the only game besides final fantasy 7 rebirth; that should get goty or award this year.(atleast for its banging soundtrack) im a big dragon age fan and theres no way veilgaurd will ever satisfy me as much as this game does. its the Turn based king of 2024 buy it.RATING: PLAY IT NOW.

_childDocuments_.review: To recommend or not to recommend, that is the question. This is kind of an odd position to find myself in.I really enjoy this game. It's not perfect, but nothing is. It has its own unique flair and draw that it mixes with elements taken from Persona and SMT, with a few adjustments to better fit the game's own design perspectives. I even prefer some of the changes made to the life sim elements - like the fact that Social Links no longer have "right" or "wrong" answers. I never was a fan of the fact that in order to build an unbreakable relationship with your friends, family, and allies you had to basically manipulate them - telling them not what you actually thought but what they wanted to hear; so the change that links deepen regardless of what you choose to say is a nice change. In general, all of the life sim elements are more streamlined because the time frame of the game is shorter (from a calendar perspective, not so much an hour perspective). The number of points you get towards increasing a social stat increases the further into the game you get, to consolidate the value of your time slots. But there's plenty I'm not a fan of like the fact that the game is far too grindy. The best way to level up is to use a mastered Archetype and convert your exp into exp items you can use on other Archetypes, because you get an exp bonus on mastered Archetypes. But doing this is time consuming. In the later games, leveling up Elite and Royal Archetypes can take not just dozens of exp items but dozens of minutes because you can't use exp items in bulk.The story also feels very disjointed and all over the place. Some twists and reveals don't really feel fully fleshed out and at the very least seem like they were written in to the story after the fact, with no concern for the fact that it doesn't match up with what's been shown/said/heard or rather hasn't been shown/said/heard. Very vague that, but I don't wanna spoil it. TL;DR: Probably the biggest issue though is the simple fact that I regret buying this game. Why? Because Atlus made it. Which means sometime in the next five years, they're going to rerelease this game as a definitive edition at full price. At some point, that really starts getting old. Why not just delay the game until its actually finished? Or release the definitive edition content as DLC? I don't know why I'm asking that, I know why - because money.EDIT: I have now beaten the game, and oh my god this game's finale just keeps dragging on and on and ON. Based on what my additional playtime and the time my achievements were earned tell me, it took me roughly six hours to get through the finale. I was also at max level when I did this - absurdly over-leveled for the finale meaning I spent as little time in that section of the game as I could.EDIT 2: This may be the one Atlus game that has an English dub that is vastly superior to its Japanese dub. My first playthrough used the Japanese dub - because I always do the first playthrough of any Japanese game in the original Japanese dub; that was mistake. The English dub fits the setting far better than the Japanese dub.

_childDocuments_.review: It starts off promising, but after the game opens up it presents you with content that's a mixed bag. Granted, I've not done them enough to comment.The combat is fantastic, and so is the art-direction. _childDocuments_.review: Another fantastic JRPG by Atlus including everything you could ask for.- Extremely fun press turn combat with many Archetypes (classes) to choose from. Being able to customize not only the protagonist's Archetypes but also the ones of your party members is huge. You can come up with a lot of fun and interesting builds.- Lovable cast, absolutely fantastic voice acting and art style.- Intriguing story with smooth pacing overall and a unique fantasy setting. I don't mind the high school setting from the Persona games but it's refreshing to see something new and they nailed it. - Amazing OST.Only minor gripes for me:- More unvoiced dialogue than usual. The majority is voiced but i felt for the few parts that aren't voiced, it detracted quite a bit from the immersion. That said, social links (called followers here) aren't voiced either except for Rank 1 and 8. Didn't mind that personally but it felt odd after P3 Reload which had fully voiced Social Links.- The story dungeons were good but i'd have loved more unique layouts for optional dungeons. There are essentially 4 or so reused ones with slightly different textures/lighting. Some Puzzles would've been amazing as well. Easily my GOTY. Everything just clicked with me and i was so attached to the cast i didn't want it to end. I played through the game twice for all achievements and i can see myself doing a third playthrough soon. I really hope there will be DLC for this game.A must play. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome story, great characters, cool music - everything either 10 or 9 out of 10.Just remember -it's not fantasy Persona after entering dungeons, then the game becomes an SMT title. The difference? Persona is generally easier and uses a system in which utilizing weaknesses gives character one more move as long as enemy was standing while hit while invulnerable or draining enemies will end turn for just that character - Metaphor uses SMT's press-turn system, your entire team gets amount of moves equal to amount of living party members and exploiting weakness changes turn to half-turn which can be used to make a move but won't award exploting weaknesses so f.e. with 3 party members you won't get more than 6 turns - conversely hitting invulnerable enemy/missing removes 2 turns and hitting enemy drain removes 4 turns giving initiative to enemy even if you used only 1 spell, making every other party member not move at all.So remember, mechanically the game is out to get you and you are expected to use mechanics like Mage SP regen on real-time combat kills, keep this in mind and you'll quickly adjust.

_childDocuments_.review: The story and world are both so interesting and engaging, the story has had me addicted the entire time and I've never been so fascinated by a game such as this one. I can't praise this game enough! If you like Atlus games, go play this NOW! If you haven't played any games from Atlus before but like JRPG's with an in depth time management and deadline system where every character feels real and relatable in some way, not to mention a very interesting advanced style fantasy world, give this a try.Easily one of the best games Atlus has ever put out! It's definitely my personal favorite. Everything about it just hits the right spot, the amazing music which I would put up there with the masterful work that is Nier: Automata's OST. The gameplay, while mostly the same is refined and some of the best combat they've done. It's still turn-based for the majority, but there are some real-time elements to it where you're able to straight up take enemies out in the field that are weaker than you taking them out without much of a fight, but they can still attack and deal some minor damage to you but you can dodge to avoid this, or attack and stun enemies for 1 turn cycle before going into Squad battle (turn-based combat), but if you get hit by enemies around your level or higher you get ambushed and the enemy attacks first, I just let this happen sometimes because the ambush song is so dang good!

_childDocuments_.review: This game rules.  Despite being a different flavor of Persona (not complaining), what it does differently is a lot of fun.  The archetype system, while a bit bloated and repetitive in some ways, was really fun to swap between and test out.  There are lots of little mini dungeons which breaks up the gameplay cycle of Story-Social-Dungeon-Story a bit more.  And the followers system (called social links in the Persona games) has been simplified and trimmed down in really meaningful ways.  This game looks and sounds amazing, too.  I love the art, but I also love the small details, such as the little sketch textures that get overlayed onto characters' clothing.  There are small things here and there that overall make this game look very stylish and unique.  And oh MAN, that music.  I was hooked as soon as I heard the battle theme for the first time.The story was really neat too.  Louis is a great antagonist, it was a lot of fun working against him over the course of the story.  He's so interesting!  I do think that the ending does feel a bit too over-complicated at times, similar to how it can get in Persona games.  But that isn't really much of a complaint.This was a fantastic game.  If you don't like Persona, you probably won't like this game.  Otherwise, hell yeah!   Play this when you get the chance!

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 atlus have done it again. GOTY (Soejima and Hashino cooked) Another must-play JRPG that lived up to the expectation and beyond.85 hours (of which 10 spent maxing archetypes achievement-not needed since ng+ gave plenty xp) first 100% playthrough (not that hard to get even without a guide-e.g. follower xp not locked behind correct dialogue options like persona but instead rewards with a currency).105 hours save file INCLUDING ng+ and superboss. Offers 3 bad endings that cut the game short, in favor of one "true" ending. Superb music, Shoji Meguro masterclass. Excellent story, writing, artstyle and themes.Hybrid persona/smt combat, with the good addition of the dynamic action combat. A lot of options for customization since every character can select every archetype.Fabulous graphics, from the cutscenes (atlus always manage to make them very cinematic) to the combat animations, and of course the classic atlus menu visuals.Solid characters, difficulty just at the right spot (can be rewarding and punishing depending on how well the whole system is used).Overall very cool game with impressive world building, easier to get into than p5r, more streamlined calendar system and more of a "journey/adventure". _childDocuments_.review: Overall: Good, but not GREAT. 9/10Story: Arguably the strongest aspect, as it goes a bit more mature than some of the previous titles, and takes some bolder risks. A few points really threw me for a loop and I didn't see it coming. I would have loved if my choices really had more consequences than just being railroaded into what they want, but they were aiming to tell a specific story so I can't exactly complain, especially because the story IS quite good. At almost 50 hours though and at the final fight, it does feel quite short.Characters: There are a few good characters, a lot of decent ones and none that I particularly didn't care for. A couple did feel a little generic, but overall the characters felt quite diverse with good backgrounds and motivations. They have character flaws and weaknesses balancing their strength of will, and often emotional story arcs. Not all that much to really write home about or insanely memorable characters, but they're good, well written characters voiced by good voice actors. Unfortunately romance has been removed in this title, despite some quite cute characters (BUNNY GIRL TOMBOY PLEASE GOD), but it doesn't all affect much other than fan service.Gameplay: Can be somewhat of a mixed bag, but mostly good. It's an RPG made by the guys who've made mainly RPG's for like, 20 years, so they mostly know what they're doing. However, I can't help but feel like this one takes two steps forward and a step back from Persona 5 Royal with some of it's mechanics. Some of the status effects and mechanics make sense and are straightforward like attacking enemies in the overworld from behind or until their stun bar reaches zero without getting hit initiates a surprise attack being a pleasant surprise, but some others make little sense either mechanically or why they did so. Breaking up the main attacks into three categories instead of Persona 5's two was a frustrating one, as there are already six other categories, and may make one or two party member almost entirely useless in certain dungeons or fights. Certain effects such as malady or hex are frustrating to deal with as well, but near completely unable to be applied to big enemies or bosses. Another frustrating mechanic was losing multiple turn icons for a reflected attack, especially when first learning about the enemy weaknesses, not only losing the xp/money bonus for an unscathed fight, but additionally allowing the enemy to likely dish out more damage by way of the fight taking longer or even ending your turn immediately.Soundtrack: Unfortunately, the weakest aspect. In my opinion, I didn't mesh with the soundtrack all that much. Previous titles like Persona 5, Persona 5 Royal, and Persona 3 Reloaded had some BANGER soundtracks, but I feel like the attempt on giving it more medieval European style feel, often with church style choirs, just wasn't really my thing. I also feel that they didn't really write enough sad style songs for the more emotional parts of character arcs to really get one in the serious mood and that often they didn't play a sad song when they should. When a character has a village wiped out and they feel it's their fault, the music should reflect that better and I just feel like the soundtrack here just didn't cut it. I also didn't care for the small amount of battle bgm's, with one in particular having what sounds like a German guy speaking very quickly in the background very easy to hear repetitively at the beginning of nearly every battle getting on my nerves the most.Overall, it's worth your money. I would personally wait for it to go on at least a minor sale, but that's just me.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoy this game. The pros? Awesome combat and progression systems. Extremely satisfying and a breath of fresh air. _childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game - I love and have played every modern Atlus title post Persona 2. Atlus games are amazing because characters have so much depth and the story is held up by really interesting, nuanced philosophies that actually get you to think during and after the game ends. But Metaphor, at least 15 hours in, doesn't really have that - or much else.The story is really, really bare bones, stories about racism and discrimination are definitely important, but the way tribalism is depicted in Metaphor is so blatantly binary and one dimensional. The dialogue is truly just exposition and drivel, and characters don't really have heart or soul. The strength of Atlus games comes from their social sim nature and their engaging characters who actually experience growth from beginning to end; the social sim gameplay of Metaphor doesn't hold a candle to Persona or even weaker games in the genre. The first act of the game is also all over the place. This game has serious pacing issues. Important story bits hardly get fleshed out, don't ever linger when it would actually be beneficial to; it's hard to explain but I just found the first few hours of the game so jarring. If I had to try, I'd say it's because so much gets dumped on you, but the contents of what gets dumped on you is simply not immersive. In the span of a few minutes, you watch a king get assassinated, fall off a wagon, walk through sand, and end up a goon under some fat mustached man. You move through a world alarmingly quickly with hardly any world building or immersion - unless you stop and talk to an NPC in which they will a) start BMing you for your race or b) tell you how their mom couldn't afford a cancer treatment because of some racist McScrooge (sorry, they all kind of blend together after the 8880183413th time). Or uh go into the menus and read extracurricular descriptions because that's good worldbuilding????????????The characters are just really, really unlikeable. Your rivals in competing for the thrones are actually jokes. They are goofy caricatures with zero depth. They lack personality and are by nature extremely irrelevant because 99% of them are competing just to give up their spot to their big bosses, ie, generic evil church man and anime Napoleon. The majority of your party members are pretty much all mildly traumatized adults who, for some reason, defer to a prepubescent teenager. Except Gallica, Gallica is fire.It would be okay if Metaphor made up for its poor story and characters with strong gameplay, music, and art. The gameplay is actually atrocious - you can literally dodge every single hostile monster and pretty much skip your way to the boss fights because of how bad the mob AI is. And the boss fights are a breeze because of how ridiculously broken synthesis skills are. There are hardly any puzzle elements to the dungeons, and the dungeon gameplay loop is pressing A to go under obstacles, fighting the same monsters over and over, and pressing A a few times to get through dialogue. When you get out of dungeons, the gameplay loop is pretty much even more dialogue. Which I wouldn't mind - my definition of a good game is honestly just glorified reading, except your dialogue choices have no consequence at all, unlike in other social sim-esque games. The rewards for dialogue are also pretty much identical across your party members, with hardly any variety. If you are not in a dungeon, you are probably reading boxes and boxes of unvoiced lines about the 81293812795th tribe experiencing racism or classism. I actually got really excited when after hours of clicking A, I finally was given an option to travel to some location relevant to a character's history. Imagine how disappointed I was when not only could I not walk around the location, but the location itself was just a static png. With more, unvoiced, dialogue.Sound is really, really subjective, but I personally got so sick of hearing "as time marches on and the age of a new king draws nearer" literally every 3 minutes. The score does have an epic, orchestral suite, but it is so evocative of Fire Emblem that I was shocked the composer was Shoji Meguro. I haven't heard the entirety of the game's soundtrack, and Atlus titles are usually back heavy in terms of where the good music is, so I won't comment on things I haven't heard. What I have heard though are reused sound effects from Persona. A good number actually...I've been trying, and totally failing, to keep explicit Persona comparisons to a minimum because I recognize a good number of newcomers haven't played those games before (therefore not being a super useful example), but I have to mention at least once that this game borrows, extensively, from the Persona games. And not innovatively either.Now for the art. There is a big difference between style and graphical fidelity / quality. This game definitely has style. The UI is really, really nice. It's just unfortunate that the graphics of the game are straight out of a PS3 game in 2024. The graphics don't really detract from the gameplay, but it's not anything to write home about. It is, however, personally difficult to justify the 70 dollar MSRP for a game with 2008 graphics. With their Shin Megami Tensei games, Atlus showed just how incredible they were at showing, not telling. With the Persona games, Atlus showed just how great they are at writing compelling, interpersonal character dramas. With Metaphor, they will tell, tell, tell until you get sick of engaging with the repetitive dialogue, and cycle through one dimensional caricatures of characters in an overly classic, very vanilla fantasy tale. While the UI is a strong point, gameplay, audio, and visuals are sorely lacking. I really wish I could like this game, and I really wish I had it in me to drag myself through the game and finish it. Atlus games got me through the pandemic and it was a joy to boot up whichever title I was playing through for that special hour in my day. As one of their biggest fans, it is truly disappointing to not only play Metaphor, but to have the game be recommended to so many newcomers when it is in my eyes one of their weakest, worst games ever.

_childDocuments_.review: My review of this game can be summed up in one sentence: I expected more. This is a PS3 game. Its not bad. Its pretty on the surface but doesnt hold up under closer inspection.Negatives: - The game looks really ugly, no amount of lighting, shadows or effects can hide the fact that this games looks    like it was made in 2008. Visual design of the menu's and character portraits is probably the only thing i'd    give this game a 10/10 for. Everything else is like 6-7/10 at best.  - There is so many loading screens for each and every little thing. Every loading screen takes only 1-3 seconds    but there is so many of them it feels like you spend half your time playing looking at them. You cant even    skip "cutscenes"/loadin screens for activities that you repeat every day. Going to the washroom for free xp    every day ? - unskipable black screen. Positives: - One thing thats new compared to Persona and that I actually really liked was the fact that you actually get    wepons/armor/trinkets to equip which have meaningful impact on how you build your archetypes/characters. - I liked what they were trying to go for with the class system but in my opinion it doesnt work as well as it    should.  - Story can be interesting at times.Atlus made a good step forward with SMTV Vengeance but Metaphor feels like another step back.

_childDocuments_.review: After sinking about 30 hours into the game, I gotta say, this one totally deserves a Game of the Year nomination. Here's the breakdown:1. GameplayIf you're into turn-based JRPGs like Persona or SMT from Atlus, you need to check out Metaphor: Re Fantazio. It mixes the companionship system from Persona (no romance, though—like, who's got time to date when you're out here saving princes and trying to become a king candidate?) with the battle mechanics of SMT 3. It's a perfect blend.2. StoryStory-wise? It's been an absolute blast so far. If you're used to the vibe of the Persona series, you'll feel right at home. No spoilers, but trust me—it’s really, really good up to this point.3. World DesignThe game world? INSANELY HUGE. The dungeons and areas you visit are super varied. It’s a major step up from SMT V and Persona 5 Royal in terms of scale and design.4. OptimizationFor an Atlus game, Metaphor is surprisingly well-optimized. Running it on an RTX 2050, I’m getting 50–70 FPS on full high settings at 1080p (sure, it dips in crowded scenes, but still solid).OverallMetaphor: Re Fantazio is a rock-solid JRPG from Atlus. If you’ve ever wanted an SMT game with a dash of Persona-style companionship, this one’s absolutely worth your time. 💯

_childDocuments_.review: Metaphor is, perhaps without exaggeration, one of the greatest RPGs to come out in the last decade. Taking every lesson that they've learned over the many years of developing Persona, Atlus has in their efforts created a wholly unique, incredibly fresh feeling experience unlike any I've had for a while. While there are overarching similarities in terms of balance and combat, the way you get to interact with said mechanics has been tweaked much to the better, allowing for a more immersive and free way of experiencing the game itself.And that's not to say that before you even get to any of that, the sheer presentation of the game is nothing short of astounding. From the UI/UX elements looking like they had more time and polish put into it than all games that released this year combined, alongside the fact that the entire skybox looks like a beautifully painted Van Gogh painting at all times, the graphical fidelity and art direction of this game is perhaps some of the greatest modern gaming has to offer. Seriously. It's incredibly breathtaking taking in the many vistas and just how immersed it makes you feel.The laurels don't stop there, because accompanying the art is perhaps also the greatest soundtrack to date, with some of the most emotional, action-packed songs I've heard since the peaks of audio that Elden Ring introduced me to. The layers and complexity in each track is phenomenal, and the small little fact that "Music" is a magic in the game and gets addressed as being cast on the group to get you feeling pumped is perhaps the best analogy I could give to the real world effect it has had on me.If you've ever wanted an immersive experience in a world that is entirely thought through, down to its last detail, with a compendium it provides you to read up on any terminology it uses that confuses you, a world so rich with character inhabited by individuals that are fantastically written, a story that, minus a few obvious plot points, unfolds itself as a truly uniquely crafted masterpiece, sprinkled in with some of the greatest combat system that's been refined since the first Shin Megami Tensei game, then please, genuinely, try this game. Try the demo. It's 5-7 hours long, and it's barely scratching the surface, but it gives you all that you need to know about if you'd like the game, and the save carries over.There's few games that will irrevocably change the way we view games as a medium, be it based on their production or their presentation, and I believe that Metaphor is among those few games privileged enough in history to be named such one.

(and that's just the tip of the ice berg on the spoiler-free themes in the story) The music is fantastic. The UI and menus screams graphic design is my passion. (It can be distracting but, as an artistic stand point its very gorgeous) If you like both SMT and Persona games, you will fall in love with this game.Just by playing the demo alone, it can easily determine whether this game is for you. And the demo itself is like ~6hrs long. Your demo playthrough will carry over to the main game once purchased, and that is amazing!I personally highly recommend Metaphor for any J-RPG lover. But give it a try with the demo before you buy the game for $70.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - You owe it to yourself to experience the battle system, the characters, and the story. But beware the borderline offensive dungeon design.This game is so close to being PERFECT. The story--a tale of tragedy, racism, classism, and religious persecution--is expertly told. Every single major character is almost excruciatingly well-written. While some have said it's not stylish, I contend that it's incredibly stylish, but in a more muted, realistic way. The music is incredible, all sung with bombastic choirs chanting in Esperanto. The combat is very well-balanced, and rewards players with creative thinking. As much as I hated it at first, the 60's / 70's fashion of some of the cast ended up growing on me.There is, however, one giant, glaring issue with this game: the dungeons.Look...I understand that this isn't a Persona game. I understand that the handful of dungeons in Persona 5 meant that each one was tailor-made for their themes, and a lot of work could go into them because there were so few. I UNDERSTAND that, with so many more dungeons in Metaphor, sacrifices had to be made, and not every dungeon could be a world-shaking spectacle.But...come on, guys. This is just BAD. Every dungeon in the game (with one glaring exception about halfway through the game) is one of a handful of biomes: Outdoors, Cave, Temple and Other, Darker-Colored Cave. There are a few dungeons with slightly adjusted wallpaper (the inside of a regal airship, for example), but 90% of the places you conduct combat in will fall into those categories. Every single one--even the final story dungeons--feel lazily slapped together, copy-pasted ad nauseam, and kicked out the door without time to brush their teeth. There are only a handful of what can only charitably be described as "puzzles" across the entirety of the game's length, and those are anemic and boring. It all boils down to sprinting through samey corridors, briefly praying that the next room has a powerful monster in it, just to take away the sheer, suffocating BOREDOM.It's a crying shame, because every. Other. Piece. Of this game. Is incredible. Whoever decided that the little man-bat in the goofy booties (whom I originally mistook for the game's 'mascot character') should be the oldest, deepest-voiced and most badass little sawblade with the darkest backstory, should legitimately be given a writing award. The music can make simple basic attacks that do pitiable damage feel like the crescendo of a victorious opera, and you its frenzied conductor. The writing is absolutely incredible, with a story that is as topical as it is prescient. More than once, a single dismissive line of a characters dialogue unraveled entire twists MOMENTS before the twist itself is even revealed. There's no instances of the game's plot not playing by its own rules, and yet it can still keep you guessing all the way to the end.There's also very little pigeonholing in regards to character roles: with a few exceptions, every character can play any role in combat, and while they do lean towards certain roles with their base stats and their final character classes (called Archetypes), clever job and equipment assignment can make it so that even your big tough greatsword-wielding noble scion can become a damage-dealing mage, an efficient healer, or even a dagger-swinging wild card. There's also no more "wasting" resources and days, as opposed to Persona 5: your Social Links (called 'Bonds' in this game) don't need to be worked up to, but become unlocked at certain story points as long as you've done their previous quests. This means that there's no more pestering Ryuji to devour ramen and work out together in the hope that MAYBE tomorrow he'll be ready for an upgrade. Disappointing your allies in conversation only nets you less Magla (the resource to unlock jobs and abilities, primarily gained through combat). Gone is the need to adhere to a walkthrough to maximize relationship efficiency. Even playing as a job you've already maxed out is free of waste; every thousand experience you gain on a completed Archetype will give you a little token to give a thousand experience to any job, on any character. This means that, if you wanted to, you could have every character play only one Archetype for the entirety of the game, while they still level other Archetypes and unlock their skills. All in all, this game gets a solid recommendation. The themes and emotions at the heart of this story are something every gamer should experience. Combat's a joy. If you can manage not to nod off during the dungeons, then Metaphor Re:Fantazio will earn a place of pride on your shelf.

_childDocuments_.review: Atlas is a shining example of a studio that still values releasing a game that is truly finished; it's polished, and with minimal bugs (if any, I haven't encountered one yet). The story of this game had me hooked in about an hour; it's incredibly unique and fun to play out so far. It's a beautiful game as well. It's no Baldur's Gate 3, but if you have any appreciation for well made art that maintains an aesthetic and with nice design, then you'll be immersed and impressed. Metaphor is heavy on the "anime" side of story-telling and game content, if you couldn't tell already, but don't let that deter you if you're unsure if that would fun or immersive for you. Literally every aspect of this game is robust and fun to play (combat, characters, progression, story lines, menu's/UX, etc.) It's just that rock solid and worth trying, if not at least for a few hours. I have some criticisms, but I won't even write them because they're so small and subjective. Expect a game with challenging bosses, but unique combat that stays fresh. Mistakes are punished, and there is such thing as "optimal" game-play. Oh, also expect a slow burn--Atlas games are typically quite long... like over 100 hours for the main story.It has everything you'd expect from a Persona game (and even SMT a bit). Yet Atlas has this game feeling both familiar, and unique in it's own right. It's not a clone of any other game they've made, but still feels very "Atlas". Metaphor feels closer to P5 than anything else. P5 might feel more "cozy" of a game, but this one makes up for it with much more dynamic combat (you can essentially change what "persona" a character has, for instance). You make friends, build trust, improve your own qualities, and have a calendar-based story with quest deadlines, all that. If you have high expectations, they will be met and perhaps exceeded.

_childDocuments_.review: 85 hours (+ 10 from the demo) to complete my first playthrough (where I got all but 2 achievements)Right after finishing the demo, I knew this was going to be a masterpiece. This is what I sent to my friends to convince them to play the demo before the full game released (they did and they fell in love too):"I think the gameplay is really good-- the press turn system is nice and strategic, and the archetype system is like the standard job/class system like in Octopath so there's a lot of variety in how you can approach turn-based battles. Even better though is the overworld combat you can do to instantly wipe out weak enemies for fast and easy grinding. The music is really banger because it'll be some epic orchestral soundtrack with Buddhist chants that are rapped in the background (turns out they are Buddhist sutras that are chanted by an actual monk, Keisuke Honryo, head priest of the Myojoji temple). And instead of a yapping cat like Morgana in Persona 5, you have a cute fairy as your sidekick who isn't as bossy. Metaphor has my wholehearted recommendation. (It runs fine with intermediate settings on my 3070ti, consistent 144 fps)And regarding the premise of the game...Persona 5: we have 30 days to change the teacher's heartMetaphor: we have 5 days to assassinate the candidate for king"Now after beating the full game I have to add, regarding the characters and story:Amazing. All the characters are very memorable. Their designs are whimsical and varied. Someone who looks and acts very serious turns out to be the silliest character of the crew. Someone who looks small and cute turns out to be an old man. There is a character whom I feel looks straight out of One Piece and his one-track mind leads to hilarious situations. All of the characters have unique personalities and come from unique backgrounds, and throughout the whole story they mesh very well in such a way where you want to keep playing the game not only to find out what happens next in the story, but also to see more of the crew's dynamics with each other.The story/theme of the Metaphor is very heavy and serious, but there are plenty of silly, absurd moments woven throughout the whole story so your heart and mind aren't constantly burdened with heavy topics like racism, grief, suicide, etc. And the whimsical moments of the story are made even more hilarious when the characters themselves realize the ridiculousness of their actions and decide to commit.Ultimately, I think Metaphor: ReFantazio is Atlus's best game yet. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to have the review be spoiler-free as possible. Pros:- The 2D artsyle is beautiful. It’s different from Atlus’ other games like Persona, but it worked wonderfully deciphering the characters in the world of Metaphor. I love the portrait arts not only of the main cast, but the side characters as well. - From the chara arts/designs alone I can say that I love the female characters more than the male ones. This is rare because I usually love husbandos the most in the games I’ve played. But the waifus in this game are so eye-candy. I loveeeee their designs so much. Brigitta, Fabienne, Hulkenberg. I especially love Junah and Eupha because of the patterns on their outfits. Other games usually avoided using ONLY repeated patterns for their character’s outfits, but it just works here. I don’t know why. That being said, I can also say that most of the male characters are all handsome in their own way. Strohl, Basilio, Neuras, The key characters of the Church, Louis, Grius. They are all so unique and each have their own charms. - From personality alone I can assure you that all characters, even the villains are all very well-developed and likable. This is the first JRPG where I love all of the main cast and the social link characters. Heck, unlike Persona, all social link only characters even have their own role in the main story. Their stories are better as well because they’re not just someone you met somewhere random and being there to talk about their problems. Everyone here has their part towards the betterment of their own tribes, family and groups. It’s so amazing to see the people of the world in Metaphor all slowly coming together through these stories, and how they’re all tied to the main story in the end. - The story is darker here than Persona 3-5. Racism everywhere. The game wasn't afraid to show blood or people’s corpses literally lying on the street. I’m so glad the game didn’t have another random God appear out of nowhere at the end like Persona games. To me, even though there are anime-cliche scenes here and there, the story until the end was wrapped wonderfully. Not perfect, but I enjoyed it a lot. I couldn’t believe I actually shed tears, shocked and smiled widely in one sitting doing the final boss and the ending. The ending is one of the best I’ve ever seen in JRPGs.- OST and UI. It’s Atlus. What else can I say?- World-building is also on point. Can’t say much about this to avoid spoilers. But it’s just so good.- Archetype >>>>>>>> Persona. From design alone, archetypes cleared. I like how all archetypes look like they have the same theme (gold/silver with fiery burning chest) but still manage to look different from one another. I love the designs a lot.- Same battle system like Persona games but everyone in the main cast has a wildcard so aside from their main archetypes, they all can switch and use each other archetypes freely. There’s also an inheritance system where we can put learned passive and active skills from one archetype to another. And synthesis systems where we basically combine corresponding two classes in the team to unleash stronger skills in battles. This is super creative because we basically have to spend some time in team building because of the synthesis skills and strategy in battles becoming more dynamic than ever. Imagine using an attack-focused archetype but can still use inherited teamwide healing/support skills. - I like how this game doesn’t have a silent MC but we players can still make decisions for him. Personality-wise, he’s not someone that is edgy or cowards. Instead he’s someone that’s determined from start to finish towards his goal and didn’t shy away from the rewards in the end.- One last thing that I love the most in this game: YOU CAN ACHIEVE MAX LEVEL ON ALL SOCIAL LINKS AND SOCIAL SKILLS IN ONE PLAYTHROUGH. This is amazing for me because on the last month before the final dungeon the game was super generous to give huge amount of time before the deadline to finish everything! This includes maxed social links (followers), social skills (royal virtue), all cooking recipes, etc. In Persona games you can't achieve this if you play blindly without using guide/walkthrough. But not in this game, which is why I love it the most. Cons:- Not really a con. But to be honest, the world design (aside from the royal capital) feels like something I’ve seen numerous times in other medieval fantasy JRPGs. They didn’t excite me. I love the design of the gauntlet runners, the landmarks/sights and the interior of all shops. But the streets and the buildings of the cities? Not so much. - The designs of the dungeons and monsters (aside from the main bosses) are so uninspiring. Repeatable design for the sub dungeons with different coats of paints. Monsters like goblins, birbs, dragons, snakes. The teeth monsters are different, at least. - I wished we could turn off Gallica’s voice in battles. I don’t mind when she told us if the characters got debuffed, but when she screamed in horror because the character got a heavy hit? Damn, definitely an ear screeching. - I wished the social link and main stories were all fully-voiced instead of just partially. It was so awkward seeing the characters were voiced in one part but silence and only saying one word five steps later.- Achievement bugs where I couldn't get the first 7 achievements earned from the first two dungeons because I clicked 'no' when the game asked to transfer save data from the demo. Re-installing or playing the game from the beginning with fresh save didn't solve this either. I'm so sad. 🙁 - Louis’ 2D portrait is too hot. If villain, why hot? :’) 9/10.All people, especially JRPG fans need to play this. I really recommend it. There’s a 5-6 hour demo that you can try for free if you’re still unsure with the game. It’s definitely the best JRPG that I’ve played this year.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is good, and I do think they made the smart decision to sell a new IP by utilizing the popular Persona calendar mechanic, but if they make another game in this vein they should ditch the Persona mechanics. The strongest parts of this game are the main story sequences and the game-play. A lot of the side content is mid, and the main cast shines at their best during story sequences, and not the side scenes. The calendar stuff just messes with the pacing too much and the only activities to do during downtime are kind of boring, like clearing dungeons that have a generic layout, or witnessing follower scenes that have mixed pacing and no voice acting until the last one. I know Persona does this too, and it's also a problem there. In this particular story, literally no character is all that important outside the main cast and the main villain, and all the filler stuff just makes me want to go back to the actual villain, so I think the calendar pacing has gotta go. The style and music are excellent of course. Some of the music tracks do sound more generic than Atlus' other series, but only because "fantasy medieval music" is kind of an over-saturated market. Any track with the weird ethnic yelling stuff are cool though. Some of the fantasy designs in this world are cool, but I really wish the actual tribes had more significant differences besides just being "humans with unique quirk." Actual unique looking races, something like Mass Effect, is just so much cooler and fantastical than just seeing basic human looking people everywhere. The only real interesting races are the Nidia and Eugief, and the cool aspect of the Nidia is barely explored. That is perhaps another issue the comes with the rigid pacing of the calendar system, in that you are never presented the opportunity to explore and learn more about the cultures and intricacies of this new world. They had a chance to do this with the follower side stories, but they all mainly serve to deliver some message that relates to the real world and play a sad piano track. Since the game doesn't give me a chance to delve into the deep culture of the world, I am left looking to their physical traits for fantastical differences, which again, is just different flavors of human for the most part. While I do think the main conflict with the villain is pretty cool, as well as the villain himself, the societal themes and message they try to deliver throughout the story fell completely flat for me. The first obvious theme is racism and discrimination, but it kinda switches gears near the end and starts focusing on how people shift their burdens and fears onto the shoulders of others so they don't have to worry about it themselves. Specifically in this game's case, the people all shoulder their worries on the king and take no personal responsibility. Okay, cool, I can get down with these topics, but the game, despite having a mainly adult cast, still handles these themes in a pretty juvenile way. The game takes every chance to show the absolute worst gradient of discriminatory acts, such as violence, murder, aggressive name-calling, and segregation, but most developed nations learn about the unethical nature of these acts in high school or middle school, and do not need a video game to show us it is bad. Of course, our world did exist in this state at one point, I won't deny that, but for a video game made in the 21st century I feel like we should be exploring more nuance in our themes. Like how these issues present themselves in very subtle ways within modern society. What is worse is that after you beat the game, in just a year the game presents itself as almost all discrimination and racial tension has faded, which is just absurd. Now there can be a little nuance found in some of the flavor text that no-name npcs give around town, but the majority of that flavor text is awfully boring so most will miss it. I will at least admit discrimination is a hard topic to tackle at least, but for such a major focal point of a lot of side and main content it could've been better. Then there is the second theme of the game, which I guess can be summarized by saying that people have others shoulder their burdens and lack personal-responsibility or something. It only kind of springs up right at the end of the game and has little time to explore it. This is the ole Atlus classic of presenting a "society are sheep" theme right at the end of the game, and then having the protagonists yap about hope and determination and kill some abstract god being. Luckily in this game the final boss is actually just the cool main villain, and not a last second god. I do think it is an interesting topic though, especially with American elections around the release date. It is hard to comment on it since it is so last second, but I wish the main cast actually had theological debating skills, and discussed more about how to tackle such issues, rather than just yap about human spirit or something. Like, deadass, the villain gave a great breakdown on why he thinks the way he does, why he is doing what he is doing, and his plan for the future. Even if his plan was, uh, a little amoral, at least he has a plan unlike my ragtag team of goobers who all take up major political positions after the game is over with absolutely zero experience or plan other than "save the world." In fact, they quite literally prove the major villain's philosophy correct by defeating him through sheer power to then instate themselves as political rulers lmao. The main cast themselves are good though, mainly during main story segments. Strohl, Heismay, and Basilio in particular stand out to me.The gameplay could certainly use some tweaks, but it is enjoyable overall. I think enabling the ability to switch archetypes mid-battle should be added, just make it use a press turn like in SMT so it isn't too OP. The main dungeons are cool, but the side dungeons are aggressively mid. They should just redouble their efforts into the main dungeons and into world exploration instead of them. Since it is a fantasy world, throw some super unique mini-game side quests into the mix, make it feel like a different world with weird recreation. The action combat is new, and makes being over-leveled slightly more entertaining as I can just mop through little baby enemies, but it is as bare-bones as action combat can get.There's probably a lot more I can write about but I'm kinda tired of typing stuff at this point. Even though I've really only complained, the game is still quite good, especially when good Triple-A JRPGs feel like they are on life support these days. It is just now that they've cemented this as a new setting I think they have a chance to abandon some of the annoying things present in their other games,

_childDocuments_.review: My first Impression after finishing the demo and now transferring my save files to the full release and playing the full game.First of all Metaphor is a fantastical fantasy setting game made by Atlus the same people who made Persona and SMT and although you can find some influence of these titles in Metaphor (obviously because the Persona directors created Studio Zero a sub studio inside Atlus SEGA and made Metaphor), the game still can stand on is own. The game has a very unique feel to it by combining gameplay aspects of multiple JRPG franchises like Final Fantasy's job class change system with the Archetypes, Monster Hunter with the bounty quests and world map what is semi-Open world where you have huge closed areas and instead of traveling from one area to another by walking with your character you actually just select set area and you travel there you have a huge very artistically pleasing map where you select the area you want to visit. Let's not forget the press turn system from Persona and SMT that clearly has a comeback in Metaphor only with a nice unique spin where you can now combine 2 characters and create a "super move" but that better move also takes 2 turns instead of 1 because you use 2 characters for it and it obviously deals more damage or has crazy buff, debuff or healing properties depending on character combination and Archetype combination and the last inspiration I can see is from Fire Emblem where the music and character designs resemble that of Fire Emblem a little bit of course is not 1 to 1 but it gives of Fire Emblem vibes at time (what is more of a praise than a critique). The story is also very well crafted giving it a very medieval-ish style atmosphere and the themes of anxiety (what creates hates, fear, discrimination...) are clearly the main focal point of Metaphor Re Fantazio.Now to the pros and cons:PROS:- Very stylish UI and atmosphere, the style is there what again nothing new when it comes to a Atlus title. This gives the game is own unique identity and the stylish decisions are also clearly connected to the overarching story of Metaphor Re Fantazio.- The gameplay is très magnifique (very beautiful) the main appeal of the gameplay is still the very classic Atlus turn based combat system will love and adore but with a new spin and the Archetype system (job classic system) is a fresh new change for the team at Atlus.- The story is very well written, it fits well with the atmosphere and art style Atlus is going with and the characters are very likable.- The music a aspect many people ignore but a very important one. The music is incredible, as usual from Atlus, they never disappoint.Having a DEMO that also transfers save file data to the final release. More companies need to implement this, huge thumbs up for this decision.CONS:- The Performance can be iffy at times although it isn't horrible as people try to make it out to be. If someone at Atlus reads my comment, although I highly doubt they will, please implement a upscaling solution, that would be very nice, something like a DLSS or FSR. You can change the rendering resolution to 75% if you have performance issues but that solution isn't perfect but it works.I don't have any more cons if I am completely honest, this is almost JRPG perfection. I hope Atlus can fix some of these performance issues and give fans more graphical options on PC, this is not a console version Atlus, we want more graphical options and a upscaling option so that everyone can enjoy Metaphor Re Fantazio. But overall if you are on the offense if you should or shouldn't get the game, I would first recommend getting the demo for free, play it, the demo is around 8-10 hours long and that will give you a clear imagine what the game is all about, then is up to you. I personally highly recommend this title is definitely one of my favorite games this year if not my favorite one! Definitely JRPG of the decade!

_childDocuments_.review: Metaphor takes a lot of influence from other Atlas titles yet does well enough to be unique and refreshing. I  this game to those looking for an RPG to play, but I'll share a few nitpicks that may turn some people away.First, I appreciate the length of this game. It took me ~70 hours to complete my first play through, which is (welcomely) shorter than their other titles. The time management in Metaphor is not nearly as strict as Persona, so I had plenty of time to do literally everything (all bosses, all quests, all bonds, everything). However, this greatly reduces any incentive to replay the game, which is required if you want all achievements. In total, it took about 100 hours to 100% the game, 30 of which was spent speed running the story a second time.The game itself is very convenient to play. Menus are super responsive and a joy to navigate. There's fast travel, menu shortcuts to nearly everything, and even reminders from your companions to turn in quests. You don't even have to battle "weaker" enemies, as you can kill them in the overworld before even initiating turn-based combat.Speaking of combat, I played on "Hard" difficulty, which is how I recommend others play. Metaphor has loads of mechanics, but fundamentally the game wants you to exploit enemy weaknesses to gain massive combat advantages. On easier difficulties these mechanics can often be ignored, but on Hard you really need to "play by the rules", as enemies can (and will) exploit your weaknesses in turn. This leads to rather swingy combat scenarios where either you kill the enemy on Turn 1 or they decimate you, giving Metaphor's combat a "puzzle" feel. If you mess up badly, you can rewind to the beginning of the battle at any time (another nice convenience).Story-wise, I enjoyed the fantasy setting of Metaphor. The world building and main cast were both great. Some people may not like the voice acting, but I thought it was quite well-done.It's obvious towards the end that content was cut from the game, as some events happen abnormally quickly compared to the much slower and more careful first half of the game. I think an entire dungeon was removed, and it results in a rather awkward character progression in the mid-game. To elaborate, characters get stronger by leveling "Archetypes", but these are unlocked slowly and require currency. I ran into a situation where I wasn't unlocking new Archetypes and didn't have the currency to acquire them anyway, which I suspect would have been alleviated by having more "time" and one more dungeon to leverage.One last nitpick is the reuse of dungeons and enemies. The main dungeons are actually all unique and (mostly) fun to explore, but the minor dungeons related to side-quests are all derivative of each other, making for a bland experience. Enemy variety was a bit lacking, as Metaphor uses pallet-swaps for "stronger versions" of enemies and repurposes early boss monsters as "regular" dungeon minions later on.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally at the end of the journey. Its been a blast exploring the world, seeing the great world building and various characters in the game.If you're coming from SMT/Persona, I would say this game sits somewhere in between but really trails its own path.There is some character development, but it isn't as deep as persona, for example. There is quite a lot of lore and world building which is very well done. They aren't shy about talking about certain topics. I think this is its biggest strength. I don't think its the best overall story compared but it talks about topics in more of a upfront way where it doesn't come off patronizing and within the theme of the story. In the other persona games like 3 reload or 5, I also found that the last quarter of the game starts to drag out until the last leg where it becomes exciting again. Hold onto this thought though for the next part.Its fun. It really is a mix of persona and SMT. Taking the best of both parts and mixing it neatly. Its definitely more accessible than Persona because of the lack of monster collecting and fusion stuff. So if you're into that, you might find its not as in depth. But the archtype system that takes place of that is a much easier way to digest as its more straight forward in presentation. Trying different classes and being able to mix abilities is really fun. I love the Overworld exploring and fighting, a very much needed QoL. I will say that the dungeon layouts are pretty to look at but that's about it. I very much liked the vertical aspect that the Persona games had more like in P5. There definitely is a lull in each section as the gameplay loop is: story -> dungeon  and repeat, but that is nothing new here as previous entries have the same issue. But I think because of the more shallow combat where it relates to type coverage, etc it gets a bit boring at the last quarter where the gameplay changes a bit again. But ultimately the game doesn't throw any new mechanics at you after the 30-40 hour mark. In some instances, you don't ever see some mechanics until the end.Think of a typical Japanese game dev studio and that is what the graphics is. It is very pretty and stylized. It definitely will hold up over a decade easily. But the issue is with performance. Performance is okay, but it definitely could be more optimized and I hope the team will take the time to learn to code effectively with their engine.Metaphor is definitely in the top 5 games I've played this year. It's really between this and Like a Dragon Infinite Wealth as far as RPGs go. You might ask why not FF7R? I think that game has some not fun open world/map things that detracted from the overall game. Its more disappointing than anything given the budget of that game. Where as LAD IW and Metaphor both have very engaging side content.-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Sega cleaned up their act from LAD IW earlier this year. No paywalls or weird dlc stuff.So far, this is to me GOTY. LAD IW would be if not for the weird stuff Sega did with the release.Will update once I'm done with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: So far I'm loving this game.If you love Atlus' SMT and Persona RPG series, Metaphor Refantazio will be right up your alley.Combat:Combat is a combination of mainline SMT and Persona 5.Exploiting weaknesses gains press turns, missing/being nulled/repelled loses press turns.There is also the ability to attack enemies in the field which is a bit of an evolution of P5's ambush mechanic, except it allows you to instantly kill enemies that are a few levels below you, or starts you with advantage if enemies are similar/higher level.Story:Story is interesting and refreshingly a departure from the usual setting of SMT/Persona.The game is set in a fantasy world with many different "tribes" (races) of people. There are strong themes of discrimination and social injustice at play. Characters are generic at face value, though the story does play with the idea of "archetypes" (which incidentally are this game's answer to personas), so this is likely intentional. I strongly suspect that the characters will develop and reveal greater depth and complexity as the story continues and I develop my "bonds" (read: Social links/confidants) with them. In short, it's a tried and true foundation supporting a more complex unfolding story.Gameplay:The gameplay loop will be very familiar to Persona fans. Each day has a certain number of time slots that you can choose to spend developing relationships to improve your Archetypes, partaking in activities that will improve your "kingly qualities" (social stats) to unlock new opportunities, or challenging the current dungeon with a view to clearing it before the deadline. Honestly it's almost identical to P5 so if you love that, you'll love this. If you hate the Persona series, you almost certainly won't like this.Graphics:Looks nice and art direction is well done with a cross between anime and storybook-style visuals.Don't expect amazing 3D realistic graphics or anything like God of War or Ghost of Tsushima, that's not what we're here for.Ticks all the usual boxes like having all the major 16:9 resolutions up to and including 4k with proper scaling, etc.Audio:Music composed by Shoji Meguro, one of Japanese gaming's greatest musical geniuses.I feel there's very strong SMT: Strange Journey influences with lots of vocalisations and drums, and an overall grim but triumphant vibe underscoring the party's struggle.Polish:There were some issues in the demo that appear to have been addressed in the full version.Audio volume has been corrected (was too quiet) and graphical performance has apparently been fixed (although I didn't have any issues with RTX 3080 + i5-12600KF system).Only thing I consider missing is support for non-16:9 resolutions like 21:9 ultrawide. When played on an ultrawide monitor, the picture will be pillar-boxed with black bars on the sides. Unsurprising though, almost all Japanese PC games do this.Conclusion:I recommend this game to anybody who loves other Atlus games, especially the Persona series.I also recommend it to anybody who enjoys a good RPG with engaging combat.I don't recommend this game to those who only enjoy online multiplayer games. This won't change your mind.

_childDocuments_.review: This game to me, as a persona enjoyer, is a 6/10~ maybe a 6.5/10~ I really wish I could call it a 10/10 Masterpiece Goty-type game like all the other people reviewing the game are doing, but it just isn't. ill start with a few things i like about the game. The music and the menu designs are on point and very stylish in my opinion. Also the JP voice acting is amazing as is expected since most games from ATLUS usually have good VA's working on them. Sadly every other aspect of the game is rather MID. What Metaphor Re;Fantazio really is, is an above-average JRPG that takes ideas from SMT and Persona but does neither well. The story in and of itself is fine—not horrible but not genre-defining either. And the characters themselves aren't that interesting; if I were being honest, I'd say they are subpar. Some of the characters' stories do tug on the heartstrings a bit. But I feel like they aren't that special compared to the other characters I've seen in games like Persona 3, Persona 4, and Persona 5.   Now let's talk about my biggest issue with the game by far. The combat, I'm going to be brutally honest it’s the worst I've ever experienced in an ATLUS game to date. It's needlessly clunky, unintuitive, and slow-paced. Its largest drawback is being unable to change your "archetype" mid-battle. For instance, I went into a battle early game (10-25 hours in) not knowing my opponent's weakness (I'm not using a guide), and all my archetypes did not deal any damage. So you then have three choices 1 fight it out (somehow), 2 restart from the beginning, or 3 just alt-f4 and restart at the previous save game, most of the time you are going to be choosing option 3 quite alot. That is horrid, why can't I just change my archetype mid-battle? It's such a crap system I don't know why they would remove perfectly working battle features from the previous games. Just to come out with this half-baked system that's frankly annoying and frustrating, to say the least. Now Later on in the game, it gets bearable around the 40~60-hour mark; since your party is much larger than it was at the beginning, you can switch people out mid-battle instead of having to alt-f4 and switch out your archetypes.  Another peeve of mine is the constant AOE attacks the bosses of the game throw at you that are bound to hit a weakness on one of the party members and then in turn give the boss more actions to destroy your team. Not only that, but buffs are basically useless the boss will just give itself 2-4 turns with their BS ability. Then it will remove all the buffs you had just put on your team and then buff itself now wasting one of your precious 4 turns to debuff the boss so you can kill it faster and it just keeps repeating over and over ugh. Every fight feels so drawn out and I'm sitting there thinking did the people over at ATLUS seriously play this and think it was fun? (Tldr; combat is very awful early game and it’s bearable late game. ) Lastly, I know ATLUS could have done a way better job with Metaphor: ReFantazio, since the best minds over at ATLUS had worked on it for many YEARS. You know the people who worked on various other successful series (ie Persona, and SMT),. Just pick it up on a sale if you really want to play this game its not worth 70 dollars. And hey I mean this isn't the worst ATLUS game by any measure, but it certainly is not the best I'd give it a solid 6.5/10, sadly this game just doesn't stack up against the likes of P3, P4, and P5, or SMT 3 Nocturne.
