_childDocuments_.review: Mild story spoilers. I won't get into specifics, but I will vaguely talk about the structure of the plot. Ignore the playtime, I had the game on pause in the background a lot. My first playthrough on hard took about 58 hours to finish while 100%ing all the content available. Minimal grinding.The story is overall better paced. The only poorly paced part is a sequence at the start of the third act that felt extremely rushed, as multiple twists are introduced and resolved in the same hour. It was extremely noticable, but the rest of the story was paced well. Every arc is building towards an ultimate, concrete goal and makes logical sense.I like the setting quite a bit. This is a game that's focused on the politics, and the politics in this fantasy world are fairly interesting, with a bunch of different viewpoints that all have a good reason to exist. It's also not afraid to point out that the idealistic endeavors of the party almost definitely won't play out the way they want it to, which is one more degree of nuance than most games have these days.The writing for the party members you get are decent. Instead of having a Haru situation where the last party member gets almost no screen time, the writers instead took cues from how P4 handled Naoto by having the last party member appear throughout the story. I found them to have the most interesting arc overall. However, every other member runs into the problem P5 had where they don't really do that much after their recruitment arc and don't have that much interparty banter. There are multiple moments where I found them sitting right next to each other in the same room, not looking at each other and not really talking. This is a huge missed opportunity, especially since you can listen to random NPCs talking to each other.The social links got compressed down to 8 levels, and that also makes them better paced. There aren't really any social link levels like in P5 where pretty much nothing happens. I did notice a trend where too many of the social links rely on "randomly running into somebody from their past" as a hook, which felt repetitive. Each social link also serves a double purpose, where they don't only advance the general themes of the game, but also help build the world. There are pretty important details you'll be missing if you skip out on these social links.Now to the gameplay. This is where most of the cons I have about this game comes from. On paper, I really like it. There are a lot of systems at play that incentivize strategic team building. Synthesis abilities depend on your party comp, enemies in dungeons are all weak to different things, and a good comp and a bad comp truly have a massive difference in effectiveness. The classes are like Fire Emblem, where they max out at level 20 and you need to get certain levels in other classes to promote, which is a progression system I find more fun than traditional Persona/SMT where you swap out your demons every few levels. Some of these classes also have gimmicks that I find way more fun than anything in their previous games.On top of that, two of the classes have an interesting meta progression where you have to craft items to augment their effectiveness. However, the final promotion of one of these classes completely ignores this mechanic (which is odd) and the other class flat out doesn't need the gimmick at all to be effective.However, the strategic element of the game is let down by too many things. The balancing, for one. There are classes that are not only blatantly better than the others, but are so much better that there's little incentive to ever touch the other classes. Why would you use a class that takes 50 mp to clear a mob when you could just run another class that can oneshot the same mob with no resource cost? Another thing is that, for whatever reason, the first three party members you get are all physical damage focused, which is just flat out weird, since the MC's best class choices are also physical focused. Another thing is how important party comps are. Much like in P5S, if you go into a boss with the wrong party setup, you quickly realize it is either impossible or will take far, far too long. Just like in that game, the only options you have are to let the boss kill you or restart the game, as there's no quick restart button that also lets you change your composition around. It's even more important in this game, as the late game bosses get very powerful very fast, and if you don't have the tools to deal with them, it's functionally impossible.Dungeon crawling is pretty lame. You pretty much just run towards the fog of war and you're done exploring. They're all extremely linear, don't have many puzzles, and lack the flair that at least made P5's dungeons fun to look at. The upside here, however, is that there are at least quite a number of optional dungeons, which still gives the game more variety than Mementos or Tartarus.If this game ever gets a sequel, I hope they iron down these flaws as I really do think the game would be extremely fun if it worked as intended. As it stands, there's too many issues for me to really love it.The graphics are flat out not good. The art style saves it a bit (I particular like scratch effect the shadows in the game have), but there's no getting around the fact that the textures all look terrible. Worse than that, the dungeons are so bog standard fantasy that there's nothing to distract you from the fact that the rock textures in the cave or the bricks in the church all look really terrible. Persona 5's textures were bad, but again, had the flair to let you ignore them.Furthermore, the enemy design. You probably heard of all the chatter of how they were designed after Hieronymus Bosch paintings. Well, I'm sorry to say that those enemies are extremely rare. Those ones in the steam store page that look ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome? They're pretty much isolated to the first fifteen or so hours of teh game. They largely disappear from then on. The ones that show up serve as generic dungeon enemies, and are way less interesting to look at. Everything else is pretty much just standard fantasy with very little to distinguish them from every other version of their species.The soundtrack is overall very good, but if it wasn't for the Esperanto chanting, it would really come across as standard orchestral fantasy. I don't really see this game having permanent brain worms like Persona does.Overall, had a good time. But the downsides aren't really small.

_childDocuments_.review: Most Persona fans will love this game. The game has much less downtime, with fewer dates where you can't do anything but save your game and go to sleep. The antagonist is more fleshed out than the 3/4/5 trilogy (only thr P5 Royal antagonist is better imo), the team feels more like a cohesive unit when compared to the phantom thieves in p5 (arguably better than SEES and Investigation Team in p4 also). Combat is very fun, with difficult bosses (on hard mode), even when you are over-leveled. You need to actually plan out an approach to a boss battle, especially late-game. The rewind mode is a good QoL feature that allows you to restart a battle as many time as you want (even on hard). While some might think that's cheating, I'd compare this to having a site of grace right before a boss in Elden Ring, you just skip the part where you die and go through the fog again. Allowing your teammates to equip any class is also a great improvement over Persona, and Archetypes are a good change of pace vs Persona fusions.A couple of downsides: Enemy and level designs in the optional areas are meh, pretty standard fantasy stuff. Music, while great, isn't something I'd put on my playlist in the car with other people listening along. Also wished the 2D anime cutscenes are in-engine instead, since the quality of those cutscenes are pretty basic, while the in-engine ones allow for more fluid movements.

_childDocuments_.review: Metaphor: Refantazio is a captivating RPG that delves deep into the realm of archetypes, offering a rich and engaging narrative. The game's story is a captivating blend of fantasy and philosophy, exploring the nature of identity and the power of belief. The characters, each embodying a unique archetype, are well-developed and memorable, drawing the player into their world.The game's true strength lies in its innovative archetype system. By allowing players to customize their characters' abilities and playstyles based on various archetypes, Refantazio offers a level of depth and personalization that is truly impressive. This system encourages experimentation and strategic thinking, adding a layer of complexity to the combat and exploration.However, the game's otherwise strong foundation is undermined by a noticeable grind towards the end. This sudden shift in pacing disrupts the flow of the narrative and diminishes the impact of the buildup. While the final parts of the game are still enjoyable, the grind feels unnecessary and detracts from the overall experience.Despite this flaw, Metaphor: Refantazio remains a compelling RPG that offers a unique and thought-provoking adventure. Its strong narrative, well-developed characters, and innovative archetype system make it a must-play for fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I pretty much never replay games, even shorter ones. This is an 80+ hour RPG (150+ with my playstyle) and I wanna replay it immediately. The cast and the characters easily stole the show for me, but I gotta commend the gameplay and especially the early story pacing. Any moment I felt like the story was getting predictable / the gameplay was falling into a lull, it changed up something major and kept me on my toes. While the last 2 months or so suffer quite a bit from dumping too much on you all at once with no room to breathe, the game already had me so hooked it didn't ruin the experience for me. As for the gameplay, I remember hearing about the class system from a trailer I skimmed forever ago, and I thought it sounded complicated / too much to juggle, but it was extremely easy to grasp since it let's you slowly dip your toes into the different classes, and they all felt like they served unique purposes so it was worth checking every class out.Outside of the endgame pacing, my only issue is the fact that there isn't any official merch of the final party member yet, they came out of nowhere and stole my heart and I need a plushie of them STAT.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm pretty mixed on this game.  While the combat is fun, to an extent, it is essentially persona 5 with some minuscule changes.  And that's not a bad thing.  The bad thing, however, is that Atlus is still riding off their popularity of persona 5 without trying to improve.  Atlus games, well, JRPGs in general, all have a similar flaw:  terrible writing and generic plots.  Atlus does a good job having a pretty aesthetic alongside a unique mechanic that people tend to enjoy.  That being said, they can't completely hide the poor dialogue, overuse of terrible npc animations and useless conversations to pad game time, and cringe storytelling at times.  So, if you just enjoy atlus games, you'll enjoy this.  Just remember there is a reason JRPGs aren't really popular anymore, and it's because nobody tries to make them good.  Supporting this reinforces Atlus that we don't want them to do better, and that's detrimental to future games.  Make your own decision at the end of the day, but this conversation really needs to be had at some point.

_childDocuments_.review: Great combat and timekeeping gameplay, and the the music is pretty good.But the characters - especially the player character - just feel boring. _childDocuments_.review: I'ved dumped so much of my time into this game and I don't think I've enjoyed playing it since hour 20 or so. I was lured into buying the game by how various review sites and gaming podcasts described the premise: You're in a race against time with a maelevolent but charismatic duke to win the hearts and minds of the people. The premise sounded fresh. However, the game does not live up to its elevator pitch.This game is a Skinner box: a game with casino-like mechanics that train players to pull the lever over and over to get to the next level, to earn the next ability you're never going to bother using, to get the next archetype that isn't practical, etc. Specifically, you'll find yourself spanking (one-shotting) enemies in the field as you run from one end of the dungeon to the other, trying to master your archetypes, since it might be another week or so before you explore another dungeon. Sometimes there are crystals that spawn enemies and make the process slightly faster, but not usually. If the minute-to-minute gameplay was fun, all of the leveling and FOMO would be worth it. But most of the game is actually spent planning around "bond" events with party members and NPCs. These visual novel-esque events happen in very cheap-looking pocket dimensions as that character deals with some personal beef that usually isn't very interesting. Your only input as a player during these dialogs is to choose how enthusiastically you want to *agree* (usually) with what the other character is droning on about. Only a handful of major cities are explorable; towns and outposts are just shop menus. Landmarks are just (pretty) vignettes were more character exposition happens. 90% of dungeons are modular and boring. This last part is especially unforgivable because this is a JRPG, where adventuring is supposed to be a big part of the experience.I'm very disappointed that a game with such a hopeful message and fresh concept has such mediocre dungeon design and undervalues exploration and experimentation.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best JRPG games I have ever played, the overworld combat with trash enemies makes grinding a level or two real quick feel less like a slog. The day system isnt too strict or anything so I have felt the freedom to do side missions in between the quest deadlines, very fun highly recommend if you enjoy turn based combat.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is quite similar to Persona's design-wise but also a big step up. Very well balanced pacing, nice story with interesting twists, engaging character progress, more depth to the combat. The downsides are that you don't have romancing options in social links, and a bit dated graphics, which is a bit compensated via astonishing visual designs.
_childDocuments_.name: Metaphor: ReFantazio

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game! It has an incredible art style and music, along with a story that puts a great twist on modern fantasy and features strong characters. The combat and gameplay will feel very familiar to fans of the Persona series, with some interesting changes. It is really nice to see this formula applied to a setting outside of high school Japan. One nice change, in my opinion, is that social links always advance to the next rank without requiring extra hangouts or gifts to progress.Every character is a Wild Card like the Fool, which means the possibilities can be endless. To a certain extent, you can mix and match abilities, but for the most part, characters have logical paths they should follow. Still, there is a lot of customization you can do for your party...until you hit the endgame. At that point, certain builds are just better than others. While not strictly required, these optimized builds will save you from breaking your controller in frustration when fighting bosses.The game does get pretty grindy, though there are ways to offset this. This grind can make endgame can feel like a slog. Despite that, I clocked 70 hours of actual game time on normal difficulty, and I still highly recommend the game while acknowledging its flaws.Also, yeah, the racism theme is brought up so often that it gets annoying, but there’s a big payoff with the endgame reveals on this topic.

_childDocuments_.review: Person: "What if we took a huge fantasy rpg and set it in the real world?"Metaphor: "What if we took a Persona game and set it in a fantasy world?"Now take the gameplay from Persona, add the job system from Final Fantasy, then the combat system from Chrono Trigger. If you understand what any of that means then this game is probably for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredible. I don't even typically like turn-based games, I get bored of them fast, but I could not stop until I had 100% achievements in this game. _childDocuments_.review: I've completed the game on hard difficulty (all followers, sidequests, optional bosses, maxed all archetypes on protagonist) and can confidently say that this game is a peak JRPG combining the greatest aspects of Atlus' Persona and SMT series.- SMT's Press-Turn combat system is used in this game instead of Persona's One More system, and I just vastly prefer Press-Turn. The game is also a lot harder than your typical Persona game but was never quite as hard as SMT, and engaging with the action component of the combat is crucial because enemy ambushes can be brutal. The game also shakes it up a bit by adding Synthesis skills where you combine 2+ people's turns and consume multiple turns at once for a powerful attack.- In typical Atlus fashion, the UI art, character portraits, animated cutscenes, and OST are phenomenal. - The game's pacing is MUCH better than your typical Persona game. You'll see from a lot of these reviews that the average play times range from 60-80 hours whereas pretty much everyone breaks the 100 hour mark with Persona, but that's not to its detriment. Deadlines are a lot more concise and the game tells such a large story within only 4.5-ish playable months compared to the 10+ seen in Persona games. Followers (Social Link/Confidant equivalent) max out at rank 8 rather than 10, and the dialogue choices don't influence your bond level. You're guaranteed to rank up whenever you meet, and you don't need to spend as much time with this system anymore.- The game's structure feels a lot less formulaic than Persona games. Persona's story arcs were very clearly defined and generally always followed a near identical formula in terms of free days, when a party member would join, the size of the dungeon, etc. Metaphor is more willing to shake up when/if someone joins (could be at the start/middle/end of an arc) and not all dungeons are necessarily massive labyrinths full of enemies and loot if the plot doesn't need something of that nature. The deadline lengths vary a lot more and they don't arbitrarily slap on 20 or so days of free time if the plot demands more urgency.- You can pretty easily knock out all Followers, side quests, and side dungeons on your first playthrough. You can level your Royal Virtues (social stats) on the gauntlet runner while travelling to new areas, and they level pretty quickly. You're given the entire final month of the game to just grind out whatever is left before the final dungeon with no story interruption. - There are a lot of side-dungeons, requests, and optional bosses to fight. This made me enjoy the free periods a lot more because there was a lot more variety compared to Persona games where you just click through dialogue boxes for several hours to level social links or social stats. Travelling to these side dungeons requires planning out travel time and routes which added a fun new dimension to free calendar periods. - The new Archetype system (classes) are a unique way of shaking up the SMT/Persona formula. I liked that they were tied to the Followers which made the social stuff a lot more exciting to engage with, and anticipating new archetypes overall was a lot of fun compared to a typical SMT/Persona game where you're basically just replacing demons of each element with stronger variants and can expect a lot of reused designs. Also, upon maxing out a class, you get an EXP consumable item for every 1000 class EXP you get which allows you to level other classes without needing to play them.- I found the story and characters to be a lot more compelling than any Atlus game to date, and I found that this game did a great job with fixing Persona's critical problem of letting characters devolve into Flanderized cardboard cut-outs when their respective arc ends. Characters maintain relevance and have genuine reason to join the party, and the game maintains a much tighter cast. The game keeps a tight focus on Louis as the antagonist which greatly fleshes him out compared to Atlus' typical eleventh-hour villains. - The action combat is pretty easy but also feels pretty clunky. Your equipped Archetype dictates your moveset, and some have really long animation locks with their attacks. You're also only allowed to control the protagonist on the field which limits your moveset even further to the class that he's using. The system also felt a bit imbalanced in that you can insta-kill enemies (without turn-based mode) when you're 3 levels above, but being 3 levels above on Hard by no means allows you to just demolish foes in turn-based combat. I feel like they made it a bit too easy to bypass strong enemies because of this, and I accidentally breezed through some side dungeons without noticing.- The Archetype system was limiting at times. You need to buy new Archetypes and skills (to make them inheritable for other classes) with a currency called Magla, and early on, it can be a bit hard to come by and may lock you into giving one class to only one character if you plan on maxing it out any time soon. Having the inheritance slots tied to Follower links sometimes inhibited me from trying new classes because some classes are very gimmicky (like only having debuffs or heals) and they need a lot of slots to be viable in combat, so these classes just became fodder to grab a few skills from. - The side content is pretty low quality. Despite the number of side dungeons, they're all re-skins of 3 or 4 basic dungeon types with different enemies and layouts. It's not only repetitive from a game play standpoint, but I feel like it hurts world building. The game already has so few towns you visit, and they keep TELLING you all this lore and geography about the regions, but you never get to explore the town outskirts or nearby wilds and see any of that. All the side dungeons look identical which creates this major disconnect (seriously, you'll be in a tropical island and there's no beach-type field or dungeon, it's just more caves and towers you blink to from a menu). All of the side towns you can visit are just a single photo with an immediate shop prompt in visual novel style, and they cannot be explored. The landmarks you visit on the way to objectives are 2D images with the 3D character models standing on them sort of like a pre-rendered background in a PS1 game, and they're a bit jarring to look at.- The party member distribution is a bit imbalanced. A lot of people skew towards building the MC as a magic user because the first 3 party members you get are physical/support oriented, and there's NO WAY to reset your attribute points from what I can tell, so you get shoehorned and locked into this build early on. Physical builds (and hybrids later down the line) are still totally viable, you just wont have a powerful, dedicated caster for very long if you don't make the MC a mage.- I didn't personally mind this at all but as a fair point of warning, the game has pretty low graphical fidelity even compared to other JRPGs. The textures are embarrassingly bad at times, and the 3D models have little to no facial animation. It's pretty comparable to Persona 5, but P5 knew to keep the camera angles zoomed out and draw attention to the character portraits, and it also has smaller, corridor-like spaces so the texture quality was less noticeable. Metaphor tends to zoom in on characters during cutscenes and has large open areas which expose some really bad floor/wall/clothing textures.

_childDocuments_.review: For everyone who was bummed that this wasn't Persona 6, I definitely think this is more than a consolation prize. I could easily see Metaphor being its own franchise in the Atlus universe that easily compares to what we've seen from SMT and Persona. It's familiar in a lot of ways that we know and love, but it manages to approach things differently just enough to carve out its own existence among those games.To be honest, I do like that it takes what I like about Persona and SMT and applies it to a completely unique world because I do find myself tiring of "angsty teenagers in japan" as a recurring setting, so this is definitely a breath of fresh air for people who wanted something substantial without immersing yourself in teen friend group dynamics. I know some people will miss that element, but chances are high that we'll get a new Persona sometime soon as well.

_childDocuments_.review: This might be one of the best games I've played in a decade.  It's the culmination of this team's games over the course of decades.  I've long wanted a game that got away from the tropes of high school protagonists, and while the character isn't much older, the world is.  It's lived in, and clearly has plenty of thought put into it.  The fact that your connections aren't based on 'best waifu' and instead on meaningful connections and ways to really enhance not just the world, but that character and flesh them out, is welcome.  I love the Persona games, but by the time I finished 5, I was long over the idea that it was basically a harem collector and the guys are just all buds.The backdrop of this game, and also getting away from a modern Tokyo is also well recieved by me.  Final Fantasy, and Dragon Quest have long felt like the only 'high end' jRPG style games with budgets that weren't based in some sort of modern setting, and I'm glad that finally Atlus/Sega has entered the foray. There's too much to mention without spoiling things, but I'll say that the 80ish hours I put into this were not a slog.  Everything was with a purpose and while I've sometimes seen it all coming a mile away, even though some of this games twists aren't super world bending, I appreciated the swings they took.I really hope with a sequel they really drill into some of the themes here and not be afraid.  I don't want them to go back to high schools and waifus, but continue on some more adult oriented, and higher level drama and intrigue.  Also, the character design is amazing, and the guantlet runners are one of the cooler ideas I've seen for transportation in a game.It's worth the price of admission, and yes, I'll admit, the lack of fully voice acted everything can sting a little -- I didn't mind reading two or three novels worth of words and emotions over my time.  I didn't even get to the job system which is also just excellent.  Give it a shot.  I really think it's worth it if you like jRPGs as a whole.

_childDocuments_.review: The review below is the most pretentious thing I've ever written, if you don't want to readMETAPHOR: REFANTAZIO IS GAME OF THE YEAR, POSSIBLY THE DECADEIf you would like to read, go on aheadIgnore my hours played, I spent much of my time playing Metaphor: Refantazio offline because my internet was knocked out after a hurricane. I write this with heavy heart, as I have finished the game less than an hour ago, but I wallow not because the game is over, but because it is not but a game. I love every character in this game, the protagonists, the antagonists, all of them. If I could I would watch movies and read books about these characters, not about their journey in the game, but about what they do after the story ends. I have played persona 4, 5, and 3, and I can say that Metaphor Refantazio has objectively better game play. And I believe the story of Metaphor is subjectively better than those mentioned, not because they are bad, but because this is good. There are morals to the story of the persona games, but they are lofty and detached, "Giving control of humanity to an evil god is bad" of course it is. Metaphor: Refantazio seeks to convey a message grounded in reality, although set in fantasy. I will not share this myself because it isn't my place to do so. But I believe that if everyone thought the way I think right now, the world may be a better place.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best modern JRPGs out there. The story is extremely interesting, the characters are lovable, there's a good mix of dark and comedic tones, it has the best battle system Atlus has ever created in my opinion, it's got a ton of VARIED content, it opens new and worthwhile activities up consistently, the cities look amazing and talking to every NPC in them is honestly worth doing, and the game isn't afraid to be a bit controversial in the topics it showcases or scenarios it makes the player work through. I like it better than SMT V and it's right up there with Persona 5 for me as well, maybe even nearly passing it but I'm too early in my playthrough to tell just yet. _childDocuments_.review: Metaphor: ReFantazio blew me away. The art, music, characters, voice acting, and story are all stunning, with so much care put into every detail. The unique accents they gave to different characters really brought the world to life, and the English dub is phenomenal!As a Persona fan, I’d been looking forward to this for ages, especially since the creators behind Persona 3, 4, and 5 were involved. It doesn’t disappoint. While this game stands solidly on its own, you can really feel how Atlus took what they’ve learned from Persona, Shin Megami Tensei, Devil Summoner, Soul Hackers, and other games, blending elements from each into something unique.For fans of Persona, there’s a lot to enjoy here, from the familiar calendar system to battle mechanics. But it still has its own identity, like a sibling to those series that’s doing its own thing while giving us some of those familiar vibes.If you’re already a fan of Atlus, this game is a must-play. And if you’re new to this type of RPG, it’s easy to dive into, especially if you’re into fantasy. I’d highly recommend it, and I can’t wait to start a New Game Plus!

_childDocuments_.review: In my opinion, Metaphor: ReFantazio in the end actually ended up being a "fantasy Persona", for all the good and bad that might entail. As someone who isn't a fan of the Persona formula, I'm mainly writing this review from that perspective. Which resulted in me tagging this review as negative, since I'll mostly be mentioning the reasons I didn't really enjoy the experience, and those originate from it being too much like Persona.Even if I didn't have high expectations for this part, I was overall disappointed with the gameplay, talking mainly about the combat side of it. The Persona game that I actually finished was Persona 4 Golden, despite the fact that I kinda hated the combat system. And even though Metaphor has been released 16 years later, there is not much innovation in regards to the base formula. The combat to me still seems like a very basic "weakness shopping list simulator", where 95 % of the battle is simply preparing the correct builds before an encounter like going through a checklist, with very little actual strategy during the encounter itself. And if you build a party around implanting weaknesses, you just beat almost every single encounter in the game. I did that early game and every boss fight ended up being almost the exact same sequence of moves where the boss got annihilated, unless it had some extra gimmick that broke that setup.Non-boss fights are even worse, as they mostly boil down to whether you ambush the enemy or they ambush you, either way the ambusing side facerolls the ambushed one. Every single encounter again ends up being the repetition of the same moves over and over, except this time you actually try to conserve your mana. I've come to loathe this type of combat system as you end up doing the same sequences of moves over and over for 70 hours. It's just simply too binary for me, based on your build you either obliterate the enemy, or the other way around, with no room for anything more interesting.But like I said, I know Persona and its combat system, so I wasn't expecting a whole lot anyway from the gameplay.The real disappointment for me however was the story side of the game.The plot, while it introduces some unique concepts at the start, ends up being played pretty much by the book the further you progress. I can't say I found it boring, but even though it didn't disappoint me, I certainly won't remember it years, or even months down the line compared to my favorites in the genre.The setting seems unique at first, but I think that's heavily carried by the art direction, both the visual and the audio parts. If you were to actually just write down the lore of Metaphor's world, you'd end up with a description of a pretty generic fantasy. There is at least one fun reveal thrown into the mix, but nothing you haven't seen before if you've experienced at least a few fantasy stories like this.But I was still satisfied with the plot and setting. The actual major disappointment that single-handedly shaped my overall view of the game are the characters. For me they. Are. Just. So. Bland.Starting with the protagonist being the biggest offender. I was happy to hear that finally a Persona like game is going to have a voiced protagonist, and we might get away from the bland voiceless self-inserts. Except it's still a bland self-insert, just voiced. The end. You might as well replace him with a mannequin. Or a wall.The main party are mostly comprised of pretty stereotypical fantasy archetypes, especially the members that you get early and spend the most time with. Which wouldn't necessarily be that bad, if there were at least some quirks or significant developments sprinkled in there. But pretty much the peak of "unique traits" is that one of the characters is really into food. And the other characters comment on that, often. The end.No problem, we can still salvage that with some fun dynamics. But there are none. The end. The main group barely feels like a group, as most of the times they interact with each other, they are just discussing the most recent plot point. Except for a few very specific instances that were perhaps my favorite moments of the whole experience. The reason for that is that most of their interactions are only one-on-one with the protagonist. Considering the MC is just a walking vegetable when it comes to personality, they might as well just be talking to a wall. So instead of a fun main group of characters, you end up with a bunch of individual archetypes talking to themselves with barely any fun dialogue among each other. So the dialogues, while extremely well localized, feel kinda empty and bland when you consider their subject matter.TLDR: If you're a Persona fan, this review wasn't really for you, as you'll likely still enjoy Metaphor a lot, it might even become your favorite. But if you're not really into the Persona formula, I advise trying out the demo first or waiting for a significant sale. Because Metaphor, in my opinion, does absolutely nothing different enough to change your opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has great music and character designs. Everything else is far worse than any other atlus game. This game has worse visuals than SMTV which is a Switch game. The enemy models are weirdly chunky and every texture looks like it was made for 480p.Persona 4, a game actually made for 480p, has crisper textures when emulated than this garbage.The architype designs are boring and the animations for their synargy moves are clunky and weak. The combat system is the worst of any RPG I've experienced in my life. Get lucky with the right architype loadout or be prepared to to fight for 50 turns while doing barely any damage.Or just die (you can't quit or use any setting menu during combot so you have to wait for death) and then switch to 3 counter picks for the enemy and melt them without any challenge.I'd say this game has poor balance but that would imply it has any balance.The story is ok but a few dungeons in and still absolute surface level with every character so far. Pretty poorly paced in that regard.Cannot for the life of me understand the positive reception for this game, maybe this year is really just that thin on big titles. I was very much looking forward to this dev trying something different again since I really enjoyed Catherine but this game is a massive disappointment.Go buy the Dragon Quest 3 remake or literally anything else.

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing the game, I can safely say that I thoroughly enjoyed it. Metaphor Refantazio easily has the qualities of a game of the year. To be more precise, it is in every sense, a triple A JRPG, with a very interesting plot, great voice acting (played in Japanese audio) and incredible animations. The gameplay  very much resembles the Persona series of course, though slightly modified, which makes it fresh, yet neither better or worse in my opinion. What I mostly feel the need to highlight though as its strongest asset is the impeccable writing, in all regards. It has very good narration, dialogues, character depth, basically everything, all while other games in 2024 seriously struggle with their own writing, even other Atlus games like SMTV. It really had gotten to a point where I was utterly disappointed by gaming as a medium for wholesome experiences, because of the lazy and subpar story - telling, amply thrown into various titles, with popular examples being Dragon Age: The Veilguard, Throne and Liberty, or even Diablo's new expansion. I won't even get into smaller titles. So yes, if you want to play a quality game, I would highly  recommend this one, since it felt refreshing and "un-dumbing" in some sense. Of course, Metaphor isn't completely without any shortcomings. Personally I found the beginning to be a bit slow, the dungeons environments kind of repeatable, and I generally felt that they didn't do everything required in terms of quality of life features. I even encountered a minor bug, where some mobs are supposed to be patrolling around an area, but they got stuck trying to move against one another. I would also have preferred if they had gotten a bit deeper in the main antagonists backstory and maybe expand on him during the final fights. Yet, this is an easy 9/10 overall and the music is also very good.
_childDocuments_.name: Metaphor: ReFantazio

_childDocuments_.review: Based purely on the first few hours, Atlus has knocked it out of the park. While the foundation of the game clearly has underpinnings in Persona (and perhaps slightly less so SMT), the new fantasy setting is very refreshing and the story captivating. The gameplay is also an excellent fusion of persona and SMT's systems, likely biased toward SMT's press turn. In terms of difficulty, so far I would say it is harder than the average Persona experience but far easier than SMT.  I have not personally run into any performance issues testing on both a high end machine (RTX 4090 at 4K, rendering at 200%) and a laptop (laptop RTX 4060 at 1440p rendering at 100%).  The one issue that I have noticed is that if you choose to play with a controller on PC, your thumbstick inputs are translated to 8 directional inputs (as if you were playing with WASD), as opposed to the full 360 movement that you would get with a controller on console. I am hoping Atlus patches this, as it can be a bit distracting at times once you notice it.EDIT: I have since completed the game, and the high quality of the first few hours and performance has persisted throughout. This is undoubtedly one of Atlus' finest works, both in terms of story and gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Plays and looks great on Steam Deck set to normal quality and 60 fpsThis is an excellent game which is NOT Persona 6. In M:RF you'll find all the usual Atlus game systems taken to the next level along with some innovative changes, an instantly gripping political drama with a beautiful medieval fantasy backdrop, and enemies that could have been plucked from Lewis Carroll's nightmares. The story has a larger scope than the Persona series and deals more directly with societal issues. Unlike the Persona series with it's more noir tales where no good deed goes unpunished and the protagonist is forced into his role. In those stories there is no hero, only a person who does what he must to restore normalcy. here we have a protagonist who has chosen to take on the hero's journey and actively seeks to change the whole of society. The journey is undertaken out of a sense of loyalty and love for a friend who accepted the protagonist for who he is. A friend who made the protagonist believe that a better future for everyone was possible. With this game we play the role of an active participant rather than a pawn as was the case with previous games. I would say it is more adult story than other Atlus games.

_childDocuments_.review: I Don't often take time to write reviews but i have to say this game is worth the time spent. I Got it as a demo & Played it to death because it was just so good. I've played games like persona and Yakuza etc but this game just hits differently in some weird way. If i could briefly sum it up as to why it hits different i would say it was like being a kid again playing Something that just hits all the right spots in gaming from look, to feel, to Story and unique concepts. I'm 28 and gamed in the womb i swear lol and recently the last 2 years at the least games have just fallen dry & Repetitive. everything online, same game just new reskins or just Flops by Developers who seem to hate there jobs. with a few exceptions of course like Wukong, Ghost of Tsushima maybe Ronin in some ways etc. But This Game just Hits from the moment you get in. Its like Being whisked away in an isekai variation (i play with Japanese VA). As of 13 hours and even in the many hours in the demo i haven't yet come across any downsides. I feel like the time keeping and planning you get in persona games is slightly better and more thought out in this game which can make it seem Easier to manage but a screw up could set you back adding a level of challenge that pushes you to think a bit but at the same time not so much as to ruin your Overall experience. The Story so far is well written and the monster concepts and ideas actually goes hard. The Human concept really just pushed the imagination. As a writer of fantasy i Cant find faults and i really think they outdid themselves with the game. If anything i would say there are bits where your like... "wow this is harder than it should be" or "why is this like this" and think of these bits as cons but then realise you missed a step or Didn't discover an easier way and then you realise its not the games fault but your own for not taking time to truly Immerse yourself & Learn what the game has to offer. _childDocuments_.review: Good things about the game:-Great Graphics-Beautiful cutscenes-Deep story- Challenging combat that requires thinking ahead and planningReasons I wouldn't recommend it:30% of game time is just cutscenes or story.Combat (at least on hard mode) is so extremely challenging that even if you level well you might still get hard stuck on early bosses.And my biggest gripe, the reason I ultimately don't recommend it, is that most quests have a deadline. The game functions on a system where you can improve stats and relationships that all cost a full or half of an ingame day. This is a very creative system but for me it's very stress inducing. I feel like I can never relax and enjoy the game because I constantly need to think "Will this action be useful enough to be worth the time? If yes will I still be able to get the quests done I have already accepted?" I still regret increasing my max mana because it cost half a day and I could have used that time to increase a royal virtue instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good in every aspect; one of the best take in turn-based combat, in my opinion.If I really had to think of downsides, sometimes the story holds you from actually playing the game for fairly long periods of time, which can be a little frustrating, but I'm honestly nitpicking, one other thing I can think of is the lack of option to change "your powers" once you're engaged in battle, as even using the retry function does not allow you to do so (unless I missed it), but then again, the game autosave super frequently which gives you the option to restart the game to make slight adjustments for an upcoming battle would you really need it.Played in hard, and I would say so far it's been a pretty good balance between the game rewarding you for making the good decisions and punishing you when doing mistakes or taking things a little too lightly. Did not ever had to grind for hours because I felt behind power wise.I don't even consider myself being super good at this type of game, just to say that hard difficulty to me has been the right choice as someone that seeked both smooth enough progression yet with a little spice added to it. I definitely had a handful of game overs but with the autosave and retry option, it never felt like I lost much progress at all, just made me trying to play better.Very, very solid game, cannot but recommend if you're a turn-based game enjoyer.

_childDocuments_.review: The story, characters and combat are some of the best modern JRPGs could possibly offer. Unlike the pretty lackluster and surface level take on social/political issues FF16 tried and in my opinion failed to deliver, this game does it so well. This is at minimum a 8.5/10, closer to 9, but a few problems kinda keep me from saying its perfect. I love the combat but since you can't change affinities like in Persona so much of the combat can feel artifically hard, like even on normal you'll be wrecked by a random enemy, for anyone coming from Persona and not the mainline SMT I can see this game being way too hard on normal. The game also doesn't do a good job in letting you know how you should be leveling your Archtypes early on and can result in you being very underpowered with little time to grind since like Persona you're always timed. And And my biggest complain are the dungeons. They just aren't good at all, they're so bland and basic. I kept waiting for them to actually become interesting. Maybe I'm spoiled by Persona 5's dungeons which no RPG or JRPG has come even close to the creativity and I was hoping they would use that to inspire a great dungeons. Its a real shame when I am enjoying the combat only to leave it and remember i'm just in generic stone dungeon #2. Besides that this game is incredibly fun and its going up there in the top 5, but Persona 5 still reigns supreme.

_childDocuments_.review: Methaphor: ReFantazio.---------------------------------------Atlus has done it again, and wow, they went all out with Metaphor: Re Fantazio. This game is nothing short of a masterpiece. They’ve taken everything we love about their RPGs and cranked it up to perfection. The gameplay? Smooth, addictive, and super satisfying. The story? Absolutely gripping once you dive into this fantasy world, you’re not going to want to leave.Let’s start with the art direction. It’s straight-up stunning. The world feels like a living painting, every scene like a canvas full of detail and life. It’s got this beautiful, hand-drawn, storybook vibe that just pulls you in. It's basically like someone mixed Persona’s stylish flair with a high-fantasy dreamscape. And the characters? Top tier. Every character you meet feels unique and full of life. The way they develop over the course of the game just makes you care about them more. They’ve got that signature Atlus charm you know, where you can’t help but get attached, just like when you maxed out those social links in Persona. You’ll have a hard time picking a favorite!Oh, and the soundtrack? Absolute fire. Whether you're in battle or chilling in town, the music sets the vibe perfectly. You’ll have those tracks stuck in your head long after you stop playing. I mean, it's Atlus, so you know they brought the heat, but this soundtrack is next-level. It gives me some serious Persona vibes, but with its own magical twist. The gameplay is a total blast. The combat system is deep but easy to get into, kind of like they took everything good about Persona’s combat and made it even better. It’s challenging without being frustrating, and every battle feels epic. The exploration is on point, too there’s always something cool to discover. The pacing is perfect, keeping you hooked from one quest to the next.Atlus has truly outdone themselves with Metaphor: Re Fantazio. It’s everything you want from a JRPG: a killer story, awesome gameplay, and a world you can lose yourself in for hours. It’s like they took all the things that made Persona great and said, “Let’s take this fantasy world to the next level.”So if you loved Persona and SMT, get ready to fall head over heels for this one. It’s a magical ride you won’t want to miss. Time to dive into the fantasy, because Metaphor: Re Fantazio is straight-up legendary.Enjoy the game !!!! a GOTY contendor and a game you will never forget.

_childDocuments_.review: is the latest title of ATLUS celebrating their 35th Anniversary of the company. This game fills to the brim with elements from a lot of their games within SMT and other games they worked on such as Etrian Odyssey. What really impresses me is how they integrate each mechanic without feeling forceful and it plays really well together. You can easily clock in 80-100 hours in this game and what it gives back to you, it definitely worth the price.The story follows a protagonist who is on the mission to save a prince, protag’s childhood friend, from a curse. The curse can be dispelled by killing its caster. Just before taking on the mission, Louis, a military genius commander, assassinates the current king. He is also the mastermind for the prince’s curse. But before we can do anything about Louis, the Royal Magic which triggers after the king dies leads to a tournament for the throne where anyone from any tribe, social status, regardless of any circumstances, can be the next king. It is now our mission to enter the tournament to bested Louis to prevent him from taking the throne.The story itself is by no means unique. What is really impressive is how the stories are told to the player. The pacing is perfect and at no point did I think the arc was too long or unnecessary. Every point and beat of the story serves its own purpose for our goal in the tournament. The story also acts as metaphor(hehe), allegory to what can happen to our world if we decide the arbitrary rules or beliefs will be our only guide to the future instead of working together as one. I will say no more about the story as it is something you really need to experience yourself.Overall it plays like a typical Persona game. The Followers mechanic is the Social Link of Persona, max at rank 8 and as you progress, each follower will give you some benefit in your normal gameplay or combat. The Followers give you more lenient and headway to progress than in Persona. Royal Virtues is the social status mechanic in Persona. Some followers do require a certain virtue rank to progress. The final obvious mechanic from Persona is the Calendar system. Main quest and some side-quests do have a time limit like in Persona, but what Persona doesn't have is travel time. In this game however, when you go to a dungeon for a quest, it will take some time to travel to, minimum of a day. During this time, we will be at the Gauntlet Runner, a vehicle we use to travel around. In the runner, we can improve our Royal Virtues, hang out with followers or do some other things like cooking.The combat has to be one of the most refined in ATLUS history. There are 2 types of combat in this game; Field and Squad combat. Field combat is used to either stunned the enemy before going in with Squad, or as a quicker way to go through lower level enemies without initiating Squad combat. Squad combat is your turn-based battle or I should say Press-turn system from SMT. Moreover the form of Press-turn this game took from is from Digital Devil Saga. The turn icon is a resource which is not exactly one action/skill equal to one icon. There are Synthesis Attacks like DDS Fusion skills where it can consume more than one turn icon. The party also has a formation; backline and frontline. Teammates in the backline will gain more defence but the physical attack will decrease and vise-versa in the frontline. The combat plays smoothly and feels snappier than their previous titles, particularly before P5R.They reuse a lot of effects from Persona 5 in particular which I always have a problem with because the sounds are so high-pitch I got my ears ringing. It’s not as bad here as P5 but still some improvement is nice. The highlight of this section has to be music. Once again this OST is done by legendary ATLUS composer Shoji Meguro. The theme this time is fantasy grandeur music with an underlying religious theme. Even though this orchestral music is not my preferred style (although I do like Strange Journey music a lot), this is by no means bad or so-so. They are really good tracks on there and some of the cutscene music or later boss theme make me shiver at how powerful the track is. The most creative thing about this is the “chant” in some tracks to invoke some religious feel in the music. The chant is done by Japanese Buddhist monk Chief Priest Keisuke Honryo chanting in Esperanto, a constructed international auxiliary language. To be frank, the OST is not my most favourite from ATLUS (that has to go to either Persona 3 or SMT IV tbh) but they are not bad, far from bad. And as someone who, let’s say, doesn't like symphony/orchestral music, the fact that this can get me to hum battle themes or area themes is impressive.Let’s just say that this game deserves a GOTY. It is the pinnacle of ATLUS game elements in one huge package that is called “Metaphor ReFantazio”. Even though nothing is really novel, or a completely new idea, you gotta hand it to them to create this masterpiece of a game from their own formula and still feel like it’s something new and fresh. Of course there are some nitpicks here and there which I came to call “ATLUS Jank”, but they are all minor compared to easily 80+ hours experience. Worth every single cents.

_childDocuments_.review: Best RPG I've possibly ever played - about 12 hours in and loving every moment. Story is great thus far, though I'm admittedly still very early in to the game - characters are good, and getting better fast - no character is too much of any one caricature or trope, which is a bit of a refreshing change from Persona series, if I'm being honest - they simply feel a lot more grounded - ironic coming from a Fantasy RPG. Graphics are the only criteria that I can scrutinize with any real seriousness: It performs fine, but it's not always the prettiest game - oftentimes textures are blurry, or they repeat very noticeably. Some areas look great, with a good amount of density and geometric complexity, but certain areas, like in dungeons, things look far less detailed- with one-too-many empty, flat wall and corridor for my liking. Speaking of geometry, there isn't much in any functional anti-aliasing, so if your game looks jagged or pixelated, you need to upsample - which obviously isn't doable for everyone. Art style and aesthetics itself are all phenomenal, and a much more endearing presentation than their prior games for myself personally.  10/10 despite those little quarrels

_childDocuments_.review: Peak game of the year material. 10/10. Everything I wanted & expected of the game. Loved it from start to finish. My only disappointments are related to NG+ mechanics & about end game. There will be SPOILERS (mostly mechanics & gameplay systems related) below.-Near the end of the game you unlock a secret prince archetype for your MC along with royal archetypes for your party members. At the end of the game I was expecting this prince archetype to evolve into an even more powerful form called hero king due to how many times characters referenced 'hero kings of old' this may also have been influenced by my playing persona 5 royal but nevertheless I was rather disappointed when this didn't happen even when it seemed as if there was a perfect opportunity for it to happen.-Near the end of the game there is a dragon trial so to speak that's ranked half a diamond away from max difficulty despite this the final boss "shadow of elegy" is actually many times more difficult to fight than the actual final operation that is max difficulty.-While initially I liked the archetypes system over the persona fusion system due it being easier to wrap your head around it the reality is it's much more limiting than the systems present in Atlus' other games.-The voice acting for the characters is spot on especially for the antagonist Louis but unfortunately a lot of times you only get a generic "what"! instead of actual voiced dialogue I understand why this is the case but the game would still be better if at least all the dialogue from main characters were voiced.Now for my let downs regarding NG+ mechanics.Upon entering NG+ you lose:-All your character levels this feels like a big f you if you grinded at any point for levels especially since there isn't a reaper like in persona games to level quickly & from what I understand SMT 5 just lets you keep your levels.-Any stat boosts you gain during the course of your playthrough whether they're from consumables, cleaning, doing laundry, or taking bath salts are lost. You only retain the stat boosts from maxing archetypes & even that is only because you retain archetype levels (you also only get these stat boosts back as you regain access to the archetypes). In persona you keep these boosts & it gives you something to work for from NG+ to NG+.-All archetypes become locked again & you have to progress through the game to unlock them again. This is extremely disappointing because the end game prince & royal archetypes are extremely fun to play with & going back to using others feels bad. Any archetypes you unlock & master should stay available to use once you get to Akademia like how you can get your personas back from the compendium like in....well, persona & again from what I understand SMT 5 just lets you keep them in your roster.All in all there's no real reason to NG+ if you get a perfect first run like I did without the power fantasy of going through it & accumulating stat boosts & playing with end game archetypes.TLDR: Having said that aside from these issues with the game (the ng+ issues being a non-issue so to speak) I'm extremely satisfied with the experience I got & I'm definitely glad I played it from day 1 release. If you've ever played any of Atlus' previous persona games & enjoyed them I would definitely recommend getting this game.P.S Very minor nitpick: There's a point in the mid game where your party gets captured by a....rope weaved into a net you really have to suspend your disbelief for it & it takes you out of the game. These guys with magic powers that can summon archetypes get taken down by some flimsy rope? Why doesn't Louis or any other antagonist just use that then.

_childDocuments_.review: Metaphor, more than anything, is Atlus utilizing everything they learned through the decades of developing JPRGs and dumping all in one place.The combination of Press Turn, calendar and archetypes systems makes for a great moment to moment gameplay, allied to the very well delivered story line and incredible character construction and development you'll have a great time with this game.Sadly the only really big negative aspect of this game is it's technical state, we are talking about a game that does not look good and also doesn't run as good as it should despite it's poor graphical fidelity. Although there are some very well made aspects in the visual design such as the menus and character portraits.Overall I felt that I got my money's worth with this game and I would recommend it to anyone even if they never played a JRPG before.Positives- Combat and overall moment to moment gameplay- Buildcrafting is expansive and doesn't require much grind- Calendar system delivers a feeling of adventure that matches the setting and plot pace- OST is great with a lot of impactful tracks- Characters have interesting story lines/progression and are all well played (VA) Negatives- Main story line has some pacing issues during certain events- Tecnhical aspects as a whole- Menus UX could be improved to minimize scrolling through dozens of items to get where you want

_childDocuments_.review: "Is fantasy a powerless creation?" This is the question the game asked me the moment I booted it up. And the game is partly about answering that question. It's a game that wears its heart on its sleeve. Unsubtle and hokey, but often profound. I alternated between rolling my eyes to feeling a well of inspiration. It's a smart game in many ways, drawing inspiration from historical figures like Thomas More and contemporary political issues, but the plot itself is as hokey as it comes. The gameplay is solid. I think it's a step down from Atlus's other games like Persona 5 and Shin Megami Tensei 5, but its still top tier rpg gameplay. It has the slick style you've come to expect from Atlus, complete with a banger soundtrack and an immaculate user interface.

If you have time to waste and long hours of reading ahead of you, you are in for a masterclass of JRPG's. If you like Persona's combat, that is.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate the direction Atlus has been going, and I hate the way P5 ended up. It was boring and pretentious- and I say that looking at its inner message of critiquing japanese society. That critique was necessary, but made into a boring, badly scripted mess.This game grabbed my attention and hasn't let up. It isn't a revolutionary RPG, but it's pretty good. They've broken their stale standard of making things guide-necessary (as far as I can tell). You aren't punished for not having universal knowledge at the outset. Every failure state still gains you some reward. You don't lose weeks of ingame time if you obtain an objective before the last day it's due. There isn't a guaranteed 'best' (and in the P series, usually only) good way to progress day-by-day. There's an exception here where some classes grant god-tier abilities to opponents early on, which bottlenecks you, but you still get something out of it if you've already max'd out the classes that can be used, and still progress in a semi-normal way. They actually use the system that's been developed in the Persona series in a way that's meaningful for the most part- you are still punished by trial and error quite a bit, but there's usually a way to win instead of the game forcing one standard group on you the entire time which enforces a guide-necessary mentality. The characters are still made script-stupid in a couple of cases, but it isn't as bad as usual in things like this. You can actually see how they might fail to understand a situation instead of the answer being directly in your face and the characters being completely braindead. The class-mixing is not FF5 or FFT levels at the start- you're bottlenecked into only a couple of classes having more than one slot until later. It works out ok, but the limiter is a currency you get by battling and interacting with other characters. The translation isn't a complete pile of woke ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as far as I can tell, and your knowledge of the characters and locations you're in pays off more than some 4th party activist translations would get you. I absolutely hate the music and have had it muted. I'm not a fan of the over-stylized menus, but they keep adding onto them as you unlock things in a sensible way. The character interactions mostly make sense, and the game appears to not lock you out of too much time. As in, some cat smothering you unconscious every night when the game director didn't want you to interact with the world. You still lose quite a bit of the time that's available due to plot, but usually they made at least some effort to make it make sense.Game's alright.

_childDocuments_.review: Metaphor ReFantazio Review:Atlus did it again purely for the love of the game. Metaphor has left me in such a good mood. They took their chances with the SMT/Persona formula and somehow made it even better. This is a genre defining JRPG.Story in this game has been refreshing, especially for an Atlus game. Atlus going off into the medieval fantasy aesthetic has been a true treat. The game really does feel like an Anime. The characters, plot and pacing are all handled well. The social aspects of this game let it soar to great heights as well, especially how it's so important to gameplay this time around. Having to go make friendships and connections to unlock new job classes really drives this game's overall feeling of enjoyment. The story may be pretty straightforward and digestible but it really takes its time to make you really invested on the journey to become king. The twists and turns were great all the way through.The gameplay has been crafted to its peak form. This is the perfect union between SMT and Persona. I dare even say it may have the best turn based system in the genre. The game does a magnificent job handling an expansive class system mechanic. The class system is up there with the all time square enix greats such as Bravely Default, Final Fantasy and Octopath Traveller. The amount of customization on movesets is a dream to play around with. The battles overall are quick and fluid, never feeling like it's overstaying its welcome. Dungeons are such a fun place to be now that they are not very confusing to get through (unlike persona 5). Overall the gameplay is fantastic and the world it takes place in is awesome.Music has always been a highlight in Atlus games and it did not disappoint. They took a step away from the persona games and have decided to forgo lyrics. It's honestly awesome getting to see the same composer go off and take on an entirely different genre and still come out hitting bangers. Some of these tunes are definitely hitting the playlist especially the Airship theme.Overall this game is peak Atlus. I enjoyed everything the game offered. I usually am not that invested in gameplay but this game really broke through with me in that department. This is a winning formula for Atlus and is probably their greatest game now that they have perfected their art. This was truly a dream to play.Score: 94/100

_childDocuments_.review: Overview:Metaphor presents an engaging main plot full of unexpected twists and a well-executed main antagonist that keeps players invested. Coming from a background of Persona 5 Royal, the narrative held my attention, but there were some notable differences that impacted my overall experience.Storyline and Characters:The main story in Metaphor is intriguing and layered, with moments that genuinely surprise. However, when it comes to characters, there's a noticeable difference. While they are well-developed, each with their own backstories and motivations, they often feel too morally perfect—as if plucked from a fairy tale. Each one embodies the idea of being "against all bad, for all good."In comparison, Persona 5 shines in this department. Its characters felt alive, showing a wide range of emotions, humor, and camaraderie that made them relatable. In Metaphor, character interactions lack this depth, boiling down to simple motivations like “They killed many people, I’m angry, let’s fight.” This reduced emotional engagement makes the cast feel less dynamic.Gameplay:Metaphor features a calendar system, meaning that each main mission—and some side quests—has a deadline. This mechanic adds a layer of strategic decision-making to each day, as players must choose between pursuing side quests, strengthening bonds with companions, or completing smaller activities to improve the protagonist’s stats.Main missions take place in expansive dungeons that can take several hours to complete. Battles are conducted in a traditional turn-based JRPG style where one team makes moves, followed by the opposing team. Players can opt to use items, cast spells, or attack during each turn.One interesting aspect is that characters can study any class (warrior, mage, etc.), each starting with a unique default. Choosing the right combination of classes for the team is essential based on the dungeon at hand. However, a significant drawback is that classes cannot be changed mid-battle. This limitation can be frustrating, especially when facing unexpected bosses that require a different strategy. To adjust, players must either lose the fight or restart the game to load a previous save.Random encounters in dungeons sometimes catch players off guard after cutscenes, which compounds the issue. In one instance, my main character's class automatically switched right before the final battle, disrupting my carefully prepared setup.Combat Mechanics:Despite the class-change limitation, the combat is well-designed, with distinct, varied classes and engaging mechanics that require strategic thinking. It kept me constantly engaged, which was a major highlight.Final Thoughts:While Metaphor didn’t resonate with me as deeply as Persona 5 Royal—largely due to its medieval setting and the less emotionally vivid characters—I still thoroughly enjoyed the gameplay. It’s a game I’d recommend, especially for those who appreciate JRPGs with strategic depth and strong storytelling, even if it doesn’t fully replicate the magic of Persona 5.Final Rating:Recommended for fans of the genre who are looking for a strategic and well-executed JRPG with a fresh twist.

_childDocuments_.review: Metaphor is exactly how I expected, and that's why I'm leaving a positive review.If you're a Persona or SMT fan, you know what you want. You know how it works, you start grinding your social skills and your relationships, and then you get benefits for combat and all the technical stuff. You're obviously required to accept a few factors, just to name two of them:- There's a time system which almost forces you to do certain things at a certain time.- Dialogue options are sometimes useless or they shouldn't be options to begin with: usually one of them is correct, the other mid, the last one definitely wrong, and since you're short on time you want to achieve the best results possibile out of social bonds, so you'll be compelled to look for a guide rather than give your honest (or roleplayed) answerr most of the times.In lesser words: the game doesn't offer you freedom, it's not one of those RPGs where you can play, do and say whatever you want. I mean you still can pick whatever dialogue option you want, but it won't make changes in the story, just give you less points.Aside from that, I think Atlus games are great once you learn how to play them, and this one has its own, unique concept and style that makes it even more special. _childDocuments_.review: Atlas's magnum opus.; I truly mean that. On a technical level it feels like all the best parts of the Persona series, refined from bloat & tedium. An engaging Job system much like that from Bravely Default, where each leveled Archetype, can, in-turn, empower the next with passives & unlocked skills. As well as absolutely stunning UI that feels like the end point of the past Persona colour theory entries. But truly what places this game so high for me is its writing. Its proof that politics & social issues can enhance a game, they just need to be handled properly. It is a story about the anxieties of life that make us all too human. Prejudice, racism, classism. The corruption of power like nobility, religion, wealth & misguided ideals. But also a story of unity, diversity, inner strength & utopian ideals. Of the possible good mankind can achieve. A self aware game that tells us that fantasy is not just a pointless distraction. But something that gives up hope, inspires us, & provides safe haven when the real world seems too dire to face.So long as we don't remain within, for that only leads to self-destruction. Its characters are masterfully written, making you care deeply for some & utterly dispise others. There are no duds here, & each & every one of them deliver their lines with beautiful voice acting in which I could feel the emotion.Due to such emotionally impactful writing, it left me in tears a multitude of times throughout the journey.Its my new number one example of videogames being art. Without question, my 2024 game of the year.
