_childDocuments_.review: Metaphor: ReFantazio is overall a great experience. It's a copy pasta of Persona with some modifications for the better. Combat is more dynamic and difficult (for most of the game), social links are easier to manage and the story carries a much more serious tone. The gameplay and story have their short comings, but its a good experience overall.I'll write this review from the perspective of someone coming from Persona, deciding whether this game is worth their time.The story of this is much more serious than Persona and it maintains this tone throughout. There's no mid-year beach party episode where everyone is cracking out their bathing suits and having a good time. The story touches on many themes of hope, death, discrimination, social change, religion etc. It's went into some topics I have not seen any games touch before. This makes the plot quite interesting, the end of the story also gets rather meta. The big downside to all this seriousness is that, while the characters are given some depth from this, they're not really "likeable" in the same way Persona characters are. They don't feel like a close-knit group of friends or are "buddy buddy" with each other, there is seldom silly moments or light-hearted scenes between the characters. Given this, some people coming from Persona games may find it harder to engage with this cast of characters.The overarching plot itself is quite slow in the beginning. For the first 10-20 hours, it feels like bog standard RPG plot of "we let us take down the comically over the top villain". Sprinkled throughout, some of the writing feels REALLY forced. One example showing discrimination. Opening cinematic? Shows discrimination. Every side conversation in town? Someone discriminating against a race. I sit down on a local park bench to raise my wisdom, my little fairy friend goes "GEE, THERE SURE IS A LOT OF DISCRIMATION AROUND HERE HUH?" (I ♥♥♥♥ yee not that's what happens). This is just one example, but there are many others. Thankfully the game tones down the discrimination stuff eventually or perhaps I just ignored it better. In the mid to end of the game, it throws twist after twist which was much more engaging. You know in college when you're writing an essay and you name it "final final final final V2 final V5.2.txt"? That's what the end of this game feels like. Every next encounter is "the final battle, for sure this time guys!". The story begins to grate at points due to this, you see more forced writing and dialogue repeating itself too. It has a big problem of "no showing, only telling". Despite this, most of it is fine it is lines here and there, but it happens often enough it is noticeable.I find the villain of this game very interesting, but also oddly written. It's like they wanted to write a nuanced villain, but had to put him into the shoes of a moustache twirling villain. By which I mean, the villain communicates in the story with a lot of nuance, but he'll do things that make very little sense in context with the beliefs he describes. One example is that he portrays he is honorable in his fight for "who takes the throne", but then results to using underhanded tactics. Which he never acknowledges ever again, but continues to display this nuanced motivation. I wish this character were more consistent, it certainly detracts from the overall plot.The VA really stands out in this game. Generally I find Persona-style animu games to have the same-sort of voice actors or types of voices, which all end up sounding the same from game to game. Most voices sound very English (or put more simply Bri'ish), which just makes the VA a joy to listen to moreso than anything. The gameplay is dramatically better than Persona. No more "all out" attack insta-wins in fights. Each party member has configurable "personas". Only one can be equipped at any one time. Each unlocked persona can inherit skills from any of the other ones, with a cost of some currency. This basically makes every single character like the "wild card" protagonists of persona games, there's nothing that makes your main character special vs every else in this regard. Everyone has access to the same personas. This adds a great amount of strategic depth to the combat, which the game even encourages use of through its "hint" system.Sadly this tapers off end-game. You become so overpowered, the game lacks any challenge. Firstly if you're high enough level, you can just one-shot the monsters in the overworld. This is nice avoiding trash mobs, but if you accidentally over level, you'll see entire dungeons require zero fighting as you poke each monster to insta-death. End game becomes just that and the enemies barely get to move since you get abilities that can skip their entire turn. Which was a shame. For context, I played this on hard difficulty. Overworld combat also feels quite clunky. It's very stiff, hard to see what's going on and when there's too many enemies, you're bound to get hit and enter an ambush encounter. Which can easily see your party wiped in a matter of moments, which can be quite frustrating, as sometimes getting hit in the overworld is just instant death. This is because of the turn system. In this game, if you hit an enemies weakness, you use 1/2 a turn. Same goes for enemies. So if you have 4 party members, you get 4 turns, you can attack 8 times if you hit the weakness each and every time. So imagine getting ambushed by 5 enemies, who get lucky criticals or hit weaknesses on every attack, almost an instant party wipe. It's hard to see a good solution to this problem though, other than maybe making it so you can't physically die from an ambush turn, which would be odd.Another somewhat clunky thing, also lacking in polish is the UI. The UI, visually, looks great. As it has done in most modern Persona games. However, because the game demands you reconfigure your party very often, you'll spend a lot of your time in these menus, changing equipment, equipped personas etc. Some examples of this clunk are when you need to modify your persona skills and gear. They live in two separate menus, but you usually want to edit both. So you need to exit the gear menu, go to the persona one, go back to gear etc. Or when you change persona, it changes your weapon type, so the game "auto equips" the "best one", but sometimes the "best one" for you, is not the one with the highest damage number. Which can cause entering some fights with unexpected gear and fighting the UI, which is annoying. Most of the game however was incredibly enjoyable for combat. The little things such as making combat animations faster, the rewind mechanic, "passing turns" were all welcome editions to streamline combat. The combat system does have other minor downfalls as well, but overall, it is very good.I found the music quite disappointing. You won't find any head bangers like the Persona OSTs. Most of this is choir, orchestra and some more choir. Some of the tracks grow on you after a bit, but most were forgettable to me or outright unimpressionable. The "velvet" room theme sounded way to gaudy for me, I actively despised it. Outside of just the general genre shift of the music, it feels like in distinctive music. There's a very low variety of tracks, 10 hours or so in and you've heard every track the game has almost. Even some of the final bosses had the generic boss theme, which was very surprising. I was prepared for something boppin', but alas. The final final (for real final) boss did have something unique, but it wasn't that distinctive honestly.In general the game has small flaws here and there, but nothing earth shattering that should majorly detract from your enjoyment of this game. The themes and messages of the story are also something that will stick with you, with plenty of reading between the lines (when they're not force-feeding lines in there anyway).

_childDocuments_.review: Tips: Get Healer to R10 ASAP, Max Alonzo and Brigitta,  This is a new high for Atlus, even with their history of innovative JRPGs. It takes the best and most distinctive parts of Shin Megami Tensei and Persona and builds them further. The story is among the most ambitious I have ever experienced. There is a LOT of lore, and Atlus fans will be able to see all of the years of philosophical, psychological and anthropological research for Shin Megami Tensei and Persona titles in how they've created a world full of realistic people, philosophies and relations between them. They don't pull any punches regarding the politics they explore in this game, but it's executed in such a tasteful way. Buyers can expect dedicated exploration of philosophies, nuances, ideals and, of course, the classic, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ CLASSIC Atlus MO of asking their players massive questions about who we are as people. The characters are written wonderfully, especially the central heroes and villain, and all of the secondary "Follower" characters have highly compelling narratives, in which they explore deeply personal themes that resonated with me, and put my problems into a healthier perspective.The pacing of the story is the BEST in Atlus history, staying compelling and engaging right from the start, so full of hooks and twists and turns. The writing in this game is among the best of the past 20 years, although personal taste does get in the way of fully enjoying the Tolkein-esque hammed up and pompous approach to dialogue. It's great, sure, but it's not for me. Small nitpicks with localisation aside, the writing gets a 9, due to it's tendency to beat you over the head with it's meaning at times; one would think a game called Metaphor, that continually shoves all sorts of metaphor in your face, would at least give you the credit to decode it yourself, instead of sapping the fun out of it. With that said, one can never give gamers too much credit these days, so I understand.The combat is straight up 10/10, it's another full on evolution in terms of strategy, creativity and joy of play. It's the classic Press Turn system with some new rules around switching and activating Half Turns. Difficulty wise, it sits right in the sweet spot between Shin Megami Tensei and Persona. Hard Mode doesn't allow for wasted turns, and there are definitely some classic SMT moments, but doesn't straight up punish players the way SMT 3-5V does. Real time combat is also implemented in the overworld, it's very basic, in a Breath of the Wild early-game kind of way, but it's honestly the best possible way to grind lower level enemies, and it feels so slick and satisfying to play, with a nice variety of weapons at players' disposal.The archetypes are an AMAZING take and full on evolution of the Persona system, and streamlines it in a way that allows for more fleshing out, and the gameplay necessitates constant re-evaluation of your lineup, so battles never get too repetitive and you're always learning new things.Visuals and worldbuilding are near immaculate. Can't say much else. The music is 9/10, only because SMT Vengeance set the bar that high a few months ago. Eht Ria's theme song is one of my favourite Atlus tracks ever, with an absolutely splendid spotlight on South Asian traditional music that perfectly complements Eht Ria itself, being a beautiful homage to Indigenous and pre-industrial cultures. Across the board, the music has done wonderfully with capturing the atmosphere and essence of every corner the fantasy world they've built.On a personal note: I have never ever ever ever thought that I could be so seen and so understood by a video game. Perhaps recency bias comes into play, but in terms of a holistic and personal experience, this might be my favourite RPG yet. It has brought immense perspective and much needed joy to my life. I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: The king is dead, long live the king. Slain in his sleep by the ruthless yet charismatic upstart Griffith, erm… I mean Louis, the king of Euchronia leaves his kingdom in utter disarray. An anxiety-riddled country torn apart by inequality, oppression, racism and religious fanaticism. To top it all off, bloodthirsty monsters, so-called  roam the earth. Turn the wrong corner in Euchronia and you might end up being devoured by a freakin walking Hieronymus Bosch painting.So, the departing king does what any good king would do – turn the royal palace into the f*cking moon from  and lift it up in the sky, then announce a popularity contest that will grant the crown to the one candidate that will win the hearts of the people, a true . And what an illustrious bunch these candidates are. On a surface-level, every popular real world political ideology is represented here, sometimes in a straight-up way, often times as a skewed parody of the actual idea. The , an unabashed theocratic organization, just exudes big d*ck energy in this contest. These guys are just like “We hold the power. We oppress you. We will continue to oppress you. Vote for us now!” One candidate is a textbook libertarian nitwit who wants to abolish all taxes and the state as a whole. Then you have Rudolf f*cking Hitler over here wearing a sleek medievalized Hugo Boss leather coat and calling for the segregation of the kingdom into – I sh*t you not – ethnostates for each tribe (tribes are basically fantasy equivalents of ethnicities). Another dude (It’s always guys, isn’t it?) plans to implement a societal hierarchy based on his perceived level of attractiveness… yep, only cuties get a seat in his parliament. Fortunately, some candidates have commendable actionable ideas like Catherina, who wishes to put a bounty on every noble’s head and calls for rolling out the guillotines for the entire wealthy upper class; she’d definitely have my vote.As you can probably tell at this point – the game is anything but subtle. Followers of sanctism literally shield their eyes as a religious gesture and they say  (close-your-eyes) as a mantra. Yeah game, I guess blind faith is bad, huh? Same goes for how Metaphor portrays racism. That is a core theme of the game but it is never really discussed all too deeply. Racism here is the in-your-face open bigotry people of “lesser” tribes experience in the street. Being spit on, being falsely persecuted or labeled as bad omens for things to come, that’s how the game depicts racist behavior. It’s not about the devious little subtleties and nuances of racism that people experience in the real world. You won’t go around in the capital trying to find an apartment and getting rejected for looking like a dog person. Rather, you spend most of the time in-game getting verbally abused for being of such low descent only to  your worth to the people which convinces them that, maybe, you’re not so bad after all. That’s a pretty sh*tty approach to deal with this subject matter if you ask me.Same goes for the portrayal as Louis as an antagonist. He’s just pure evil and he  Kill the king, burn down villages, kill literally everyone in his path and he just keeps getting away with it and is hugely popular to boot for some reason. So yeah, the character writing can be a bit cheesy and tropey in places. But it’s not all bad. Seriously, without spoiling anything, there are some powerful character-driven moments here. In best Persona fashion, you make connections to a wide range of followers which are this game’s social links in the spirit of the whole  affair. And I have to say, these are some of the more memorable characters Atlus has ever put in a game. Sure, there is the occasional mid arc that kinda goes nowhere but for the most part, these guys have interesting stories with satisfying resolutions. That’s not always the case though. Like there is one questline concerned with members of an oppressed tribe going around stealing and robbing out of sheer hopelessness. At the end, the solution is just “Yeah guys, just get a job lol” and everything turns out fine? I mean, yeah sure, that’s a quaint idea but I’m not sure that’s how this works.So yeah, I have my gripes with the writing. It sure is optimistic, wide-eyed and endearing in a way but when you tackle heavy topics like racism and zealotry, a superficial depiction of these topics does not suffice imho. You don’t solve racism by showing racists that the people they are racist against, are actually alright. You don’t solve poverty by shaming poor people for committing crime and telling them to get a job. You don’t solve religious fanaticism by exposing the church’s vile acts of corruption without looking deeper into how this organization gained such a position of power in the first place. It’s all a bit too simple for my tastes. Gameplay-wise though, this game is a blast. The archetype system is a welcome change. Instead of collecting and summoning personas, you can study archetypes that represent different RPG character classes. And every party member can unlock every class! The possibilities to rearrange your party composition to deal with a specific combat situation are just endless. I had so much fun with this system. The game actively promotes changing archetypes all the time. You can go ape sh*t and you are never punished for trying out the wildest combinations. It’s fun, it’s cool and it does feel fundamentally different from Persona. Fighting itself is fun as hell too. The separation into real-time overworld combat and turn-based squad battles is a godsend. They actually found a way to make grinding fun! Going around a dungeon in Metaphor after clearing it, one-shotting every monster and collecting that sweet sweet experience never got old for me. Squad combat is great too and brings some fresh ideas like positioning to the table. One thing I didn’t like here was the fact that archetypes can’t be changed mid-battle. That is too bad because sometimes you are thrown into battles you cannot prepare for. This happens only rarely but when it does, it’s extra frustrating. I remember having to fight a sandworm with the freaking  archetype equipped. Throw money at a sandworm and see how that works -> it doesn’t.Before wrapping up let me tell you that this game’s audiovisual design is just peak. Anyone telling you this game is ugly is either blind or suffering from a severe case of RTX brainrot. Show me a game this confident in its bright Art Deco style. Just look at these menus alone and tell me how this isn’t the coolest sh*t you’ve ever seen. Yeah, some textures look like a$$, the PS3  kind of a$$ but who cares? The art direction is strong and bold, an absolute treat for the eyes. And the music? Whoever thought mixing hip hop with classical music and bloody Buddhist chants deserves the highest praise, just listen to . The best thing is, music in this game is diegetic, it is described as a form of magic which is just the coolest thing.I’ve been fairly critical and yet, I would absolutely recommend this game. It sure is somewhat naïve in its core message, some moments are really nonsensical and over-the-top and not all of the plot points make perfect sense when you think about them too long. But this game has heart. There is some truly grotesque stuff in here (the  WTF), some heart wrenching moments, amazing gameplay, audiovisual design off the charts and some of the best voice acting I’ve heard recently (Basilio, I love you). Even though the end of the game is super stretched out, I am glad to have experienced this epic journey. May Fantasy live on.

_childDocuments_.review: I couldn't tell you the last time I played an Atlus RPG and walked away completely satisfied. My biggest criticisms are with some story beats that are well set up for the start of the third act but that we speed through without allowing more build up that would help the particular beat feel more natural, but its a moment I could see coming in a way that I still felt satisfied when it happened. It's less a disappointing moment and more a "I wish this had about an hour more development to it."And that's all before the amazing game play. One issue with modern Atlus RPGs is that they lack difficulty. Sure, you get bapped in a fight by a cheep shot and die but you very rarely feel challenged. Fights in SMT5 and Persona 5 are very much feast or famine. While the Combat in Methaphor is super breakable that's only well into the late game, and the enemy encounters are designed to usually counteract your growing knowledge of the games systems. You very rarely feel like you can't win, even in fights you arent ready for, yet when you do lose you would be hard pressed to get discouraged because it almost always feels like the tools are at your finger tips to over come adversity.If you were wondering if this game is worth $70 USD, the answer is yes. But if you were as burned out by the quality of writing in a lot of Atlus games for the past ten years trust me when I say you will not regret buying it when its even ten dollars of.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot believe there was a time where my thought process for this game was, "maybe I'll get it, but not at launch." And then I played the demo, and in less than an hour I was invested. I NEEDED to play this the day of its launch. And I was not let down in the slightest, this game is a fine work of art. Continue reading if you want, I've got some things I want to cover that might be pretty minor spoilers.I ADORE this game's cast. They bounce off of each other well and have such great interactions with one another, and not just making the protagonist "the silent character you imprint your own actions upon" was a great change. It makes him feel like an ACTUAL character you end up attached to and liking who doesn't just have two lines of dialogue, and I find it hard to even call them that. While on the topic of the characters, I'd like to say I really appreciate the characters getting development outside of the follower bonds/ranks. A major issue many people have (that I agree with) with the Persona games after 3 is that the cast hardly gets any major growth or development outside of their social links, whereas 3 had something more akin to "side stories" for all the main cast members where you see more aspects of their character. I will say, in this game there is a bit of development that appears exclusive to the follower ranks, but it's all still really good and I love to see the characters change and grow outside of them.The game's soundtrack is TOP NOTCH. Expected nothing less from the man Shoji Meguro himself. Expertly done tracks befitting of every moment.If I somehow haven't sold you on this yet, I know that $70 is a high price, but you're getting so much for your money. A game with a fantastic story, cast, gameplay and music. And you can also check out the demo. Bravo to everybody who worked on this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid ⭐ 8.5/10Metaphor feels like a love letter to fans of Persona and Shin Megami Tensei, with just enough innovation to stand on its own. The stunning hand-drawn art immediately immersed me in its world, and the diverse voice acting — complete with a fully voiced protagonist for the first time — adds welcome new layers of depth to the experience. Combat is a standout, striking a really nice balance between familiarity and freshness that makes it intuitive for someone like me who's only other JRPG experience was Persona 5 Royal.The freedom to tackle challenges in your own way is a welcome addition, with only minor instances of “illusion of choice” detracting from the mostly engaging narrative flow. The story doesn’t shy away from grim, thought-provoking themes, though its emotional impact occasionally falls flat due to underdeveloped non-main cast side characters and a somewhat predictable final act.Despite its attempts to separate itself from its Persona lineage, Metaphor sometimes feels hesitant to break completely free. Still, its brilliant monster designs, thematic depth, and strong core mechanics make it a high recommendation for JRPG fans looking for something familiar yet refreshingly new.TL;DR: A gorgeously crafted, emotionally engaging JRPG that fumbles slightly in originality and pacing, but ultimately succeeds in delivering a memorable adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Persona, but set in medieval fantasy land, where humans were the monsters all along.EDIT: Okay, having actually finished the New Game+ let me stop being snarky and actually be a bit helpful.Metaphor "wears its Persona roots on its sleeves" to be sure, but if you go into this game expecting a pure Persona style experience you'll be missing that this is really more of a Bravely Default game at the gameplay level: while the classic resistance exploit mechanic of SMT/Persona is in full force, the choice to use turn icons and partial icon use for exploiting weaknesses (rather than the good ol "knock every enemy down then all out attack" approach of P3 through P5) creates a bit of a differrent experience. Moreover, damage type negation (for your party) is far fewer and far between than you'd see in a Persona game; you need to be able to hit multiple damage types to maximize your offense, but doing so isn't an auto-win, and unless you explicitly prepare your archetypes for each encounter knowing what damage types the enemy is about to deal, you're a lot more likely to have your weakness hit than you are to have your resistances really be a big deal.Without the ability to swap out personas mid-battle, the dynamic is a lot different, and unlike in your Persona titles, you're actively building not just the protagonist, but your entire team. If you enjoyed Final Fantasy Tactics' job system where you had to reach a certain job level in such and such class to train in such and such other class, Metaphor is basically that-gated behind Persona social links. But it works! It works a lot! Even doing a new game plus, because progression in social links is in calendar and story line gated, you can have a 100% maxed out set of archetypes but you'll still spend time playing with early game archetypes in the early game, unlike in most Persona games where you can just whip out your level 99 Personas the moment you can afford to summon them.As for the story, there's not a whole lot I can get into without spoilers, but the game feels poignant and on point, without being too preachy, even though it very clearly has a message. All in all, this is my favorite Atlus title, bar none.

_childDocuments_.review: I had very high expectations for Metaphor ReFantazio, especially after playing Persona 3 Reload, and it absolutely delivered. The story is excellent, with each character being deeply developed, and the soundtrack is epic. The graphics are impressive, though slightly inferior to Persona 3 Reload, but they’re still far from bad. A particular standout is the game’s menu art, which is one of the most beautiful designs I've seen in video games. The turn-based combat is highly varied, and the archetype system offers players great freedom in customizing their party. However, I found the level progression a bit unbalanced. Even after completing all the available missions, I still had to grind significantly to reach the required level for certain quests. If you enjoy Persona or turn-based RPGs, this game is a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: Try the demo - don't just assume you'll like it cos you liked Persona. I did that, and now I'm mad as hell at myself for it.First off, it lacks really -any- of the charm or humour of the Persona games. The characters are not particularly memorable and most of their dialogue is very tedious. The music, too, is orchestral and epic, rather than quirky. The visuals are polarising, it seems, and, imo, absolutely horrible, but are also fairly drab and routine high fantasy (seriously, you could have gone all Roger Dean / Shadow of the Beast psychedelic fantasy or whatever, but no) -- which makes it all the more jarring when suddenly its throwing wacky and surreal  Archetype powers all over the screen. So, the stylings are always at odds with the devs' desire to be offbeat and crazy. (One exception: the designs of the humans are wonderful!)The Archetype system is frankly a mess. Thankfully, it does do a good job of autoequipping your best gear when you switch to a new one, on the whole, but if you do have to swap gear manually (say, cos you're going up against a boss who's immune to your default best pick) it's just stress to have to remember to swap everything back again 15 mins of cut scene later. The inherited skill aspect is basically a way to slightly alleviate the issue of not being able to ensure a good spread of ability types from your themed archetypes. It's especially annoying when you find yourself having to use an archetype you've already maxed instead of one you're wanting to level, because the situation demands it. Similarly, the Informer gimmick, whereby you pay for clues to what your next enemy's vulnerabilities will be, is to help you pick the right archetypes for dealing with them (cos it doesn't let you change archetypes mid-fight, for some stupid reason.)The travelling around the world aspect is basically pointless. It may as well be on rails, really, since the story requires you to go to certain places by certain dates anyway. The only flexibility you have is what order you choose to do side quests in. (Standing outside on the gauntlet runner while it's loping along is undeniably cool though.) They added a teleport mechanic so you can revisit previous locations without burning time, presumably once they realised that they'd need you to continue checking in with previous contacts, shops etc. Seems like bad planning -- P5S managed to have you travelling around without needing any of that. Sure, you could revisit previous dungeons, but you never needed to return to previous towns, so it can be done.The story's themes are interesting, I'll say that for it, though it's not very coherent. The quests are a mixed bag. Taking two minutes to teleport halfway across a continent to buy a bunch of flowers for a random child was a particular low point. The rewards for them rarely feel worth it. So all in all, kinda disappointing tbh. Try the demo though, I'm an outlier.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best JRPGs I've ever played for one of the most important reasons, which makes games "good/fun" to me: the gameplay mechanics! If you like turn-based games in general, you will LOVE this one right away. The implementation of the "Turn Icon"-system adds enough nuance to the combat to remain interesting throughtout the game and more importantly fun/challenging (particularly if you play on "hard", since the enemies get one additional turn icon, which is HUGE. You get caught off-guard/ambushed by an enemy cause you didn't pay attention? You better start praying lol... a much improved mechanic over the P5 "1 more!"-system imho. Kudos!). On top of that, the Archetypes/class combinations with the different Synthesis-attacks flesh-out the ressource management during combat even more, allowing for so many fun ways to approach encounters in the game: If your "planning phase" before an encounter becomes "fun", because you think "oh, awesome, if I combine this and that class I can get these and those abilities to work together PLUS I get some awesome class-combined abilities on top of that, but I must pay attention how many turn-icons I burn with them, as to not over-extent myself", for instance, you know you've done something correctly as a dev studio!  All of this bundled into the classic, compelling ATLUS/Studio Zero (Persona Series Devs) package, meaning great music, presentation, congruent character arcs, with an overarching and refreshing take on societal issues, "Utopian dreams" and handling of personal anxieties. I enjoyed the more "serious tone" of this story and game a lot! Awesome new IP: I hope there will be a Metaphor 2 in the distant future. My expectations for P6 are even higher now, after playing this. GOTY 2024 for me, 100+ hours well-spent! Buy it!

_childDocuments_.review: Metaphor is a party based JRPG from Atlus, the creators of the Shin Megami Tensei and Persona series of games. It is a party centered game with the same calendar and relationship system that can be found particularly in the Persona games. It's a game about self discovery and overcoming individual anxieties, lets talk about it. This review will be as spoiler free as possible and only reveal direct information found within the first 3 hours of the game. I will detail and review each section of the game individually and give each part its own score with an aggregate score at the end.TLDR: Solid game. Higher difficulties can and will slap you silly if you're not prepared. Characters are compelling, music is good to great. If you're looking for a new Persona game considering the gap between P5R and, allegedly being anounced at the Game Awards this year, Persona 6 then this game is probably right for you. Its a competent party based JRPG for sure.Story:Metaphor's story is that of a power struggle for the empty throne of a kingdom. It is laced twists and turns when it becomes extremely unclear as to every key player's motivations and allegiances. The main themes of the story are those of interpersonal connections, struggles with low self-worth and anxiety, sacrifice, and obligation. It spins a heavy tale of a kingdom deliberately kept in turmoil by censorship of information and dissidents. The story of this game will be fairly ageless.8/10, a few of the twists felt rushed and not given proper time to settleMusic: Its unique. Very bombastic, very loud. Choirs in combat, in dungeons and especially boss fights. The music wasn't trying to be overpowering or overly unique, but certainly painted the picture of a land with far different cultures in its own territories and different musical tendencies.6/10, unmemorable but unoffensive.Characters: As this is a party based JRPG, the ensemble of characters is what will drive the story. Metaphor has very well written and developed characters for the most part, with only a few that get mishandled in my opinion. Some of their arcs feel well done, and others feel rushed or anticlimactic. I personally feel that the shortening of ranks from a standard 10 that is found in the Persona games to only 8 hurt the ability to flesh out these character's arcs more. The dialogue outside of those activities is great for giving each one a unique identity and flavor though. I think the less interesting brother survived, personally8/10,  Good cast but some seriously missed opportunites. The Faker ending is superb, though.Graphics: Good enough. Its not super high fidelity, and some monster's overworld models do look a little too uncanny, but its not bad. I would recommend those with better PCs download the 4k mod from Nexus as it cleans up a lot of fuzziness overall. The enemy models and designs are good, but there is a lot of reskinning. This game does not support ultrawide monitors either, so you will need the Metaphor fixes mod for that as well. Even that isn't perfect, but it makes 85% or so of the game ultrawide compliant. You will see some funny instances of character models standing off to the side before entering or suddenly stopping as they leave because a 21:9 or 32:9 aspect ratio was never intended.6.5/10, good but unimpressive. Audience: Teen and up. Not a lot of strong language, a few instances of the words "Damn" "♥♥♥♥♥" and "arse" but thats about it. Cartoon violence, cartoon blood, etc etc.Gameplay:It plays a lot like SMT 3 and a lot less like persona. There is no swapping of your Archetypes mid fight, buffs have multiple tiers, and the turn system closely mirrors SMT 3's. There is not a true "1-more" system like in the Persona series, but there doesn't need to be. Overall it is classic SMT gameplay. Buff, debuff, attack. Simple, but very deep with the ability to induce weaknesses with certain skills, being able to make skills from specific archetypes transferable to all the archetypes for that character, and strong synergy skills to tie the archetype chemistry closer together.9/10, I really enjoy the depth to the combat and the challenge it presented on higher difficulties. One of the achievements in this game is to beat the final boss without weakening him throughout the dungeon. Absolutely brutal, and I love it.Difficultly:Since we've just mentioned it, this game can be supremely punishing. You miss an attack? Just like SMT 3, thats 2 actions gone. You hit an immune or absorb target? Thats your turn over. You get hit by a critical or a weakness? combat system works the same for the enemies as it does for you. Some of the boss fights are genuinely brutal. You can run into a level 60 boss by leveling up your companions far before you're ready to fight it. You can make the final boss incredibly punishing if you're going for the achievement on non-storyteller difficulty. There are also 2 other optional bosses that are very difficult in their own right. One at the end of a chain of quests that itself is an annoying boss gauntlet, and one that is the game's "super boss" only available in NG+.That being said, there are ways to still cheese these harder fights. Just get used to doing a lot of fishing in NG+. This game is about as hard as a typical SMT game, which is fantastic considering how easy P5R and P3R were.9.5/10, storyteller existing removes the half point.Price: If you're not an Atlus/SMT/Persona fan, then i would tell you to wait for this game to go on sale as is my typical advise. Its a good game, but i still feel $70 is a lot for any title. I'd look for it around $50 or lower personally.Bugs;Had a few random crashes, but the game's timely autosave feature meant that nothing was ever really lost. In my time with the game it crashed 6 times, but that easily could've been the mods i mentioned before.Final score:7.8/10 Closing thoughts:Metaphor is a good game, and a promising start for Atlus to expand their IPs. While there are parts of Metaphor I think could've been done better, like the graphical fidelity and the music style, I know those are mostly personal preference. The game at large is good, bordering on great. I dont see it as a GOTY contender like some do, but i wont dismiss it entirely either. As it stands in the current industry, there are only 3 game studios that I would trust to consistently make good to great games. Atlus, From, and Larian. That hasn't changed here.

_childDocuments_.review: So, where to start without spoiling anythingThe game focuses on our un-named main character as he starts his journey to deliver a message, a simple task that very quickly leads him on a new path to try to right wrongs and unite the tribes, along the way you'll meet a host of different characters all hailing from different races across the country and will grow and develop along the wayFirst and foremost, if you enjoyed the gameplay style of the likes of Persona 5 then you will feel right at home as every mechanic and gameplay system will feel familiar, from exploiting elemental weaknesses to strengthening characters and archetypes, they are essentially the same as the persona's from the franchise of the same name, meeting new characters and forming bonds will unlock more options for you to equip, you are also able to inherit skills from other archetypes you have unlocked on that character in order to give a warrior access to magic or access to healing abilitiesThe combat is your standard turn based affair with MP being the common cost of using abilities, deciding if you want people on the front lines or the back lines, with units in the front gaining attack and lowering their defense and units in the back gaining defense and the cost of offensive power, which gives you more ways to tactically approach each battleThe soundtrack is impressively on point with even the default battle theme for normal encounters going far harder than any default battle theme has any right to go and it reminded me a lot of how hard the FF XIII battle theme went during longer encountersThe graphics are definitely good enough, no photorealistic models and textures required, the game does break up the important scenes with anime style cutscenes for you to lean back and enjoy, without buying the DLC there is no way to change your characters default appearance so if you're not a fan of the character designs you will be stuck with them for the 60 odd hours it will probably take most people to go through this gameThe bond system is about the same as expected with no romance options like the persona games have, which isn't really an issue for me but i get that some people might be interested in having a romance option, raising bond levels is normally done by spending time with a character during your free periods or in some cases when travelling to different towns or dungeons, you should generally be able to max these out in a single run of the gameAll in all i think this is a solid new (for the most part) IP and i look forward to seeing if we will maybe get another game set in the same universe in the future, given the reception this one got i like to think there is a high chance of that happening, but we shall see what the future brings.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start this review by saying that I played Metaphor kind of in an "Atlus RPG fatigue", since I've played 2 of their games this year (3 if you count Episode Aigis as a full on new RPG, which I do, ♥♥♥♥'s long as ♥♥♥♥), but even then it's honestly one of the best Atlus RPGs I've played. The story captivates you very early on, with several interesting themes, the art and menus are all beautiful to look at, the spritework on this game genuinely made me smile and feel happy just by seeing the characters smiling. The music in this is also borderline insane with how good it is, Meguro does it again, man can't stop winning.The character's designs and "Social Links" are really well written, Maria's link made me tear up (also gave a real good bonus skill, go do that as early as you can, it's like Mishima's bonus, but Maria doesn't suck), Heismay's story also connected with me on a personal level, since it's about dealing with loss and moving on and Brigitta might be my favorite design in this game. The villain is also one of the best Atlus has put out so far.The gameplay is essentially SMT with added features, like Synthesis Skills (which honestly are a bit busted, Junah was in my party to pretty much buff the ♥♥♥♥ out of everyone else, Heismay made it so no enemy had a turn by dodging like a madman and Hulkenberg was.... Well, I like her, so she gets to stay)Not everything is perfect, the menuing to unlock or change Archetypes can be a bit excessive, at one point I was tired of opening the menu to unlock something for someone and having to press X a bunch to skip through dialogue I had seen multiple times by now. I also had a problem with voices, where I had to pretty much download and install bloatware on my pc to fix it, because for some reason the voices in scenes would default to surround sound and lower to 2%, making it so the characters sounded like they were inside a tin can across the street. Some bosses can also be a bit of a chore to fight at certain points, where it's several turns of a battle of attrition, draining down my MP to debuff/clear off buffs on a boss and then chip away it's health with damage, it's not really engaging, fun or hard, just boring. Anyhow, the good far outweighs the bad in this game, to be honest a lot of the bad are gripes that I had myself (with exception of the audio issue), definitely a recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Metaphor: ReFantazioStory 10/10: Metaphor is a wonderfully well written story, that challenges the concepts of fantasy (idealism) with the reality of an imperfect world. Through many clashes and interactions, the protagonist challenges a world of classism, racism, and xenophobia. With plentiful twists and turns, the story of ReFantazio is something to not be missed. Definetley one of Atlus's deeper stories. To talk to much beyond over vague generalizations would spoil too much. Please enjoy this game spoiler free.Music 9/10: The heavy medieval themed music Atlus chose for this game fits this fantasy world quite well. The tracks with the Monk chanting are really interesting. Not my favorite Atlus OST, but certainly not bad.Difficulty 7/10: While Metaphor's story is fantastic, i do have one small bone to pick with the difficulty of this game. I played through my entire playthrough on normal, and had no problem with the majority of the sidequests and fights, but that final boss is a ridiculous difficulty spike. I had to put the difficulty on story to beat it, and even then it was a slog. Just a fair warning to those who get frustrated easily. That final boss is no joke.Overall I enjoyed Metaphor in my 56 hours of playing. I'd rate the game a 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent JRPG. Combines the best parts of Persona/SMT with a pronounced Dragon Quest influence. It's not perfect, but it's pretty close, and the highest highs more than make up for a few moments of weaker writing and minor polish issues. Yes, some of the themes are a bit on-the-nose, but tropes don't drag down the quality when the writing around them is so strong in general. I grew up playing JRPGs, and my favorites (i.e. FFVI, Earthbound) aren't perfect either, but they're still some of the best games I've ever played, and Metaphor sits alongside them in my opinion. 95/100.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough one for me, because I can totally understand plenty of people, especially Atlus fans loving this game. I, personally am not a fan of the stereotypical "anime" tropes that plague that industry. What I am referring to is the standard, boiler plate immature writing and generic characters. Usually, Atlus writing turns these tropes on their head in a satisfying way, but here, I am sadly far too turned off by childishly simple characters and bland motivations. They reach for the stars, as usual with their projects, tackling serious themes and many are saying that the themes in this game are far more mature, but i actually disagree. I think that Persona 5, specifically handled very serious themes of sexual assault, suicide, addiction, etc. This game benefits from deviating from the high school dating sim, but suffers from not capitalizing on the high fantasy setting enough.I find the biggest turn off to be the writing in an otherwise servicable fantasy RPG experience. I have spent plenty enough time, completing multiple dungeons and story threads to know that this isn't for me. Without beating up too much, I can distill it simply:The overall story has an overly long intro and needlessly drags its feet getting you through a painfully on-rails experience that barely lets up. The concepts they try to reach for are embarrassingly dropped or not properly given enough maturity or nuance. Generally, this is an extremely basic succession crisis storyline that doesn't offer near enough to keep one interested.The characters are the most egregious part for me. Everyone speaks in moral platitudes and uses flowery prose to muse on their opinions about power, freedom, death and honor, but when the chips are down, the game really boils down to "I'm enjoying being a bad guy and dress in dark colors. Androgony and emo clothing is COOL!" and the heroes are simply preaching and chastising the lunatics who love being evil, emo anime robots. It's truly a disappointing affair and I found myself saying out loud, numerous times "That's it?" when a character would reveal their reasons or motivations for their choices. Nothing has enough depth, and the worst part is that they are constantly cautioning against finding simple solutions to complicated problems in the world, such as inequality, but ultimately it's just a simple "good guy fights for freedom, bad guy fights for selfish things." That sort of world can certainly work in the right creative hands, but here, it just feels annoyingly shallow.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Verdict: Story: 8/10(Beginning - 8/10)(Middle - 8.5/10)(Ending - 7/10)(No spoilers, but the game goes in hard to start making you get ready for this mountain of a journey. The story set has many twists and turns that blind sided me in a good way, but the ending was sadly Persona "WTF" that did not make sense and then it was assumed it did. Though it missed a little with me, the post game was still fun and entertaining and would recommend to anyone)Character Development: 6/10(Unlike Persona, the characters don't really interact with each other outside of the main story. While each the main character and his party are well written and have clearly defined motives, I would have loved to see them interact with eachother. They only seem to talk with the MC and make the occasional comment to one another. I also feel that some of the character's story is somewhat shallow. The Main character and maybe 3 of the 6 that hit close to home and that you feel for, the others feel very cookie cutter story. One of them, practically has the same story as another character from specifically a persona game)Music: 6/10(Game Music+ Ambiance- 7/10)(Battle and Boss Music- 5/10)(Memorable Music- 6/10)(Sadly the music in Metaphor falls short from the standard I have felt in many games similar and done by the franchise. The one song that you remember the most is sadly over used and can get somewhat tiring after a while. There is no differences and the boss music is a slightly more tense variation. The Final boss's OST sadly falls short from its memorability and did not give the same threat or vibe as "Battle for Everyone's Souls (P3) or Rivers in a Desert (P4) I went to listen to the OST for the final boss again while writing this and really felt no connection. Sadly a miss there.Gameplay and Difficulty: 9/10(This game does not disappoint when it comes to its combat, as it never does. Mana is always a finite resource and is well managed making it hard to complete a dungeon on the first run unless your well equipped to do so. Though there are skills and The Mage that will make it easier to regain lost mana with a bit of grinding. The grind is rewarding if you choose to do it and does not punish you for going back and slapping a few mobs with its gameplay systems. battles are fast when you are over leveled for the enemy, ending them in literal seconds while mobs your own level and above are still a challenge if your not prepared. Boss battles are difficult, but are a breeze if your over-leveled for them. In addition, some bosses can be cheesed hard if you have a simple reflect skill and counter buff and Debuff clensing skills, ending your opponents turn in without some of the more painful mechanics start to crop up. One good thing I like, is every character can fit every role. The knight? Ima make you my healer! The warrior fighter? Nah mage please. Its a great system that rewards you to take the time to level multiple classes, which is a requirement for the endgame "Elite" ClassesOverall Score: 8.5/10Good Game, Good Mechanics, Falls short a little with story development and character development, but still a good burn(Note: My first run took me 70 hours to complete, This included a fair amount of the grind. I was able to complete all aspects of the game which did not require a New Game Plus to complete. The only thing I missed was a time exclusive book and the all masks and cooking recipes cooked. The game was completed on Hard difficulty from start to finish without any alterations during the story)

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game, with a much better main plot and social links than P5. The Archetypes (basically classes from FFV) lend a real mix and match aspect to the dungeon crawling that was never in Persona, since with Persona fusing higher level Personas was usually the best bet. You can also upgrade your classes from the main menu, no more going to the Velvet Room all the time. Voice acting and direction in particular are stellar in English, with great and funny emotional line reads from the main cast.It's strange how SOME of the dialogue in the social links isn't voiced, feels like a missed opportunity. The game's textures and environments occasionally look like a meh PS3 game, and not in a charming mid budget JRPG way, in a "they did texture wrapping lazily" way. The artstyle hard carries for the game. Lots of quality of life improvements from Persona and SMT including a reset to battle start button, but no back out of a boss battle option. You WILL fight bosses it may be hard to beat with your current Archetype setup (resist / null your attacks etc.) and want to switch, but can't run from boss battles, so you'll have to close the game and reload a recent save. In the request lists for sidequests, you should be able to select a request you completed and just teleport to the questgiver, seems an obvious fix. So far the music is more bombastic classic JRPG fare, horns chanting and the like which I love, but I can see fans of Persona with it's rap / jazz / j-rock influenced OST feeling left out.Overall, it's a strong 9/10 for me so far and is most likely my GOTY, beating P3 Reload and FF7 Rebirth. Fellas, they cooked.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly good so far. I was worried the fantasy setting would feel generic compared to SMT and Persona, but that isn't the case at all. The four main characters (Protagonist, Strohl, Hulkenberg, and Heismay) were fantastic characters. Sadly, the later 3 playable characters didn't hit the same (except for their archetypes, which were great and very useful in combat). The main story starts out boring, but gets very intense and exhilarating at the 10 hour mark. I loved every single side character and their bonds. I love how big the reward can be for talking to them. In conclusion, at the moment It's my favorite Atlus game. It has some problems with the late game playable characters, but besides that, I loved the game. 3/10

_childDocuments_.review: I will never try to tell someone how to play a game, but seriously just focus on the story and the missions. I have done exactly zero grinding, and I have maxed out every single stat, every single relationship, and I have done every single mission. I am towards the end of the game at level 70, and I was incredibly impulsive in my resource usage. I didn't plan anything. There is NO need to try to 100% you can almost do that without trying if you just take your time and engage with everyone. Don't worry about failing dialogues, I sucked at that and I still casually got everything maxed out in time. I'm not even sure if the triangles do anything lol. Anyways, you are doing the story and the game a disservice if you don't take the time to enjoy it. There is never a point where I felt rushed. I just talked to everyone and did everything. I have talked to every single NPC, and it actually felt rewarding to do so. There is no reason to rush, just be yourself and make it your journey, and I promise you won't regret it. I don't think I've ever left a review in my entire life. This game by far, is the best game I have ever played in my entire life: It has an amazing and powerful story. 10/10The voice acting is quite literally the best I have ever heard, in any format, for any medium. The combat is Atlus refined, and is very unique in its own way. Its turn based, with a combination of over world combat elements. The characters are...so fudging amazing. I mean every character has personality, even the dorky ones. Every character feels central to the story. The relationships aren't bogged down by trying to rizz the characters, but they are just real connections in a weird way. Not like literal real relationships, but you can almost imagine a world where the characters exist. Every single character you meet is a part of the story. There are just so many small elements that feel useless or unimportant in other games, but they allllll somehow play a part. I don't want to spoil anything, but honestly if this game goes off the records, I can see it being one of the most incredible modern art pieces of our time. Forget the fact that its just FUN.

_childDocuments_.review:
From the creative minds behind Persona 3, 4, and 5 comes Metaphor: ReFantazio, a unique fantasy world, where your protagonist will journey alongside his fairy companion, Gallica, to lift the curse from the kingdom’s lost prince. Control your destiny, face your fears and awaken magical "Archetype" powers that lie dormant in your heart. By awakening to an “Archetype,” you will unlock the power to channel and combine the abilities of unique job classes. Strengthen your bonds and build your party to take down powerful foes and discover the kingdom’s true nature.

-Go on uests, dungeon dive, & hunt for treasures by day. Strengthen relationships, build bonds, & increase virtues by night. Choose your actions wisely, time management is key to achieving your goal. 

Ride your “gauntlet runner” to faraway dungeons & towns across an expansive world. Discover beautiful landscapes  accompanied by captivating music, immersive UI, & anime cutscenes.

A unique battle system combining turn based & real time action grants strategy & exhilaration at every turn. Party customization through “Archetypes” provides freedom to personalize your adventure. 

A mysterious & exciting story unfolds in a world where people must fight their own anxiety. Join the high-stakes Royal Tournament that promises hours of captivating exploration and discovery.

name: Rails Across America
detailed_description: Rails Across America is a game of railroad empires in North America, covering the period from 1830 to the near future. It is a real-time strategy game with a 'sim' flavor. Rails allows hundreds of tracks with thousands of trains crossing the continent. Players must focus on strategic decisions: where to expand, where to compete, and when to call in favors from government officials, union leaders, and other powerful figures. Sophisticated cargo routing system enables large-scale play enabling hundreds of routes and thousands of engines. Influences let you directly affect other players: cause a financial panic, start an investigation into the player's company, instigate a strike, petition a city for route assignment or force independents out of business. 60 different engines and cars. Intelligent AI modeled after 12 real world rail barons. Up to 8 players in multiplayer over LAN. Create new worlds using the Map Editor and unleash your creativity to craft your ultimate train fantasy.

name: Ufouria: The Saga 2
detailed_description: Upyo! How's everyone been? SUNSOFT's Ufouria is back! - An authentic evolution of the original 'Ufouria'! Rampage through the fluffy feltwork arts-and-crafts recreation of the world of Ufouria, with your trusty crew from the original game in this exploration-based action side-scroller. Of course, newcomers to Ufouria are welcome too! - Adventure in the lovingly crafted wacky world of Ufouria! Familar characters and stages of the original game are back, transformed from their formal pixel art to charming handmade feltwork. Iron bead artwork also plays homage to the nostalgic pixelated look of the original. Look for all the similarities and differences if you've played the original before! - Different courses each time you play!? The various stages from the original game now change randomly every time your enter, making for a fresh new challenge each time! New characters joining your crew let you reach more areas. You might even find areas that weren't in the original game at all... - Popoons are now a super powerful cleaning agent! A new threat, one that wasn't in the original...the icky Bumyon makes an appearance! The troublesome Bumyon sticks to everything and everyone and is quite the annoyance, but somehow Hebe and crews can counteract them perfectly with their Popoons. Clean up the Bumyons that litter the planet and thwart the Utsujin's evil plans! Visit the never before seen Hebe's house! Meet rare characters that were only ever seen before in Ufouria art books! A Collection feature lets you read up on enemies and their backgrounds!

_childDocuments_.review: Ufouria the Saga 2 is twee.It’s a fact that supersedes any conversation about its genre or its gameplay or its progression. All of those things are just vehicles to deliver a vibe—and thankfully that vibe is immaculately curated with a beautiful craft and felt aesthetic.This is a dumb little world inhabited by dumb little creatures with dumb little problems: like Mr. Jennifer and his unwillingness to join you unless you get him Pepto Bismol to alleviate his stomach issues.It effortlessly weaves non-urgent slice of life scenarios into a short but sweet metroidvania format. It’s mechanically light and beatable within an afternoon; but if you’re willing to embrace what Ufouria has on offer, that afternoon will be damn cozy.You start as a singular character, Hebe, waking up in his treetop bedroom/bathroom that’s also the central hub that all the other zones sprawl out from. Not too sprawling, mind you: part of Ufouria’s short duration is owed to the fact that those zones are only ever a hop and a skip away from home-base and easily fast traveled back to when needed.It’s pretty frictionless by design: though you do have an alien with nefarious plans you have to take down, most of the game is really just doing favors for your three buddies and exploring to find secrets. The map borrows some rogue elements in its design. The world itself is consistent: Popoitto Caves is always to the east and Ufouria fields is always to the west, but once you go into one of those zones it becomes its own mini-instanced platformer level with semi-randomized layout and completion bonuses for finishing.You’ll want to get to the end and fight the boss while collecting as much currency and collectables as you can on the way, then you’re usually met with the option of proceeding to an adjacent level or porting back to home base and spending what you’ve accumulated.There’s two semi-discrete phases of the game: your first hour or two will be gathering the crew, which is a sequence of finding them out in the world, beating them in a boss fight due to some sitcom-level misunderstanding, then completing some sort of collection task for them. The second half of the game is using all of the accumulated abilities of the crew to get to all the previously inaccessible zones and collecting the prerequisites for a final boss push.Regardless of which step of the journey you’re on you’ll frequently want to take trips back to the vending machine at home which has a variety of health upgrades, utility spells, and other ways to enhance your exploration.Its randomized take on level layouts add a different texture to those metroidvania ‘come back here when you get the double jump’ moments. It’s not a specific obstacle getting in your way every time because it's random, it's usually a genre of obstacle. Getting the climb with Hebe lets you get to the high levels, getting the swim from Mr Jennifer lets you descend into the water, but outside of the non-randomized hub, it’s not like there are exact coordinates you need to remember. Just know that the swim helps you with water and make a mental note of which zones have water, rather than recall particular puddles within that zone.It’s less gratifying than your average ‘aha!’ moment that usually comes with this kind of game, but it works within the context of Efouria’s effortless difficulty.The combat and general movement style is simple by design, harkening back to its retro origins and also aligning to Ufouria’s felt style. Everything is just a little frumpy. Even the simple act of killing an enemy demands getting above them to butt stomp, and if you want them to sit still to enable that cleanly you’ll need to press a button to take one of your Popoons from your pocket, then another to throw it at a fixed angle at your foe.It’s not smooth, it’s not physically satisfying and, yet, it all kind of works? I couldn’t imagine your basic mode of attack being a simple strike with modern flare and tight control because that’s not what Ufouria is or what it’s going for.If that sounds like cope just remember it was like this 30 years ago, too. The first game was tone first and this one is as well, and it’s that tone’s success that makes Ufouria worth playing.The tweeness is overflowing from the screen. It invites comparison to the few times where Nintendo’s cutsier mascots found themselves in craftlike environments but the production here gives it a different feel. Look close enough at any of your characters and you can faintly see the individual strands of felt that construct their bodies and clothing. Whereas something like Yoshi’s Wooly World feels like it was made from fabrics that came together within its universe, Ufouria feels like it was made with fabrics that came together from our universe. Seemingly small distinction, but it gives the game a vibe a little closer to the best British cultural exports that put physical toys and models into fantastical environments for kids, like Thomas the Tank Engine and Brum. It’s a wonderful style whose only problem is that I wish it was pushed further: the random generation that the levels lean on limit Ufouria’s ability to produce meaningful setpieces and memorable singular objects in this style, as opposed to just tylesets and backdrops.That vibe is communicated beyond just the aesthetic, though.That old menu switching between characters is now a little high-five animation where they tag each other in. Everyone gets their own goofy walk cycle and their own chirpy little animal crossing voice. You’ll be hearing them a lot because friendly debriefs are a frequent occurrence.I’m largely willing to come to the defense of the fact that Ufouria’s actual gameplay can sometimes be intentionally simple, but there’s two areas where I found that the game's structure was inhibiting the tone and not helping it.The first is in Efouria’s ‘prepare for the final boss collection phase’, that has you going to new zones and completing them with whatever parameter that level defines (such as not getting damaged, doing it in under a time-limit, etc). It's the only notable difficulty spike within Ufouria and the spike isn’t the problem as much as the framework around it is: there’s no way to quick retry when you fail, demanding that you go home and trek all the way back to the zone to repeat its challenge. It’s annoying in a way the game otherwise never is.The second is that its random generation and collection focus fits horizontal levels far better than vertical: which is largely fine because vertical sections are the minority, but you can frequently miss a collectable you didn’t know was coming (its random, remember?) and lack an effective way to get back up to it—usually requiring a full retry. Hebe eventually learns to climb, but certain level layouts prohibit climbing due to ledges or other protruding objects.Ufouria is a beautiful little game. Its lean on randomly generated worlds prevent the artstyle from producing memorable setpieces and occasionally cause some annoying pathfinding snags. It’s a game that’s at its best despite and not because of its gameplay, but it effectively recreates the tone of its 33 year old predecessor and infuses that recreation with its own style. Its blend of cartoonish characters with real fabrics and craft materials give the game a twee feel and it sustains that tweeness with its low stakes platforming and friendly themes. It’s only got a few hours of game, but that’s a slice of life worth giving.

_childDocuments_.review: This game bills itself as a sequel to classic Metroidvania Ufouria, but it's not really that. It's not a game I'd describe as a sequel or a remake due to its very strange nature.If anything, Ufouria 2 is more of an incremental platformer. The desicion to completely move away from Metroidvania roots in favor of buying upgrades was likely chosen due to tight budget as it means the player will traverse levels over and over again.The levels themselves are somewhat random with pre-determined chunks building a new level each time. However, they're not that different each time.By all accounts, I feel like Ufouria 2 is a bit of a cheap trick. A weirdly grindy platformer that asks you to go through the samey levels, complete missions, collect coins and cans to purchase more things. However, it never feels bad. Each level is very short and the aesthetic is absolutely beautiful. There's also plenty of dialogue which reminds me a lot of Japanese 4-koma comics: silly, not exactly laugh-out-loud funny, but pretty witty and charming.It should also be mentioned that Ufouria 2 is a short game. If I wasn't going back to the beaten levels to collect stuff and see new things it's very likely I would've finished the game in 2 hours. I still recommend this game, but only if you understand what kind of game it is: it's not Ufouria again, nor is it a fully-fledged sequel, just a charming game about collecting stuff to buy more stuff. I liked it, but it might not be your cup of tea.
_childDocuments_.name: Ufouria: The Saga 2

_childDocuments_.review: A long time ago a friend of mine had a NES so I went to his home every now and then, one of the games he had was something called "Ufouria" that I never heard of, but I was immediately hooked on it: it gave me an interest in metroidvanias (when they weren't called like that yet) and many years later brought me to write a series of articles about all the games in the series, that you can read .So, when I heard that Sunsoft was bringing Ufouria back after like 3 decades, I was quite interested in what they were going to do with it so many gens later. The answer is: not that much. I found it not terrible but quite disappointing for what it is and its price.- The new graphic style is really charming and a good innovation of the simple shapes and bright colors from the original 8-bit sprite-based graphics. Even rendering said pixels with perler beads is a cute choice and ties in with the "arts and crafts" new style.- Good arrangements of the already good soundtrack of the original game.- Good translation and adaptation that perfectly captures the goofy humour of the characters and their attitudes.- Extremely easy, linear and railroaded. The plot is not that good that you can appreciate the game always pointing you on the right track instead of letting you explore more.- The "roguelite" structure makes it really repetitive. Procedural generation of the levels probably would not have worked, but the variations in levels are so minimal and you'll have to revisit them so many times in order to buy the required stuff from the machine, that you're going to get bored after a couple hours of always doing the same stuff.- The 4 new endgame areas are just rehashes of the previous ones.- Several buyable items are just cosmetic stuff that don't really change the gameplay in any way. When you have enough money and cans to buy the TV item that supposedly makes the game harder, not only the game is already close to the end, but there seems to be no difference in difficulty at all.- Characters' special moves are irrelevant (being buyable and, again, optional). The game is so easy that you will never need to use Hebe and Sukezaemon's special attacks, and by the time you get O-chan and Jennifer's special ability to reach cans in hard places, you've probably catched so many of these that you won't care to use them. Unless you're a completionist, but there's not even an achievement for that.- The achievement for gaining 50K coins at once is absurd and just a means to artificially increase the game's length, since it's way more than you need to buy all the stuff put together.- Not about the game itself, but it's not good that there's no option in the menu outside of changing the language, not even for the volume or screen resolution, or multiple save slots if you decide to start over.- The barrel cat/smiley face boss is missing.- The Donadona enemies (crawling guys on the giant tree) no longer spare Sukezaemon when he's crawling towards them.- Hebe clones/doppelgangers are present in other games, so it would make more sense to fight them in the boss rooms once you defeated your friends, instead of having to fight your friends' clones even if they are in your party already (mirror matches included).This is all... I would've preferred an 1:1 remake with new graphics or a totally new sequel instead of this strange and boring reboot/sequel hybrid.

_childDocuments_.review: I had an amazing time playing Ufouria: The Saga 2.The world of Ufouria is truly unique and you can tell how much personality the game itself has. The characters are charming and their dialogues and interactions are super cute and funny.  The UI is extremely polished and original, making menu navigation really enjoyable.The gameplay is really straightforward, you go exploring various platforming areas and collect coins you can use later in your HUB to buy upgrades in a vending machine. These upgrades can help you progress in new areas and even power up your characters. There is a boss fight at the end of each area too.I personally enjoyed the audio, it seemed fitting for the game atmosphere and the sound effects felt accurate.It took me around 5 hours to finish the main story while collecting various achievements. I still have some things to do in the game to obtain all achievements.The game felt extremely polished and I didn't find bugs during my playthrough.Most importantly: I had a LOT of fun playing this game. I totally recommend it to anyone who likes simple platformers and vivid game worlds.Looking forward to seeing more of the world of Ufouria and its characters in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: yeah i dont know about this one. its carried entirely by its novelty. you play as some platforming mascot rejects who buy their character upgrades through a vending machine. everything is just at face value which is pretty funny. the music is great but its just remixes of the first game's music which just goes to show how great 8-bit music can be at setting the mood.but man the gameplay can get boring. the level design is NES tier random platforms and enemies everywhere. eventually it just turns into a coin grind. overall this game is worth it for its charm and it does try its best to carry the game. but it's definitely overpriced for what you get, i would say it's worth maybe $15.
