_childDocuments_.review: If it feels more like a DLC that is because it technically is. It is a Standalone Expansion like Dragon Age Awakening was so you do not need the Original game to play it. The price point also reflects this. Do I recommend it? YesIs it better than the first? NoIs it dumbed-down mechanics? YesIs it less rpg and choices? YesIs the story convoluted? Yes but so was the first one. Is the battle system the same? Yes but not as fun. AOE is essentially gone. Are the classes the same or better? No. They are different. The only element is fire with some poison shots and electric random damage if you choose the LAR for it.Did I still enjoy it? YES!I hope they make more content in this series.

_childDocuments_.review: It was incredible to hear that King Arthur: Knight's Tale was getting a sequel, unfortunately, this game failed in every aspect to improve or innovate on any of the ideas and actually managed to simplify and remove ideas that made the original so incredible.The Pros -        - The combat still feels great       - The art style hasn't changedThe Cons -        - Just about everything is a reused asset from King Arthur: Knight's Tale       - The game offers almost nothing new, the one thing that was introduced were "UItimates" and even then they are           very generic and uninspiring       - The voice acting is atrocious and sounds like a generic AI prompt the entire game        - The Morality chart is just a slider from Good to Evil and the benefits to either side are negligible       - There are 6 characters in the entire game that are forced upon you with no choices to be made       - Your town is incredibly bland and uninspiring       - Some missions are literally reused exactly from King Arthur: Knight's Tale       - "Side Missions" are actually mandatory and don't really offer anything besides some loot which is majority of the           time sub par       - Overall skills for each character have been reduced        - Your characters cannot get injured and full heal in between missions automatically           (This can be seen as a positive for some but I did enjoy the injury mechanic from the first game.)       - The game only manages to introduce 2 new enemies that ultimately are just re-skins of enemies from the first           game. Even then you are still fighting Picts, Knights, Fomorians, Seelie/Unsellie the majority of the game.Overall it feels as if no one wanted to work on this title. This game should have been sold as a DLC to King Arthur: Knight's Tale and not as a stand alone.The game offers around 20 hours of content for a play through, I would only recommend buying this game on a decent sale which is a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Challenging tactical combat with different difficulties to choose from. Some encounters propose different approaches to be defeated, and it makes for interesting tactical approaches.- It offers an alternative story with a varied cast of historic figures, and a variety of morale choices- It's mostly bug free, with nothing game-breaking, which makes for a smooth gameplay experience.Cons:- Most of the maps and enemies are reused from King Arthur: A Knight's Take, so it's basically different encounters and story with the same assets. It's basically a DLC marketed as a stand alone game, but even then, most DLCs usually offer new asssts. This game does not.- Very poor QoL. You can't organize your inventory, you can't see what talents or gear you have equipped during missions, you can't even see what value you have on some crucial stats like Dodge or Double Damage. In general, it feels like it has been made with laziness and disinterest. - The missions are quite lower quality than King Arthur: A Knight's Tale, and the voice acting is also worse. A lot of things have been simplified, and rarely in a good way. In general, a worse experience.I can't recommend this game for anyone in general. If you're a die-hard fan of TB RPGs, there is a niche for you here, but there are also plenty of alternative that offer more, especially in the QoL department.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: An underwhelming DLC (sequel?) to a good gameGOOD: the setting, undead Roman legionRespeccing your characters have never been easier, might be even too good. I wouldn't mind if the game had a gold cost applied after the first respec.Customizable difficultyBAD: horrible voice acting, your undead Romans sound like a bunch of hipsters grabbing a morning coffee at Starbucks. How did this pass QA is beyond meOnly six characters, should have been at least eightBuilding bonuses and progression (except blacksmith) is an insult even to my low intelligence, I could design a better system in a day probablyA lackluster morality systemThe devs making story choices for you like killing of a certain prisoner, even though you made dialogue choices to keep him alive and promised to RELEASE him ALIVE. Lararium is a TRAP. You might think that Lar statues give you interesting choices, but playing WITHOUT them was a better experienceWhere is Sir Tewelyn???MIXED: classes and skills - just meh, not bad, but not good either; most items weren't great, even the relic onesMISSED OPPORTUNITIES: importing a save from the previous game that reflects our choices and shapes the story in this gameHOW TO FIX: Add at least two more characters, a caster and ranged dps. But another tank would be also goodRedesign morality system and add a third progression line Undeath. So instead of a horizontal line we get ∆ or three-pronged star. Storywise it could work as following: 1) Demonic means following your Big Bad Boss, i.e. Emperor Sulla; 2) Humanity means working towards an alliance with the Knights of the Round Table; 3) Undeath means uniting your forces with Sir Tewelyn to create your own Undead kingdom in AvalonUse AI to tweak existing voice lines and add new onesAdd a toggle to skip all in-game cutscenes, they aren't worth re-watchingCONCLUSION: Almost in every aspect this game offers less than its predecessor and it's a case of less not giving you more.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome so far! Much harder than expected and many surprises, which is good. Playing on very hard though. Atmosphere is great and characters have pretty unique skills. I don´t care about the story in this game. King Arthur already had bad writing but since you can easily skip all dialogues very fast this doesn´t matter. This game is about gameplay and characters and they nailed it. They improved a lot since King Arthur. AI is much better and much more challenging. If you play on harder difficulties, you have to plan really well without the game being unfair. King Arthur was very easy, even on very hard. Of course people can complain that there is less content than in King Arthur but it is also much cheaper and planned as a DLC. The missions are linear here but usually longer than King Arthur. I just finished 5 and I am already 10+ hours in. You can do so much micromanagement after each mission because all characters level up and you get many ressources while many missions in the original game were just fillers. I am usually busy in the city for quite a while between missions.And the big PLUS: You play undead romans. You even have an undead roman vestal that can summon fire birds. _childDocuments_.review: Like many other have said, I wish I could give a sideways thumb or something. I was so hyped for this game, and maybe that's my fault, but this just feels like a downgrade overall from the original game. This isn't by any means a terrible turn-based game. However, when compared to the original, King Arthur: A Knight's Tale, Legion IX leaves so much to be desired it's downright saddening. The game itself without comparison is solid. It's a great turn-based game with excellent tactical camera capabilities, hero builds, and even morality/decisions to change your adventure. The game-play, items, leveling system, and general base upgrades feel and look the same as the original, characters even seem a little more involved with the story, but man I am just so disinterested. I'll finish it, eventually, and then maybe I'll go play Knight's Tale again to finally get around to being a good guy.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure if this was supposed to be a proper sequel, but it certainly felt more like an expansion to King Arthur: A Knight's Tale than anything else. Whatever it was supposed to be, it didn't hit the mark. Most of the visuals, characters, enemies, and mechanics are recycled from the first game. Other than some Roman costumes for the new heroes and a Roman reskin of the player's base everything looks and plays exactly the same. It definitely sounds worse than before, though, because the voice acting is terrible this time around. Most of the dialogue revolves around badly timed jokes, poorly conceived banter between friends, and badly executed insults between enemies. Some of the actors sound completely bored with their roles.The story doesn't make any sense either. Here we have a handful of Roman warriors who have clawed their way out of the underworld and constantly refer to themselves as demons and vanguards of the Ninth Legion yet the story relies upon a morality system where you're supposed to choose between kindness and  brutality without ever actually giving you the chance to embrace either one. There are six new heroes, but for "story reasons" you will spend a significant chunk of the game fielding five at most. Words like "conquer" get tossed around a lot even though the supposed conquest of Avalon takes place behind the scenes and has no impact on gameplay. Worst of all, the Ninth Legion itself never makes an appearance outside of cutscenes. Don't waste your time on this one.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed the other installment of King Arthur: Knight’s Tale, this somewhat shorter (and priced accordingly) sequel is easy to recommend. The game improves upon the shortcomings of its predecessor in some areas by allowing you to take more than 4 heroes on missions, and it’s refreshing to not feel so restricted and limited with party composition.  Unfortunately, you’re limited to a small number of heroes so your party doesn’t ever really change.  I honestly would have preferred to pay more for another full-fledged game—more characters to choose from, more story missions, expanded items and progression—but that’s more of a compliment rather than a critique.Speaking of, the base building in the first game felt lackluster and uninspired, and this trimmed-down experience doesn’t deviate much from that path. You never really get a sense that you are rebuilding or developing a town at all and it’s a bit of a letdown. I’m not expecting an X-Com Long War degree of detail in the base management portion of the game, but I would prefer if there were more meaningful choices to be made when it comes to upgrades, buildings, and assigning characters to tasks.  The town screen as a whole almost feels like it could be eliminated entirely and not much would be lost for how unrewarding it feels. The game is good, but improving this area of the game would really put it over the top for me into *great* territory. I’m hoping the developers take some of these lessons to heart as a lot of the elements of this game feel like a trial run for an inevitable Legion IX/Knight’s Tale follow up and I am looking forward to it.

_childDocuments_.review: The first King Arthur had it's issues but sadly, this game went backwards. The game play gets old pretty quickly with no new mechanics really added after the first couple missions. Additionally, the overworld management part of the game is incredibly boring and unimpactful. I generally love the management parts of games but there's no sense of growth or progression with it here.The worst part though is by far the writing and voice acting. I normally can tolerate both being subpar in a game but it's so bad here. The writing tries to be quippy and funny while the background is trying to sell a grimdark universe. One moment your character will say things like, "Yep, still dead." after you rest in camp or, "Wow, they're really trying to kill me!" (all while the text on screen doesn't match the actual words said at all) and then the next, they'll try and pitch you on super serious and threatening lines.The problem that makes all of that writing even worse is the voice acting. I honestly cannot tell if they used AI or if the voice actors were just terrible/poorly directed because it's the worst I've heard since late 90's/early 2000s games and terrible anime dubs. The voice actors aren't consistent at any point in a sentence, their tone never matches what the situation is, and they brutally mispronounce so many words. I'm honestly shocked that there was voice acting like this in a modern game.tldr; was interested in this game pre-release since I mostly enjoyed the first one, managed expectations so wasn't expecting more than an 8/10, was still disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: I have close to 1000 hours in King Arthur: Knight's Tale, and around 80 in Legion IX now (many hours of beta testing prior to launch!)I think is an innovative stand-alone expansion to King Arthur: Knight's Tale. It's certainly not a new game, but it delivers a unique and fun twist on the King Arthur formula.Here's the innovation: the game removes some of the strategy layer from the original King Arthur (injury system, permadeath, some of the more long-term resource management elements, scarcity of things like respecs, etc.) -- but leverages that to deliver a much more focused, complex, and challenging tactical experience. Because your characters can't permanently die, the devs have the ability to develop much more ambitious fights and much more wild enemy types -- you can use your heroes lives as resources to complete an encounter. They no longer have to balance encounters around the strategy layer of injury management -- instead, the game can focus on challenging fights.I think the result is something that feels truly unique and compelling to me as a veteran tactical RPG player. The new difficulty settings (Brutal and Brutal+ or Custom) are both phenomenal additions that greatly raise the ceiling for how far you can push your builds. Hero skill trees are completely new, with a lot of very creative and interesting skill choices to build around. They've taken many of the basic hero archetypes from KA:KT that were spread across close to two dozen heroes and refined them into 6 heroes with their own unique playstyle/interpretation of the archetype. And with the newly added free Skill Reset, you can constantly build and rebuild these characters to match new gear or to try new build ideas.Again, this makes for a game experience that stands apart from KA:KT in significant ways -- ways that, I think, improve the basic formula of the series for the better.And for $20 bucks, it's 30 hours of content for just one playthrough of the main campaign -- not counting the endgame or additional playthroughs. Huge recommend -- a game I will play and replay for a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: Salvete, legionarii!With all my time on this platform, I don't usually write my opinion about games, but I can't stay silent this time, due to my obsession with tactical games and products I wanted to see in better shape.I quite liked the main game, but I felt it is lacking a lot of QoL features, so I thought "this time they changed everything to better state". Oh boy, how I was wrong.This is not a separate game as the devs said, this is not an expansion like people write in other reviews. This is oversimplified mod / reskin of the main title. Done so lazy, my eye started twitching. The game has all the same assets: some maps were taken from the main title, same foes, skills, icons, mechanics as before, plus some small new features. Experience system was abolished and equipment lost it's level restriction, which fits new system actually. I got sapphires as a drop, that never used anywhere, because the forging mechanics was simplified, lol. Another bugs? There are, but not critical. Loyalty system is unnecessary due to some plot twist happening anyway. Ah, yes, thanks for taking away relic equipment I was choosing so well (won't spoil more).Devs said there will be 30 hours of play and taking in account my speed of sloth I thought it will take 50+. However, I finished campain on hard in 14 hours and it felt easy after playing the main title. There is no replayability for me, last mission doesn't count. Endgame "exists", but meh, you don't get any more levels and can't fill the loss of your contubernium members.I actually liked the idea of the story and how the two games can intertwine together. But implementation is bad. That's a huge step back.Optimo precāre, sed pessimum parā.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tale of revival, resurrection and revenge; the chronicle of how the greatest adversary of King Arthur came into power – and the terrible price he had to pay.Our journey begins in Eboracum, in one of the greatest cities built in the Roman provinces of Britannia. But that was a long time ago, and Eboracum slowly turned into a magnificent graveyard of marble palaces, populated by the living, breathing ghosts of a fallen empire. Until a young monarch in the south, a Briton called Arthur pulled the enchanted sword out of the stone and changed everything.And now, after the catastrophe has struck in the south and the Once and Future King lies wounded, the time is right to make the former provinces great again. The fate of the Romans lies in the hands of a noble man called Septimus Sulla. Betrayed and full of anger, he embarks on his quest to restore the glory of Eboracum. Nothing will deter him: he will wage war against both the savages of the north and his fellow nobles; he will unearth the secrets of Hadrian’s Wall and he will even venture into the mists of the underworld to find to the fabled ghost legions of Rome.

It's still a good story with exceptional gameplay, but its not as epic or big or tactical as the base game.So with that being said, King Arthur: Legion IX is worth its money. NeocoreGames created a fantastic combat, resource and armor system, making the King Arthur series maybe the best turn-based strategy game from a gameplay perspective. _childDocuments_.review: Full Gameplay Walkthrough - Invading King Arthur’s realm in Avalon with an army of zombie Romans was not on my to-do list for 2024 initially, but you know what? There’s a first for everything. I can confidently say I’ve never played a game in a setting like this one before. It’s a nightmare version of the dream of an Eternal Rome that will have you make some tough choices: Will you embrace your demonic side or restore your humanity?Combat reminds me of Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader a little in that enemy waves often outnumber you by a shocking scale, though many foes are simple cannon fodder to get that power fantasy of being an undying Roman demon soldier across. Look, as a self-confessed Romeaboo, that works for me. That said, you can ramp up the game’s difficulty and actually face some really tough challenges, so there’s room for those enjoying a hardcore run and those just being there to relax a bit.Legion IX’s combat really rewards good positioning and planning. Since all of your characters can take action at the same time on the player’s turn, you can set up powerful maneuvers and use everyone’s abilities to their fullest without having the enemy ruin your plans – of course, all foes will take their own turn at the same time as well, so you’ll always need to be prepared for a mass of attacks coming your way.You can change up your overall style quite a bit with different equipment and buffs gained from your settlement – for example, there is one buff you can activate that gives all your characters lifesteal in combat, but prevents you from healing at campfires during missions. Aside from the resting places, mission maps will include some puzzles, hidden treasures, and shrines to get temporary buffs from – overall, it feels quite rewarding to scout every last corner, especially as you sometimes can begin encounters from a more favorable position by going to them from a different direction.King Arthur: Legion IX is a solid RPG with crunchy and satisfying turn-based combat that takes place in a setting you won’t soon forget – a bit janky and rough around the edges, but good fun.Score: 7/10Version tested: PC

_childDocuments_.review: You take control of Gaius Julius Mento, a Roman Tribunus and his group of companions and lead incursion to Avalon. There is also big endgame content where you clash swords with all knights and heroes from previous game.Core content are missions on almost identical maps from original game and fighting same enemies and bosses. You can usually field all heroes (5-6) and fights tend to be bigger. You have few upgradable buildings in your city and less character maintenance (no training/healing). _childDocuments_.review: I bought this game as soon as it came out, taking advantage of the special launch offer discount for owners of King Arthur Knight's Tale, a game I wrote an enthusiastic review about. It has to be said that this is more KAKT light than KAKT II; while being fully playable as a stand-alone game, it feels more like an excellent DLC, or even more precisely a mod, than a full fledged sequel. The game is basically the same, just more streamlined and much shorter (which does not mean simpler). While the tactical level, which was the core of the main game, is still deep and gratifyingly challenging, the strategical level, which was a bit of a weak point, is now almost completely gone. Not having to worry about persistent injuries and having just six characters takes away much of the strategical challenge. Also replayability is a lot lower, as there are no mutually exclusive heroes to recruit, and the moral axis is reduced to two sides. Also the plot is a lot more superficial, and the heroes have a more generic feel. Which is pretty logical, not having the Camelot mythos to back them up. However, there still are 20+ missions, so this game still offers good value for money, just not as good as the original. I also noticed that while in KAKT the missions after completing the main storyline presented a big difficulty spike, here, on the contrary, they seem for now rather easy, while the hardest challenges were in the first few missions. I still have to fight Morded himself at the time of writing however. In conclusion, I can recommend this game. But if you do not yet own it, go buy KAKT first!

It misses many of the things that made the original game worthwhile, it's shallow.If you loved the original games tactical gameplay, tis for you.But for enjoyers of the original game, it may be missing a lot of what made that game special.
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: Voice acting sounds like it was made with AI, along with some weird humor that doesn't work with this kind of setting.Everything except pure combat is downgraded. Only 6 heroes where you can use all of them in every mission except for a few. Morality chart is just good or bad with very little incentives either way. Nobody can die or even get injured, so basically zero risk in combat. Also very poor performance. I'm using a 2070 super and even on the lowest settings I can barely get 40fps.
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, if you liked King Arthur: Knight's Tale then it's basically another 20-30+ hours of a similar experience. The smaller focus on a core team of 6 characters and a more focused story is definitely a plus. If you didn't like King Arthur: Knight's Tale due to the commitment and length then give this game a try. For 20$ it's definitely worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: Put 60 hours into "Knights Tale" to prep for Legion IX as I was stoked for this release. I am not very far into it but it *feels* like the other game in the series in terms of atmosphere and UI making it feel more like an expansion and the price reflects that as well, note this is not a negative. I love the Roman theme and the characters feel authentic and different from any of the Knights of the Round making me very excited to see what is to come. I am enjoying it and see no future reason to feel otherwise.
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: So far, its a smooth and bugless experience of a really good turn based tactical rpg.You play as the undead reborn roman legionnaries of the 9th, on a mysterious fantasy island of avalon.If you played king arthur, this one is no different, the gameplay, mechanics and skills are pretty much alike.I would absolutely recommend this to any1 who likes games like pillars of eternity, xcom or similar great titles.The game was gifted to me, but i wouldnt change my review even if i bought it. Kudos to the devs, i wish all games would launch as smooth and bugfree as this one.
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: A great expansion to a great game! If you liked Knight's Tale, you'll probably like this one too. It's a lot shorter and, in some aspects, simpler than the main game, which is reflected in the price. Most of the negative reviews don't seem to realize that this is essentially a very big DLC, and as such, it delivers completely. I, for one, had my expectations fully met, and would love to see what else this series has in store for the future!
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed King Arthur: Knight's Tale, then you'll enjoy this. Most of the mechanics, gameplay, and levels are the same, just with new characters and a briefer campaign.Totally worth it for the low cost, good for a solid weekend. I'd be very happy to play another expansion if Neocore does this again.
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: If you liked Knight Tale, you'll like this one, it's the same but shorter, simpler, with new combo and synergies to discover.Completed the game, and End Game, in less than 15h in Hard. In retrospective, I should have cranked that up, the game was pretty easy, and the moment I hit full humanity, I ended every mission with more life than I started with, even the last boss.For those who didn't play the predecessor, it's a fantasy square base tactical game. Using Action Point and Movement Point as ressources, you have a set number of specific skills per characters. The format work well, and each character is pretty unique in it's gameplay intension, and you'll have a decent amount of variety of build and synergies to come up with. To note, this opus doesn't offer the possibility to swap characters, there's 6 and that's it.In the end, the game is shorter, but also denser, everything is open at the start, every skill's available, and you can respec at will, legendary gear come pretty quickly, and there's no health management between mission, you just get a faster, neater, more restrain version of the previous game, which frankly isn't bad.I would recommend aiming for hard or higher for anybody that did beat the first game, the free respec, high access to legendary equipment, and lars combo can make the game pretty easy. For context, as I said, beat the game in less than 15h in hard. Every missions I finished with more vitality than I started with, I have not rest in a camp or use a potion for my entire playthrough passed the second mission.
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: This game is even better than the orginal.Played whole day yesterday and did not encounter any bugs.New heroes their abilities are interesting. Maps even tho reused a lot make sense in new plot.Everything feels fresh and well polished.Been playing on hardest difficulty and the challenge is there.I like there is no grind in this game, just planning guilds and executing strategy. GG!
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the new characters and their play styles. The story was good for the 15 hours or so for a single play through completing the initial story mode. I did the good play through first and just started the evil play through. I m looking forward to pushing the limits as both good and evil and the future DLC hopefully will bring some fun fights :)
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: I'm having fun with it. There are a few things I like better than knights tale and others that I like less. Some of the simplifications might be good thing actually. Voice acting is not great as they say but it's ok, yup, sounds like it may be AI generated? I recommend it if you liked the first one or you like the roman setting. Will update this once I finish it.
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't an improvement from the first very slow combat (u need to press and hold a button to speed it up) I fixed it with a toggle macro anyways the graphics feel outdated and the writing is very cheesy and bad, the walking speed is very slow, bad map, I think all the money went towards the intro movie and then the game itself.
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: 6.5/10A solid Turn-Based game. The story is interesting enough to cause me to want to see more, although not interesting enough to be driven toward. I did not play what appears to be the prequel to this game, but the themes are very familiar to any Arthurian legends fan. Nothing really new, just a rehash of the old.The mechanics are good, no issues other than the seemingly random 'backstab' bonus that opponents receive. There is a sense of repetitiveness to the game, which brings a bit of boredom after 3-4 missions in a row. There is a very real sense of "Oh boy, here we go again doing the same thing as last mission."All in all, a good outing and worth the price of admission.
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review:
King Arthur: Legion IX is a turn-based, character-centric tactical RPG in the King Arthur: Knight's Tale universe - a dark fantasy version of the Arthurian myth.

Play through a Roman-themed campaign as Gaius Julius Mento, a tribune of the undead Ninth Legion, as he discovers Avalon. Battle the monsters of nightmares, challenge the Pict tribes, the monstrous Fomorians and the cunning Sídhe. Experience the might of the Old Faith and Christianity and face the knights of Sir Mordred's Round Table through 15 handcrafted missions.

Find, rebuild and protect the remains of the only Roman colony in Avalon and choose your path to victory. By the end of the campaign, you'll have to choose: do you want to become a powerful demon, or will you reject the might of Emperor Sulla and restore your humanity?
_childDocuments_.name: King Arthur: Legion IX

_childDocuments_.review: The game is made for multiplayer. I bought this game to play it as singleplayer. The only way to play singleplayer is by playing 1 vs 1 games. Come on! I want to play a huge game with lots of AI players, but that is not possible. I don't have time to play multiplayer. I consider myself lucky if I'm able to play 30 minutes without interruption. The AI in the game is also very dumb. Good luck getting them to build up an army. All they do is build up a few soldiers, but once you have defeated them, they will not build any more soldiers, even though you don't destroy any of their buildingsThe game also contains no randomized maps. It only comes with a few select maps. I saw earlier it was mentioned the reason for this is the landmarks they have put in the game. Those landmarks are places where if you do something, you get something. For example some places they could give you some stones if you give them a hammer. These landmarks in my opinion just makes the game worse. Please feel free to remove them from the game, to make the game more funOne thing I always loved about some of the earlier Settlers games was the exploration. Not knowing how the map looked like or where you could put what kind of mine is one of the important parts of the game series. Here you know from the start where everything is. There's nothing left to exploreI also hate the fact that food production is not as important as it used to be. In the old Settlers games, you couldn't mine anything, if you didn't have a good food production. Here food production just gives you a bonusOn the positive side, it does look great
_childDocuments_.name: The Settlers: New Allies

_childDocuments_.review: As already said in many other reviews: not a Settlers game, not worth the full price.It's just a fighting game now (which is apparently called a RTS).I'm at the level 3 or 4 of the campaign and this is why I'm so disappointed, after years of waiting for a new edition of The Settlers:- the only focus for the player is to raise military units as big and as fast as possible.- resources management has almost disappeared from the game, economy and basic needs (food chain, etc) are not that important to maintain your colony happy or efficient.- The depth and complexity of the previous Settlers is clearly missingIt looks like all the dev efforts were put on making new awesome graphics.Because honestly, this is the only positive thing I can mention about this version of "The Settlers": it's a very pretty but empty shell. Bummer!At least I got it on sale..I still can't figure out how Ubisoft can justify its full price tho.This game will just stay in a corner of my Steam library, collecting dust while I play Pioneers of Pagonia.
_childDocuments_.name: The Settlers: New Allies

_childDocuments_.review: Honest review from someone who has played all the settlers games, this, and the new tales of pagonia (created by the original settlers dev)5.5/10Would recommend simply due to the amount of content in the campaign and while it's on sale. would never have paid more for it.The downfall of this game is having settlers in the title. This alone is enough to rile players, because it is not and should never have shared the settlers title. if they renamed it they'd probably have more positive reviews.The gameplay is shallow but enough to keep you progressing. It's mostly focused on military, which again is limited. The economy is bare bones. Everything can be built with wood and stone, for some unknown reason. There's very little complexity to the economy system, which is its downfall. Oh and lets not even mention the awful story narrative and voice acting. the campaign story itself was garbage.That said tales of pagonia was even worse, i know it's in Alpha but it will need years of content to even match this or become what it's supposed to be.Nice little time waster, but a quick uninstall from me once completing, can't imagine i'd want to come back and play again unless they released a huge DLC pack and actually diversified the different cultures buildings, economy and military, rather than a reskin. Added a bunch of complex economy systems, and refined the military actions.
_childDocuments_.name: The Settlers: New Allies

_childDocuments_.review: This has got to be the biggest pile of garbage ever produced by Ubisoft. The balance factor for missions is non existent.My current mission is to defeat the enemy but blueprints will disappear after a certain amount of time:1) After 2 minutes you will no longer be able to build the toolmaker and the guild. 2) After 5 minutes you will no longer be able to build mines, defense towers or houses to get more settlers.Dear Ubisoft... NEWSFLASH: It takes 4 minutes 30 seconds to expand the territory to even get to a point on the map where you can build a mine. 3) Even if you are able to build the mines the enemy will attack at the 10 minute mark so you have 5 minutes to build the mines, build the forge and build the blacksmith and the training grounds to create troops by the 10 minute mark.I've tried every way possible:A) Make a gold mine and mint coins and buy armor to create troops after building a harbor.B) Build the iron mine and charcoal mine to create your own weapons and armor to recruit troops.I was finally able to create 20 archers as I thought maybe I could snipe and kill a few enemies at a time and retreat back.Now for the absolute best part and biggest joke about this stupid game. I had 20 archers firing at a single warrior and it did zero damage.Tell me Ubisoft, who is designing your current games? I would rather go back and play Settlers 7 with its ridiculous combat system.Do not waste your money on this piece of garbage!
_childDocuments_.name: The Settlers: New Allies

_childDocuments_.review: First, the positive. I think this game has some beautiful artwork and good music. Also, the menus and UI in general are very well made, imo, and feel smooth to interact with and can be easily navigated and understood with their clear structures. During gameplay, I felt like the scale of the game just felt right. the size of the maps, the size of units and buildings and the max amount of them. I never felt unnecessarily and artificially restricted. I feel like there have been some talented people working on this.However, there's a lot missing in this game, most of all a unique selling proposition. There is nothing this game has or does that you cannot get in a better form with some other title.I was disapointed that there are whole sections of buildings that are quasi useless. Decorations serve no purpose, food is only used to boost production in some buildings, should you choose to do so, making the whole food production chain and its buildings optional. I did not expect much, but I thought there would at least be some population or settlement management mechanics. Without anything like that, the only thing you can do is build troops and crush the other player on the map. Which makes it puzzling to me why this game even has a creative mode where you are alone on the map, if there is nothing to do.But also the military in this is not very deep. There are 7 unit types, which is ok i guess, but they all use the same ressources. So you either get those resources fast or you don't get any troops. There is no possibility to build a mass army of cheap soldiers, if you don't have access to better ressources, and of course also no possibility to build an elite force if you have a prosperous economy and fancy resources.The campaign is not great, not terrible, but it feels like they put it in after they had already decided what the game is going to be, not that the game would be built around the story, like a user made campaign, where they used the game's existing assets to tell teir own story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Settlers: New Allies

_childDocuments_.review: I used to be a fan of the old Settlers games, particularly the ones that came out on the Commodore Amiga and eventually on PC, such as Settlers II and The Settlers II 10th Anniversary. These were the original ones I played (and still do) until the series took a different direction.This new game comes close to the old days but still falls short in some areas. For instance, the AI doesn't expand its land and only tries to attack with its army, which is easy to wipe out. However, I wouldn't say it's a terrible game; it has its moments.What I don't like are the microtransactions in the game, and I miss the large maps and a map maker. I wouldn't recommend buying this game at full price; instead, wait for a big sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Settlers: New Allies

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals and the audio are well done. But it's not anything new that you haven't played before. In fact, the units are fairly simplistic: archer, defender, attacker, healer, siege and race special. It requires setting up a Ubisoft ID, even if you plan to play offline. The micro transactions don't make much sense, nor do the gems and xp meters. It might be entertaining if you haven't played many RTSs in the past. Otherwise, I'd skip.
_childDocuments_.name: The Settlers: New Allies

_childDocuments_.review: I spent hundreds of hours playing the previous version of Settlers, and I have to say, this new installment falls far short. The entire game feels excessively simplified, failing to live up to the legacy set by Heritage of Kings. I eagerly awaited its release, but unfortunately, I neglected to read reviews before making the purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: The Settlers: New Allies

_childDocuments_.review: After the very disappointing Open Beta, I wanted to give the game another try (since it was just on sale for 15 bucks), because supposedly a lot had changed since then.I didn't really notice that much change in terms of gameplay. The game still feels uninspired with superficial mechanics. The campaign, which after more than an hour still consisted of build this, get checkmarks, do that, get checkmarks, didn't impress me at all, and in PvE the AI is still very easy to defeat without much strategy, with minimal building effort.In theory, this Settlers game should be right up my alley. I like a manageable amount of goods, short production chains, and an AI that's not a hard nut to crack. But everything here is so streamlined that I can't get into any kind of creative flow, and I always feel like I'm being robbed of the very opportunities to play the game in a way that I would enjoy, and the charming sounds and mostly good graphics can't hide that fact.Maybe this game has something to offer for PvP players, but for me as a single player, the game has absolutely nothing to offer with its paint-by-numbers campaign and the underwhelming depth of both the building and RTS parts of the game. And that's still true, even if you forget that this is supposed to be a Settlers game that ties into the old parts. At least that's how it was announced back then.Personally, this game is not worth my 15 bucks or my time. There will be players who will enjoy it, but I can't recommend it as a Settlers game, as a (city) builder, or as an RTS.
_childDocuments_.name: The Settlers: New Allies

_childDocuments_.review: Let's be honest, this is NOT a Settlers game. It is in the same genre, but it's far enough that it shouldn't have the same name. At a 67% discount (so a price of $20) you can think of it as a decent indie game that tries to mimic the franchise but that's about it.So if you see it for $20 or less, sure, give it a go and try to forget that it's called Settlers; but NEVER buy this at anything above $30, it's not worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game despite many negative reviews, and when it was on sale. I usually don't bother writing reviews, but I'm making an exception here because I feel bad for Ubisoft and think this game deserves a better rating. For people who played the latest editions of Settlers, this game could be a surprise because it's very different in terms of graphics and multiplayer options. As someone who played one of the first editions of Settlers in my teens, I actually think Ubisoft goes back to the original Settlers very much in this game (engineers broaden the boarders manually, there are cute blue houses etc.) For me, it's the editions in between this one and the first one (like Settlers 7) that were a wild variation and a different game all together. That said, I enjoyed it just as much, it was at times really challenging strategically, especially with the ressource management which is an element not present in this game. New Allies is a different story all together, for now (29h in the game) it's slower-paced and relaxing, with the design really a pleasure to look at and a strong woman characters featured as leaders. I haven't experienced any bugs either, except for one when I had to click on a video twice for the game to move to the next stage. Overal, I'm really enjoying the game so far. I hope it will get more challenging as the story advances, but even if it doesn't, I won't regret my purchase for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fine on sale for $20. The skirmish mode is extremely bare bones, feels like a game demo or early access. _childDocuments_.review: I got this on a steep sale so I figured okay fine I'll check it out. Despite knowing it's not really a Settlers game and being a long time Settlers fan (tho they've all been mediocre to bad since #4). I really tried to like it, even evaluating it as a completely separate entity from the Settlers IP. But there's a bunch of baffling and not so baffling (about what we'd expect from Ubi) yet still bad decisions.So it's trying to be a more RTS focused game, yet the unit control is really awful. Imagine playing StarCraft but the units reacting 2 seconds after you give them an order, and half of your army standing around doing nothing when attack moving. Secondly, the game is extremely hurt by there being a 500 max population cap no matter how much housing you build. Now in a game like SC2 this isn't an issue, but here it's a massive problem because units, carriers, engineers (basically pioneers, geologists and all the other specialists rolled into one unit) all take from that shared population. In SC2 all you have outside of your army is some workers harvesting minerals and gas. Over here your entire economy runs on a massive workforce. A medium sized village (by earlier Settlers standards) can eat up almost the entire population cap of 500 just having enough workers to have some going idle. If they want a hard pop cap, it should be applied to the army alone. Third, defenses are absolutely mind numbingly overpowered for their cost. A tower only costs some rocks and wood, and a few placed together will wipe out armies unless microed around heavily. Armies that cost advanced resources. Fourth, I don't really agree with what some other people have said that food is optional. You don't need to use it, per se, but doubling the output of your buildings for easily available resources is massive. If it wasn't for the pop cap issues, you could run a fairly huge production line off of just one iron mine (1 iron mine doubled, serving two foundries that are doubled again, serving four blacksmiths). It's optional the same way spreading creep with creep tumors or injecting larva is in SC2 for Zerg. Aka not at all if you want to be competitive.Lastly, the story is god awful. Extremely dislikeable and irrational characters. Strong independent wamen types. This is the usual Ubisoft release where they're just running down a diversity checklist and not really creating any good characters or story. And characters accept completely unreasonable statements because they just automatically have to defer to whatever the indigenous people/wamen say and so on.If all of these things were addressed, you'd have at least a decent game on your hands. Although not really a Settlers game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Settlers: New Allies

_childDocuments_.review: No idea what all the negative reviews are about and that it's not like other settlers games.  It's reminiscent of the original games.  Settlers 1, 2 and 3 back in the 90's.  A lot less complex than the more recent games though, but I couldn't be happier that the Victory Points system is gone.  It has for now at least, 4 levels in.  Those that it was nothing like settlers are very wrong, have short term memories or never played the originals. I did heed some advice from one of the comments and wait til it's on sale, I did that but would've gladly have paid full price now I'm 15-16 hours in.Yes there's lots of fighting, no there's not much strategy in the fighting, biggest army wins (just like every settlers game ever), but the strategic warfare isn't why you buy settlers now is it!?   Most of my time spent on this so far has been creating the settlement, the economy, the resources.  You don't need to dive in to the fighting straight away.If you're a fan of the originals, then get it.  If you're a whiny bell end, or prefer epic strategies, then it's probably not for you.  Although I'm all for an epic strategy game when the mood suits.
_childDocuments_.name: The Settlers: New Allies

_childDocuments_.review: The Settlers has been butchered, it has become a monster. This game is riddled with MTX, poor gameplay, no Australian server support (it keeps desyncing and you cannot recover as there is no online saving). The people they have working at this studio have absolutely ZERO respect for The Settlers games. ZERO. Instead you have what has become a weak amalgam of a city builder meets an RTS game. It does NOTHING different for the genres. Its just the absolute minimum of both put together and called Settlers. The only positive things I have to say are that the graphics are quiet nice and working very smoothly for me, I know this isnt everyones experience, but I have the hardware for it. The worlds feel so bland and empty however, vert lazily made. Zero feeling of ambience for the environment, its just kinda there. The campaign so far (because online coop is absolutely atrocious) is what I have spent my time playing, and I must say its a good campaign so far. Im only on Act 1 but they seem to have put alot of work into it. And I do appreciate it for what it is.In saying all that, this game is no city builder with complex economical prodution lines. It is the bare minimum that The Settlers could be, and for that reason I would no recommend you spend more than $15 USD on it. And 100% do not pay for the MTX rubbish.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot of good here. Some interesting ideas with a city-builder RTS that I haven't seen before.The big problem is the price and the current state of the game. The game REGULARLY crashes, it's infuriating to constantly lose your progress with your city. _childDocuments_.review: This game is seriously horrible, first of all like every Ubisoft Game it is required to install their crappy launcher. I hate Ubisoft Connect with passion.But I played the Settlers the first time when I was 6 years old. I really love the series. But this game just seems like Ubisoft tried to make a quick buck by creating a sloppy and loveless reboot.For me on Linux I had horrible performance and stutters the entire time. It always changed my resolution to 4k even tough I have a 1440p display. And even worse, the settings menu got stuck on my screen and I had to Alt + F4 to play the game again.I played the game with friends, this game makes that process horrible as well. You are not able to play a  game that is not 1vs1, 3x3, 2x2 or 4x4. We were 3 people, so we had to wait for a forth to join from the random player queue. After the 5 min ran out without me connecting my entire settlement got removed. What the hell where they thinking?Even Settler 2 had that functionality and that game is from 1996. _childDocuments_.review: The game could have been lukewarm enough for a positive review. However the Steam overlay and Ubisoft connect conflict turns this into a thumbs down. The Ubisoft crash launches often, often enough that Ubisoft's technical support has it's own dedicated advice site to solving the problem by deleting the Ubisoft folder at the local app data. However that treats the symptom, not the root cause. Usually I can expect anything to +10 crashes a day, worst being blue screens. This conflict only seems to happen when playing the settlers through steam.  Then there's the choice between the pest and the plague, as I noticed that disabling the Ubisoft game overlay allows me to play the game indefinitely without crashes. However then It is replaced with another bug where I cannot exit the game . So when I hard quit the game the saves are not synched, as I found out after losing few hours of ingame progress more often than once. So hopefully I get to proceed the game usually in 10-15 minutes intervals before I get the message about ubisoft detecing an unresolvable error, and having to shut down.  Gameplaywise. I remember how older installments of the game used to have this philosophy of certain professions having to be easily recognizable. Like (meat) smokers house would look like smoking house, with the worker looking like walking cigar with singed black hair and all that. Most of the buildings in THIS game look generic and similiar to each other, with uniform color themes and bland worker routines. The game has 3 - different biomes, where the professions are still the same, but building "skins" are different, at least there was a little bit of creativity in creating 3 - different styles for same type of building, but in a different surrounding.  The combat Ai meets the minimum, though it has these silly moments where I target enemy, and the enemy and my units bumb to each others trying to run past each other.Following the movement in the settlement itself is satisfying enough. With one settler being for each task, or idling. On other games like Anno 1800 you can have the lively city population with alot of population going through this "theater" of daily live. In this Settlers everyone occupied is doing excactly that, which I like to follow. Though sometimes it feels a little bit silly to look at this idiot conga line spanning through my settlement, when for example I sell 200 units of wood , and 200 settlers start moving the  wood, one piece each, leading to this long line where they politely wait on one road to the harbor to unload that one piece of timber.  Granted you will be able to get donkey carts that can move 8 - units of anything, which helps to avoid congestion like that. But sometimes I still don't use them because I simply enjoy watching the Hell's traffic jam  that is suddenly having several hundred settlers moving several hundred products at the same time.Speaking of delivering. If the delivery is interrupted, it is not picked up from where it is interrupted. I had build a watchtower relatively far from closest storage, and it would take roughly 3 - minutes for a settler to deliver the stone needed for construction. Only the settler got intimidated by enemy military unit and runs away. So when they start re-carrying the material, it's a different settler, and all the way from the storage all over again from the start, not for example from where the carrying process was previously interrupted. Also other lacking life quality improvements. Like It would be nice to be able to queue research, and not having to click them one by one everytime research is finished.

_childDocuments_.review: Would not recommend at full price. At 75% off? Go for it.I play single player exclusively so, naturally, this review is for SP mode only. The game world is beautiful and overall it reminded me of Warcraft (the old games, not the WoW abomination). It’s accessible, relaxing and easy. Compared to the previous titles in the franchise, this game is what we nowadays politely call streamlined. The Castle and the Cathedral are gone with the wind. Only the Warehouse remains. Ir’s not upgradable but you can build multiple warehouses. Your army consists of swordsmen and archers supplemented by various specialists trained in the specialized advanced facilities. However, there is no Hero to lead your troops. There is a Sad Weak Guy called the Guildmaster, his Strong Woman Cartographer assistant who looks like Ms. Shrek and who bosses the Guy around like there is no tomorrow, a couple of Allies and a misguided Bandit Queen. You just periodically watch cutscenes and that’s about it. Your input is not requested. As for the warfare, you cannot build any walls in this game, sadly, but the towers and some other structures placed strategically will protect your city quite well. Speaking of strategy, it’s not much different from the older games. You know the drill. Recruit a huge army while defending your own city, find a weak spot in the enemy defenses, destroy the enemy warehouse(s), win, profit.Academy is one of the best buildings available to you. Research done at the academy makes your troops basically invincible. Build it at the first opportunity.The main campaign is rather short and simplistic and heavily hints at the future expansion. The story itself is underwhelming, to say the least. Not that it was much better in the older games. The game offers a sandbox mode  if you just want to build a cute city and conquer a few bandit camps, and also some other modes. For the single player that means a few maps where you can compete with AI. These maps are rather small. I wish there were more maps (bigger and better designed, with less symmetry and predictability, maybe even procedurally generated) AND some interesting scenarios for us single players. There is a huge unrealized potential for a more enjoyable gameplay than is available right now, in my opinion. Overall, 7/10. Casual fun, don’t expect much depth.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay, but really not okay for 60 dollars.At least if you're like me and was more excited about the economy/building aspects of Settlers. It's a very pretty game with lots of little sounds and animations to help with the immersion, but the gameplay has completely diverted all attention into RTS mechanics and the like. Settlers don't even have to eat or have needs anymore, they just work and work and the food is meant to be used to help boost the buildings for a short time. Outside of surveying potential mining sites building a full city takes maybe few minutes which is just too fast for me to enjoy. The RTS mechanics are mostly just using waves of cheap soldier to kill towers (there are only a handful of unique soldier types, although it's a nice addition from previous titles).With them adding faction-unit cosmetic micro transactions (the day the game came out) and just the way many of the new mechanics work I feel they're trying to appeal to the online-versus community for longevity. They've also kept a working skirmish mode with multiple player-counts (1v1, 2v2, 3v3 and 4v4) which you can also play against bots, something other recent RTS games have for some reason neglected to have. TLDR: Overpriced RTS game, not really like the older games but trying to do some newer things with the IP. Good online multiplayer/AI skirmishing potential. The single player story is very basic and the tutorials will more than likely take over two hours if you do them all. Not for me but maybe someone else will like it.

_childDocuments_.review: The campaigns dialog is horrible. You cant customize maps, you can only play skirmishes against 1 ai by yourself. The worst part however is the supply chain. The way supply chains are handled is nothing short of atrocious. The most glaring issue is with the carriers, who don't seem to have any sense of locality or preferred warehouses. In a game where managing resources is key, you'd expect carriers to move goods efficiently between warehouses, especially when they are spread far apart. For instance, if you have warehouses A, B, and C, and a building site next to C, it would be logical for the supply chain to work as follows: wagons transport goods from A to B, from B to C, and then local carriers deliver them from C to the construction site.However, the system is even more flawed because wagons are unable to carry different kinds of goods at once. The whole point of using wagons should be to increase efficiency by carrying significantly more items (8 rather than 1) and moving faster. If a building requires 4 wood and 4 stone, you would expect a single wagon to handle the delivery. Instead, the game requires two separate wagons, one for each resource. In most cases, however, wagons aren't used at all. Instead of a single delivery by a wagon carrying 4 wood and 4 stone, the game opts for 8 individual carriers, each transporting just one item. This makes the supply chain almost 90% less efficient and utterly frustrating for players trying to manage their economy effectively.The overall supply chain management is even worse. Since carriers aren't local and don't prioritize nearby warehouses, you'll often see carriers trekking across the entire map, back and forth, picking up and delivering goods in the most inefficient way possible. Imagine a carrier walking from warehouse A (the starting warehouse), all the way to a production building near C, just to pick up a good, only to place it in warehouse C and then run all the way back to A. It’s mind-numbing and destroys any sense of logical flow in your economy.In a game that should be about careful planning and strategic management, the randomness and inefficiency of the supply chains turn every decision into a frustrating ordeal. If the developers don’t address these issues, it’s hard to recommend this game to anyone who values the core principles that "The Settlers" series was built upon.Edit: Seems like not even the selection of where to get resources from works correctly. When building and i guess in general the game doesn't select the closest warehouse where the required resource is available

_childDocuments_.review: Based on campaign so far:TLDR score: 7,8/10Decent mix of newer versions of Settlers and Northguard. Certainly not as bad as i expected due to the rather bad reception this game had.First of all: Great graphics! The feel and look of the game pays good homage to earlier settlers titles.The Boost system for foods, a toggle to get double outputs (I would've prefer older style with miners needing food or similar, feels very generic to just toggle on a button)I would've also preferred 3 separate campaigns, one for each faction, like the old games - You would start by learning each production line, units and different faction traits (at least the ones above basic chains) instead of having everything available basically from the start.The Academy for upgrades is a neat idea - However, I feel there's too many niche upgrades, maybe having a bit fewer and longer, more focused upgrades, would feel better. Also there's no ability to queue research, so you gotta go click the academy again every 30secs, depending on if you have the resource or not.Last point 60Euro price-tag seems steep, for a game that could still use some more balancing and gameplay polish.I would prefer if they leaned more towards the Settlers side, rather than the Northguard unit management with "Abilities and Spells"If you're into settlers games in general and can get it on sale (i paid 20euro) then i would definitely recommend Settlers: New Allies.Best Regards

Pros: - Beautiful graphics- new additions (not existing in previous games) have been worked seamlessly into the experience- Relaxed and stress-free gaming- Did not experience bugs or other technical issues- nice small improvements - easier to make roads, a farm only takes up the initial space (you don't have to account for additional fields), the addition of healersCons:- Campaign is very short,  missing additional maps- No way to speed up the clock- Difficulty level is too low- Far too many useless short cut-scenes with ramblings - they do not add to the story unlike cut-scenes in previous Settlers games. _childDocuments_.review: I loved Settlers 6, Rise of an Empire. I had issues with the 7th, yet was able to love it for that time.This iteration is a scam, a shame, it does not deserves to be a Settlers.The gameplay itself is fine, way less restrictive than it was for the 7th (pretty hard to get into it) while still being quite harsh compared to the 6th, that's not my main complain.The narration is a straight downgrade from the last iteration, no more no less than that, It doesnt make any sense, illogical, is sloppy at best, with little to no connexion between each stages. I've seen quite a few people say the graphics are alright... I disagree, not for 2024's standards. Yes, they are great when you compare them to previous game, but not that much. The 3D is pretty messy, but most of the game being played with an above view, it does not matter that much. What does matter tho, is that this view itself is quite lacking to be perfectly honest ! I 100% prefer the DA from the 6/7th, and the graphics are here comparable to a early 2010s game. Age of Empire IV came out a year ago and is leagues beyond that game, in a kind of game where the difference shouldnt be that drastic !I have no problems with Ubisoft ID or microtransactions as I am not a buyer of such stuff, and did not bother me when playing solo.The different factions feels a lot similar to me, without that big change I hoped from the "about this game" information.They do not differ that much in look, and their story is abysmall at best.The story driven campaign promised is a pure sham, with caracters with no substance, low effort, no charisma, a simply failed narration from start to finish.That game lacks both the narration, the gameplay (compared to the 7th, that one is just a disapointment), and did not held up its promises.I have received that game for free, gifted from my brother as it was a licence that was with us as we grew up. I feel sorry for him to have spend that much for both of us on that scam. Do not recommend above 5e/usd. Go play Settlers 7 or something else like Northgard...

_childDocuments_.review: This new Settlers branch is sold as a fully functional game. It is far from it. Exit function of the game is broken. The save functionality is broken. The game pretends to save the game in the gui. In fact the save is never made. Playing the game for several hours at the time will almost garanty you a game crash at least or a fully locked OS. For now I was just playing along with the campagne. Some chapters I had to play multiple times because of the crashes and the total screwed save/load functionality. I mostly could finish campagne chapters only by playing them straight through if managed to go without a crash. Sometimes I got lucky. Then the game would actually saved the actual state of the chapter. In which case I could continue were I left off. The game is maybe at the level of beta testing at best. Within the campaign it seems the game still needs working out the balancing.What I expected was a game that works without any issues on all levels. We all know why one should avoid assumptions, right. That will show me.PC specs: I9, 64GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 12GB, DirectX v12, SSD storage for OS and Steam storage.

_childDocuments_.review: I played all the old Settlers games back in the day.  This one was on sale so I bought it.  The cutscenes are boring.  The gameplay is OK but no boats so far.  Anyone who played the earlier games will be familiar with it but it feels more simplistic than I remember.  Graphics are fine but you cannot zoom in and out far enough.However an absolute game-breaker for me is that the manual saves mostly do not work.  Not only that but the game does not save when you go to the "leave" option as the screen promises.  It then does not let you quit without forcibly closing it via Steam.  When reloading all progress on a level is lost and the game goes back to the beginning of whatever level you ,have reached (I have only played single-player campaign so far).  Strangely the game saves worked on the first few levels but then stopped working.  All this means that for me to finish a level I have to do it all in one go.  As some take several hours, I am not prepared to do this so will not be playing the game any more until the save problem is fixed.I know I am not the only one with this issue - there are threads about it on Steam and other negative reviews highlighting the no save problem.  How Ubisoft have the brass neck to release a game that cannot be saved only they know.  I do not recall any similar issues with the old games so  maybe the interface between Ubisoft and Steam is the problem.I  would strongly recommend against buying this game atm unless the saving issue is fixed.Edit: The May 7 patch said "Fixed issue that could cause players getting stuck in Exit Game popup" - clearly not fixed (on Steam at least - see below) and no mention of save problem.  I have tried launching the game from the Ubisoft app rather than Steam and at least some of the time, the saves and exit screen are working so it would seem that something is going wrong between Steam and Ubisoft.  Edit 2:  Have now finished the Campaign and tried Skirmish mode vs AI and Sandbox (there are still some enemies in Sandbox).  Saves/Loads work OK as long as Steam not used, just Ubisoft.  Campaign needed more maps and more gameplay variation.  Suggest the devs have another look at the old games and incorporate some of the additional elements those games had into any updates. There is nowhere near enough content to justify the high price on Steam for this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Settlers: New Allies

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautiful game, the care and attention that has gone into crafting the models, textures and sounds is fantastic. However, all this promise is let down by: A badly crafted tutorial (Completely separated from the main campaign as a small series of minigames where it jumps back and forth between concepts early and late in the gameplay loop. Then expecting you to remeber all of that for when its time to put into practice. Why is this not a part of the campaign instead?). A horribly "homebrew chatGPT crafted" story in the campaign with soulless characters and weird disconnected/nonsensical dialog (Basically its about a skippy nonchalant archeologist ordering her tribes weak leader to attack and murder an infinit amount of settlements. So she can go sightseeing in ancient ruins, looking for her ancestors. Under the pretence that its ok because they are "pirates". Even though most settlements seem setup more like gentle farming communities).Repetative and quickly booring gamplay loop, with over simplistic production chains (1. Wall yourself in with towers and decoys 2. Farm resources 3. Build a huge army 5. attack and win. Rince and repeat).Lastly some specific annoying features: 1. Why cant you destroy roads in any other way than to place a building on it then cancelling?2. The hero mobs in the campaign are not introduced in any other way than, why did my 50 man army die trying to kill 5 bandits...3. The gameplay wiki in the game forgot descriptions of the buildings available.4. The scores at the end of a game have no desciptions of what they actually include. And you can win a game and still have a lower score than the opponent that lost.5. There is a real money shop. I dont really care, but some people dislike that sort of thing in a 60 euro game...Thats all of it I think, I wont be playing this again unless the game is changed in a fundamental way. But I think that is unlikely to happen.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not worth a settlers name for this game, There is only a campaign no scenerios.The game is heavily focused on fighting, towers are OP and you more or less need atleast 30 units to destroy a tower and getting the infrastructere takes time. The AI is not hard in any of the mission prioritize building 1 tower on each of your entries and you are golden for the rest of the game. So you can take your time to build up the necessary infrastructere.I hate the cutscenes in the campaign. The voice acting is bad, to say it mildly. The story is bad. I don't know why, but it feels like the voice acting is catering to social justice warriors. The BGM is bad they have these high pitched noices which makes you think you finished something important, but no that is just the BGM. I bought it 50 % off, which i to be fair I do not regret it is not much of a city builder but it is some. They have also improved upon the previous recipy. For instance you can now hire builders that are vulnerable to attack. you can move them in advance if you know you need to build in area so they don't start moving once you have started construction. It is also much appreciated that idle workers are the ones to collect material from shops and deliver it to the nearest warehouse.All in all, if you are a fan of the settlers series you will get disappointed. But if it is on sales and you have nothing better to do you can go for it. It is a decent game leaning towards the bad side. Every mission is a repetition. Didn't care much for the multiplayer part, so you can try that for yourself and make your own mind :)

_childDocuments_.review: The Settlers combines a fresh take on the popular gameplay mechanics of the series with a new spin. It offers a deep infrastructure and economy gameplay, used to create and employ armies, to ultimately defeat opponents. 3 playable, distinctive factions – the Elari, the Maru and the Jorn – can be found in The Settlers. Each with a unique look and play style. At the heart of every match is gaining resources and building up your economy to recruit new settlers and a directly controllable, winning army. Research upgrades for your army and strengthen them by recruiting support and siege units. Various online multiplayer modes with up to 8 players offer thrilling skirmish battles against other players or AI for long-lasting fun. A story driven campaign will immerse the players into the world of The Settlers, while new players can learn the basic mechanics in a separate tutorial.

name: Kong: Survivor Instinct
detailed_description: A sudden Titan attack prompts massive evacuation efforts-but not everyone makes it to safety before the devastation ensues. Caught in the crossfire between battling monsters, many residents become trapped in the collapsing city—your only daughter among them! Kong: Survivor Instinct is a 2.5D action-adventure game that combines realistic platforming, challenging combat, and metroidvania-style exploration during a thrilling quest of survival worthy of the Monsterverse franchise. TRUE MONSTERVERSE ADVENTURE Influence the Titans with Monarch tech and use their enormous strength to your advantage as you navigate a treacherous maze of collapsing buildings, toxic leaks, and raging fires. Scavenge for resources, weapons, and tools to solve environmental puzzles and defend yourself against both human and monster enemies. FACE THE LEGENDARY KONG Explore and survive as you encounter Kong in all his majestic glory, face the formidable Abaddon, and confront other new and returning superspecies and Titans! Whether you scavenge through half-destroyed buildings or fight off mercenaries, these enormous monsters are nearby, directly or indirectly impacting your gameplay. Though the Titans pose a lethal threat, you can - and must - influence their behavior with the ORCA Σ, a new prototype inspired by Monarch’s technology. ALAN JONAH RETURNS Discover an official Monsterverse story set shortly after the events of Godzilla vs. Kong . Stand your ground against the Hyenas, a mercenary group led by Alan Jonah. Reemerging after the events of Godzilla: King of the Monsters , the former eco-terrorist leader returns in Kong: Kong: Survivor Instinct with a new villainous scheme. A FATHER’S MISSION TO RESCUE HIS DAUGHTER Take on the role of David, an oil rig worker braving a crumbling city to find your only child, Stacy. Make your way through the districts while encountering fellow survivors taking shelter among the rubble, mourning their loved ones or on the verge of giving up hope. Feel the awe-inspiring terror Titans bring upon a city through the eyes of a father desperate to find his daughter!

_childDocuments_.review: Sideways thumb.I can't bring myself to leave this a negative, it just wasn't my type of game.It's barely a metroidvania.  I mean it has branching paths, fast travel, permanent health & ammo upgrades to find.. but everything so far has been item or key gated, not ability gated.  I would argue that finding the gun which you use to shoot off locks is an ability gate, but that's all I've seen which resembles one.  I expect proper traversal upgrades in a metroidvania.I will say that the map was nicely marked, locked doors, collectables and the like.No, this is far more like games like ,  and .  Minus the horror theme and with combat and some branching paths (though each path hits a dead end quickly and it's ultimately linear with side-rooms ..at least so far anyhow).I'd only pick this up if slower games like the aforementioned appeal to you.
